name: Michigan Advance
title: Meet the Michigan climate candidate on Trump’s radar
description: Less than two months ago, William Lawrence was a relatively unknown progressive climate group co-founder and a dark-horse candidate for Congress running in a Trump district in the middle of Michigan.  But his August victory in the Lansing-area primary — where he capitalized when moderate Democrats split votes — has catapulted Lawrence firmly into the […]
text:
William Lawrence speaks about data centers and artificial intelligence in Mason, Mich., on Sept. 17, 2026. (Photo by Robin Bravender/Michigan Advance)Less than two months ago, William Lawrence was a relatively unknown progressive climate group co-founder and a dark-horse candidate for Congress running in a Trump district in the middle of Michigan. 
But his August victory in the Lansing-area primary — where he capitalized when moderate Democrats split votes — has catapulted Lawrence firmly into the national spotlight. The 36-year-old vying to represent Michigan’s 7th Congressional District is suddenly under heightened scrutiny from the Democratic Party, national news outlets and even President Donald Trump. 
The high-profile race, which pits Lawrence against incumbent Republican Rep. Tom Barrett (R-Charlotte), could tip the scales of power in Washington next year. It’s also a microcosm of some of the biggest debates playing out in national politics in the midterms that are likely to carry into the 2028 presidential race. The contest could offer lessons about voters’ opposition to data centers, their willingness to shrug off controversial social media posts and their appetite for left-leaning candidates promising drastic changes in the Trump era. 
Michigan’s 7th District is “one of the quintessential swing districts in the entire country,” said Kyle Kondik, managing editor of Sabato’s Crystal Ball at the University of Virginia Center for Politics. It’s been historically competitive, voting narrowly for Joe Biden in 2020 and for Trump in 2024, Kondik said, and it’s “the kind of swing seat that Democrats probably should be winning in a year like this.” 
The left is hopeful Lawrence can capitalize on anti-Trump sentiment to win the race. Democrats’ congressional campaign arm recently added Lawrence to its “Red to Blue” program — signaling a boost in support from the national party. 
But Kondik and other political analysts still view the race as a toss-up, due in part to Lawrence’s past as an outspoken climate activist and progressive. 
“He’s the kind of candidate that I think Republicans are sort of dreaming of running against,” in part due to his track record of saying “a lot of pretty out-there things,” Kondik said. “But it’s also not obvious to me that he’s going to lose. I really think it is still a toss-up.” 
William Lawrence speaks to a voter at an “Ask me anything” event outside Lyon Township Hall on Sept. 8, 2026. (Photo by Robin Bravender/Michigan Advance)
Trump attacks
One complication for Lawrence: His controversial social media posts during his years as a progressive activist and climate organizer. 
Some of his now-deleted social media posts surfaced in a CNN report this month, including a post from 2021 in support of communal living. “Biggest W of my late 20s was finding a long-term stable co-op house. F*** isolation and the nuclear family domicile,” Lawrence wrote in one of the posts. In another post from 2022, Lawrence wrote that the “nuclear family home is an isolating, individualistic, violent way of organizing society.” 
For Republicans, Lawrence’s old posts and his activist record are political red meat. 
Days after those old posts resurfaced, Trump blasted Lawrence during a speech at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas. “One of the Democrats’ top congressional candidates is a self-described Marxist who says he hates family households, oh, that’s nice, and wants to destroy the American way of life,” Trump said. 
Lawrence told Michigan Advance that he learned about the president’s comments when the House Republicans’ campaign arm tagged him in a clip of the speech on social media. He welcomed the president’s attention. “I thought, ‘Hey, here we are. We’ve arrived,’” he said. 



Quotation







He’s smart and aggressive — I doubt he’s going to Congress just to have a job.


– Environmental activist and author Bill McKibben, who has known William Lawrence since his undergraduate days.


Barrett is also seizing on Lawrence’s old posts. “My wife and I live in a small town in this district and I’m raising a nuclear family — something that my opponent says is a violent way of organizing society,” Barrett told the Advance in a phone interview. 
Barrett, a U.S. Army veteran running for his second term representing the district, said Lawrence has been a “radical activist for his entire life as an adult. And you can’t then divorce yourself of that when you decide to run for office in a very, very competitive congressional district. You can’t just say, “Ah, well, don’t pay attention to anything I said.’” 
Lawrence addressed the resurfacing of his remarks in an interview earlier this month. 
“There’s things that I have said that … I stand by saying them at the time, even though I wouldn’t say them in the same way now,” Lawrence told the Michigan Advance in a parking lot where he sat next to a sign that said “Ask me anything” and took questions from locals.
There’s things that I probably disagreed with even at the time, and it was a moment of frustration. And there’s things that I … changed my mind in response to new information,” he said. 
Like others in his generation, Lawrence said, “I’ve just done a lot of time thinking out aloud on the internet. … And I think folks understand that.” He’s changed his approach since then, Lawrence said. “I’m in a different role now, and that requires me to hold myself to a higher standard.”
Lawrence specifically addressed his past comments about marriage during a recent news conference in Mason. “I’ve been happily married for four years,” he told reporters. 
William Lawrence speaks about data centers and artificial intelligence in Mason, Mich., on Sept. 17, 2026. (Photo by Robin Bravender/Michigan Advance)
Climate roots 
Before he was an aspiring congressman, Lawrence was a climate activist who helped launch the youth-led Sunrise Movement. 
He worked on a fossil fuel divestment campaign as an undergraduate at Swarthmore College and met up with other students around the country interested in cutting their universities’ ties with oil and gas companies. 
That eventually led to the creation of a national network of student divestment organizers and ultimately the co-founding of the youth-led Sunrise Movement in early 2017. That effort injected energy into the environmental movement as young activists staged a sit-in at then-House Speaker Nancy Pelosi’s office in 2018 and went on to prod the Biden administration on climate change. 
Lawrence’s links to the climate movement are still strong. Stevie O’Hanlon, another Sunrise co-founder and the group’s former communications director, is managing Lawrence’s campaign. 
Sunrise’s current executive director, Aru Shiney-Ajay, traveled to Michigan last Friday to train Michigan State University students and get them fired up for Lawrence’s election. 
She sees Lawrence’s political rise coinciding with a new era of climate politics. 
“I actually do see climate anxiety spiking among young people again” and data center and AI concerns are “a big part of that,” she said. “I think having Will in power would just be an incredible way to show how movements can go from taking the streets to the halls of Congress.”
Environmental activist and author Bill McKibben has known Lawrence since his undergraduate days. McKibben thinks Lawrence’s climate and activism background could help propel him to victory in the moderate district. 
“I think people are plenty ready for fighters — he showed in the primary that that was an asset,” McKibben said in an email. And he thinks Lawrence will be in prime position to shape the national debate on climate and data centers if he wins in November. “He’s smart and aggressive — I doubt he’s going to Congress just to have a job,” McKibben said. 
Data center drama
Lawrence’s allies say his roots as a climate activist and affordable housing organizer make him uniquely suited to harness opposition to data centers in his district. Those opponents include the younger university crowd worried about the centers’ climate impacts as well as moderate voters wary of the impacts on the environment, property values and utility costs. 
Lawrence is campaigning relentlessly on data centers, calling for a one-year federal moratorium on new construction. He appeared at a Lyon Township board of trustees meeting earlier this month to promote a moratorium to local officials. And he recently unveiled a plan to rein in data centers and artificial intelligence. 
A sign in Mason, Mich., near the site of a proposed data center on Sept. 17, 2026.(Photo by Robin Bravender/Michigan Advance)
Barrett calls Lawrence’s stance on data centers an “absolutist” position. 
“I’m taking the approach that local residents ought to have the decision, and that data center developers — along with local elected officials — ought to make that case to the local residents and allow them to decide what’s right for their communities,” he said.  
Lawrence is slamming Barrett for voting for Trump’s 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act that included tax breaks available to tech companies for data center construction. 
Barrett said the law included “broad tax reforms that certainly changed tax policy for all kinds of different things,” and didn’t single out data centers for support. 
Barrett touts his own past opposition to direct incentives for Michigan data center developers during his time in the state legislature. And in August, Barrett introduced legislation in Congress to ban the federal government from overriding local zoning decisions about data centers. 
U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett (R-Charlotte) at an event hosted by the America First Policy Institute in Charlotte, Mich. June 16, 2026. | Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance
“Local opposition to rapid data center expansion is emerging as a critical issue,” said Marty Jordan, an associate professor of political science at Michigan State University. 
Lawrence’s “consistent opposition to data center expansion” resonates strongly, Jordan said. “While Barrett has recently advocated for greater local control over these projects, his position is complicated by President Trump’s support for AI data center growth.” 
Ultimately, the candidates’ diverging views on data centers and other key policy issues may matter less in November than their party affiliations, said Erin Covey, House editor at The Cook Political Report. 
“For most House candidates, people are ultimately going to be voting for you based on the letter that is beside your name,” she said. “So even if they have disagreements with their own party’s nominee, we live in such a polarized era that keeping the other party out of power is always going to be the driving consideration for most people.”

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: A GOP power player and lobbyist is a key advisor to House Speaker Lisa Demuth
description: House Speaker Lisa Demuth has had several defining moments in her campaign for governor thus far. She lost the Minnesota Republican Party’s convention endorsement in May after 10 ballots, though her team successfully raised doubts about the tabulation process to dampen the endorsement of Kendall Qualls. Later, after missing out on what had been considered […[...]
text:
Lisa Demuth attends her campaign's watch party at Burger Moe’s in St. Paul on Tuesday, August 11, 2026. Demuth, center left, with Ben Golnik, center at computer, monitor results. (Photo by Tony Nelson/MinnPost)House Speaker Lisa Demuth has had several defining moments in her campaign for governor thus far. She lost the Minnesota Republican Party’s convention endorsement in May after 10 ballots, though her team successfully raised doubts about the tabulation process to dampen the endorsement of Kendall Qualls.
Later, after missing out on what had been considered a must-have endorsement of President Donald Trump, she went on to win the Republican primary for governor.
On the convention floor and on primary night as the returns came in, Demuth had at her side a GOP operative and lobbyist who is well known at the Minnesota Capitol, but less so to the general public: Ben Golnik.
Golnik is an advisor to Demuth’s campaign, armed with a vast network of GOP politicos, donors, delegates and operatives. He’s doing all of this work without receiving a paycheck from Demuth’s campaign, according to campaign finance reports.
But Golnik very much gets paid in his day job as a registered lobbyist who represents Big Pharma, the tobacco industry, a horse racing track and other clients.
Golnik didn’t respond to interview requests, but he told the Reformer in a text message that he volunteers for Demuth’s campaign like he has for campaigns in the past.
“I first met Speaker Demuth when she ran for the House in 2018. Speaker Demuth is a friend and I’m a volunteer on her campaign for governor,” Golnik said. “I’ve volunteered for dozens of campaigns over the years and enjoy being helpful.”
Lisa Demuth complained to Ben Golnik (left), about malfunctioning clickers amid voting irregularities at the Minnesota Republican Convention in Duluth, Saturday May 30, 2026. (Photo by Glen Stubbe/Minnesota Reformer)
Golnik is hardly alone. Many lobbyists raise money, drum up research, consult on ad copy and even knock on doors for candidates, which allows them to take the temperature of the electorate and maybe even get face time with the candidate. Democratic-Farmer-Labor lobbyists like Brian Rice and Larry Redmond are known to get deep in the weeds of campaigns. 
(U.S. Sen. Amy Klobuchar, the DFL nominee for governor, was once a registered lobbyist during her days in private law practice.)
Norman Ornstein, an emeritus scholar at the American Enterprise Institute, said many lobbyists volunteer and raise money for campaigns, but said a decision-making role for a lobbyist would be unusual.
The problem with the arrangement is whether Golnik’s free and apparently important work with the Demuth campaign would create an obligation to him or his clients if Demuth is successful in November.
“There is nothing illegal about this that I can point to, but a lobbyist for Big Tobacco and Big Pharma? Not a great look,” Ornstein said in an email.
Demuth at a Capitol press conference Thursday said her campaign has a number of volunteers and staff to help get their message out. Asked about Golnik’s responsibilities, Demuth declined to provide any details.
“We have volunteers that are on our campaign,” Demuth said.
Golnik is hardly the same as the legions of Minnesotans stuffing envelopes, however. He comes with a long resume of GOP political work and would be a candidate to be Demuth’s chief of staff, or some other key role, formal or not. 
As executive director for the Minnesota House Republican caucus, Golnik was former House Speaker Kurt Daudt’s right-hand man when the Crown lawmaker was among the state’s most prominent Republicans between 2014-2019 and was frequently discussed as a potential candidate for governor.
Daudt praised Golnik in a statement, noting that any candidate would be happy to have his assistance and that people in politics “wear different hats in campaigning, in public service, in advocacy and strategic advice-giving.”
“There are dozens of DFLers and Republicans who play such multiple roles. It is normal and legitimate for anyone involved in public life and cares about our communities to do so,” Daudt said.
Golnik founded the Minnesota Jobs Coalition after the Republicans’ 2012 debacle, which gave Democrats their first trifecta in recent memory.
Under Golnik’s leadership, the Jobs Coalition — which is still hammering Democrats today —  went on to help Republicans take the House majority in 2014 and then expand it in 2016.
When House Republicans lost the majority in a 2018 landslide, Golnik left the Legislature to take up lobbying.
His most prominent client is the Danish drugmaker Novo Nordisk, which manufactures weight loss drugs Ozempic and Wegovy. He also represents PMI U.S. Corporate Services — a subsidiary of the tobacco company Philip Morris — and the North Metro Harness Initiative, which does business as Running Aces.
Running Aces, which operates a casino, racetrack and restaurant in Columbus, Minnesota, donated $500,000 in June to the Restore Sanity political action committee, a super PAC supporting Demuth’s campaign for governor.
Running Aces President Taro Ito didn’t respond to the Reformer’s request for comment.
Golnik is friends with Tommy Merickel, an influential, behind-the-scenes business executive and fundraiser who succeeded Golnik at the Jobs Coalition. Merickel — who has worked closely with billionaire Glen Taylor for decades — is fundraising for the Restore Sanity PAC this election cycle.
The super PAC in recent weeks received a $10 million cash infusion, cutting into Klobuchar’s longtime financial advantage in the race.
According to a 2017 Star Tribune profile, Golnik is driven less by ideology than a competitive desire to win.
“When I’m playing chess with my kid, I don’t like to lose,” Golnik told the Star Tribune.

name: Nevada Current
title: Educator challenges incumbent for Nevada State controller
description: Republican Nevada State Controller Andy Matthews is seeking reelection this November as the state’s independent fiscal watchdog, while his challenger, Democrat Michael MacDougall, hopes a blue wave will help launch him to victory.  The state controller is responsible for administering the state’s accounting system, conducting state audits, settling claims ag[...]
text:
Michael MacDougal, Andy Matthews (Candidate photos)Republican Nevada State Controller Andy Matthews is seeking reelection this November as the state’s independent fiscal watchdog, while his challenger, Democrat Michael MacDougall, hopes a blue wave will help launch him to victory. 
The state controller is responsible for administering the state’s accounting system, conducting state audits, settling claims against the state, and collecting debts owed to the state. The controller also serves on the state’s transportation board and the executive branch committee, which oversees annual internal audits. The state controller is limited by the state constitution to two four-year terms and yearly compensation is around $100,000.
MacDougall said he hopes voters give more attention to down ballot races like his when they hit the polls – or send mail in ballots – this November. He pointed to recent polling showing Democratic Attorney General Aaron Ford has a lead over Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo in the Nevada race for the governor’s seat.
“I think the national conversation will play a role in the local conversation here in Nevada, and I think that will help me. That’ll help up and down the ballot,” MacDougall said. 
Matthews, however, has the advantage as an incumbent with a strong fundraising arm. Matthews reported raising nearly $50,000 in campaign funds through July, compared to MacDougall’s nearly $24,000.
That fundraising also helped Matthews launch an advertisement in September highlighting his accomplishments in office. The 30-second ad, shows Matthews counting pennies as he touts the website his office launched that provides real-time information on state spending.
“Fundraising is only one part of running a successful campaign, MacDougall said. “I’m focused on meeting voters where they are, and being in the public eye, and being at events and meeting with people. I think that that has more of a sway than the dollar amount raised.”
Matthews did not respond to the Nevada Current’s request for an interview. 
Before being elected controller in 2022, Matthews served in the Nevada State Assembly. Prior to that he led the Nevada Policy, a conservative think tank.
On his campaign site, Matthews highlighted his work helping local governments create their own transparency websites. He also noted his work to modernize the state’s financial, human-resource and information-technology systems. 
Matthews also noted he enacted significant reforms to the state’s financial reporting. 
MacDougall criticized Matthews for delaying the release of the state mandated Nevada Annual Comprehensive Financial Report, a report that details the state’s financial position and is required by law. Matthews released the report more than two years after the fiscal year ended. 
Delays in audits erode trust in government, while timely audits demonstrate effective government and help build trust in the state, said MacDougall. 
“Citizens and businesses lose faith in government when audits are not conducted in a timely manner. Trust is crucial for effective governance, and delayed audits undermine this trust,” MacDougall said. 
On his campaign website, Matthews said if reelected he would prioritize the creation of a Nevada Office of Inspector General in his second term. 
During the 2025 Legislative Session, Matthews proposed the creation of a Nevada Office of Inspector General to independently audit recipients of state funds. Although the bill did not advance, Matthews promised to reintroduce it in 2027 and has submitted a bill draft request. 
MacDougall said he’s open to the creation of a Nevada Office of Inspector General, although he said he would have to examine the bill’s language.
“I think oversight is a good thing,” MacDougall said. “Any sort of oversight to ensure that people are behaving correctly is a good thing.”
If elected, MacDougall said his top priorities would be to conduct a state audit, support better access to public transportation, and recover millions in uncollected tax revenues.
MacDougall works as an educator teaching social studies at The Adelson School, a private Jewish community school in Las Vegas. He earned a bachelor’s degree in political science from Allegheny College in Pennsylvania, and a Master of Arts from the University of Iowa and one from the University of California, Los Angeles.
MacDougall said he views the role of the state controller as a referee that serves as a check on state finances, auditing every dollar in and out, including taxes and federal funds, said MacDougall. 
When it comes to recovering unpaid back taxes MacDougall said the office should explore targeted enforcement measures to improve tax collection, including punitive actions and streamlined services that could help bring in more revenue.
He said his campaign is focused on practical solutions to existing problems and forward thinking. He emphasized the importance of collaboration with other agencies and elected officials to find solutions.
One practical solution that could improve quality of life for Nevadans is expanding access to transportation. The state controller sits on the Nevada Department of Transportation board, influencing public and commercial transportation within Nevada.
MacDougall said he wants to make public transportation more accessible and affordable, including reduced or free fares for young people.
“It’s a service that is being provided and funded through tax dollars, so it behooves us to make sure we are making it the best we can,” MacDougall said.
MacDougall has been endorsed by SEIU Local 1107, the Nevada State Education Association, the Southern Nevada Building Trades Union, AFL-CIO, Teamsters Nevada, and Smart Local 88. 
Matthews has been endorsed by Lombardo, the Nevada Republican Party, Nevada Young Republicans, and the Keystone Corporation Nevada.

name: Nevada Current
title: Workforce development specialist, former state legislator face off in regent race
description: Five Nevada Board of Regents seats are on the ballot this year, but only one is an open seat not featuring an incumbent. That race, for District 5 in Southern Nevada, will bring to the board either a former state legislator or a current higher education professional with a background in workforce development programming. The […]
text:
Stephanie Molina, Mo Denis. (Candidate photos) Five Nevada Board of Regents seats are on the ballot this year, but only one is an open seat not featuring an incumbent. That race, for District 5 in Southern Nevada, will bring to the board either a former state legislator or a current higher education professional with a background in workforce development programming.
The Board of Regents oversees the Nevada System of Higher Education, which is composed of two research universities, a state university, four community colleges, and a research institute. NSHE enrolls more than 100,000 students, according to their website, and has a biennium budget of more than $2 billion dollars.
In 2023, the Nevada State Legislature passed a bill to reduce the number to regents from 13 to nine. They also shortened the term length of regents from six years to four years beginning with the 2028 election. To align with those changes, the winners of this year’s regents races will have truncated terms and have to run for re-election in 2028.
Regents run in nonpartisan races, but the board often features elected officials with experience in partisan politics.
District 5, which covers areas of North Las Vegas and Winchester, is currently represented by Patrick Boylan. Boylan, who was elected in 2020, has been the subject of much criticism for making racist, discriminatory and anti-transgender comments. He ran for re-election this year but came in fourth in a crowded six-person primary.
Former Nevada state legislator Mo Denis came in first in the primary, receiving 30% of votes. Stephanie Molina, a workforce development program coordinator at Nevada State University, came in second place with 20% support.
Now, Denis and Molina will face off on the general election ballot.
Denis, a Democrat, is no stranger to public office, having represented the area for 18 years in the Nevada State Legislature, including a stint as Senate majority leader. His legislative experience includes playing a major role in the 2019 revamping of the state’s K-12 education funding formula.
Denis told the Nevada Current earlier this year he hadn’t planned to run for another office after he termed out of the Legislature in 2022, but he felt compelled to run for regent because he felt the board was being “sidetracked” and “losing focus on students.”
Molina, also a registered Democrat, would be a newcomer to elected office, though she has previously served as president of the executive board president of UNLV’s Graduate and Professional Student Association and been a voting member of the Nevada Student Alliance. According to her campaign website, she wants to bring her experience with workforce and economic development programming to the board and “help build a higher education system that is more accessible, accountable, and responsive to the people it serves.”
“Having seen the system from multiple vantage points, as a student leader, a participant in faculty governance, and a higher education professional focused on workforce development, I am prepared to bring a thoughtful, data-informed, and service-driven perspective to the Board,” she wrote in a candidate survey for the Nevada Faculty Alliance.
In his survey responses, Denis wrote he views higher education as “central to Nevada’s economic diversification, workforce development, and community engagement. It creates pathways to opportunity, supports innovation, and strengthens communities across our state.”
The Nevada Faculty Alliance has endorsed Denis, as has the Culinary Union, Laborers, Progressive Leadership Alliance of Nevada, Clark County Education Association, and Nevada State Education Association.
According to her most recent campaign finance report, filed in mid-July, Molina did no fundraising during the first half of the year.
Denis raised nearly $39,000 during that period and spent most of it, entering July with $5,780 on hand. About a quarter of the amount raised was self funded. Other top contributors include the Clark County Education Association, Vegas Chamber, and Assemblymember Selena Torres-Fossett (D-Las Vegas).
The next campaign finance reports are due in mid-October.

name: Missouri Independent
title: The Fairness Project remains largest funder of effort to stop Missouri abortion ban
description: Since 2017, a D.C.-based nonprofit called the Fairness Project has poured more than $13 million into Missouri campaigns.  Every campaign it backed that has reached Missouri voters has won. And now it is making its biggest investment yet in the state. In 2024, The Fairness Project gave more than $4.5 million to a citizen-led ballot […]
text:
Abortion rights advocates gather for a canvassing kick-off event on Aug. 29 in St. Louis County (Anna Spoerre/Missouri Independent).Since 2017, a D.C.-based nonprofit called the Fairness Project has poured more than $13 million into Missouri campaigns. 
Every campaign it backed that has reached Missouri voters has won. And now it is making its biggest investment yet in the state.
In 2024, The Fairness Project gave more than $4.5 million to a citizen-led ballot effort to overturn the state’s abortion ban. This year, it has donated $5.3 million to Stop the Ban, making it the largest donor to the campaign seeking to defeat Amendment 3.
The amendment, placed on the Nov. 3 ballot by Republican lawmakers, would repeal the abortion-rights measure Missouri voters approved two years ago and replace it with an abortion ban with limited exceptions. It would also place a constitutional ban on gender-affirming care for minors, which is currently banned in state statute. 
The Fairness Project’s prominent financial role — and the fact that, as a federally registered 501c4 nonprofit, it is not legally required to publicly disclose its donors — has also made it one of the main targets of conservative and anti-abortion leaders who argue that out-of-state interests wield too much influence over Missouri elections.



Need to get in touch?
Have a news tip?


CONTACT US



James Lawson, campaign manager with Her Health, Her Future, the group supporting Amendment 3, said he finds the influence of out-of-state funders on the abortion-rights campaign “deeply troubling.” Lawson is on a leave of absence from the Missouri Attorney General’s Office where he worked in communications through early November so he can help manage the campaign. 
“They don’t have a dog in this fight here in the state of Missouri, except to push a radical agenda,” he said, accusing the Fairness Project of trying to make Missouri “a battleground” for progressive movements.
The latest SLU/YouGov poll found Missouri voters almost evenly divided: 43% supported Amendment 3, 44% opposed it and 13% remained unsure. In 2024, the abortion-rights measure won with 51.6% of the vote. Their polling over the past several years has continuously shown the majority of Missourians remain in favor of abortion access with gestational limits.
The Fairness Project, which backs progressive ballot measures across the country, declined a request for an interview or written comment. But the nonprofit’s leadership has been vocal in the past about its partnerships in Missouri.
In September 2024, Kelly Hall, then executive director of the Fairness Project, spoke with The Independent about that year’s reproductive rights campaign. Hall recently stepped down as executive director.
While money is a necessary ingredient to a successful campaign, Hall said, “it is only possible to do anything at all if we are supporting the work that is being driven by grassroots organizations, grassroots donors, regular people speaking to their neighbors and an electorate that is enthusiastic about the issue that these advocates have put forward.”
The coalition behind the reproductive rights campaign, called Missourians for Constitutional Freedom in 2024 and Stop the Ban this year, also includes the ACLU of Missouri, Abortion Action Missouri, Action St. Louis, Planned Parenthood Great Plains Votes, Planned Parenthood Great Rivers Action, PROMO and Beacon Reproductive Health Network. 
Stop the Ban did not provide a comment for this story.
Chris Melody Fields Figueredo, executive director of the Ballot Initiative Strategy Center, which partners with the abortion rights campaign, said as ballot campaigns get more expensive, funders become more critical. 
“There is a partnership that is critically important between state and national organizations,” she said, “to ensure that Missourians have the freedoms that are so fundamental to what the people of Missouri want.”
 The Fairness Project

The Fairness Project was started by SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West leaders in 2015 after the group’s president, Dave Regan, hoped to support ballot efforts to raise minimum wages and expand healthcare access beyond the west coast.
“ … The Fairness Project has made it possible for regular people across the country to create meaningful economic and healthcare improvements in their lives, when their state governments have refused to do so,” a 2020 resolution signed by the SEIU-UHW executive board reads. “In short, the Fairness Project provides hope.”
The nonprofit’s revenue has grown substantially in recent years. In 2021, the Fairness Project brought in $4.1 million in revenue. In 2024, as its reach expanded across the country, it brought in $33.3 million, according to ProPublica’s nonprofit tracker.
That year, the Fairness Project injected more than $32 million into 11 campaigns in seven states, including efforts to raise the minimum wage, guarantee paid sick leave and protect reproductive rights, according to its annual impact report. In the 2024 general election, nine of the 11 campaigns they were involved in won at the ballot box.
By November, the nonprofit will have invested in more than 40 ballot campaigns across the country.
SEIU-UHW continues to support the Fairness Project, according to the union’s website. The nonprofit’s board members have included SEIU-UHW leadership, as well as Democratic political strategists and leadership with the ACLU, Planned Parenthood and the Human Rights Campaign.
Missouri labor unions, abortion rights groups turn unlikely alliance into ballot power

Leading up to the November 2024 election, the Fairness Project poured more than $30 million into reproductive rights ballot measures across the country. Nearly $5 million of that went to Missouri’s abortion rights effort, which raised more than $30 million.
“Since the start of our fight to restore abortion access in Missouri, the Fairness Project has been an invaluable partner,” Emily Wales, president and CEO of Planned Parenthood Great Plains, is quoted saying on the Fairness Project website. “They’ve helped guide in-state organizations through an effort that’s unlike any other we’ve undertaken.”
In Missouri, the Fairness Project has also put money behind efforts to expand Medicaid access in 2020, raise the minimum wage in 2024 and protect direct democracy this year. In November, the Fairness Project is backing the effort to overturn a gerrymandered congressional map, known as Proposition A, as well as Amendment 6, which would make it more difficult for lawmakers to alter or repeal measures approved by voters.
“Jefferson City politicians spent months trying to keep this measure off the ballot, showing exactly why Missourians need it,” Hannah Ledford, the new executive director of the Fairness Project, said in a statement earlier this month about Amendment 6, adding that the proposal “will protect voters from misleading ballot language, attempts to block citizen-led campaigns, and efforts to overturn laws they have already passed.”
Since 2017, the Fairness Project has contributed to the following Missouri campaigns, according to campaign finance reports: 

Stop the Ban (2026): $5.3 million
Respect Missouri Voters (2026): $375,000
Protect Majority Rule (2026): $1.4 million
People Not Politicians (2025): $250,000
Missourians for Constitutional Freedom (2024): $4.7 million 
Protect Majority Rule (2024): $64,021.
Missourians for Healthy Families and Fair Wages (2024): $322,539 
Missourians for Healthcare (2020): $496,067 
Raise Up Missouri (2018): $285,000
Give Missourians a Raise (2017): $114,276

 Anti-abortion campaign lags 7-1 in fundraising

The campaign to keep Missouri’s abortion rights amendment in place has so far raised more than seven times as much as the campaign to reinstate the ban, according to the latest fundraising data. 
As of this week, according to the Missouri Ethics Commission, Stop the Ban had raised about $13 million. Her Health, Her Future, which has the support of many of Missouri’s most powerful Republican officials, had raised more than $1.8 million.
Most of the largest contributions to Her Health, Her Future have come from Missouri donors. Only around $50,000 has come from out of state. The largest donors to the anti-abortion campaign are organizations tied to the Drury family, best known for the Missouri-founded, St. Louis-based hotel chain. Drury has donated more than $741,000 to the campaign effort across three of its businesses.
A spokesperson for Drury could not be reached for comment, but Lawson called Drury “a classic Missouri success story and family that is very committed to their faith and to the values that they hold dear.” 
Her Health, Her Future has built a coalition that includes national organizations based outside of Missouri, providing help on the ground, including by sharing expertise, he said. But many aren’t backed by deep pockets.
“You’re gonna see it even on the national level, we see a significant imbalance of funds from progressive billionaires,” he said. “Versus, the pro-life movement is made up primarily of a coalition of faith groups that are much more grassroots oriented.”
Stop the Ban has also received sizable checks from individuals and Missouri organizations. Its local coalition members have contributed nearly $1 million. Philanthropist Lynn Schusterman, who was born in Kansas City and who now lives in Oklahoma, has given $3 million, and Bloomberg donated $1.25 million. Hundreds of Missourians have made smaller donations to the cause.
While the Fairness Project isn’t required to disclose its donors, some of its top contributors can be identified through 990 forms filed to the IRS by nonprofits that have given. Top contributors to the Fairness Project include Global Impact, Hopewell Fund, Our American Future Action and Sixteen Thirty Fund, all of which are based in D.C. Public records do not show whether those grants were earmarked for Stop the Ban or other specific campaigns.
 ‘Dark money’ flows across ideological lines

Earlier this month, while embroiled in a court battle over Missouri’s congressional map, Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins proclaimed he would “proudly fall on my sword to save this great state from out-of-state special interests and their out-of-state sugar daddies.” 
“Missouri will not become another New York City or Los Angeles on my watch,” he said.
Criticism of out-of-state money has become a recurring theme among Missouri Republican leaders as ballot campaigns have increasingly drawn millions of dollars from national organizations and wealthy donors.
Missouri lawmakers last year approved a proposed amendment for the 2026 ballot that sought to raise the threshold for passing citizen-led ballot initiatives. It also would have put a ban on campaigns accepting money from a “foreign national” into the state constitution.
In a video supporting Amendment 4 — which was rejected in August by 80% of Missouri voters — Republican Gov. Mike Kehoe said “our constitution shouldn’t be the victim of out-of-state special interests who spend millions to deceive voters and pass out-of-touch policies.” 
But undisclosed money has also played a big role supporting causes backed by Kehoe and other Republicans.
By the August primary election, about $23 million in large donations came from groups that don’t have to disclose their donors. The largest donor —  giving more than $6.5 million — was a nonprofit called Missouri Action that was created earlier this year. The campaign also received roughly $2 million from Ohio-based nonprofit American Policy Coalition.
Lawson believes voters are increasingly paying attention to who is funding campaigns.
“Slowly, over time, yeah, I think voters are becoming significantly more sensitive to out-of-state dark money,” he said. “And I would even go as far as to say, we probably saw that a little bit in the primary when we saw a rejection of some of the ballot measures there.”
Supporters of Missouri’s Amendment 3, which would reinstate a near-total abortion ban and place a permanent ban on gender-affirming care for minors into the constitution, gather for an informational meeting on Thursday, Sept. 10, 2026 in St. Louis County (Anna Spoerre/Missouri Independent).
Hall in 2024 said she doesn’t bother with dark money arguments. 
“If they want to focus on this rather than on the issue that Missouri voters care about, which is making sure that everyone in their state has access to life-saving, reproductive healthcare when they need it, then that’s a misread on their part of what Missouri voters care most about,” she said.
The same model is also being used by abortion opponents.
The Love Life Initiative, launched late last year by U.S. Sen. Josh Hawley of Missouri and his wife, Erin Morrow Hawley, says it will invest in anti-abortion and pro-family messaging around the country. The organization does not publicly disclose its donors and has not donated to the Amendment 3 campaign.
Undisclosed political spending is hardly unique to Missouri — or to one side of the political spectrum. The New York Times reported last month that at least $1 billion from anonymous donors has flowed into the 2026 midterm elections through nonprofits, super PACs and other groups. 
Craig Holman, a campaign finance expert with the consumer advocacy nonprofit Public Citizen, said “dark money” was born of the 2010 U.S. Supreme Court decision in Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission which opened the door for unlimited spending on elections. 
In the 16 years since, total expenditures in politics have increased more than three-fold, he said.  The prevalence of campaign funding from groups that don’t have to disclose their donors spans party lines and political ideologies, reaching from statewide races to federal elections, he said. 
Ballot measure campaigns in particular remain the “wild west” of campaign finance laws, Holman said, as judges continue to strike down any limits on contributions and spending on behalf of ballot measures.
The prevalence of anonymous campaign cash in Missouri elections continues to give John Hancock, a veteran GOP political consultant, heartburn.
“You’re really, in a sense, taking the ball out of the hands of Missourians by having all of this influence money, and it’s dark influence money — we don’t really know who the donors are — and I think that’s regrettable,” Hancock said. “But that’s what the campaign finance laws allow.”
Editor’s note: The Hopewell Fund served as an incubator for States Newsroom, the parent organization of The Missouri Independent, from 2017-19 and does not fund the nonprofit news organization. States Newsroom lists Global Impact Fund as among its donors. Donors have no role in editorial decisions.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Developer eyes ‘GoldMine’ data center project in Fairfield, near Eagle Mountain’s Meta campus
description: In the small Utah town of Fairfield with a population of roughly 180 people — near the border of Eagle Mountain, where some 65,000 people live — a developer wants to build a project named “GoldMine,” which could include hundreds of acres for another data center in the Cedar Valley.  The “mixed-use industrial and technology […]
text:
A street sign at the boundary line of Fairfield and Eagle Mountain is pictured on Sept. 23, 2026. (Katie McKellar/Utah News Dispatch)In the small Utah town of Fairfield with a population of roughly 180 people — near the border of Eagle Mountain, where some 65,000 people live — a developer wants to build a project named “GoldMine,” which could include hundreds of acres for another data center in the Cedar Valley. 
The “mixed-use industrial and technology development” to the west of Utah Lake has so far been envisioned to include 140 acres for “ranchette” rural homes on one- to three-acre lots, and about 80 acres of commercial lots. But the lion’s share of the project (933 acres) would be devoted to a “business park” and industrial development — which would include “technological campuses” and “data centers.” 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
That’s according to Fairfield Planning Commission public documents, which include a preliminary draft plan created by the project’s development firms, EGI Real Estate and DAI Utah. 
Fairfield Mayor Hollie McKinney said the project is “still in the early, preliminary planning stages,” so it’s possible that the vision for GoldMine could change as it goes through the planning process. 
“Fairfield has not received a development application for this project, so the town has no plans to evaluate or permit at this point,” McKinney told Utah News Dispatch in an email this week in response to a request for an interview. 
A view looking east across a property that’s been proposed for a 933-acre business park that could include a data center is pictured from Main Street in Fairfield, Utah on Sept. 23, 2026. (Katie McKellar/Utah News Dispatch)
McKinney also said “the developers have been good to work with and have included Fairfield’s residents, rural character, and water use in our preliminary discussions,” while adding that as “plans become more concrete, I’ll be in a better position to comment on the project and its potential impacts.”
The proposal hasn’t yet received a vote from the Fairfield Planning Commission, nor the Fairfield City Council. While being briefed on the project during a July meeting by EGI principal Jared Westhoff, the town’s planning commissioners expressed some concerns about the project and raised questions about water use and water rights.  
But they also said they liked the direction it was headed, particularly to build out a portion of the area with rural residential homes on large lots that allow animals — to avoid the land eventually being filled with high-density housing instead. 
But to Deeda Seed, a senior campaigner for the Center for Biological Diversity who has been tracking a growing number of data center proposals throughout Utah, the “GoldMine” proposal is concerning for multiple reasons — but especially because it’s located in the Cedar Valley, where water is already scarce and emissions are increasing due to a growing number of projects.
A sign pointing toward data center construction sites is pictures in Eagle Mountain on Sept. 23, 2026. (Katie McKellar/Utah News Dispatch)
“This is just crazy,” Seed said. “The fact that this thing is called GoldMine kind of sums it up. You know, these developers are digging for gold in the form of data center development. And the harm to everyone else is really significant and is totally not worth it.” 
Seed worries small-town Fairfield won’t have the resources — from permitting staff to firefighting resources — to properly manage and mitigate impacts of the proposed GoldMine project. 
Seed also questions whether enough people in Fairfield — and its larger northern neighbor, Eagle Mountain — are aware that it’s being considered, and if they’ll have the opportunity to weigh in before it’s too late. 
“This one is totally flying under the radar,” Seed said, adding, “Look at what happened to Mona.” 
Mona is a small rural city in Juab County, where residents learned a 3-million-square-foot data center was coming near their community months after it had already been approved by county leaders. One Mona resident first heard about the project only after a Williams Gas representative knocked on his door, asking for permission to run a gas line across his backyard, the Deseret News reported.  
The Fairfield Town Hall is pictured in Fairfield, Utah on Sept. 23, 2026. (Katie McKellar/Utah News Dispatch)
Seed worries the GoldMine project could be a similar scenario for Eagle Mountain if word doesn’t get out sooner rather than later. 
“The developers love it, because they see it as a gold mine,” she said. “But for everybody else it’s a very, very big problem, and our elected officials need to get a handle on it right now. But also communities need to be aware — early on.” 
Concerns of another data center in Cedar Valley
The Cedar Valley — and Eagle Mountain in particular — is no stranger to data center development. Just roughly three miles east of the property being eyed for GoldMine, there’s already a sprawling data center campus owned by Meta, which was approved as a 2.4 million-square-foot Facebook data center by Eagle Mountain leaders in 2018. Now, Meta is expanding, planning for the data center to surpass 5 million square feet when it’s fully built out.
Seed said Meta’s data center and other projects in the airshed — including Enyo Energy’s power plant that’s been proposed in Fairfield near the Meta campus — are adding up, increasing emissions in the Cedar Valley to the point that she’s worried they’ll tip the area back into federal nonattainment status. 
A Meta data center campus is pictured in Eagle Mountain, Utah on Sept. 23, 2026. (Katie McKellar/Utah News Dispatch)
“They’re apparently intent on building this gigantic polluting complex of hyperscale AI data centers in the Cedar Valley,” she said. “And I’m telling you, if I was in Eagle Mountain, I would be very worried and asking my elected officials what the heck is going on here.”
Seed argues the Cedar Valley could be on the brink of a “full-fledged disaster in terms of air quality. And this is in the Great Salt Lake Basin, totally the wrong place to be doing this under any circumstance.”
“This is ridiculous,” she said. “These (data centers) are going to change people’s lives forever, and change the landscape forever. You know, Eagle Mountain has the potential to become a great, sustainable community, but not if they go in this direction that they’re going in with all the data centers — but also not if their neighbors are pushing in this direction.” 
An old structure is pictured on a property to the south of Main Street in Fairfield, Utah on Sept. 23, 2026. (Katie McKellar/Utah News Dispatch)
Water, public transparency will be priorities as project is reviewed, mayor says
When asked about Seed’s worries, McKinney, Fairfield’s mayor, told Utah News Dispatch in an email “I understand the concerns Deeda has raised about public awareness, water use, and emissions,” but she noted Fairfield hasn’t yet received a development application for the project, so the town isn’t positioned to evaluate or permit it at this time. 
“When an application is submitted, we will review its specific impacts and follow the applicable public process,” McKinney said. “Protecting Cedar Valley’s water resources and keeping residents informed will be priorities throughout that review.”
The GoldMine project also lies within the Utah Inland Port Authority’s Pony Express Project Area, which means it could eventually be eligible for subsidy through the port authority’s tax increment capture and bonding power. 
However, because the project hasn’t gone through Fairfield’s planning process, it’s far from any consideration by the Utah Inland Port Authority Board. 
A view looking east across a property that’s been proposed for a 933-acre business park that could include a data center is pictured in Fairfield, Utah on Sept. 23, 2026. (Katie McKellar/Utah News Dispatch)
“UIPA does not get ahead of the communities we partner with,” Ben Hart, the port authority’s executive director, said in a prepared statement Wednesday. “Local leaders determine what types of development are appropriate for their communities, and UIPA’s role is to support locally established priorities.” 
He also noted UIPA’s “position on data centers remains unchanged.”
“UIPA is aligned with the governor’s executive order and the principles outlined on our website, including respect for local land-use decisions and responsible planning for water and energy use,” Hart said. 
Eagle Mountain’s Meta data center has come with decades of tax incentives, totaling about $150 million over 40 years for the first phase of the project. Its 567-acre expansion also allows it to receive back about $780 million over 40 years, clawing back taxes that would otherwise be collected from Alpine School District, Utah County, Unified Fire Authority, Central Utah Water Conservancy District and Eagle Mountain. 
While the development has created jobs and boosted property tax revenue for the area, Eagle Mountain this year nearly doubled its property tax rate to capture about $2.1 million more to pay for more police, expand city staff and increase wages for city employees, The Salt Lake Tribune reported. That amount is nearly equal to the $2.5 million per year Eagle Mountain has forgone for Meta’s tax incentives. 
A Meta data center campus is pictured in Eagle Mountain, Utah on Sept. 23, 2026. (Katie McKellar/Utah News Dispatch)
‘We take concerns regarding water and air quality seriously,’ developer says
Jared Westhoff, the EGI principal who has been discussing the project with the Fairfield Planning Commission, told commissioners in a July 16 meeting that one of his partners went to the East Coast to look at data centers “that were done right, and a couple that were done wrong.” He said the one that was done “wrong” was because of noise. 
“We’re going to be in this community for a long time, and we want to make sure that this project is something we can all be proud of as it’s built out,” Westoff said. “And so the last thing we would want is a data center going in that has some power generation with it and the noise is driving us all crazy.” 
Planning Commission Chair Wayne Taylor told Westhoff: “From being a little town (that) we are, this whole thing is concerning, right? But we understand that things are going to change, so we appreciate the thoughtfulness you’re putting into it.” 
Another commissioner, David Riet, said the rural town of Fairfield has “always resisted development, but we understand it’s coming.” But he also said “we would rather develop it nice like this so that it’s built out, so it’s not going to turn into a mess later with high density everywhere. If we build it out this way now, then it’s going to be nice forever.” 
Homes to the north of Fairfield, Utah are pictured on Sept. 23, 2026. (Katie McKellar/Utah News Dispatch)
“So as far as I’m concerned, I’m glad to see that it is being discussed and built out this way rather than the alternative, which eventually we’d just get run over by high density,” Riet said. “So I like the way this is going for that reason.” 
They also discussed water. Westhoff told planning commissioners that developers would want the GoldMine data center to function on a “closed loop system” that uses air cooling rather than water cooling. 
“We do not want the high water use that you see at Meta,” Westhoff said.  
But Seed told Utah News Dispatch a closed loop design “doesn’t solve the problem” with water because it would be powered by “a gas plant, and a gas plant needs water.” 
“So the water consumption is still a significant issue,” she said. “And when you put all of these hyperscale facilities next to each other in a valley (with already strained water resources), it is a recipe for disaster.” 
Westhoff, in response to a request for an interview, told Utah News Dispatch in an email Wednesday that the vision and design of the GoldMine project is going through an “ongoing planning process to obtain feedback and direction from Fairfield Town.” 
“The planning process remains ongoing, and the concepts and standards reflected in the draft are subject to continued review and refinement,” Westhoff said. 
A Meta data center campus is pictured in Eagle Mountain, Utah on Sept. 23, 2026. (Katie McKellar/Utah News Dispatch)
In response to Utah News Dispatch’s questions — including whether the developer had secured water rights for the project and details about GoldMine’s expected emissions — Westhoff said in an email that the project’s specifics are still taking shape, so it depends on what ends up moving forward.
“We take concerns regarding water and air quality seriously and intend for the project to incorporate responsible, modern standards as planning moves forward,” Westhoff said.
He also said that “based on the type of development currently being contemplated, we expect the business park to have lower overall water demand than a comparable residential buildout, particularly where low-water and closed-loop systems are utilized.”
“With respect to emissions, any future user would be expected to comply with all applicable state and federal air-quality requirements and permitting standards and to incorporate appropriate emissions-control measures where applicable,” Westhoff said. “Actual emissions would depend on the specific use, equipment, energy source, and final facility design, so it would be premature to provide a meaningful emissions estimate at this stage.”
Westhoff added that “we appreciate the questions and will continue working with Fairfield to ensure the project is planned and developed responsibly.”
Horses graze in a pasture in Fairfield, Utah on Sept. 23, 2026. (Katie McKellar/Utah News Dispatch)

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri should scrutinize all schools, not just St. Louis Public Schools
description: Missouri State Auditor Scott Fitzpatrick’s demand that the president of the St. Louis Board of Education testify about the firing of former Superintendent Millicent Borishade raises a larger question: Is this really about accountability, or is accountability being selectively applied? Dr. Borishade has filed an active whistleblower and wrongful-termination l[...]
text:
(Spenser Heaps/Utah News Dispatch).Missouri State Auditor Scott Fitzpatrick’s demand that the president of the St. Louis Board of Education testify about the firing of former Superintendent Millicent Borishade raises a larger question: Is this really about accountability, or is accountability being selectively applied?
Dr. Borishade has filed an active whistleblower and wrongful-termination lawsuit against the district. Any competent attorney understands the danger of having a board president provide open-ended testimony concerning matters that could become evidence in pending litigation.
Protecting the district’s legal position is not hiding from accountability. It is protecting St. Louis taxpayers.
But if Auditor Fitzpatrick wants to make himself Missouri’s watchdog over public education, then he should explain why that watchdog seems to bark much louder at public schools than others.
Consider Kairos Academies, a St. Louis charter school. Its fiscal year 2024 independent audit identified material noncompliance, a material weakness in internal controls, and a significant deficiency in internal controls. Yet where was the high-profile intervention from the State Auditor? Where were the demands for public testimony and the accompanying political spectacle?
There have also been serious questions raised about Kairos’ finances, including concerns surrounding fund balances and retirement-system contributions. If a charter school failed to make required retirement contributions on time and corrected the problem only after it was discovered, that deserves every bit as much scrutiny as financial or management problems at a traditional public school district.
And the standard cannot change when we leave St. Louis. Missouri has more than 500 school districts, including small rural districts that have experienced serious financial problems. Yet the auditor’s own 2024 annual report says his office released performance audits of only two school districts that year and launched audits of two more.
That is precisely why selective enforcement matters.
The auditor has chosen to place extraordinary attention on St. Louis Public Schools. His office issued a “poor” rating and publicly emphasized the district’s deficit spending, even projecting when its fund balance could eventually fall to financially stressed levels if corrective action were not taken.
Fine. Hold SLPS accountable.
But hold everybody accountable.
Audit the charter schools with questionable financial practices. Investigate districts operating with dangerously low reserves. Examine failures to make required retirement contributions. Demand answers from rural, suburban, charter and traditional public schools with the same intensity being directed at St. Louis.
Accountability cannot depend upon where you live, school type or political ideology.
The State Auditor possesses enormous public power. That power should be used to protect taxpayers—not to advance the political campaign against traditional public education.
The St. Louis Board of Education should cooperate fully with legitimate financial oversight while refusing to compromise its legal position in pending litigation.
And Auditor Fitzpatrick should answer a simple question:
If this is really about accountability, why isn’t everyone being held to the same standard?

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Bill to allow politicians to spend campaign cash on security spurs warnings of misuse
description: The Assembly gave overwhelming approval to a bill that would allow political candidates to use campaign funds to pay for security measures.
text:
Assemblyman Jay Webber (R-Morris) speaks on the Assembly floor on Jan. 12, 2026. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)Legislators passed a bill Thursday that would allow politicians and candidates to use campaign donations to pay for alarm systems, bodyguards, and other security measures, despite warnings from Republicans that such spending disregards donor intent and would be misused on “Uber drivers for their kids.”
The bill would allow campaign cash to be spent on security structures like fencing, lighting, and doors; non-structural devices like motion detectors and security cameras; security personnel; and cybersecurity software and services to protect officeholders, candidates, relatives in their household, and their staff.
It bars spending such funds on guns and ammunition, home improvements the bill doesn’t explicitly authorize, and payments to family members or entities family members own or operate.
The Assembly passed the proposal by a 53-13 vote, largely along party lines, with 14 members abstaining or not voting during their first session in Trenton since recessing in June for the summer.
Seven Republicans stood to condemn the bill, which is sponsored by Assemblyman Robert Karabinchak (D-Middlesex) and Sens. Paul Sarlo (D-Bergen) and Carmen Amato (R-Ocean).
Some shared their personal experience with vandalism, threats, and harassment, and agreed heightened security is warranted as political polarization drives up such dangers. But campaign supporters should not foot that bill, they said.
Assemblyman John Azzariti (R-Bergen) said the government should cover such costs, just as federal authorities have done for Congress members.
“The money should certainly not be coming from donors who don’t even know that you’ll be spending this money on other things other than getting elected,” Azzariti said.
Assemblywoman Dawn Fantasia (R-Sussex) seconded that, saying: “I don’t believe anybody ever donated to me with the intention of: ‘I hope this keeps her alive.’”
Assemblyman Jay Webber (R-Morris) noted the state’s long history of public corruption and warned the bill risks abuse “way too large for us to ignore.”
“I mean, this is New Jersey,” Webber said. “You should be expecting bad headlines about candidates who misuse these funds, whether it’s getting chauffeurs, or shall we call them Uber drivers, for their kids to school or installing fences around their homes that they always wanted to put in.”
Webber and Fantasia flagged the “hypocrisy” of legislators supporting the bill who also have special license plates advertising that they’re state lawmakers.
“They’ll get in their cars in the garage, in their license plates with two crowns on them, their initials and their district number, and they’ll drive home, telling the whole world exactly who they are, where they live, and where they’re going,” Webber said.
Critics also noted that both incumbents and Democrats, as the majority party controlling the Statehouse, tend to have far more campaign cash on hand, meaning the bill creates new inequities for Republicans, third-party candidates, and political newcomers who might not be able to divert dollars away from their core campaign needs.

The Senate unanimously passed the bill in June. It now heads to Gov. Mikie Sherrill’s desk.

name: WyoFile
title: Trump orders plans to unlock isolated public land, revise river-trip permitting
description:
The efforts are contained in a push to bolster hunting heritage.
The post Trump orders plans to unlock isolated public land, revise river-trip permitting appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
President Donald Trump last week ordered federal land managers to boost public access to public lands, including to landlocked checkerboard parcels and to Western whitewater rivers.
The order, titled Reinvigorating America’s Hunting Heritage, could reverse federal priorities to sell or trade isolated parcels of public land. Across the West, the BLM alone has identified more than 6 million acres available for “disposal,” according to onX, a digital mapping firm, and the Theodore Roosevelt Conservation Partnership.
The order also seeks to reform online application systems for coveted western river floating permits, which have reportedly been abused by individuals using computer programs.
The order directs the secretaries of War, Interior, Agriculture and Commerce to develop access plans within 180 days. National parks and monuments are generally exempted from the call.
The plans seek “to unlock checkerboarded and landlocked parcels through voluntary access easements, land exchanges, and cooperative agreements that respect private property rights,” according to a White House fact sheet.
As such, the action could reverse longstanding federal policies regarding public land that’s hard for the public to reach. That includes parcels that are surrounded by private land or arranged in a checkerboard pattern.
The common corner of public and private checkerboard-pattern property at Elk Mountain Ranch. (Mike Vanata/WyoFile)
That checkerboard pattern covers millions of acres in southern Wyoming and resulted in legal battles over public access by corner crossing, a controversy only recently settled in favor of public access.
Today, the Bureau of Land Management, for example, has a disposal policy that targets lands that are “uneconomical or difficult to manage with respect to contiguous public lands.” Almost 800,000 acres of BLM land in Wyoming reportedly qualify for disposal.
“Disposal” means to remove those lands from the federal estate by selling, trading or donating them to either private or public entities. The order calls for the federal government to plan for means to seek public-access easements to the parcels.
On rivers, where access is governed by lotteries and first-come online reservation systems, the order calls for reforms to favor U.S. citizens and previously unsuccessful applicants. The order also seeks to prohibit “automatic computer entries into the lotteries.”
Downriver dash
On Western rivers where access is governed by federal agencies like the National Park and U.S. Forest services, boaters seeking wilderness whitewater and stillwater adventures must obtain permits. Federal agencies limit the number of floaters to protect the environment, prevent crowding at a limited number of campsites and for other reasons.
The chance of obtaining a permit for the classic week-long whitewater descent of the Middle Fork of the Salmon River in Idaho’s Frank Church River of No Return Wilderness in Idaho’s Salmon-Challis National Forest is as low as 1%, river runners say.
Some permits are released online at a specific date and time. Boaters who react quickly win in the first-come, first-served computer dash. (There’s also a permit lottery that is random, not first-come, first-served.)
Rafting on Idaho’s Middle Fork of the Salmon River in Idaho’s Frank Church River of No Return Wilderness. (Zachary Collier/FlickrCC)
The first-come permits are scarfed up “the second they are released — in 10 milliseconds,” said Heather Hansman, a river-running journalist who recently wrote about abuses of the system.
“People are making up fake bot accounts,” she said, to evade prohibitions against multiple applications under the same name and other rules designed to create a fair system. Those fake names and applications can be operated by a computer program that can secure permits faster than a human typing on a keyboard the instant the application period goes live.
A river runner suspected something fishy and created a program to see whether he could beat the system, Hansman said.
It worked.
“The guy ran an experiment,” she said. “He ended up with six or seven permits by bot and nothing doing it by hand.”
While the executive order could remedy the bot battle, other aspects of the federal recreation system also deserve scrutiny, Hansman said. Recreation.gov or rec.gov reportedly provides permits to more than 100,000 sites, including national park campgrounds and backcountry camping sites.
Booz Allen Hamilton, a private company created the system and operates it for the government. Rec.gov is unsatisfactory, Hansman believes.
“I think the river permits are one piece of a systematic problem,” she said. “The issue is with the rec.gov umbrella.”
“Journalism can change policy. It’s cool.” Heather Hansman
She recently visited Capitol Reef National Park in Utah, for example. “The entire campground was booked,” she said, with no way to get a permit for an overnight stay.
“I had had this experience trying really hard to get permits and not being able to,” she said, “then going out and finding them empty, even though they’re booked up online.
“The entire campground was booked out but probably half of the sites were empty.”
Certainly, some empty sites were the result of emergencies or other cancellations on the part of the prospective campers. But many vacancies, Hansman believes, are due to overzealous campers who are not serious about their plans or who hoard permits for flexibility or some other reason.
There’s no downside to that hoarding and non-use, Hansman said, except for loss of a first-night fee.
Park rangers who see the problem, “can’t stop you from getting more reservations,” or otherwise penalize misuse, she said.
Booz Allen didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment on the executive order and other issues.
Corner crossing case
The order that targets public access to checkerboard land ownership follows the high-profile case of four Missouri hunters who reached public land in Wyoming by corner crossing.
Corner crossing is the act of stepping from one piece of public land to another where the two share a common corner with two pieces of private land. The ownership pattern resembles a checkerboard with alternating squares of public and private property. Corner crossers do not set foot on private land.
To step from public land to public land in such an area, a person necessarily passes through the airspace above the private property. A prosecutor in Carbon County charged the Missouri hunters with trespass in 2021, but a jury found them not guilty.
The landowner whose private ranch enmeshed some 6,000 acres of public land the hunters sought to reach sued the four in civil court. Courts cited the 1885 Unlawful Inclosures Act in siding with the hunters in a case that went all the way to the U.S. Supreme Court.
The 1885 act prevents landowners from blocking access to public land in the checkerboard.
Camouflage-wearing attendees at a February 2026 legislative meeting wait to testify on a bill that clarifies the legality of corner crossing in Wyoming statute. (Mike Koshmrl/WyoFile)
The high court declined to hear landowner Fred Eshelman’s appeal of the 10th Circuit Court of Appeal’s decision. The two cases brought national attention to corner crossing and the checkerboard land ownership pattern. (WyoFile covered the issue over five years with some 80 articles.)
As a result of the ruling, corner crossing is legal in the checkerboard area of Wyoming and in Colorado, Utah, Arizona, Oklahoma and Kansas. Nevertheless, the executive order could boost access in these states.
That’s because a caveat in the 10th Circuit decision allows corner crossing when it is the sole means of reaching public land. Depending on how new rules are formed and what new access easements the government may obtain, access to public land could become easier and less complicated than stepping over a hard-to-find survey monument at a common corner.
Southern Wyoming has about 2.4 million acres that are considered corner locked – inaccessible to the public without corner crossing. Across the West, the area is estimated at 8.3 million acres.
Hansman said the executive order may illustrate one point.
“Journalism can change policy,” she said. “It’s cool.”

title: Bucking the wind: Wyoming artists transform wind blade into snowfence
description:
The "Windborne" art installation transforms a discarded wind turbine blade into function inspiration, Casper artist says.
The post Bucking the wind: Wyoming artists transform wind blade into snowfence appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
A collection of Wyoming artists is hoping for a few good, blustery snowstorms this winter in the Esterbrook community in the Medicine Bow National Forest — an opportunity to test a new art installation, and to inspire.


“Windborne,” functionally, is a modern-day snowfence made of a single wind turbine blade, chopped into a dozen pieces planted in a row. It’s designed to pull swirling snowflakes down into a pile instead of allowing the white stuff to drift across a road near the Wyoming Rescue Mission Recovery Camp.


‘Windborne’ dedication
A dedication of the installation is scheduled for 11 a.m. Oct. 3, at the Wyoming Rescue Mission Recovery Camp, located at 3046 Esterbrook Road.


There’s about 500 miles of snowfencing — typically of the wood variety — across Wyoming. It’s practical infrastructure in a state that battles snowdrifted highways. 
“Windborne” is also art intended to inspire, Casper sculptor Chris Navarro says, because it demonstrates how a group of artists can repurpose what’s commonly regarded as industrial waste that typically crowds landfills.






Wyoming artists collaborated on an art installation near Esterbrook that repurposes a discarded wind turbine blade. (Chris Navarro)






The crew of artists helped paint a galloping band of mustangs across “Windborne.” The art installation in the Medicine Bow National Forest also serves as a snowfence. (Chris Navarro)


“It costs more to recycle them than it does to bury them,” said Navarro, who typically works in bronze. Several years ago he saw a photo in a local newspaper of a dozer pushing dirt over a massive pile of decommissioned wind turbine blades at the local landfill and was moved to do something about it. “I saw that and I just said, ‘Wow, what a waste of material! There’s got to be something better to do with them.'”
He found co-conspirators at the Rescue Mission Recovery Camp and coaxed Colorado-based Vestas to supply and cut up a decommissioned blade, which it was more than willing to do, Navarro said. Vestas, like other wind energy manufacturing companies, is eager to find new ways of making better use of the industry’s byproduct.
This schematic depicts how the “Windborne” installation is constructed. (Chris Navarro)
The nearby Mantle Ranch Wild Horse Adoption and Training Facility was also integral, Navarro said. He tapped several other local artists to paint a band of wild mustangs running across the blade sections. “When I look at those 40 mustangs, I don’t see horses running away. I see a herd moving forward.”
Navarro said he hopes the installation’s sense of “moving forward” inspires a solutions-oriented resolve to tackle challenges like discarded wind turbine blades. In fact, the Wyoming Department of Transportation will monitor how well the installation prevents drifts, and may consider wind turbine blades as part of its snowfence program.
