name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Mountain strong: North Carolina marks the 2-year anniversary of Hurricane Helene
description: Before there was Helene, there was Katrina. The destructive Category 5 hurricane that devastated New Orleans in 2005 convinced Alex Webber to move from Louisiana to the mountains of western North Carolina. Webber thought she’d found a climate-safe area in the picturesque town of Marshall until 2024, when Hurricane Helene brought catastrophic flooding and lan[...]
text:
A rainbow shines above downtown Marshall on September 18, 2026, a week before the town marks the two-year anniversary of Hurricane Helene.  (Photo: Courtesy of Sky Walsh)Before there was Helene, there was Katrina.
The destructive Category 5 hurricane that devastated New Orleans in 2005 convinced Alex Webber to move from Louisiana to the mountains of western North Carolina.
Webber thought she’d found a climate-safe area in the picturesque town of Marshall until 2024, when Hurricane Helene brought catastrophic flooding and landslides to her backyard.
This weekend marks the two-year anniversary of Helene, and Webber brushed away tears as she recounted 24 months of trying to rebuild the life she had before the storm arrived.
Alex Webber gets emotional as she thinks about rebuilding from Helene. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)
“Our business was completely gone,” said Webber. “At home, our driveway was destroyed and that was $7,000 to rebuild.”
Webber said claims made to FEMA and her insurance company were turned down.
“We came back through Go Fund Me,” Webber said in a call with reporters organized by the nonprofit Extreme Weather Survivors. “It was almost easier in Katrina.”
Fellow Marshall resident Gina Heath says she’s grateful for the parts of town that have made a comeback. But it’s hard not to think about the loss. Twenty-five of the 27 homes on her street were lost to Helene.
“After the hurricane hit in late September, most of us were not able to do income-generating work,” said Heath. “For me, I was juggling, supporting, getting my kids through a very uncertain time, creating normalcy however I could.”
Heath said she thought FEMA would have a bigger presence on the ground in helping her community recover.	

Hurricane Helene by the numbers:

More than 100 lives lost.
$60 billion in damage
Over 73,000 homes were damaged or destroyed.
150 Renew NC single-family homes completed with about 2,000 more in the program pipeline
1,100+ Homes repaired, rebuilt or weatherized by nonprofit and volunteer partners with state funds
6M+ Cubic yards of Helene-related debris removed to date
99% State-maintained roads reopened
169,000 individuals received behavioral and mental health services offered through Hope4NC



“Eventually, secular and religious nonprofits came and helped people to rebuild. We never got anything significant from FEMA,” said Heath.
Two years later, Heath said two-thirds of Marshall is thriving. Even though many municipal buildings, including Marshall’s century-old courthouse, remain untouched, she said she feels fortunate.
“Not every town in Western Carolina has that same story at this point,” said Heath.
Chronicling a slow recovery
Extreme Weather Survivors, a national network of individuals and families impacted by climate-fueled disasters, surveyed 300 North Carolina adults directly affected by Hurricane Helene.
What they found was that 1 in 4 still have not returned home, even though they plan to. Seventy-one percent personally know someone who is still struggling financially, nearly two years later. And 60% said they felt abandoned by the government during and after Hurricane Helene.
Webber said the one exception was Gov. Josh Stein.
“Our state governor has been coming in very quietly. He just comes in with his wife and checks on downtown,” said Webber. “He’s been seen around town multiple times. They’ll come for the weekend, no cameras.”
Stein has made numerous trips to the mountains in the months after Helene, while back in Raleigh the Governor’s Recovery Office for Western North Carolina (GROW NC) is facilitating a collaboration across state agencies to support the recovery, while also managing federal and state reporting requirements.
Recovery efforts continue across western North Carolina. Madison, Yancey and Mitchell counties sustained some of the worst damage. (Google maps)
Matt Calabria, director of GROW NC, is in charge of  answering to frustrated state legislators who want to know why the program is not moving faster, while trying to get as much money as possible from the federal government, which has been slow to respond.
Calabria told NC Newsline this week the state has reopened more than 99% of roads closed or affected by Hurricane Helene. More than 1,250 homes have been repaired or rebuilt through Renew NC and with volunteer partners. And recently, the state announced funding for 828 new affordable housing units for the region.
Calabria is aware some survivors are tired of waiting and feel the process is slow and cumbersome. He doesn’t disagree. Instead, he uses the feedback to sharpen his funding requests to the N.C. General Assembly and to Congress.
“Hearing from folks is never unwelcome, and it’s never a distraction from the job. It is the job,” Calabria said.
‘In the thick of it’
On Friday, Stein and the recovery office will be in Mars Hill to unveil the Western North Carolina Economic Recovery Plan, a long-term framework to rebuild and grow the region’s economy. It’s intended to build on work already underway by counties, chambers and small businesses.
Leo Sharp (left) and Tessa Reed Sharp enter year three of rebuilding their homestead. (Photo: NC Newsline)
Sixty miles away in Green Mountain, Leo Sharp and Tessa Reed Sharp will spend the day continuing to rebuild their century-old homestead that was heavily damaged by Helene’s floodwaters.
The couple moved to Mitchell County in 2022, hoping to renovate their home and create a small business selling tea, eggs and honey from their beehives. Helene washed away the chicken coops, toppled the hives, and left them with an early estimate of $120,000 in damages.
As construction continues indoors, the couple is dividing their time between the living room and a tent pitched on wooden scaffolding across their property.
“It’s kind of become like our little staycation,” said Tessa Sharp with a smile.
Rebuilding a century-old homestead after a once-in-a-century storm

The couple was working this year to replace some kitchen cabinets and flooring, when they discovered supports underneath the house had been washed out by the floodwaters. They didn’t catch that before, adding to the list of things that would need to be addressed.
“There’s a lot of blessings in disguise with progress,” Leo Sharp said. “A couple steps back, couple steps forward, but all in all everything, every step that we take forward is a good source of hope.”
The rebuild has taken longer than they expected, but Tessa Sharp finds comfort in their tight-knit community.
“Knowing that we’re not in the thick of it solo, that really helps,” she said.
The Sharps, like many others, are not waiting for  government funding for their recovery. The two have opened an online store to sell their artwork to bring in additional revenue for rebuilding the homestead.
Leo Sharp sells prints of his artwork to raise rebuilding funds. “Vantage” is a symbol of hope. (Artwork courtesy of Leo Sharp)
“Vantage” is a piece Leo Sharp created to remind the couple to remain vigilant. It features a heron soaring above the mountains of western North Carolina.
“From up high, everything else seems so small,” he said.
‘We start working’
The couple credits Stephanie Johnson with helping the region slowly recover.
Two years ago, Johnson was just planning to set up a short-term aid distribution site in the local Roses parking lot. But the need in Yancey County was tremendous. The rural county had 7,000 structures damaged or destroyed, including 1,500 homes. People were desperate for building materials to start fixing their houses.
“I was very much like, ‘Oh God, now you want me to get into building materials?'” Johnson recalled.
The next day, unsolicited, a trailer arrived with 100 front doors to donate.
“They were beautiful doors,” said Johnson. “That was very much a clear answer to me that yes, God intended me to end up organizing building supplies.”
She founded the nonprofit Rebuilding Hollers Foundation, and began by asking on social media for tools, shingles, sheetrock and lumber. With each ask, the donations slowly started to arrive.
With a background in commercial contracting, banking and real estate, Johnson and others developed Rebuilding Hollers into a fully operational community-based nonprofit. The group received over 593 requests for help.
Stephanie Johnson poses with students in the carpentry program at Mountain Heritage High School. The innovative program is helping people repair their homes sooner in Yancey and Mitchell Counties. (Photo courtesy of Stephanie Johnson/Rebuilding Hollers)
“We have met the needs of 301 of those projects. We still have 292 projects that need help,” said Johnson.
They keep the application process simple.
“Do you live in Yancey or Mitchell counties? Were you affected by the storm? Then we go see the property,” Johnson explained. “We come up with a plan. We start working.”
A partnership with the carpentry program at Mountain Heritage High School, also made possible through donations, is helping with the rebuilding process..
“We get the site ready and prepped up. The school builds the subfloor, the framing, and then a home delivery truck moves it to the site,” said Johnson.
Local contractors then finish out the house.
Rebuilding Hollers has recently opened a storefront where storm survivors can shop for free to replace household goods like light fixtures and linens.
An online store and an October fundraiser provide a steady stream of income to keep the nonprofit moving forward.  On Friday, Rebuilding Hollers will be accepting donations at a community concert and voter registration drive in Burnsville, NC sponsored by Extreme Weather Survivors. The national group is hoping to engage voters on the issue of climate change.
Heading into year three of the recovery, Johnson said she has 25 neighbors still living in campers, waiting on her group to help.
“We stick together as a rural mountain community,” said Johnson. “It’s really pure faith and absolute determination that this storm will not define our community.”
Each rebuilding project comes with unique challenges. Two walls of this structure were blown out by the force of Helene’s water. This is the first project Rebuilding Hollers completed. The nonprofit has 292 projects that still need help. (Photo courtesy of Stephanie Johnson/Rebuilding Hollers)

title: Colorado’s first state fair opened in 1876 with displays of produce and a pigeon shooting match
description: Colorado’s first-ever state fair opened in Denver on the afternoon of Sept. 26, 1876, and “every means of transportation in the city was pressed into service” to ferry passengers to the 40-acre fairgrounds on its eastern outskirts, according to the Rocky Mountain News. All week, wagons and railroad cars had transported goods from all across […]
text:
Denver is pictured in a photograph dated between 1875 and 1879, including a bridge over the Platte River and the Denver City Water Company's Holly water works. (Courtesy of Denver Public Library Special Collections, X-18534)Colorado’s first-ever state fair opened in Denver on the afternoon of Sept. 26, 1876, and “every means of transportation in the city was pressed into service” to ferry passengers to the 40-acre fairgrounds on its eastern outskirts, according to the Rocky Mountain News.



← Sept. 17–23
Sept. 24–30 

This story is part of Colorado at 150.

All week, wagons and railroad cars had transported goods from all across the state to be put on display at the fair — technically, the annual exposition of the Colorado Industrial Association, which had been held in Denver since the 1860s and would later move to Pueblo, where it was officially incorporated in 1886.
“Of course every person feels a certain pride in having the first fair since Colorado became a state especially successful,” reported the News. “And then there is the national pride engendered of the Centennial year which spurs men on in their liberality.”
The central attraction inside the fair’s main exhibition hall, courtesy of Denver’s Bellevue Gardens, was “a circular stand covered with pots and vases of flowers, among which were many rare exotics, exhaling delicate odors and adding materially by their brilliancy of color to the attractiveness of the scene,” said the News.
Other booths showed off “every variety of fancy needlework”; oil paintings and engravings; tanned animal hides and furs; luxury furniture and “some excellent articles in the plumbing line”; and a cornucopia of agricultural products.
“The Clear Creek Valley Grange has on exhibition a large amount of all varieties of produce, among which are mammoth squashes, beets, potatoes and melons, besides some freshly cut grass measuring over six feet in height,” the News continued. “The El Paso County Cheese Company shows enough of that article to surfeit the whole state.”
At Ford’s Park, adjacent to the fairgrounds, 40 entrants contested a pigeon shooting match, with prizes ranging from $100 in cash to a sack of flour. But the fair’s biggest draw was five straight days of horse racing. The trotting and running races on Sept. 26 were won by “Tempest” and “Bay Billy,” respectively, with each winning a $150 top prize.
At the request of 50 petitioners representing the “bankers and business men of the city,” Denver Mayor R.G. Buckingham declared Friday, Sept. 29, an official holiday, “with a view to the encouragement of a project which, if properly furthered, will inure to the benefit of the entire community.”
“To a stranger within the gates, it seemed as if the whole state of Colorado had turned out and was upon the grounds,” the News reported the following day. “The grand stand was filled so that it was impossible to find sitting room and almost impossible to find standing space, before one o’clock in the afternoon, although the races were not announced to begin until two o’clock.”

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Everett Wess campaigns against long odds
description: Everett Wess has a very difficult road to being Alabama’s next U.S. senator. The Democratic nominee is trying to become the first person in his party to be elected to the Senate from Alabama in a general election since 1992. Republican nominee Barry Moore, a congressman from Enterprise, has name recognition and a solid warchest. […]
text:
Attorney Everett Wess, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, is in an uphill battle against Republican nominee Barry Moore.(Photo courtesy of candidate).Everett Wess has a very difficult road to being Alabama’s next U.S. senator.
The Democratic nominee is trying to become the first person in his party to be elected to the Senate from Alabama in a general election since 1992. Republican nominee Barry Moore, a congressman from Enterprise, has name recognition and a solid warchest. Through the end of June, Wess raised slightly less than $4,000 in campaign funds compared to Moore, who has received almost $2.5 million in donations, according to the Federal Election Commission website.
Both the Cook Political Report and Sabato Crystal Ball rate the seat as “Solid Republican” and “Safe Republican” respectively with about a month and a half until the election.
“It is a tough state to start out with,” said J. Miles Coleman, associate editor for Sabato Crystal Ball at the University of Virginia, of the Democrats’ chances for winning the contest. “(President Donald) Trump carried it by 30 points in 2024. None of the main national parties really seem very invested in it.”
Despite that, Wess continues to attend events to meet with voters to discuss the issues he believes are important for Alabama residents.
“I am the type of individual where all I can do is work on winning this election for the people of Alabama,” he said in a recent interview. “That is what I am doing, meeting with the citizens of Alabama, speaking with the citizens of Alabama, listening to the citizens of Alabama, and in the end, they will make their decisions as to who they think is the best candidate to represent the state of Alabama.”
The contest will determine the successor to U.S. Sen. Tommy Tuberville, who is the Republican nominee for Alabama governor. A message was sent to the Moore campaign on Tuesday seeking comment.
Despite the structural disadvantages, Wess said he will continue to discuss the priorities he laid out for this campaign. He chose to be a candidate after he sensed that voters are dissatisfied with Trump’s performance.
“It looks like hope is lost,” Wess said. “People are uncertain about what is going to happen next. There is confusion with the current administration, uncertainty with the current administration.”
Wess hopes to seize on many of the same issues that other Democratic nominees have made their priorities, particularly the economy and inflation.
“That has been happening since Trump took office,” he said. “Prices have really not come down, and especially with the start of the (Iran) war. Gas prices are high, groceries are higher, prescription drugs are also high.”
Democrats nationally have a favorable environment. But in Alabama, party advantage favors Moore. Alabama does not require voters to register with a political party to be eligible to vote, so membership numbers among the different parties are not publicly available. However, the Independent Voter Project, a nonprofit organization that promotes election reform, estimated almost 2 million people in Alabama, roughly 55% of the electorate, favor the Republican Party while about 1.2 million people in the state, about 36% tend to favor Democrats.
“You have a bunch of strongly Republican exurbs and rural areas in Alabama,” Coleman said. “Yes, you have some Democratic beach heads in Jefferson County and Mobile, the area around Huntsville is slowly getting a little less red, but not enough to offset some of these really Republican parts of the state even in a year that is probably going to be good for the Democratic Party.”
Republicans also outvoted Democrats during the primary election for this race in May, with about 340,000 voters casting a ballot for one of the Democratic candidates for senator. More than 480,000 people cast a vote for a Republican candidate to be the next U.S. Senator.
Democrats have overcome the Republican party advantage in the past. Doug Jones, currently the Democratic nominee for Alabama governor, bested former Alabama Supreme Court Justice Roy Moore for a special election in 2017. But the contest was the only one on that ballot, and Moore, who had already alienated many Republicans, faced allegations of sexual abuse and misconduct during the campaign, which he denied.
“If you are extraordinarily, personally noxious to people, you can neutralize your party’s advantage, and really importantly, if you face a credible opponent,” said David Niven, an associate professor of political science at the University of Cincinnati.
Despite the long odds, Wess believes he has a path to victory.
“I am on the ground working, listening to the people and listening to the needs and desires of the people, and I think that is going to make a difference in race,” Wess said.
Wess currently works as an attorney for the Wess Law Firm in Birmingham. He has also served on the executive committee of the Jefferson County Democratic Party, taught classes at Faulkner University and served on the board of Legacy Works, an organization mentoring at-risk youth.
Wess says he would prioritize healthcare, public safety and education as the issues he will prioritize should he be elected. He said he wants to bring federal dollars to the rural parts of the state to invest in rural hospitals and strengthen their emergency departments. He wants to recruit additional physicians and medical staff to the area and help make prescription drugs and healthcare more affordable.
Wess has seized on many of the same campaign issues as other Democrats with respect to the economy.
“I was talking to a lady just yesterday who said she was buying bread at the beginning of this year, and now it is a dollar more,” Wess said.
He also spoke of problems with the budget reconciliation bill that Congress and that Trump signed into law. The bill substantially shifts the cost of the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program to states and could reduce the number of people who are able to receive food assistance. The bill also did not extend the tax credits allowed by former President Joe Biden that people could use to reduce the premiums they pay for health insurance with the Affordable Care Act.
“I thought I could do a good job,” Wess said. “I thought I could put the Alabama citizens first before the wants and the needs of the administration.”

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: There’s an easy way to save lives from sudden cardiac arrest
description: On Oct. 24, 2021, dressed as a zombie and dancing in Lexington’s annual Thriller Parade, I collapsed from sudden cardiac arrest and died in front of the Kentucky Theatre. Main Street was packed with a thousand zombies and 10,000 spectators, making it impossible for an emergency vehicle to navigate through the horde of zombies. If […]
text:
Charlotte Callan and Sarah Katzenmaier are trying to map every AED in Lexington. Callan saved Katzenmaier's life by doing CPR during the Thriller Parade, not knowing there was an AED inside the Kentucky Theater. (Photo provided)On Oct. 24, 2021, dressed as a zombie and dancing in Lexington’s annual Thriller Parade, I collapsed from sudden cardiac arrest and died in front of the Kentucky Theatre. 
Main Street was packed with a thousand zombies and 10,000 spectators, making it impossible for an emergency vehicle to navigate through the horde of zombies. If not for the heroic actions of Charlotte Callan, who performed CPR for over 10 minutes, I would not be here today. She kept oxygenated blood flowing to my brain until paramedics arrived to shock my heart back to life with an Automated External Defibrillator. Charlotte was later honored by Mayor Linda Gorton with the Spirit of Lexington Award.
 The irony of my story is that while Charlotte was desperately pumping my chest in the street, there was an AED inside the office of the Kentucky Theatre. But no one knew how to find it, because Lexington doesn’t have them mapped! Knowing where AEDs are, saves lives; this asset could have saved critical minutes. In a sudden cardiac arrest event, every second matters; survival rates drop by 10 percent for every minute that passes without defibrillation. Having an AED nearby and accessible while waiting for an ambulance can mean the difference between life and death.
 Today, Charlotte and I are working together on a grassroots initiative to ensure that no one in Lexington dies next to a hidden defibrillator. We have launched the Cardiac Crusade / Lexington Re-start a Heart initiative, with a volunteer team of Cardiac CATS. Our goal is to make Lexington a more heart safe community.  
 If you download the PulsePoint AED app (NEAR) and look at Lexington, you can see all our mapped AEDs. Only the gold shields represent verified, functional AEDs that 911 dispatchers can use to direct bystanders. If you look at our neighbors in Nicholasville, or at progressive cities like Buffalo and Boston, their maps are filled with gold shields. Boston over-achieved and has grown to include areas all over Massachusetts.
 When I started laying the groundwork for this campaign in January, Lexington only had 4 Verified AEDs on the map.  Since then, we have mapped over 150, but we need a lot more.
 The data shows that mapping AEDs saves lives. Cities that have successfully mapped their AEDs and made their communities aware of this initiative—such as San Diego—have seen sudden cardiac arrest survival rates skyrocket from less than 10 percent to greater than 60 percent. This initiative helps every single citizen regardless of age, health status, or zip code, because sudden cardiac arrest can strike anyone, anywhere, with absolutely no warning.
 I am leading this initiative and have been working with city leaders to prepare for this campaign to map AEDs across Lexington.  The Lexington Fire Department, E911 unit and PulsePoint, along with Cardiac Crusade, are working together to ensure the software supports any needed upgrades. Our local emergency responders are already collaborating directly with their counterparts in Buffalo to replicate their success. Councilmember Tyler Morton, City Council and the Mayor’s office have promised their support in spreading the word.  Governor Andy Beshear supports this initiative, and we hope to include all of the Commonwealth in the future.
 We still need more volunteers and more healthcare sponsors to help us complete our city’s map. UK Healthcare has generously pledged to recruit medical students who can earn practicum hours by mapping AEDs, as the PulsePoint AED app tracks AEDs mapped in your profile. The American Heart Association has stepped up as our foundational sponsor and provided capital funding. Now, we need your help!
 You can become a “Cardiac CAT” today. Download the PulsePoint AED app (NEAR) and look for AEDs at the places you regularly visit—your office, gym, or grocery store—and see if their AEDs are on the map. You can take a free online training course through the Cardiac Crusade website to become a certified verifier, allowing you to log and verify AEDs while running everyday errands. This is not limited to Lexington; you can add an AED to the PulsePoint AED map anywhere you see one!
 I invite everyone—citizens, business owners, and potential corporate sponsors—to join us for our campaign kickoff press event on Oct. 16 at 5:00 p.m. at West Sixth Brewery, another sponsor. Let’s work together to make Lexington and all of the Commonwealth a more heart-safe place to live.

title: Virginia health committee considers mandating licensed nurses in every school
description: Virginia schools could be required to have a licensed nurse in every building starting in 2028, under a legislative proposal introduced Wednesday. The measure is designed to close healthcare gaps by placing experts in schools to manage complex medical conditions. Virginia permits school divisions to employ nurses, but state law doesn’t require it. About 8% [[...]
text:
A newly proposed legislative measure would require all school districts in Virginia to employ a licensed nurse in every school. (Stock photo Sewcream Studio/Getty Images)Virginia schools could be required to have a licensed nurse in every building starting in 2028, under a legislative proposal introduced Wednesday. The measure is designed to close healthcare gaps by placing experts in schools to manage complex medical conditions.
Virginia permits school divisions to employ nurses, but state law doesn’t require it. About 8% of Virginia’s schools operate without a nurse.
At the School Health Services Committee’s Wednesday meeting, speakers and committee members supported the proposal. As written, it offers districts facing nurse shortages two-year waivers if they can show they made a good-faith effort to hire.
“School nursing is public health,” said Paula Nichols, school health administrator at Washington County Public Schools, during a video call on Wednesday. 
She said during Hurricane Helene, school nurses helped serve whole communities, not just students during the school day, going door to door to bring cases of water and medical care while wading through high water.
They also helped run community supply drives with other local partners.
“When the next emergency comes, and we know they always do, we need those relationships already in place,” Nichols said.
The proposed policy would require each school board to provide at least one licensed school nurse per building or per 325 students. The requirements would not take effect until July 1, 2028.
Schools have to compete with hospitals, clinics, academic institutions and nursing homes for nurses, according to workforce data collected by the Virginia Department of Health Professions.
Stacy Haynie, a lobbyist representing the Virginia School Board Association, supported the goal of having nurses in school buildings but raised concerns about implementing such a mandate because of a persistent shortage of nurses statewide. 
She noted that even when school boards want to hire nurses, they lack applicants for those positions.
“Regardless of what this committee does with this particular proposed legislation, I think we need to make sure that we don’t lose sight of the fact that there is a shortage of nurses across the commonwealth.”
Senate Education and Health Committee Chair Barbara Favola, D-Arlington, who also chairs the state’s school health services committee, said lawmakers are working to address the shortage.
She also backed the school nurse proposal, calling it a compromise and the main reason the committee was formed. 
“At the end of the day, we have to allow our teachers and school administrators to teach and manage the school, and having a nurse allows them to do their job,” Favola said. “A nurse is there to help with health issues that more and more of our children are facing every day.”
Betsy Looney, a committee member, said, “school nursing is not band-aids and ice packs,” emphasizing the central role nurses play in school safety.
“A nurse in every public school is not an additional service layered into the educational system,” Looney said. “It is the professional infrastructure necessary to safely and effectively implement the health responsibilities Virginia has already placed on its schools.” 
The committee will vote whether to send the proposal to the General Assembly for the upcoming session starting in January at its next business meeting on Nov. 18.

title: After Obama-era Chesapeake Bay executive order rescinded, environmental groups brace for fallout
description: Virginia environmental advocacy organizations are trying to determine the full extent of impacts from President Donald Trump’s rescission of a landmark Chesapeake Bay pollution reduction law last week.  “We’re still waiting to find out what all of the fallout is going to be,” said Jay Ford, the Virginia policy manager for the Chesapeake Bay Foundation. […]
text:
Map of Chesapeake Watershed states. March 30, 2026. (Photo by Shannon Heckt/Virginia Mercury)Virginia environmental advocacy organizations are trying to determine the full extent of impacts from President Donald Trump’s rescission of a landmark Chesapeake Bay pollution reduction law last week. 
“We’re still waiting to find out what all of the fallout is going to be,” said Jay Ford, the Virginia policy manager for the Chesapeake Bay Foundation. “The immediate impacts are a clear weakening of federal leadership right after the signing of the new Bay agreement.”
Trump rescinded Executive Order 13508, signed in 2009 under former President Barack Obama. The federal effort brought states and localities together collaboratively to identify pollution sources and ways to reduce sediment and nutrient loads.
The order also charged Chesapeake Bay watershed partners with creating stormwater management best practices.
“As of 2025, the jurisdictions of the Chesapeake Bay watershed — New York, Pennsylvania, Maryland, Virginia, the District of Columbia, Delaware, and West Virginia — have collectively met 100 percent of their goal for sediment reduction, 90 percent of their goal for phosphorus reduction, and 57 percent of their goal for nitrogen reduction,” Trump said in the rescinding statement.
These reductions are due in part to the Chesapeake Watershed Agreement, a multi-state agreement formed in the 1980s that brought together the states whose waterways feed into the Bay. The partners pledge to collaborate on goals and benchmarks to meet pollution reductions. 
The latest iteration of the agreement was signed last year and established four main goals and 21 outcomes the states can strive towards over the next 15 years. 
“Given this significant progress, and the need to provide clarity on how to continue improving the environmental health of the Chesapeake Bay, it is appropriate to revoke Executive Order 13508,” Trump said.
But leading environmental groups said it’s not the right time to pull back on the provision that has helped make so much progress. 
“The irony is that the success touted in (the) executive order was made possible in part by the executive order that was just rescinded,” said Hilary Falk, president of the Chesapeake Bay Foundation. “Weakening federal leadership makes it harder for localities and communities to tackle pollution, flooding, and other major challenges that we are facing.”
Trump framed the original order as overly broad and unclear on implementation standards, stating “this lack of clarity has led to harmful economic impacts on affected Americans.” He used stormwater management fees, which he dubbed “rain taxes,” as an example of this dynamic. 
A representative of the federal Environmental Protection Agency supported Trump’s move in a statement this week, saying it “emphasizes that Americans don’t need to choose between clean water and economic prosperity. With practical and focused actions, they can have both.”
Stormwater fees, which are not directly related to the previous executive order and can’t be repealed by Trump’s order, are used to fund stormwater infrastructure that aids in managing flooding, which contributes to pollutants flowing into the Bay. 
Many Virginia localities have put these fees in place. The Chesapeake Bay Foundation is concerned that the president’s repeal of the former order will encourage localities to pull back on those investments, amping up the risk of floods devastating communities statewide, especially in the coastal region. 
“In an area like Hampton Roads, the stormwater management is important for water quality, but it’s also important for habitat,” said Alison Prost, CBF’s senior vice president for programs. “It’s important for resiliency and what it means for the communities down there. So, if the federal government is not going to take that holistic approach, I think it may make those challenges harder.”
While the latest Bay agreement is still in place, Ford said there are also worries about potential breakdowns in state partnerships on reducing pollutant loads in the Bay. It’s also unclear if federal funding that previously supported many of these efforts, could be lost.
“All the states have their jurisdictional bounds, but the federal government is really the umbrella that helps make sure everyone’s communicating appropriately and they’re sharing best practices,” Ford said. “Federal agencies, they figure in pretty much every major work group and, you know, scientific tact component of both the Bay program and the work that flows from it.”
Members of Virginia’s congressional delegation have urged the president to reverse his actions. 
Sens. Mark Warner and Tim Kaine, both Virginia Democrats, and U.S. Rep. Bobby Scott, D-Newport News, condemned the move.
Scott serves on the Chesapeake Bay Watershed Task Force and said the repeal represents the federal government “walking away from that responsibility,” which “jeopardizes the hard-fought progress we have made.”
“Rolling back efforts to clean up the Bay is dangerous not just for our environment but for our economy,” Kaine and Warner said in a joint statement. “We should be building on the progress we’ve made instead of walking away from a framework that has guided restoration efforts for more than 15 years.”

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Three summers after costly cyanobacteria treatment, a small NH lake is still in the clear
description: Clear waters in Moultonborough’s Lake Kanasatka this summer strengthened residents’ hopes that an expensive, last-ditch chemical treatment undertaken several years ago was paying off. This year has been a “beautiful” one on the lake, said waterfront resident Kevin Kelly. Conditions have improved each year since the treatment was applied in 2024, after anguis[...]
text:
A team of researchers with the UNH Lakes Lay Monitoring Program heads out to track water quality on Lake Kanasatka in Moultonborough Thursday, Sept. 24. At the helm is lakeshore resident Kevin Kelly, who has helped measure water quality on the lake for decades. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)Clear waters in Moultonborough’s Lake Kanasatka this summer strengthened residents’ hopes that an expensive, last-ditch chemical treatment undertaken several years ago was paying off.
This year has been a “beautiful” one on the lake, said waterfront resident Kevin Kelly. Conditions have improved each year since the treatment was applied in 2024, after anguish and health concerns over recurrent cyanobacteria blooms peaked the year before.
For Lake Kanasatka, the treatment “is doing what it’s supposed to do,” said Amanda McQuaid, director of the UNH Lakes Lay Monitoring Program. She spoke by the lake’s shore on Thursday, a bald eagle crying from somewhere in the pine branches above her head. 
Yet experts, including McQuaid, have been clear that the treatment, which for Lake Kanasatka cost more than half a million dollars, is not permanent. Nor is it necessarily well-suited to all of the many other water bodies across New Hampshire dealing with similar bloom struggles, McQuaid said.
“We don’t want everyone to be like, ‘Oh, let me try to do that now,’ because it’s not going to work,” she said. 
Cyanobacteria blooms occur when a type of bacteria normally present in water bodies at low concentrations begins to grow unchecked. Excessive nutrients, such as from erosion or fertilizer runoff, and rising temperatures linked to climate change can both worsen the blooms; the bacteria can sometimes produce a range of toxins harmful to both humans and animals.
The treatment pursued by the Lake Kanasatka Watershed Association involves depositing alum into the water, where it binds with the nutrient phosphorus and settles to the lake floor. Scientists hope it will last at least a decade, McQuaid said.
Kirk Meloney, former president of the Lake Kanasatka Watershed Association, said he was convinced a chemical treatment to the lake that cost more than half a million dollars to implement had proven worthwhile. The occurrence of potentially toxic cyanobacteria blooms has fallen sharply on the lake in the three summers since the treatment, which scientists said is not a blanket remedy for the many other lakes facing challenges from cyanobacteria. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Some consider it experimental, and the decision to pursue the treatment felt risky at the time, recalled resident Kirk Meloney.
“It was a concern to me, dumping all this stuff into this precious water body,” said Meloney, who at the time was leading the Lake Kanasatka Watershed Association as its president. But he wanted to “listen to the science,” he said. 
The condition of the water seemed to warrant the drastic move. Recalling the years before the treatment, McQuaid likened the color of the lake’s water during the summer of 2020 to Gatorade. By 2023, she said, the water body was in the thrall of blooms worse than any previously observed at the site.
“This whole area was solid green, scummy — like, thick,” she said. Some of the affected water spilled over into Lake Winnipesaukee, to which Kanasatka is linked.
Conditions have steadily improved since the 2024 treatment. 
Last year, the lake still saw some blooms, including in September, Kelly recalled. But this year, the water has been mostly clear.
The cyanobacteria “blips” that still occur now and then, McQuaid said, are often linked to heavy rain, which dumps nutrient-laden runoff into the lake. But on the whole, phosphorus levels are a fraction of what they were before the treatment, and the lake ecosystem seems to be bouncing back.
On Thursday, a loon and its chick drifted on the water, disturbed occasionally by predatory dive-bombs from the bald eagle. On a pontoon boat nearby, McQuaid’s team lowered a cone-shaped net to the deepest reaches of the lake, bringing up water teeming with typical algae and twitchily swimming zooplankton. These, McQuaid said, are signs of a healthy ecosystem.
“All of this is related to those loons,” she said, holding the bottle of plankton in the sun. “A good base of the food web supports the fish, supports the loons.”
Diverse plankton and algae, like those in this flask, are signs of a healthy lake ecosystem, said Amanda McQuaid, director of the UNH Lakes Lay Monitoring Program. These plankton were collected and concentrated from the depths of Lake Kanasatka, in Moultonborough, on Thursday, Sept. 24. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)
It’s likely that the alum treatment is only part of the explanation for this year’s happy conditions on Lake Kanasatka. Cyanobacteria blooms were generally less severe this year in many lakes, McQuaid said.
The summer’s rainstorms were mild, McQuaid said. And on Kanasatka, residents have also stepped up their preventative work, such as by taking steps to better manage stormwater on their properties and nearby roads. 
Steps like these are fitting for most water bodies, McQuaid said. But the alum treatment, she cautioned, isn’t as universal.
 The treatment targets an overload of nutrients that have built up over time in a particularly affected lake, not cyanobacteria themselves, she said. 
It is also expensive. Lake Kanasatka’s treatment cost about $600,000; the grant the watershed association received from the state, for $500,000, halved the million dollars that the Legislature had initially allocated to the Cyanobacteria Mitigation Loan and Grand Fund in 2023. (Though another million dollars in American Rescue Plan Act money was later allocated to the fund, as of fall 2026, its balance had fallen to about $200,000 after multiple attempts by the Legislature to find ways to replenish it were voted down or sent to study committees.)
Thus, even in cases where such a treatment may be warranted, not every lake will be able to fund it. Those on Lake Kanasatka feel fortunate. 
The Lake Kanasatka community raised more than $400,000 themselves for the project; once the chemical treatment had been paid for with help from the state grant, Meloney said, the watershed association was able to leverage the additional money for more preventative work to stay ahead of the blooms.
“That put us into such a great position,” he said.
Six years ago, the waters of Lake Kanasatka in Moultonborough were the color of “Gatorade,” said UNH Lakes Lay Monitoring Program Director Amanda McQuaid. A costly chemical treatment seems to have brought the incidence of cyanobacteria blooms on the lake closer to historical norms — and closer to their ordinary blue color, like that pictured here on Thursday, Sept. 24. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Indiana officials expect saving $1B a year as teacher pension plan hits funded status
description: State officials say a $1 billion annual payment to an Indiana teacher pension fund won’t be needed within the next couple of years.
text:
Indiana Public Retirement System Executive Director Executive Director Steve Russo, right, speaks during a state legislative committee meeting on Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026. (Screenshot from livestream)State officials say they expect a $1 billion annual payment to an Indiana teacher pension fund won’t be needed within the next couple of years.
Republican legislative leaders hailed Thursday’s announcement from state pension officials that the fund covering teachers hired before 1996 could be regarded as fully funded as soon as Indiana’s 2028 fiscal year.
That fund’s large unfunded liability has been a persistent worry of legislative budget writers.
They’ve directed $4.3 billion in extra payments to the fund since 2018, when annual state appropriations to cover its pension payments were expected to continue until at least 2037.
The largest of those extra payments was ordered in 2022 with $2.5 billion directed to the pension plan from state reserves that were swollen with federal COVID-19 pandemic relief funding.
Steve Russo, executive director of the Indiana Public Retirement System, told a legislative committee that projections were that a $160 million state payment in 2027 would get that fund to 100% funded status.
But he cautioned that poor investment returns in coming years could mean more direct state money for what is known as the pre-96 pension fund covering about 52,000 retired and 4,000 active teachers.
“I don’t want to, in any way, portray that once we think we get this thing to 100% funded, and we make a payment that gets it there, that that means you’re done,” Russo told the pension oversight committee. “There’s risk going forward with this.”
Top legislators, however, cheered the pension fund announcement as giving the state “financial freedom and fiscal flexibility.”
“It’s a big win for Indiana and an achievement many other states can’t attain,” Senate Appropriations Committee Chair Ryan Mishler said in a statement. “This is a result of our commitment to pass balanced budgets, work within our means and keep our financial promises to retired teachers in our state.”
House Speaker Todd Huston said taxpayers would benefit from the state avoiding future $1 billion annual payments to the fund that was designed decades ago under a “pay-as-you-go” model. That money would be freed up for other priorities or tax relief.
“Through increased annual contributions to the teachers’ retirement fund and additional one-time investments, Indiana has strengthened retirement security for our teachers, saved our schools billions and reduced a major long-term cost for taxpayers,” Huston said.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Changes could be coming to Blueprint education plan
description: The board overseeing implementation of Maryland's sweeping education reform plan could propose some changes to the plan, as another looming budget shortfall makes it a likely target for cuts to some lawmakers next year.
text:
Koen Hawk, a third grade student at Arbutus Elementary School in Baltimore County, colors on the first day of school Aug. 31. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)The board overseeing implementation of Maryland’s sweeping education reform plan could propose some changes to the plan, as another looming budget shortfall makes it a likely target for cuts to some lawmakers next year.
A few of the changes being eyed by that Blueprint for Maryland’s Future Accountability and Implementation Board include adding more pathways for educators to achieve National Board Certification or other academic accreditation; providing funding for more college and career readiness classes; and conducting a study to assess how much to increase the base level of per pupil funding.
Those recommendations and more were discussed by board members at their meeting last week and could be finalized when the board meets again next month.
They come as the state faces a projected $3 billion budget gap for the upcoming fiscal year, about $1.8 billion of which is tied to education under the Blueprint, according to the Maryland Associations of Counties (MACo).
The projected budget shortfall for fiscal 2028 also comes in the first year in which Blueprint costs will exceed dedicated revenues. To cover the balance, the state will have to dip into the general fund, as a first-in-the-nation digital ad tax meant to help pay for the education plan remains in legal limbo.
Gov. Wes Moore (D) on Wednesday praised the Blueprint due to the work of educators and state Superintendent Carey Wright, such as improving math and reading test scores. But he also said, at the J. Millard Tawes Crab and Clam Bake in Crisfield, that “we have to be able to take a look at the Blueprint to ensure that all these things are not just effective but also scalable.”
“Our remarkable educators are helping to lead what has been one of the greatest rebounds post-COVID of any state inside of the United States of America,” Moore said. “This is some of the best work that’s happening in the country right now, and we want to make sure we’re continuing to support that.”
Sen. Mary Beth Carozza (R-Lower Shore) at J. Millard Tawes Crab and Clam Bake in Crisfield Wednesday. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)
Sen. Mary Beth Carozza (R-Lower Shore) said she will work in the upcoming legislative session on proposing legislation to bring more flexibility under the Blueprint for the state’s 24 school districts.
That could include, for example, changes that would let a school district use resources or funding for prekindergarten that may be designated for career and technical education (CTE) in a district is already “doing well in CTE.”
“In other words, instead of that one-size-fits-all mandate, we go to the locals and work with them in good faith knowing that we have the same goal, which is a quality education for all students,” she said.
“We are facing very serious, long-term fiscal budget challenges,” Carozza said at Tawes. “So therefore, we’re going to work a little bit more with the individual counties, the school systems, so we can have a win-win.”
Legislative recommendations
The Blueprint board met Sept. 17 to review proposed legislative recommendations, which would ultimately need approval by the legislature.
One recommendation in the 15-page document would be to ease certification requirements for private providers who employ educators who teach prekindergarten students.
Such a change could build on House Bill 748, sponsored this year by Montgomery County Democratic Dels. Bernice Mireku-North and Julie Palakovich Carr, that creates another pathway for individuals to qualify as an early childhood teaching assistant. The law went into effect July 1.
Not all the possible changes are cost savings. Another recommendation is to require that multilingual learners and students with disabilities automatically receive Tier I funding, which provides free full-day prekindergarten for families at or below 300% of the Federal Poverty Level, or those experiencing homelessness. That policy had been in place from fiscal years 2024 to 2026.
“So making this change permanent will have a fiscal impact,” said Joy Schaefer, government relations director for the AIB.
Another recommendation would be to conduct a study on the impact of National Board Certification for teachers, especially in “high-need student populations.”
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
The Learning Policy Institute, a national education research organization headquartered in San Francisco, recommended in a March report that policies should provide salary increases for teachers who receive not only advanced credentials, but also teach in subjects like special education or in rural and high-poverty schools. In February, the National Board for Professional Teaching Standards said Maryland led the nation last year with 1,435 of those teachers who received that designation.
The Blueprint currently requires that teachers who get National Board Certification get a $10,000 salary boost, and another $7,000 for those who teach at an “identified low-performing school.”
Not all local school officials are fans of the automatic pay bumps. Worcester County Superintendent Annette Wallace said last month that she vehemently disagrees with the Blueprint salary requirement.
“There’s no data in Worcester County Public Schools to suggest that National Board Certification makes you more of an effective teacher,” Wallace said in an interview last month. “Just because you’ve been teaching a long time doesn’t mean that you’re a great teacher. Quality is what’s more important to me, not number of years.”
The Blueprint board could vote on the legislative recommendations Oct. 15.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Don’t just say ‘no’ to school referendums and data centers
description: What do school referendums and data centers have in common? They are all unpopular but not all of them are bad. That’s why I hope Hoosiers consider each proposal on their individual merits instead of automatically opposing all of them. And there are key things you should think about when weighing the pros and cons. Let’s […]
text:
A rendering of Meta's massive data center campus coming to Lebanon. (Courtesy photo)
What do school referendums and data centers have in common? They are all unpopular but not all of them are bad.
That’s why I hope Hoosiers consider each proposal on their individual merits instead of automatically opposing all of them. And there are key things you should think about when weighing the pros and cons.
Let’s start first with referendums.
Thirty-eight school districts in dozens of counties are asking voters this November to approve a property tax referendum that will give their schools additional money. Most of these are for operational dollars, but there are a few construction and public safety levies as well.
This is a record for one election in Indiana — spurred by lawmakers’ recent limits on when school districts can take these requests to the voters. The new law restricts the requests to once every two years rather than the previous maximum of twice a year.
Americans for Prosperity’s Indiana chapter launched a targeted digital ad campaign urging voters in counties across Indiana to vote no on school property tax referendums.
“Government spending accountability should come before tax increases, and we’re making sure voters have the facts they need before they go to the polls in November,” the group said.
This approach is bad for Indiana. Each community has its own needs and voters should consider that when casting their ballots.
Here are a few things I think provide important context for referendums:

Has the school district asked for a referendum before? It could be that a district has already cut costs and now needs an infusion of funding to accomplish its goals.
Does the referendum actually raise property taxes? Many of the proposals this year simply renew an existing levy that is set to expire. This means you won’t see an increase (which also means you won’t see a decrease.) Sometimes a district might have a bond payment obligation ending, so the referendum would simply takes its place on your bill.
What will the money be used for? Paying for an extravagant new building is different than continuing base course offerings or even offering new programs for students. A public safety referendum could hire school resource officers or harden schools against outside attacks.
Is the district responsible with its dollars? This is in the eye of the beholder, of course, but I hope you look into whether its budget has grown at an unreasonable rate or if administration salaries are out of line. If district leaders have been good stewards, then take that into consideration.
What are the costs of saying no? In some areas, a referendum could lead to teaching jobs or an arts program being eliminated — especially if an existing referendum isn’t renewed. In others, a defeat could mean remaining status quo but forgoing new opportunities.

Now, let’s talk about data centers.
Hoosiers have revolted against the hyper-scale projects that eat up electricity and water. Dozens of counties and communities have put temporary or permanent restrictions on developments. Many state Republicans, however, support their growth and President Donald Trump believes they are important to win the global artificial intelligence race with China.
So, here are a few things to consider if a data center is proposed near you.

What benefits will flow to the community? This could include direct payments from the company, increased property tax revenue and even jobs. Employment is high during construction but generally dips to lower levels for operation. I live in Lebanon and Meta is spending millions on roads, infrastructure and community programs.
Are they paying for the investments in the electric grid needed to operate? This is important so those one-time upgrades don’t fall on existing customers. Companies in the beginning of the data center boom weren’t paying those costs. After residents pushed back, lawmakers established a threshold of covering 80% the costs, whether it be new generation or transmission lines. And many are paying 100%.
What about the water? Some communities have plenty of water resources and some don’t. If water supply is ample, that is a big part of the equation. But if, like Lebanon, water has to be brought in via an extended pipeline, it might not be the right fit. And where will the wastewater go? These are all considerations you should research.
Where is it located? Many of these data centers are gobbling up productive farmland, which I see as a negative. Or they are located close to homes where residents might be bothered by the noise and additional traffic — especially yearslong construction traffic. Vacant industrial land seems a better fit or at least land already zoned for business activity.

I don’t think either referendums or data centers are inherently bad if you consider all the factors involved and allow local communities to decide.

title: High-risk pregnancy doctors publish new standards for care under state abortion bans
description: As physicians continue to navigate care for patients with complex pregnancies in states with abortion bans, a group of maternal-fetal medicine specialists has developed new guidelines to help providers in those states navigate legal risks for themselves and medical challenges for their high-risk patients.  Maternal-fetal medicine specialists handle some of t[...]
text:
A sign outside a hospital's maternal-fetal medicine department sets aside parking for patients. The Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine issued guidance earlier this month encouraging physicians who care for high-risk obstetric patients in states with abortion bans to establish systems of care and build agreements between providers and healthcare administrators to provide the highest level of care. (Photo by Kelcie Moseley-Morris/Stateline) As physicians continue to navigate care for patients with complex pregnancies in states with abortion bans, a group of maternal-fetal medicine specialists has developed new guidelines to help providers in those states navigate legal risks for themselves and medical challenges for their high-risk patients. 
Maternal-fetal medicine specialists handle some of the most high-risk pregnancies, including patients with high blood pressure, diabetes, cancer, fetal anomalies or other complications. In states with abortion bans, those conditions can become even more dangerous for a patient if a doctor is unsure when they can terminate a pregnancy without potentially jeopardizing their medical license or facing criminal penalties that can include jail time.
“Individuals at high risk for pregnancy-associated morbidity and mortality have unique needs for reproductive health services, including abortion care,” the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine wrote in a special statement published this month. 
Abortion could return to Supreme Court, this time with a focus on women’s health

Ten states plus the District of Columbia allow abortion access without gestational restrictions, while 13 states ban abortion at all stages. Following the implementation of those bans since 2022, many hospital systems and clinics have offered different interpretations of how to avoid legal jeopardy under the bans and what qualifies under exceptions, leading to confusion and delays in care that have been documented in many states nationwide. 
To mitigate those problems, the guidelines encourage providers and administrators to set up referral networks across state lines, work to find agreement on what is permissible under state law and counsel patients on their options even in states with restrictions to deliver the highest-quality care. 
“We are uniquely positioned as high-risk pregnancy experts to make that case to our leaders,” said Dr. Justin Lappen, who leads the maternal fetal medicine section at the Cleveland Clinic in Ohio and chaired the committee that developed the statement. “And a statement like this would give providers and our colleagues some confidence to be leaders in this space.”
The Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine and the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists agree that access to abortion and counseling about options is the standard of care for obstetric patients, but there are conscientious exceptions for doctors who do not want to provide abortion care. 
Some doctors choose to affiliate with the American Association of Pro-Life Obstetricians and Gynecologists, and offer their own guidance about approaching complications, which still includes termination in some situations. The group is officially a partner of the Alliance Defending Freedom and several anti-abortion groups, as well as the Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine, which is the group that sued to revoke federal approval of one of two drugs used to terminate a pregnancy or treat miscarriages.
A representative from the American Association of Pro-Life Obstetricians and Gynecologists could not be reached for comment before publication.
Worse outcomes for high-risk patients
Nationwide, women in states with bans have reported difficulties receiving care when experiencing pregnancy complications. 
One of the most common emergencies occurs when a patient’s amniotic sac breaks before a fetus is viable. If left untreated, it can quickly turn into a deadly infection. The statement noted that after Texas passed Senate Bill 8 in 2021 banning abortion at an early gestation, waiting to treat patients in those medical situations dramatically increased negative health outcomes. According to research cited in the statement, complications such as blood transfusion, intensive care admission and serious infection resulted in 57% of cases, versus comparable research in states without restrictions that showed a complication rate of 33%. In all of the cases, the fetus did not survive.
Federal judge’s order allowing an Idaho doctor to perform certain abortions is put on hold

The guidance states hospitals and clinics should expand their abortion care to the extent allowed by law, and recognize maternal-fetal medicine specialists as sources of best care practices. It also instructs providers to work with legal teams in their networks to understand the federal Emergency Medical Treatment and Labor Act and when it may require abortion care, as well as encouraging training for basic termination procedures. 
Dr. David Hackney, a maternal-fetal medicine specialist in Ohio who published a book in August about navigating high-risk pregnancy care under Dobbs, said the statement will be useful for many providers nationwide.
“We don’t always focus enough on hospital administration, care and systems, but there’s always so much that can be done in those regions that is almost — if not more — important,” Hackney said.
After the Dobbs decision in June 2022, Hackney said, many individual healthcare systems didn’t know what to do when faced with certain situations where termination might be needed, and set a patchwork of policies that increased confusion for providers. But in the years since, providers and administrators in some healthcare systems have come together to reach informal agreements about what they are comfortable doing within the confines of an abortion ban.
“You have some defense if everyone has agreed to do the same thing,” he said.
When laws are unclear, he said, people will most often lean toward over-complying, which can create worse outcomes for the patient. 
“Even outside of abortion, medical care tends to work better when you have consensus and you have common best practices, even if it’s on a regional level,” he said. 
‘When they need me, they call me’
Many specialists’ cases aren’t emergencies, but rather pregnancies that put a patient at risk because of underlying health conditions, whether they existed before a pregnancy or developed during pregnancy, or late-term diagnoses of fetal anomalies that upend a wanted pregnancy. 
In those cases, the maternal-fetal organization says, patients should be told that their options include termination, even if that can’t happen in their home state.
Dr. Leilah Zahedi-Spung, a maternal-fetal medicine specialist who co-authored the special statement, moved to Colorado from Tennessee in 2023 after that state enacted a near-total abortion ban.
She said she saw firsthand how difficult it was in Tennessee to try to take care of patients without clarity around the law and without leadership that was willing or able to try to provide support. One goal of the statement is to help provide that kind of support to physicians, she said.
“We know you’re in a tough situation, we’re not blind to that. No one is blaming you for what you can and cannot do,” Zahedi-Spung said.
The society’s statement suggests that providers establish relationships with leaders within their clinical settings as well as in the community, region and state to agree on legal interpretations of abortion restrictions, particularly those who might hold leadership positions themselves. It also encourages doctors to establish referral networks locally and between states to ensure patient access.
“I have lots of people from Texas who have my phone number, and when they need me, they call me,” Zahedi-Spung said. “That is a system that works. And then those patients go back to safe providers who can take care of them.”  
Stateline reporter Kelcie Moseley-Morris can be reached at kmoseley@stateline.org.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Diesel fuel prices in Connecticut hit record high
description: The head of the Connecticut Energy Marketers Association said consumers likely will face shortages and more price increases in coming months.
text:
Despite diesel prices hitting a record high this week and home heating oil up 50% in just three months, the state’s fuel distributors warn the problems are far from over.
The head of the Connecticut Energy Marketers Association said consumers likely will face shortages and additional price increases this fall and winter.
“There’s no limit to how high [prices] could go if these wars continue,” Chris Herb, the association’s president and CEO, said Wednesday, referring to ongoing conflicts between the U.S. and Iran and between Russian and Ukraine, both of which interfere with petroleum production and exports. “I am immensely concerned.”
The average retail diesel price hit a record high Wednesday in Connecticut, approaching $6.48 per gallon, then ticked another 3/10ths of a penny over that mark on Thursday, according to AAA. That’s up 71% from the $3.78 average price recorded here one year ago.
The national average hit a record Tuesday at $6.53 per gallon and stood at $6.51 on Thursday, AAA reported. One year ago, the national average stood at $3.69 per gallon.
Besides the ongoing wars, diesel prices also often surge each autumn as farmers in the U.S. and other Northern Hemisphere nations need fuel to run equipment for harvest, said Herb. “We have two events colliding at the same time,” he added. “Unfortunately, it’s beyond our control on how we would attract supply.”
The U.S. Energy Information Administration reported this week that diesel and other related fuel stocks were about 12% below the seasonal average, and Herb warned that could mean tight supply conditions for months to come, depending on whether President Donald Trump’s administration restricts fuel exports to preserve domestic supplies.
Further complicating matters, the Connecticut Department of Energy and Environmental Protection reported an average price of $5.91 per gallon this week for home heating oil. That’s up 50% from the $3.95 price noted the week of June 22, but still below the $6.37 cost the department listed in early May of 2022, two-and-a-half months after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine began.
Home heating oil is very similar in chemical structure to diesel fuel. Both are distillates, produced by boiling crude oil and then cooling it back into liquid form. And because of their similarities, both are subject to the same political and market pressures.
The heating oil situation is particularly troublesome here for low-to-moderate residents who rely on the Connecticut Energy Assistance Program to keep warm.
While the demand for aid has grown steadily in recent years, demand for the federal Low-Income Household Energy Assistance Program funds that the state doles out via the CEAP program has not.
The state Department of Social Services projects the poorest and most vulnerable households that qualify for the program would receive $1,995 this winter, down 33% from the $2,980 maximum grant provided in 2019-20.
Members of a state energy advisory board, including Connecticut AARP Director Nora Duncan, have urged Gov. Ned Lamont and the General Assembly in recent years to add state dollars to the program to bolster grant levels.
Many legislators from both parties also have endorsed the use of state funds to expand energy assistance.
Lamont and lawmakers have set aside $550 million from past state budget surpluses to mitigate federal human service programs cuts. About $260 million remains in the response fund, which already has been tapped to bolster healthcare and nutrition programs and to assist immigrants whose legal status has been challenged by the Trump administration.
A spokesman for Lamont’s reelection campaign, Rob Blanchard, said, “Trump’s war in Iran [is] driving up gas, home heating oil and diesel prices on everything we buy, and instead of helping, the White House keeps trying to gut LIHEAP, the program families need most right now. Connecticut deserves a partner in Washington, not more chaos.”
But minority Republicans in the state House and Senate say local Democrats’ policies have done plenty to make Connecticut unaffordable. The GOP released a tax relief plan that includes repealing a highway mileage-based levy on large commercial non-farm trucks.
“Connecticut didn’t become one of the most expensive states in the country the day President Trump took office,” House Minority Leader Vincent J. Candelora, R-North Branford, said two weeks ago when Republicans rolled out their tax-cutting options.
According to state analysts, that truck tax will generate $62 million in revenue this fiscal year for the state’s transportation program, which holds more than $640 million in reserves and projected surplus.
But that $62 million cost, along with spiking fuel expenses, is passed onto shoppers at supermarkets, department stores and other retail outlets that rely on deliveries from diesel-powered trucks, said John Blair, president of the Motor Transport Association of Connecticut.
Blair, whose association represents more than 500 trucking and related businesses, called the rising diesel prices “a grave concern” for his industry, predicting consumers would benefit from any repeal of the highway tax.
“Any cost that we can reduce,” he said, “we can pass along.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: The cowardice of masked law enforcement: Recent Kansas immigration raids remind us why faces matter
description: “Disgusting,” a voice on the Facebook video says. Captured in Kansas City, Kansas, this summer, the footage shows a handful of law enforcement officers — most of them masked — detaining a man. Their black SUVs surround his white pickup at the intersection of 6th Street and Central Avenue. After two minutes and 16 seconds, […]
text:
A masked ICE agent stands guard outside as ICE and other law enforcement agents raid a restaurant in Minneapolis, Minnesota, last year. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)“Disgusting,” a voice on the Facebook video says.
Captured in Kansas City, Kansas, this summer, the footage shows a handful of law enforcement officers — most of them masked — detaining a man. Their black SUVs surround his white pickup at the intersection of 6th Street and Central Avenue. After two minutes and 16 seconds, the officers have the handcuffed man in a back seat and drive him away.
The most common face covering among the officers is a black elastic cloth pulled up to cover their chin, mouth, cheeks and nose. As they mill around the intersection and inspect the truck, the thin fabric keeps each of them anonymous.
“They can’t even show their faces,” the bystander’s voice continues, before using an expletive to describe the agents.
As unprecedented immigration enforcement continues this week in Kansas and nationwide, the masks worn by law enforcement create a looming, yet cowardly, specter: law-enforcement officers so morally compromised by their work that they can’t show their faces, whether in Liberal or Garden City. Their work is so counter to the wishes of the community that they must hide themselves.
For the sake of this column, please reserve all of the other political and moral objections to the immigration raids — and there are many: separation of nuclear families, coordination with local law enforcement and insistence that you not record their public actions, because of a Kansas statute.
For a moment, let’s focus on the anonymity of the mask.
I could have written this column about masked agents in Kansas this summer or this spring or last year (as my Kansas Reflector colleague Max McCoy did). Choose your month and week. Federal immigration raids persist.
This week, local news outlets along with Kansas Public Radio reported that “ICE agents with masks covering their faces” were “stopping cars and questioning passengers” in Liberal. During a Kansas City, Missouri, raid this summer, another operation “involved at least six unmarked vehicles with Kansas and Missouri license plates,” as reported by KCUR. Immigration officers in Kansas are faceless and nameless, stripped of even the most basic identity, back story or credentials. 
Chilling photos by KCUR news intern Cassandra Isobelle Flores give us a clear look at the standard faux-military costumes the agents prefer: a backward baseball hat, a T-shirt, a tactical vest bulging with hidden gadgets, jeans and boots — every face covered in a mask.
If you had shown me these photos in 2010, I would have assumed they were from a country gripped by paramilitary violence. In 2015, I would have assumed they were actors on the set of “Homeland” or “24,” taking on the role of a CIA operative spiriting terrorists away to a black site for questioning.
We would all be terrified at being confronted by beefy men with badge numbers hidden, intent to stuff you into an unmarked car while refusing to identify themselves. Given the civic instability that their anonymous presence causes, it’s a stretch to even call them law enforcement. 
The federal agency alphabet soup decorating their vests is another matter. While they might claim that it helps to identify them as federal agents, it only makes them more mysterious because the acronyms are esoteric.
Most Americans and immigrants know the meaning of “POLICE” and “ICE.” 
But test yourself. I am going to give you three acronyms. Which two are actual immigration enforcement agencies? And which one is not? Your options: HSI, USIC and ERO.
Two of these acronyms appear on the tactical vests of agents in Kansas. Did you guess ERO, which stands for Enforcement and Removal Operations? What about HSI, Homeland Security Investigations?
(If someone is wearing a USIC vest, they are likely coming to locate underground utilities in your backyard.)
A law enforcement uniform is supposed to be exactly that: uniform. The crisp blues and badge of a traffic cop. The brown-on-brown of a sheriff’s deputy. The full range of military uniforms that designate: “This is who I am. This is my authority.”
The gear of today’s masked immigration officer as he walks main streets in southwest Kansas is intentional sartorial anarchy, saying: “I might look like this. Or like this. But regardless, you must obey.”
While I now live far from small-town Kansas, I once lived in a midwestern town smaller than Liberal, Dodge City and Garden City. I can imagine how residents would have reacted with alarm at seeing strangers dressed for insurrection. After all, the wonder (and claustrophobia) of rural life is how familiar you are with everyone. In the small towns of Kansas even more than big cities, masked strangers — especially a pack of swaggering and largely untrained strangers — creates outsized chaos.
The counterarguments from the Department of Homeland Security are shot through with hyperventilation, falsehood and distraction.
Why must their agents use masks?
Without masks, their identities could be revealed through doxing online.
Without masks, they would be “targeted by highly sophisticated gangs like Tren de Aragua and MS-13, criminal rings, murderers, and rapists.”
Officers are “flanked by vehicles marked with the name of the department,” a ludicrous claim that I needed to re-read three times.
This is normally the part of my column that I reserve for pointing at the prospect of change through state legislation. However, legislation in other states that aimed to unmask federal immigration agents has fallen flat. In New Jersey and New York, judges have paused state laws. In New Jersey, the Department of Justice argued in a court filing that the “supremacy” clause means that federal authority holds more power than a state law about masks. In New York, a judge cited the federal government’s designated role to police immigration as reason to defer to their masking policy.
In Washington state, a law has proven essentially toothless. Federal officers simply continue to wear the masks.
An executive decision by President Donald Trump has trickled down to small-town Kansas through Homeland Security instructions and policies with no recourse for normal citizens. This federal department and this careening president are aligned in wanting agents with masks on American streets.
But why?
I agree that one key reason for the masks is to create fear, of course. But another is shame.
Consider the pride of other civil servants and law enforcement: municipal police, firefighters and the military. The holiday parades. The public adulation. The local heroes. Compare that with the shameful image of an immigration agent — claiming to simply be doing his job — while hiding behind a scrim of facial obscurity.
Among the wash of jarring visuals from the Trump era, masked agents will be one of the most enduring. We will remember the sinister image: eyes perched above an anonymous male face tightly and darkly wrapped.
We will also remember the message of that image: one of impunity, cruelty and xenophobia, cloaked in the reassuring, condescending lie of “law and order.”
Eric Thomas teaches visual journalism and photojournalism at the William Allen White School of Journalism and Mass Communication at the University of Kansas in Lawrence. Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate.
