name: Washington State Standard
title: ‘Better than before’: WA reopens historic Capitol campus building
description: More than two years of construction and $131 million later, a historic building on the Washington state Capitol campus is reopening.  A cadre of top state officials cut the ribbon and welcomed the public into the transformed Joel Pritchard Building on the south side of campus Thursday afternoon.  Lt. Gov. Denny Heck said the 77,000-square-foot […]
text:
The expanded Joel Pritchard Building on the Washington state Capitol campus after a ceremony on Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026. (Photo by Jake Goldstein-Street/Washington State Standard)More than two years of construction and $131 million later, a historic building on the Washington state Capitol campus is reopening. 
A cadre of top state officials cut the ribbon and welcomed the public into the transformed Joel Pritchard Building on the south side of campus Thursday afternoon. 
Lt. Gov. Denny Heck said the 77,000-square-foot building wasn’t just expanded but built “better than before.” It faces the Capitol Dome with legislative office buildings on each side.
“It is truly magnificent,” Heck said.
This marks the latest step in the modernization of the Capitol campus, which has included the tear-down and rebuild of the Irving R. Newhouse Building, which houses Senate Republicans, and renovation of the John L. O’Brien Building, home to many state House members. The O’Brien Building work is set to wrap up in the coming months. The General Administration Building on the north side was demolished this summer, and skylights are coming back to the Capitol building.
The Pritchard Building, designed by architect Paul Thiry, joined the Capitol campus in 1958, the last addition to the Olmsted Brothers-designed grounds. It cost $1.3 million to build, at the time. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2015.
The north face of the Joel Pritchard Building is shown in this undated photograph. (Photo courtesy of the Washington State Archives)
For decades, the building served as the Washington State Library until the 2001 Nisqually Earthquake underscored seismic risks. The earthquake damaged the building, leading the state to relocate its library collection to a Tumwater facility. 
For years, most of the building served as an empty, windowless former book-storage facility. The massive renovation is meant to turn it into a bright legislative workspace.
There had been talks of demolishing the building, but instead it was restored and expanded.
“I think as we celebrate today, we made the right choice,” said Rep. Steve Tharinger, D-Port Townsend, who is chair of the House Capital Budget Committee.
Construction started in March 2024. The state appropriated over $131 million for the project.
The facade looks much the same, but the construction added a new wing with offices for some state House members. Staff from the state Office of the Code Reviser and Legislative Technology are getting new work spaces. Tenants will move into the building next month. There will also be a new cafe.
And the historic Washington Room was restored, including the 117-foot-long, somewhat abstract mural by artist Kenneth Callahan that adorned the walls when the building opened. The four-paneled, 360-degree mural depicts the arc of humanity, from its primitive start to modern day. It was transported to New York for refurbishment before returning to the Washington Room.
Two visitors take in the Kenneth Callahan mural in the Washington Room of the reopened Joel Pritchard Building. (Photo by Jake Goldstein-Street/Washington State Standard)
The Du Pen Fountain outside will flow with water again soon. A James Fitzgerald mosaic and Mark Tobey painting remain inside.
The work also included stabilization of the steep hillside next to the building that leads down to the banks of Capitol Lake. This involved driving many concrete columns deep in the ground to support the building, Tharinger said.
The building is named for the state’s former two-term Republican lieutenant governor. Pritchard also served in Congress and the state Legislature, and is considered the “Father of Pickleball” for inventing the sport with friends in the 1960s. Gov. Bob Ferguson said his parents were active in Republican circles campaigning for Pritchard’s runs for elective office.
“The thing about Joel is, almost unfortunately, he’s better known as the inventor of pickleball,” Heck said, “which I think overshadows what a significant contribution he’s made to our state, what a magnificent public servant he was.”

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Advisory group suggests adding member of the public to South Dakota Open Meetings Commission
description: A member of the public could have a vote on South Dakota’s Open Meetings Commission if the state’s incoming attorney general, legislators and governor back a proposal recommended Thursday by an open meetings task force. The commission is a five-member board established in 2004 to hear complaints about alleged violations of open meetings laws and […]
text:
Attorney Sara Frankenstein speaks to members of the South Dakota Open Meetings Commission on Nov. 18, 2024, in Pierre. The commission's membership consists entirely of state's attorneys or assistant state's attorneys, but a task force has recommended legislation that would change the commission's makeup to include a member of the public. (Photo courtesy of SD Attorney General's Office)A member of the public could have a vote on South Dakota’s Open Meetings Commission if the state’s incoming attorney general, legislators and governor back a proposal recommended Thursday by an open meetings task force.
The commission is a five-member board established in 2004 to hear complaints about alleged violations of open meetings laws and issue censures to public bodies that have broken them.
Per state law, its five members have always been state’s attorneys or deputy state’s attorneys, all appointed by the attorney general. 



Need to get in touch?
Have a news tip?


CONTACT US



The South Dakota Advisory Task Force on Open Meetings Laws, a 15-member group, was created by Attorney General Marty Jackley last year to consider updates to the state’s transparency statutes that apply to public meetings.
Every member of the group present for Thursday’s virtual meeting voted in favor of a proposed change that would expand the Open Meetings Commission to seven members and adjust its makeup to represent a wider range of voices.
If the proposal is adopted, the group would have four state’s attorneys or deputy state’s attorneys, two attorneys representing public bodies other than counties, and one member of the public. The attorney general would maintain the sole discretion to appoint members.
‘Defensibility’ with a public member
The idea of adding a member of the public to the commission came from Dave Bordewyk, the director of the South Dakota NewsMedia Association, which includes South Dakota Searchlight as a member. He was absent for Thursday’s meeting, but his proposal was backed by Steve Willard, president of the South Dakota Broadcasters Association.
Given that members of the public or media representatives arguing on their behalf are typically the ones who file complaints, Willard said, a layperson’s voice would add credibility.
City council and town board violated open meeting laws, commission finds

“For their purposes, I think there’s some comfort, and some defensibility on this particular group that it’s not so insular, that it includes a member of the public,” Willard said.
The proposal was one of four up for consideration on Thursday, including the one that was endorsed, which was modified to include seven members. 
Two other proposals would have added lawyers for public bodies other than counties, whose voices are represented by state’s attorneys, but not a member of the public. As written, all four kept the commission’s membership at five.
An informal survey of advisory group members found that most supported the idea of including at least one member of the public, but with reservations. Several expressed concerns about appointing a non-lawyer to a quasi-judicial role.
“I’m of the opinion that an attorney representing something other than a public body would be a good thing,” said Geoffrey Gray-Lobe, a Clay County commissioner.
Majority would remain prosecutors
Michael Smith is the state’s attorney for Clay County and a member of the Open Meetings Commission. Smith said he understands the value of a public voice, but also said the work of determining whether a public body broke the law is akin to prosecution. 
“There is a deep need to understand the law,” Smith said.
Open Meetings Commission finds two local boards violated South Dakota law

Austin Hoffman, who’s the McPherson County state’s attorney and also serves on the Open Meetings Commission, said he’d be comfortable with the idea of a layperson serving alongside him if the group’s makeup remained a majority of prosecutors.
Kellen Willert, the city attorney for Belle Fourche, agreed that a prosecutor-led group is ideal, but said the commission’s authority is limited. 
“The worst thing they can do is issue a censure,” Willert said. “I think it makes sense to have a member of the public on it. Nobody’s right to life or property is endangered.” 
Hoffman and the others who’d expressed reticence at the idea of a layperson interpreting the law coalesced around the seven-member, majority prosecutor proposal, in part because two extra people would make it easier to have a quorum and hold hearings if some members are absent.
Idea would need legislative, governor support
To take effect, the change would need to take the form of a bill in the next legislative session, which begins in January. That bill could be presented at the request of the attorney general or introduced by a lawmaker.
Jackley formed the advisory group, but won’t be around to pitch its proposal. He’s a candidate for South Dakota’s seat in the U.S. House of Representatives.
Fall River and Oglala Lakota County State’s Attorney Lance Russell is running unopposed for attorney general in the Nov. 3 election after securing the Republican Party’s nomination for the post. He will take over the job in January. 
He’s also currently a member of the Open Meetings Commission. In an email to South Dakota Searchlight, he said he’s a supporter of the group’s mission and its current five-member makeup, but has yet to talk to the task force members about their decision on Thursday.
“I am keeping an open mind on its recommendation and look forward to hearing the rationale for the proposal,” Russell said.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico education officials propose new budget with 2.9% increase
description: The New Mexico Public Education Department on Thursday laid out spending plans for a proposed $5.9 billion budget for the Fiscal Year 2028 budget, a 2.9% increase over FY27. PED requested, in the wake of the landmark Yazzie/Martinez case, $30 million for Indian education and $1.7 million for bilingual multicultural education, among other education initiative[...]
text:
New Mexico public education officials proposed a $5.9 billion budget request to a joint interim Legislative Finance and Education Study committees on Sept. 24, 2026, which included increased funding for school improvements. (Photo of Mayfield High School students in Las Cruces by Leah Romero for Source New Mexico)The New Mexico Public Education Department on Thursday laid out spending plans for a proposed $5.9 billion budget for the Fiscal Year 2028 budget, a 2.9% increase over FY27.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In a joint presentation to the interim Legislative Finance and Education Study committees, PED officials detailed budget priorities, which include building on improvements with literacy rates and chronic absenteeism, and continuing to work to address lower-performing schools.
Specifically, the proposed budget includes $15.5 million for literacy and reading support; $16.6 million for literacy coaches; and $29 million for reading and mathematics intervention, among other items. 
In a statement issued Thursday, PED Secretary Mariana Padilla said the proposed budget “will help schools build” on the gains that have been made, while also addressing critical needs in mathematics, student engagement and educator recruitment. “These investments focus resources where they can make the greatest difference for students and give educators the support they need to succeed,” she said.
Another priority for PED in the proposed budget was student attendance and engagement — $35 million for career technical education; $10 million for summer internships; $60 million over three years for afterschool programs.
Padilla said that the department received a grant from the U.S. Department of Education that it plans to use for “career connected” education in middle schools throughout the state. She also highlighted summer programs served with the funding.
“Students build their job skills, their life skills, and are able to really develop some strong mentorship opportunities,” Padilla said.
PED requested, in the wake of the landmark Yazzie/Martinez case, $30 million for Indian education, $1.7 million for bilingual multicultural education, $1.5 million for Hispanic Education and $500,000 for Black Education.
Rep. Derrick Lente (D-Sandia Pueblo) acknowledged the funding priority, reminding the Legislature that before 2019, the Indian Education budget was $2 million. Student groups identified in the case saw the largest literacy and mathematics proficiency gains in grades three to eight from 2022 to 2026, according to PED statistics.
“We are not fighting over crumbs anymore,” Lente said. “We are seeing the capacity being built at a number of our pueblos, nations, and tribes — and seeing real results at this point.”

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Douglas County sheriff plans to investigate county program for the poor
description: OMAHA — The Douglas County sheriff on Thursday announced that he will open an investigation into the practices of a county program designed to help the poor. Sheriff Aaron Hanson said his intent is to ensure that taxpayer dollars have not been criminally spent. The move comes on the heels of a report by the […]
text:
Douglas County Sheriff Aaron Hanson. Aug. 2, 2024. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)OMAHA — The Douglas County sheriff on Thursday announced that he will open an investigation into the practices of a county program designed to help the poor.
Sheriff Aaron Hanson said his intent is to ensure that taxpayer dollars have not been criminally spent. The move comes on the heels of a report by the State Auditor’s Office, which flagged alleged and potential improper distribution and use of gift cards intended for low-income county residents.
“We owe it, not only to every citizen in Douglas County, but especially to those this program is designed to assist, to ensure that hard earned property tax dollars are not being impermissibly or fraudulently misspent to the detriment of taxpayers and those who actually need the help this program is designed to provide,” Hanson wrote in a  media release.
Attached to Hanson’s media release was a letter addressed to Douglas County Board Chair Roger Garcia and Vice Chair Mike Friend. Referencing State Auditor Mike Foley’s findings, Hanson said he had consulted with Douglas County Attorney Don Kleine about the matter.
Nebraska auditor criticizes Douglas County’s ‘high’ cost to administer program for the poor

Both Hanson and Kleine are up for re-election in November. 
Hanson, in the letter, told Garcia and Friend that he had financial crime investigators in his office and would be “happy to assist” the county’s general assistance staff in vetting applications for potential fraud.
In addition to “problematic” distribution and use of Dollar General gift cards, Foley criticized the county’s general assistance office for high administrative costs, contending that for every $100 of financial aid to the poor in a three-year period, the county spent roughly $74 on administrative expenses. He said the top three salaries among 18 people ranged from $166,614 to $105,000.
Friend said county officials were analyzing Foley’s report. While he said he was concerned about the findings, he doesn’t think at this point that the matter merits a law enforcement investigation. 
Melissa Sewick, director of the county’s general assistance program, has defended her team’s efforts to “responsibly” administer public assistance, which she said includes a range from determining eligibility to helping clients connect with other resources. She said, however, that county officials recognize the importance of efficiency, have made some changes and continue to evaluate their processes in light of the auditor report.
Garcia was out of town and deferred to a statement by the county’s chief administrative officer. In that, Patrick Bloomingdale said: “I will discuss the proposed investigation with the County Board in executive session next Tuesday.”
Mike Friend, vice chair of Douglas County Board. (Courtesy of Douglas County)
Hanson thanked county officials in advance for their cooperation in the investigation, which he said was likely to be complex.
The sheriff previously had  sent a letter Jan. 7 to Garcia, Friend, Bloomingdale, Kleine, Commissioner PJ Morgan and County Finance Director Lori Pirsch.
That letter talked about a “worthwhile concept of renewing the working relationship” between the county’s office that handles general assistance and the Sheriff’s Office. 
Hanson said that in the past, the two offices had worked “proactively together” to investigate fraudulent applications that he said resulted in inappropriate disbursements to people. That “interplay” steadily declined over the decade, the sheriff wrote. 
According to Hanson, the general assistance office sent 14 referrals to the sheriff between November 2020 and May 2021. Since May 2021, there have been no referrals, he said, adding: “I suspect the drop-off was the result of personnel changes in that office.”
Hanson’s Jan. 7 letter included a memo from Chief Deputy William Niemack, who told the sheriff that he would like to “examine the current status of criminal fraud against Douglas County, specifically regarding general assistance.”
Niemack wrote that the sheriff’s criminal investigation division was not yet at full capacity at that time, but was increasing to 10 investigators. He asserted that a past proactive partnership led to efficient use of funds and violators being held accountable.

text:
(Photo by Mint Images/ Getty Images)Maine Attorney General Aaron Frey is urging residents to check if they bought certain generic drugs, in which case they may be eligible for new settlement funds. 
Maine and 47 other states and territories plan to use settlement funds from drug manufacturers to refund consumers that paid inflated prices for certain generic drugs from May 2009 and December 2019, according to a press release from the Office of the Maine Attorney General. 
The coalition filed a series of antitrust lawsuits against drug manufacturers, starting in 2016, arguing the companies conspired to raise the prices of generic drugs. The coalition has reached settlements with several manufacturers, totalling roughly $96.5 million. 
This month a federal judge gave initial approval to the coalition’s plan for the settlement funds.
Consumers can check the list of eligible drugs at https://aggenericdrugsclaims.com/, or call 1-866-290-0182 and email info@AGGenericDrugs.com. Consumers can then submit a claim for the drug purchase until March 8, 2027.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico Election 2026: Commissioner of public lands
description: This November, New Mexicans will elect a new leader to the office that manages millions of acres of state lands at a time of record-high oil and gas prices, increased corporate interest in data centers and uranium extraction, and ongoing environmental threats posed by wildfire and drought.
text:
Democrat Juan de Jesus Sanchez III, left, and Republican Michael Perry are facing off in the Nov. 3 election to become New Mexico commissioner of public lands overseeing the State Land Office. (Source NM file and courtesy photos) This November, New Mexicans will elect a new leader to the office that manages millions of acres of state lands at a time of record-high oil and gas prices, increased corporate interest in data centers and uranium extraction, and ongoing environmental threats posed by wildfire and drought. 
Republican Michael Perry, a longtime official in the state Department of Wildlife and New Mexico State Land Office, is running against Democrat Juan de Jesus Sanchez III, a former political director for U.S. Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) and natural resources specialist with the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers. 
Current Land Commissioner Stephanie Garcia Richard, a Democrat, is running for lieutenant governor.
Her successor will be tasked with balancing the state’s need for revenue with environmental considerations, as well as diversifying the office’s revenue streams to reduce reliance on the volatile oil and gas industry. 
In recent years, an oil and gas boom has meant the Land Office has received more than $2 billion a year in revenues, largely from oil and gas royalties, offsetting costs of public services that would otherwise fall on taxpayers.
Looming over the race is President Donald Trump’s administration, which has sought to roll back a number of policies aimed at protecting federal public lands from timber harvesting and oil production in a state with 27 million acres of federal land. 
Garcia Richard has spent much of her second and final term in office seeking to push back against Trump’s policies. 
She has blocked a 0.6-mile gas pipeline on state trust lands for a controversial data center in Doña Ana County; imposed a moratorium on oil-and-gas leasing on state lands near Chaco Culture National Historical Park; and earlier this month announced an executive order banning new uranium mines on lands her office oversees. 
Source NM spoke to both candidates about their visions for the office, including where they would differ from Garcia Richard and support or oppose Trump’s public lands agenda. The state land commissioner receives a $149,714 annual salary each year during a four-year term. 
 The candidates’ answers below have been edited for clarity and concision.
Michael Perry
Michael Perry, Republican candidate for New Mexico public land commissioner, stands in front of a sign from a rancher who supports him in an undated photo. (courtesy photo)
Republican Michael Perry said his decades of public lands experience and bachelor’s degree in wildlife science from New Mexico State University make him the practical choice to succeed Garcia Richard at the State Land Office.
Perry spent more than 20 years with the New Mexico Wildlife Department, previously known as the Department of Game and Fish, ultimately overseeing all of the department’s law enforcement operations in southern New Mexico. That commitment to conservation and wildlife still guides him today, he said. 
“I absolutely believe in, and I was willing to give my life for, wildlife and conservation efforts,” he said. 
He served as assistant lands commissioner at the State Land Office between 2016 and 2019 under former Commissioner Aubrey Dunn, overseeing watershed health, forest remediation and habitat restoration. He is also currently a Chaves County commissioner. 
What makes you the most qualified to be land commissioner?
I have 33 years of specific experience that can help the State Land Office, and I was also the assistant commissioner over restoration or remediation, forest health and watershed management. I have a specific degree that is attributed to this job. Chaves County placed me on the Public Lands Advisory Committee where we go to Washington, D.C. for natural resource management issues and to secure funding. 
What is one aspect of the State Land Office that the public should understand better? 
The public should understand that the state land is entrusted to raise money off of the land to pay for public education and public hospitals. I don’t think the general public knows the importance of that. If you took the state land office and the functions and the money that they make, which is about $2.5 to $2.6 billion a year, out of the mix, you’re going to have to make up that funding somewhere else. The other thing the state land commissioner is supposed to do, which I don’t think we do enough, is take care of the land for the next generation, so they can take care of the land for them, so they can make money off it. 
And I actually think that needs to be No. 1. I think we need to take better care of the land first, and then make money off of it second. Right now, it’s vice versa. 
What new initiatives would you implement at the State Land Office upon taking office?
The absolute No. 1 initiative for me is to bring back habitat management and forest restoration, so we can have a resiliency built up in our forest that counters catastrophic wildfires and counters catastrophic flooding after the wildfires. I want to bring our watersheds back into shape, so we can get our rivers and tributaries flowing, and we can get water down the way to Elephant Butte, so our farmers can make crops. Our watersheds are in bad shape because we have too many trees or too many stems per acre on the landscape.
If elected, will you uphold incumbent Land Commissioner Stephanie Garcia Richard’s ban on new uranium mining on state trust lands? Why or why not?
If it’s really an important topic, why did she wait until the two-minute drill of the fourth quarter of her eight years in office to implement it? So I think it’s just a political move, honestly, to get to grab some ink off of the news. 
I would want to look at uranium exploration pragmatically. Anybody who’s against environmental protections or the land in New Mexico, whether it’s Republican, Democrat, I’m against them. I want to make sure we take care of the land first, but I also want to say I think it would be short-sighted to say that we’re not going to have uranium exploration. I’m not saying I’m for it, but I’m saying let’s look at the area, let’s look at the geographic location, let’s look at the social parameters that (exist) where they’re talking about having it. 
How will you use your office to support or oppose President Donald Trump’s push to remove Chaco Canyon buffer zone protections from oil and gas extraction? 
I can’t do anything against it. I mean, I’m not in charge of federal lands and the federal government. I think we need to communicate with the people on the ground that live off the land in those areas and have a seat at the table for them, and say, ‘What would you like?’ Now, the lion’s share of the property belongs to the federal government, so they’re the ones that are driving the bus, so to speak, on oil and gas expiration. But I do support protections on state land.
If elected, will you continue to prohibit the use of state Trust land for the Project Jupiter gas pipeline or other data-center-related infrastructure? 
I am not for data centers on state land. I think we can have better uses. When you build a big footprint of property on state land, you’re covering up a potential grazing allotment, a grazing lease, a right of way. Once you put that huge footprint of buildings on there it’s going to only be used for one thing. So you better make a lot of damn money off that one thing because you’re taking that land out of other uses forever.
(Regarding the Project Jupiter pipeline), she is going against her fiduciary responsibility, which is to make money for the schools, by not allowing that right-of-way. She is not doing what she’s supposed to do: Make money for the land. If she’s going to be an advocate and say I’m not going to allow this right-of-way, all they’re going to do is go around it. So now you’re causing a larger footprint and a larger land disruption, because now they’re going to drill this right away around it on BLM land, which is going to cause more hate and contempt on the landscape. 
Would you continue to implement a proposed State Land Office rule that would increase the minimum bonding requirements for oil and gas operators from a minimum of $10,000 to $150,000?
I think the bonding needs to be increased. I haven’t researched it enough to see if the numerics are correct.
What is the ideal mix, in your view, of state trust land leased for oil and gas production versus wind, solar or alternative energies? 
I think we’re doing pretty good on both right now. I think we need to be objective and say, ‘Are we going about this the right way?’ Because the end goal is to make money off the land for the schoolchildren, not to drive people and productions off the land because of overregulation and an increase in prices. So I absolutely support green energy. I want more green energy. I want it to be viable and vibrant, but I want it to stay in our state to help New Mexicans. And currently, I think the state land has been an advocate for green energy that is of no beneficial use to New Mexicans. 
Juan de Jesus Sanchez III
Juan de Jesus Sanchez III, left in cowboy hat, listens to U.S. Rep. Gabe Vasquez (D.N.M.) introduce him to Democratic party delegates at the party’s pre-primary convention March 7, 2026 in Mescalero. (Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)
Juan de Jesus Sanchez III describes himself as a 13th generation New Mexican whose family ranch near Belen relied on a state Trust land grazing lease. He worked as a natural resources specialist for the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers and at the New Mexico Acequia Commission before becoming the political director for U.S. Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-New Mexico.)
He defeated two other Democratic opponents in the primary, including state Rep. Matthew McQueen (D-Galisteo) and Jonas Moya, the former New Mexico director of the U.S. Farm Service Agency under President Joe Biden. 
“I think I’m bringing the lived experience, the professional experience, but also the values and principles to make sure our land is taken care of, not for a short-term economic benefit, but for long term sustainability,” Sanchez said. 
What makes you the most qualified to be land commissioner?
I’ve got a lot of both professional and lived experience tied to the land, and the other part of it is also being able to come into the office really ready to make sure that we advocate for the land, not only in a  short-term situation, which I think the the Trump administration is trying to do with things like uranium mining, drilling around Chaco Canyon, mining in the Pecos River. They’re trying to get money in the short-term instead of thinking about what the long-term consequences of these things are.
What is one aspect of the State Land Office that the public should understand better? 
The main goal is to be able to generate funds for public schools. What that means is that rather than us getting taxed at a higher rate to be able to go pay for our education, our lands help foot that bill to make sure that we have less of a tax burden, and we also have the opportunity to go out and enjoy these lands in the outdoors as well. 
Public lands serve so many different purposes, and I think they’re one of the most important and unique things that make New Mexico special.
What new initiatives would you implement at the State Land Office upon taking office?
One of the things I really want to do is open up a new office of outdoor rec and stewardship. Create a new position for an assistant commissioner for the head of the new office of outdoor rec and stewardship, and start building up an office from there. Essentially, what this office is going to do is look for opportunities to create more outdoor rec opportunities and work on the stewardship and restoration of our trust lands. They’re going to be focused solely on making sure we get people out in our outdoors.
If elected, will you uphold incumbent Land Commissioner Stephanie Garcia Richard’s ban on new uranium mining on state trust lands? Why or why not?
Our state has a very, very bad history with uranium mining. On state trust lands alone, there are dozens and dozens of uranium mines that need to be cleaned up. Our focus needs to be focused on cleanup of uranium mining, not continuing to mine and consider more development that could be harmful to our communities.
How will you use your office to support or oppose President Donald Trump’s push to remove Chaco Canyon buffer zone protections from oil and gas extraction? 
This is not an issue that you can kind of tiptoe around and be half in, half out of. I need to be all in. I will absolutely be ensuring that the land in that 10-mile radius around Chaco Canyon remains protected and remains so that we don’t use it for extraction. And the step beyond that, if the Trump administration does remove the boundary, move it from 10 miles to 5 miles, or remove it as a whole, as they’re doing the infrastructure to build roads out there, needing easements, needing infrastructure like pipelines or transmission line, or whatever it may be, is that the land office will not cooperate in any way.
If elected, will you continue to prohibit the use of state Trust land for the Project Jupiter gas pipeline or other data-center-related infrastructure? 
If the alternative is that they will be going around state Trust land, which I’ve heard is a strong possibility, then I think it’s worth sitting back at the table and negotiating more strongly with Project Jupiter and trying to figure out what kind of leverage the land office has there. 
I’m going to be advocating in this first legislative session for very strict guardrails around data centers. After that, each  data center is different. I have six different levels of things that are important to me for me to even consider a data center on state trust land:public input before decisions are made; community benefit programs to make sure that the communities are taken care of in some way or another; making sure that water we use for drinking or agriculture is not used for data centers; project labor agreements and ensuring that labor is being taken care of; these need to be off grid and at least 50% renewable energy from the offset; and the sixth is bonding around these infrastructures. 
Would you continue to implement a proposed State Land Office rule that would increase the minimum bonding requirements for oil and gas operators from a minimum of $10,000 to $150,000?
I wholeheartedly support the current bonding rule proposed. I’ve told (the) oil and gas industry that I will be implementing that. I have told advocates I will be implementing that. 
What is the ideal mix, in your view, of state trust land leased for oil and gas production versus wind, solar or alternative energies? 
I don’t think we need to be thinking in a mixed percentile. We need to be thinking about responsible revenue generation. So oil and gas right now generate about 97% of the funds that are brought in from the land office. I would like to bring that down, but really, it’s going to be dependent. Oil and gas is a boom and bust industry, and it’s booming right now. If it ends up busting, then the percentage that we get from renewables will ultimately go up.
We need to continue to increase our renewable energy opportunities: wind, solar, transmission, and now geothermal and continue to make sure that we are getting our the revenue from oil and gas, as long as we’re holding all those who use our land accountable and making sure they’re cleaning up.
Have you learned anything about who might have been behind the PACS that supported you during the primary election?
The super PAC is still something that I have no idea who put in the money behind it, and I could say that they did not help me. They did a disservice to my campaign. If we need to be taking care of some of the loopholes that they were able to take advantage of, I’m happy to advocate with legislators to make sure we take care of that, because I still don’t know what the background was there.
As for the (Chevron-backed) independent expenditure, that was all public. There was nothing that was behind the curtains. I haven’t had any conversations with some of the contributors about why they did support me.

name: VTDigger
title: Its selectboard mired in controversy, Weston to hold special election
description:
Weston selectboard resignations and complaints from residents may point to a broader trend in Vermont.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Its selectboard mired in controversy, Weston to hold special election.
text:
A sign directs voters to the polling place in the municipal building in Windsor on August 11, 2026. Photo by Noel Clark/VTDigger

Town politics in Weston have been contentious in recent months, with the selectboard and residents pitted against each other in recent meetings over ethics and open meeting law complaints. 
Now, Weston is holding a special election on Sept. 26 to fill empty selectboard seats after two members of the five-member board resigned this summer amid rancorous meetings. Some residents have even called for the remaining selectboard members to resign.  
The board vice chair says the issues residents have brought up are mostly procedural and that the board is working on addressing complaints.
Residents say board members are slow to respond to the ethics and open meeting law complaints. Weston resident and attorney Susan Morris said the board has failed to take accountability when responding to complaints.
“The dysfunction, infighting and disregard” are blatant and seemingly driven by some personal motives, said Morris when calling for members’ resignation on Aug 11. “The board is not functioning responsibly.”
The brouhaha escalated after resident Kenneth Hall filed several open meeting law and ethics complaints against the selectboard beginning in May, including alleging the board did not properly call for a special election in an open meeting. 
There has been a minor outbreak of town dysfunction in Vermont, and several other towns have similarly tumultuous local political landscapes. In Killington this summer, a selectboard member faced ethics complaints, and the former town manager faces potential disciplinary action after a monthslong gridlock over removing a staff position from the town budget. Woodstock, Weathersfield and Waterbury are all facing their own versions of political upheaval in town governance. 
Some of the infighting in Vermont towns has come in the wake of legislation passed in January 2025 adopting a Vermont municipal code of ethics. Before the legislation was passed, there was no uniform mechanism for town residents to file ethics complaints against local officials, according to Christina Sivret, the executive director of the Vermont State Ethics Commission. 
Municipalities had to adopt a process for investigating ethics complaints after the statute passed, Sivret said, which Weston did during the Tuesday selectboard meeting, giving the town clerk the role of complaint receiver.
“It’s not uncommon that municipalities didn’t put this in place immediately, so there’s varying levels of knowledge in terms of what the requirements were and how to go about it,” Sivret said.
Vermont municipal strife may be a reflection of broader trends, according to Christina Barsky, professor and director of the Masters in Public Administration program at the University of Vermont. She said some of the discord may reflect the national political landscape and the public’s attention to ethics and accountability.
She also sees Weston’s situation as indicative of a possible enforcement gap, because towns can adopt their own ethics complaint procedures, potentially amounting to “self-policing,” she said. Weston is an early test of this new law and system, Barsky said, as residents are using the complaint process the law has given them to address concerns and shine a light on what’s happening in their community. 
“Many small towns are running on really thin administrative capacity, and the Weston case maybe gives us a reminder that governance basics — things like trainings, procedures, independent ethics review — are sort of infrastructure to governance in the same way that we could think about, you know, roads or bridges as physical infrastructure,” Barsky said. 
Jim Lindville, vice chair of the board, said board members chose to call for the special election in September rather than appointing new members in order to avoid selecting “winners in a situation where people are looking at our actions with critical microscopes,” as well as to give other candidates time to step forward. 
Lindville said he wants to see “peace in the village” and for the board to no longer be shorthanded so that it can take on town matters, including infrastructure projects aimed at improving Weston’s flood resiliency.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Board of criticized North Dakota business financing program plans meeting to address audit
description: Officials overseeing a state-backed business financing program that drew critical audit findings and a sharp response from lawmakers plan to meet in coming weeks to address the situation. The North Dakota Development Fund Board met Thursday in a special meeting by videoconference, two days after the Legislature’s audit committee voted to recommend the full L[...]
text:
A screenshot of the North Dakota Development Fund Board meeting by videoconference on Sept. 24, 2026. 
(Screenshot from Microsoft Teams)Officials overseeing a state-backed business financing program that drew critical audit findings and a sharp response from lawmakers plan to meet in coming weeks to address the situation.
The North Dakota Development Fund Board met Thursday in a special meeting by videoconference, two days after the Legislature’s audit committee voted to recommend the full Legislature shut down the program and to refer the audit findings to the attorney general for investigation.
Audit findings included a lack of documentation for millions of dollars in transactions, unverified job data reported by borrowers and inconsistent conflict of interest procedures. Commerce Commissioner Chris Schilken told lawmakers improvements are underway or complete and emphasized the problems predate his and Gov. Kelly Armstrong’s tenures. Sen. Jeff Magrum, R-Hazelton, who chairs the audit panel, called the findings a disaster and said nothing has changed.
Fund Executive Director Brian Opp announced a planned “strategic session, in-person meeting” in upcoming weeks for the fund’s board of directors to address the audit findings in depth, “where we’ve been, where we are and where we’re going with those items.” 
It’s unclear when that meeting will occur. Fund staff will schedule it to align with board members’ availability, Board President Jim Albrecht told the North Dakota Monitor. Parts of that meeting will be public and other portions might be closed in an executive session, he said.
The board’s next monthly meeting is scheduled for Oct. 8 by videoconference. 
Opp also complimented the board and staff on “the work that has been done in the past couple of years,” specifically the improved collection and retention of conflict of interest forms, improvement of the form itself and a policy prohibiting “related-party loans.” 
The 2019-2024 performance audit found nearly $4 million in funding for five organizations that had relationships with one or two fund board members.
“Today the Development Fund has no related-party transactions, loans or investments,” Opp said.
Lawmakers seek AG probe after audit finds problems with North Dakota business financing program

Board Member Lyndsay Ulrickson said she looks forward to the future discussion and added it will be important to share with the public how the board has made improvements, such as the fund’s partnership with the state-owned Bank of North Dakota for the bank’s expertise. 
From there, the board moved into an executive session and closed the meeting for about one hour and 45 minutes. Reporters were moved into a virtual waiting room just as board member Joel Brown asked whether the board should make a motion to enter the executive session.
To enter an executive session and close a meeting, a board must first meet openly, then cite the legal authority for closing the meeting and what topics will be considered during the closed session, according to an attorney general webpage on closed meetings and executive sessions.
Some reporters were removed from the meeting during the board’s discussion of the executive session motion. It’s unclear what topics the board discussed. Albrecht called the matter “a simple timing thing” he said was a mistake on his part to not have the sequence in order. 
Later, the board returned to a public meeting and took three votes on items related to businesses. Those matters were not listed on the board’s agenda posted to the Secretary of State’s website. The public portions of the meeting lasted about 18 minutes.
The board president told the Monitor the Development Fund has provided value to the state, but he said the direction for its future is ultimately left to the Legislature and the governor. He referred the Monitor to Commerce for comment on the audit findings.
“We’re trying to do what we’ve been asked to do for the state of North Dakota, and hopefully we’re doing it in a way that is fulfilling what the mission is,” Albrecht said. 
Attorney General Drew Wrigley told the Monitor he has not received anything regarding the Development Fund audit. 
The Development Fund was created in 1991 and offers loans and investments as gap financing to new businesses that might not be able to obtain loans from traditional banks. The fund touts having aided more than 900 projects and created more than 9,000 jobs in its existence.

title: Colorado to get $250M in federal funding for electricity grid improvements
description: The Colorado Energy Office will receive $250 million from the federal government to improve electricity transmission links between Eastern and Western grids, the U.S. Department of Energy announced Thursday. It’s part of $1.9 billion total to help fund 31 grid-improvement projects. “This means lower costs and fewer outages for Coloradans,” Colorado Gov. Jare[...]
text:
Colorado Gov. Jared Polis on Thursday announces a $250 federal grant for Colorado to improve electricity transmission between Eastern and Western power grids. (Photo courtesy of Gov. Jared Polis Facebook)The Colorado Energy Office will receive $250 million from the federal government to improve electricity transmission links between Eastern and Western grids, the U.S. Department of Energy announced Thursday. It’s part of $1.9 billion total to help fund 31 grid-improvement projects.
“This means lower costs and fewer outages for Coloradans,” Colorado Gov. Jared Polis, a Democrat, said in a statement. “By strengthening Colorado’s electric grid and expanding our ability to share power with other regions, we can better protect families and businesses during extreme weather and periods of high demand while continuing to save people money.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Colorado and Oklahoma will get the most federal funds, both at $250 million. Some projects, including those in Alabama and Mississippi, are aimed at increasing capacity for large-load data centers, and in total, the 31 projects will add 23 gigawatts of capacity to the country’s transmission system.
Colorado’s project will “expand interregional transfer capability, improve system reliability, enhance operational flexibility, and strengthen grid resilience across Colorado, Texas, and neighboring regions,” according to a DOE summary.
The project will move a transmission connection between Colorado and Texas to the higher capacity May Valley substation in southeastern Colorado. Higher voltage wires will more than triple the amount of electricity that can move between the two regional grids, from 210 megawatts to 700 megawatts. It could one day carry 2,000 megawatts of electricity.
It is part of a larger set of investments to improve the multi-state transmission system, known as the Colorado-to-Texas Western-Eastern Interior Modernization Initiative, or CO2TX.
“Xcel Energy Services Inc’s proposed project will allow optimized use of clean energy resources across a much larger geographical footprint which will save Coloradans money on energy costs,” Will Toor, executive director of the Energy Office, said in a statement.
Because the project involves modernizing existing equipment and lines, it is in line with a March executive order from President Donald Trump that seeks to maximize existing right-of-ways instead of new construction.
“Modernizing the Lamar Tie will strengthen the connection between the Western and Eastern electric grids, helping us better serve customers during extreme weather, meet growing energy needs and make the most of affordable energy resources across the region,” Robert Kenney, president of Xcel Energy–Colorado, said in a statement.
The money was made available through the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act of 2021. Xcel is contributing an 80% funding match for the project.
In July, Polis and other Western governors started a task force to prioritize upgrades for the region’s energy grid.

title: Southern University announces semifinalists for system president’s job
description: Two Louisiana community college chancellors and a North Louisiana district attorney are among the six semifinalists for the Southern University System presidency, the search committee tasked with filling the post announced Thursday.  The three in-state contenders to lead the state’s historically Black college system are: Willie Smith, chancellor of Baton Rou[...]
text:
The F. G. Clark Activity Center at Southern University in Baton Rouge is also known as the "Mini-Dome" and is a multi-purpose facility used for campus and community events. (Photo provided by Southern University)Two Louisiana community college chancellors and a North Louisiana district attorney are among the six semifinalists for the Southern University System presidency, the search committee tasked with filling the post announced Thursday. 
The three in-state contenders to lead the state’s historically Black college system are: Willie Smith, chancellor of Baton Rouge Community College; Larissa Littleton-Steib, who holds the same job at Delgado Community College in New Orleans; and John Belton, district attorney in the 3rd Judicial District, which covers Lincoln and Union parishes.
The four out-of-state candidates are: Brian Bridges, New Jersey’s former higher education secretary; Jaffus Hardrick, previously president at Florida Memorial University in Miami Gardens; and Roscoe Jones, former dean of Drake University Law School. 
The six candidates will be invited to interview with the search committee Oct. 7, after which its members will recommend one or more candidates as finalists for the job. Those finalists will then do another round of interviews with groups of students, faculty and other stakeholders before the Southern University Board of Supervisors votes on who to hire. 
The search committee’s chairman, New Orleans City Councilman Jason Hughes, said the semifinalists were chosen from among more than 60 people who expressed interest in the job.
“They bring a wide range and diversity of experience,” Hughes said. 
Southern’s system presidency has been vacant since former Dennis Shields was fired late last year after serving in the position since 2022. Shields is now chancellor of the Camden, New Jersey, campus of Rutgers University, where former LSU President William Tate was hired as president in 2025. 
Southern AgCenter Chancellor Orlando McMeans has been serving as interim president since Shields’ departure. 
Littleton-Steib has led Delgado since 2019 and was previously chancellor of Baton Rouge Community College. Smith took the BRCC job after Littleton-Steib left, and he previously held several positions in the Louisiana Community and Technical College System. 
Belton has served as a district attorney since 2014. He has prosecuted several high-profile defendants, including bringing a case against the state troopers involved in the 2019 death of Black motorist Ronald Greene, who died after being beaten by police and dragged along the roadside while handcuffed. 
Belton previously was a member of the Southern University Board of Supervisors from 1990 to 2005, serving as its chair from 2001-02. Another prosecutor, 18th Judicial District Attorney Tony Clayton, currently leads the Southern board.
Before becoming dean of Drake’s law school, Jones worked extensively in Democratic politics, including as chief of staff for former U.S. Rep. Abigail Spanberger of Virginia, who’s now the state’s governor, and assistant chief of staff to former U.S. Sen. Dianne Feinstein of California.
Hardrick served as president of Florida Memorial University from 2018 until he resigned in 2024 due to health concerns. Hardrick received his undergraduate degree from the University of Louisiana at Lafayette. 
Bridges had worked in numerous roles in both higher education policy and at academic institutions before becoming New Jersey’s secretary of higher education under former Gov. Phil Murphy. His most recent university job was as vice provost for diversity, equity and access at Ohio University.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC inmate guilty in stabbing death of 3 during prison riot, jury decides
description: Larry White performed a rap for the judge just before receiving three life sentences for joining a mob that killed three.
text:
Inmate Larry White was found guilty at the Lee County Courthouse in Bishopville, S.C., pictured on Dec. 5, 2023. (Photo by Skylar Laird/SC Daily Gazette)A Lee County jury found an inmate guilty Thursday of participating in a mob that killed three people during the nation’s bloodiest prison riot in a quarter-century.
Larry White, now 30, was found guilty of criminal conspiracy and three counts of assault and battery in the first degree. White was one of 47 inmates indicted in connection with the 2018 riot that killed seven and injured 20.
White was the third inmate to go to trial and the third to be found guilty on all counts. Two dozen of those charged have pleaded guilty, and two have died in prison while awaiting trial, according to the Department of Corrections.
The jury handed down its verdict after about two hours of deliberations, ending a four-day trial.
Larry White, 30, was convicted Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026, of joining a mob that killed three in a 2018 prison riot. (Photo courtesy of SC Department of Corrections)
White will serve three life sentences, one for each of the assault and battery charges he faced, decided Judge Ferrell Cothran. When the riot began, White was serving 15 years for attempted murder and burglary, with a projected release date in 2031. His lengthy disciplinary record dates to 2017, soon after his sentence began, according to the state prison system.
Just before Cothran handed down his sentence, White gave a statement in the form of a rap. Calling the prison system “crooked and manipulative,” White said he gets to talk to his 13-year-old daughter just once a week and called himself “a decent person.”
“Justice is never served because our stories are never heard,” White said.
Prosecutors argued White was part of a group that killed three men: 28-year-old Raymond “Twin” Scott, 38-year-old Corey Scott and 33-year-old Joshua Jenkins. Video showed White repeatedly stabbing one of the men, whose identity was unclear, as he laid on the ground outside the fence.
“Every time someone dies, the world is less,” prosecutor Barney Giese said during his closing statement. “That includes people in the Department of Corrections who have a right to live and go home.”
White and his attorney contended the violence arose as part of a fight among gang members, not as part of a premeditated plan.
Violence broke out at the maximum security Lee County prison around 7 p.m. on April 15, 2018, after a group of inmates attacked Michael Milledge, a well-liked fellow prisoner, in his cell. A rival gang retaliated, killing the inmate who stabbed Milledge to death.
Word of the attack spread using contraband cellphones, and rival gangs went head to head across the prison’s seven units.
White, a member of the Crips gang, lived in the only unit where other gang members outnumbered the Bloods. After 9 p.m., as tensions rose, White joined gathering gang members, security video played during the trial showed.
The Crips and Gangster Disciples, who wore jackets and other clothing made out of plastic from mattresses meant to protect them from blades, met outside the dorm’s showers. There, they hatched a plan to kill the dorm’s Bloods, prosecutors said.
But White testified Wednesday he only knew the Bloods had to leave.
A group of Crips and Gangster Disciples chased the dorm’s Bloods outside, into the rain. They cornered the rival gang members against a 12-foot razor-wire fence with a locked gate. Some of the men climbed over the fence to escape, many injuring themselves on the razor wire or in jumping to the other side, prosecutors said.
The attacking inmates repeatedly stabbed the four inmates who didn’t make it over, killing three and severely injuring another, prosecutors said.
White joined the attackers for four minutes before returning to his dorm room, where he retrieved a second shank before running back to join his fellow gang members, White said when prosecutors questioned him. He admitted to standing over and stabbing at least one of the men left behind, though he said he didn’t remember who.
The three men killed had a combined 163 stab wounds, prosecutors said. Investigators said White inflicted at least 16 of those wounds, though White said he did half that.
Under state law, any single person in a mob is responsible for the group’s actions, making White responsible for every wound, prosecutors said.
Attorneys recall chaos, bloodshed of Lee County prison riot at trial of inmate

Before inmates chased the Bloods outside, White knew the gate was locked, prosecutors said. White agreed.
After tensions first began to boil in his dorm, White went outside to check the gate and discovered he couldn’t get through, he testified.
That knowledge of the gate was key in showing White and his fellow gang members planned to attack the Bloods, said Giese, a special prosecutor for the attorney general’s office who works with the Department of Corrections. If they really had wanted to let the gang members leave peacefully, they wouldn’t have led them into an ambush, Giese said.
“They had a plan, and when they executed it, they executed three people,” Giese said. “They had no chance down there. They had no chance.”
White’s return to the action after going to his cell for another weapon also showed his intent, prosecutors said. White could have removed himself from the fighting then and hid out there, but instead he decided to return to continue attacking, Giese said.
White rejoined the attack because it seemed “worth doing at that time,” he testified. When Giese asked White if he found the attack enjoyable, White said he did.
“He admits to chopping people up,” Giese told the jury during closing arguments. “He admitted enjoying it.”
Although White didn’t dispute joining in on the attack, he called it a fight that broke out after one of the Bloods threatened a fellow inmate.
White carried a shank because everyone did, he said. He joined the group of gang members because he worried about being alone in his cell and because he knew he’d be asked to answer for himself if he didn’t defend them.
“My purpose was to assemble for self-defense and to defend them if anything were to happen,” White said.
White returned to his cell to check on his cousin, who was still in the dorm, he said. He saw blood on his face when he looked in the mirror. Believing someone had hit him, he ran back outside for retribution, he said.
“When you left your cell, you’re coming all the way back down, and you were going to stab some Bloods, weren’t you?” Giese asked him.
Inmate in deadly SC prison riot guilty of murder, jury decides

“Yes,” White replied.
Much of White’s defense focused on issues in the prison the night of the riot.
Just one guard was responsible for more than 200 inmates in his dorm, and she barricaded herself in a guards’ station after fighting began. Contraband cellphones and weapons were rampant, many doors didn’t lock, and attacks happened often, said defense attorney Christopher Thompson.
“That environment created what happened to these poor victims here,” Thompson said.
The Department of Corrections agreed in 2021 to pay $6 million to settle 81 lawsuits over the riot.
Regardless of the culture at the prison, White should have known it was wrong to stab fellow inmates to death, prosecutors said.
“The buck stops here,” said prosecuting attorney Margaret Scott. “Larry White’s excuses need to stop. Today is the day that Larry White will finally be held accountable for his actions.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Iowa Medicaid Fraud Control Unit highlights efficiency; critics call for more funding
description: Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird said Thursday that recommendations about increased staffing and funding for existing Medicaid fraud elimination efforts will come at later meetings of the state Medicaid Fraud Elimination Task Force. The task force was established by executive order July 1 by Gov. Kim Reynolds. It is charged with submitting a final report […[...]
text:
Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird, joined by Jeremy Ingrim, director of the state Medicaid Fraud Control Unit and other members of the state Medicaid fraud task force for a meeting Sep. 24, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird said Thursday that recommendations about increased staffing and funding for existing Medicaid fraud elimination efforts will come at later meetings of the state Medicaid Fraud Elimination Task Force.
The task force was established by executive order July 1 by Gov. Kim Reynolds. It is charged with submitting a final report by Oct. 29, 2026 for the governor and lawmakers with recommendations on how to reduce and prevent incidents of Medicaid fraud. While the members did not deliberate on any specific planned recommendations, leaders gave updates from work groups about their efforts to find areas for improvement.
Members also got an update on work currently underway by the Medicaid Fraud Control Unit to address fraud within Iowa’s taxpayer-funded healthcare program. Jeremy Ingrim, the director of the unit, said federal evaluations and data have shown Iowa’s Medicaid Fraud Control Unit is more efficient than those in other states, “despite being one of the smallest units based on staffing and funding.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Ingrim said in federal fiscal year 2025, Iowa’s unit was ranked 10th highest in total convictions with 37 total convictions, above the national average among all 53 units of 22. With total operating expenses for the Iowa MFCU at $1.3 million in FY 2025, he said the approximate government cost for the unit was $36,700 for each conviction, the lowest conviction cost among all units nationwide.
“In other words, the government got the most bang for its buck in Iowa for criminal convictions in federal fiscal year 2025, and the unit remains on track in the current federal fiscal year for similar results,” Ingrim said.
Iowa’s fraud control unit was created in the 1970s and exists within the Iowa Department of Inspections, Appeals, and Licensing (DIAL).
Dean Lerner, who served as director of Iowa Department of Inspections and Appeals under former Democratic Gov. Chet Culver, told reporters after the task force meeting the funding for Iowa MFCU was “woefully inadequate compared to other states with similar budgets.”
Lerner, as well as Kevin Techau, another former Iowa Department of Inspections and Appeals director, held a news conference in July calling the task force a “sham.”
Lerner said hiring additional staff and providing more funding for the MFCU would be the most effective way to tackle Medicaid fraud in the state, because 75 cents per dollar spent comes from federal funding, and he said between $4 and $5 are recovered by the unit for each dollar spent.
According to Ingrim, the Iowa MCFU has nine staff members — five investigators, an assistant attorney general, a data analyst who also serves as an auditor, a paralegal, as well as a director. The unit is authorized to have 11 total staff and currently has two vacancies.
Bird said the task force has not yet made funding or staffing recommendations for the MCFU, but said, “that would be something that would be in a final report.” She praised the Iowa MCFU is “a very efficient unit,” but said the task force’s goal was to provide new avenues to find instances of fraud.
“It’s important that we are not just reactive, but we are proactive when it comes to fighting fraud,” Bird said. “And so it is very important that we get those tips from people, and that those are investigated and followed up on — but we also need to be more proactive, looking at where the fraud may be occurring, rather than waiting for someone to discover it and report it. … Even though we have a great and efficient unit, which I do appreciate, we should take a look at everything. Everything’s on the table to make sure that we are doing what we can as a state to eliminate fraud in our state, especially when it comes to taxpayer dollars.”
Working group leaders shared ideas and discussions they had since the August task force meeting on finding ways to allow Iowans to report instances of fraud, as well as to use data and analytics to identify cases where fraud may be occurring by flagging issues like overlapping claims or unusual billing.
Ingrim also told the task force increasing enforcement of the state’s Civil False Claims Act “could increase Medicaid fraud recoveries” in Iowa. The MCFU already has an assistant attorney general who works to ensure Iowa’s participation in nationwide civil cases involving Medicaid programs in multiple states, he said, but said there could be increased efforts to expand enforcement of Iowa Code on actors attempting to present false or fraudulent claims for payment to the state of Iowa.
“Establishing procedures and coordinating available DIAL and Attorney General’s office resources to pursue violations of Iowa Code Chapter 685 may serve as a force multiplier to increase Medicaid fraud recoveries and assist in deterring healthcare fraud in Iowa,” Ingrim said.
Lerner said the Iowa AG’s office is responsible for investigating Iowa Civil False Claims Act cases. He said Bird should increase a focus on pursuing cases against care facilities that do not provide services Medicaid pays for under this law.
“There are numerous opportunities to file those cases against nursing homes that are providing woefully inadequate care to people and killing people,” Lerner said. “Those dollars that are spent on those nursing homes for Medicaid residents should be sought from the nursing homes and put back into the state coffers, and they’re not being done, and that would be one area that should be a big focus.”
Bird said while the task force will create a report on ways to reduce Medicaid fraud, it will be up to state lawmakers and the governor whether to implement their recommendations.
“This is the first step in the process, but a very important one, because we want to make sure that the solutions that we’re proposing, the ideas that task force members have about how to make things better, are things that will work and be effective, and that we are doing everything we can to eliminate fraud in Iowa,” Bird said.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Oklahoma can’t deny Jewish charter school from opening, federal judge decides
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — In a decision that could enable the nation’s first religious charter school to open, an Oklahoma City federal judge has ruled in favor of a Jewish school seeking to operate with taxpayer funds. Oklahoma Western District Judge David L. Russell decided Thursday that the Statewide Charter School Board violated the First Amendment […]
text:
Oklahoma Western District Judge David L. Russell decided Thursday the state cannot exclude religious applicants from accessing charter school funding. Russell heard arguments in the case on Aug. 5 at the William J. Holloway Jr. United States Courthouse in Oklahoma City, pictured Dec. 4, 2023. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/ Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — In a decision that could enable the nation’s first religious charter school to open, an Oklahoma City federal judge has ruled in favor of a Jewish school seeking to operate with taxpayer funds.
Oklahoma Western District Judge David L. Russell decided Thursday that the Statewide Charter School Board violated the First Amendment when it voted against establishing Ben Gamla Jewish Charter School solely because the school would teach a particular religion. 
The board had denied opening Ben Gamla in light of a 2024 Oklahoma Supreme Court ruling that rejected taxpayer-funded, faith-based charter schools.
“The Oklahoma Statewide Charter School Board wanted to follow the First Amendment, but regretfully, they were bound by Oklahoma law when reviewing Ben Gamla’s application,” the board’s attorney, A.J. Ferate, said Thursday. “The court’s ruling today affirms that religious charter school applicants should not be excluded from consideration simply because of their religiosity.”
Attorney A.J. Ferate speaks to news reporters after a hearing Aug. 5 in Oklahoma City federal court over a Jewish charter school. Ferate represents the Statewide Charter School Board, which denied the school. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
The board will review the court order at its next meeting and take the appropriate next steps, according to a statement from its hired legal firm, the First Liberty Institute.
The decision allows the school to proceed toward opening. However, attorneys on all sides of the case have said the matter could be caught in a string of appeals ultimately leading to the U.S. Supreme Court, which deadlocked on a previous attempt to open a Catholic charter school in Oklahoma.
Two groups of state residents intervened in the Ben Gamla case to oppose the school’s creation. One, mostly made up of Jewish Oklahomans, is represented by local and national legal organizations, including the American Civil Liberties Union and Americans United for Separation of Church and State. 
The judge’s conclusion “opens the door to a dangerous sea change for our democracy,” the group’s legal team said in a statement.
“Forcing taxpayers to fund religious public schools violates state and federal law,” the attorneys said. “Ben Gamla will not only indoctrinate students into a particular religion — it will discriminate against families that don’t share the school’s beliefs. We will continue to fight for all Oklahomans, who deserve public schools that are secular and open to all students.”
Charter schools have long been considered to be public schools because they primarily rely on taxpayer funding, though they’re run by non-elected boards and are exempt from certain regulations.
Attorneys supporting Ben Gamla contend charter schools more closely resemble private entities that should be free to espouse a religion.
Former Democratic U.S. Rep. Peter Deutsch, of Florida, applied to open Ben Gamla as a free online charter school. Ben Gamla would teach the tenets of the Jewish faith along with typical school subjects.
Former U.S. Rep. Peter Deutsch speaks to the Statewide Charter School Board on Jan. 12 in Oklahoma City to present an application to open an online Jewish charter school in Oklahoma. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
Deutsch, a plaintiff in the lawsuit, said Thursday the court decision is a “victory for educational freedom, religious equality, and families in Oklahoma.”
“The state cannot single out religious schools for exclusion while welcoming everyone else into the charter school program,” he said in a statement. “We’re eager to open wide the doors of educational opportunity in Oklahoma.”
The federal judge agreed after listening to arguments from all sides of the case in an Aug. 5 hearing. Excluding private applicants from opening a state-funded school just because of their religious character violates the free exercise of religion, Russell decided.
Unlike the state Supreme Court, the federal judge determined charter schools are not government actors who must remain secular.
An Oklahoma law that requires charter schools to be nonsectarian “expressly discriminates” against religious schools that would otherwise be eligible for state funding, he decided.
However, Attorney General Gentner Drummond contended in a separate lawsuit that the board intentionally excluded other concerns raised about Ben Gamla’s viability outside of the religious element when voting to reject its application. Drummond alleged the board did so to benefit the school’s chances to succeed in court. 
That lawsuit, filed in Oklahoma County District Court, hasn’t had any movement in months, records show. The Attorney General’s Office confirmed Thursday that the case is still active.
Drummond, who led the legal fight against the Catholic charter school, originally was listed as a defendant in the federal lawsuit over Ben Gamla, but he had himself removed from the case.
“In 2024, the Oklahoma Supreme Court ruled that a religious charter school violates the Oklahoma Constitution, state law and the U.S. Constitution,” Drummond said in a statement Thursday. “The U.S. Supreme Court left that decision in place last year.”

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Indiana nabs $175M from feds to fix regional electricity ‘choke point’
description: The project will unlock 2,000 to 4,000 megawatts of transfer capacity for an Indiana grid interconnection that Gov. Mike Braun dubbed a "choke point."
text:
U.S. Department of Energy General Counsel Jonathan Brightbill announces $1.9 billion in transmission grants, while Indiana Energy and Natural Resources Secretary Suzanne Jaworowski looks on, at the Statehouse in Indianapolis on  Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Indiana has won $175 million in federal funding to upgrade a critical “choke point” between two regional electricity grid operators, officials announced Thursday.
“The challenge isn’t simply generating more electricity,” U.S. Department of Energy General Counsel Jonathan Brightbill said. “It’s making the grid so that it can move power where it is needed quickly, affordably, and reliably across one of the most important regional seams in the country — and that comes and lands right here in Indiana.”
The “seam” is where the Midcontinent Independent System Operator’s service territory meets that of the PJM Interconnection. The border between the two regional transmission organizations runs through Illinois, Indiana, Michigan and Kentucky.
Gov. Mike Braun speaks on Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026 at the Statehouse in Indianapolis. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Brightbill said the project will unlock 2,000 to 4,000 megawatts of transfer capacity for an interconnection in the Hoosier state that Gov. Mike Braun dubbed a “pinch point” and a “choke point” in comments to reporters.
The work is expected to save ratepayers in and outside of Indiana between $50 million and $150 million annually by relieving congestion at that interconnection point.
“Congestion, that may cut off access to generation that’s available,” Brightbill said. “The way the bulk power system works, you end up with pockets. And then with dynamic pricing … you can end up with prices spiking in localized areas that then will cost those local ratepayers a lot of money.”
The four-year project will include:

Replacing old power lines with new ones with materials that carry electricity more efficiently.
Implementing dynamic assessment of the lines, allowing them to carry more electricity under ideal weather conditions. Static lines are set more conservatively, for the worst-case scenario.
Adding topographic software so grid operators can direct electricity from cheaper sources along more efficient routes to where it’s needed.

The project’s sponsors will put up an additional $150 million for a total price tag of $325 million.
Brightbill was in Indiana to announce the selection of 31 projects nationwide worth more than $5 billion. The $1.9 billion in federal investments are set to leverage an additional nearly $3.4 billion.
“Selected projects will reconduct or rebuild more than 1,500 miles of transmission infrastructure. They will deploy cutting-edge, grid-enhancing technologies across nearly 21,000 miles of transmission lines,” Brightbill said. “And, together, we are expected to unlock more than 23 gigawatts of additional grid capacity. That’s a lot.”
Money for the initiative was authorized under the 2021 Bipartisan Infrastructure Law during former President Joe Biden’s administration.
Originally called Grid Resilience and Innovation Partnerships, President Donald Trump’s administration has renamed the program to SPARK, which stands for Speed to Power through Accelerated Reconductoring and other Key Advanced Transmission Technology Upgrades.
Nuclear regulation deal inked
Also on Thursday, Indiana became the 41st state to take over responsibility of non-energy nuclear and radioactive materials used in medical, industrial, academic and fusion technologies from the federal government.
The U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission can hand down oversight under the Atomic Energy Act of 1954. Kentucky became the first “agreement state” in 1962. Dozens of states have followed in its stead, with Indiana the latest.
The announcement has been in the works for years. Then-Gov. Eric Holcomb in 2021 submitted a letter of intent to pursue a deal.
“Agreement state status gives us better customer service, faster permit review times — which was always an issue — faster incident responses, and lower regulatory fees,” Braun said.
Gov. Mike Braun, front left, and U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission Chair Ho Nieh sign an agreement giving Indiana control over nuclear permitting and inspections within the state, on Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026 at the Statehouse in Indianapolis. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
The Indiana Department of Homeland Security will manage the program.
Spokeswoman Ashley Morgan said the agency will have five health physicists responsible for handling licensing and inspections.
The work will be largely funded by licensing fees. An eight-page fee schedule shows costs, mostly in the thousands, for each type of license.
The state Department of Homeland Security also houses a dedicated radiation team managing nuclear emergency response and risk, and works with communities exploring nuclear — in collaboration with the Indiana Office of Energy Development.
“Making more licensing and permitting decisions here in Indiana rather than in Washington means Hoosiers have more control over Indiana’s energy future,” Braun said, calling the deal a “necessary step for Indiana to meet our nuclear energy generation goals.”
