title: Ohio GOP lawmakers tee up votes for gas tax holiday after Acton, then Ramaswamy, back idea
description: Ohio Republican candidate for governor Vivek Ramaswamy introduced his plan Wednesday for a 90-day gas tax holiday. It comes on the heels of Democratic candidate Amy Acton calling for a similar halt to the tax. Ramaswamy insisted his proposal is different because he’s working with the legislature “to lead through action rather than through tweets […]
text:
Ohio Republican candidate for governor Vivek Ramaswamy. (Photo by Nick Evans, Ohio Capital Journal.)Ohio Republican candidate for governor Vivek Ramaswamy introduced his plan Wednesday for a 90-day gas tax holiday. It comes on the heels of Democratic candidate Amy Acton calling for a similar halt to the tax.
Ramaswamy insisted his proposal is different because he’s working with the legislature “to lead through action rather than through tweets and statements.”
“The level of detail from her gas tax proposal? Non-existent,” Ramaswamy said. “This is why this woman, I think, is disqualified from leading the state. I mean, the answer is if she can’t offer specifics, if she can’t stand shoulder-to-shoulder with us on a debate stage, she doesn’t have what it takes to lead the state.”
In a statement, Acton campaign spokesperson Addie Bullock said, “Dr. Acton has been clear throughout her campaign; she will work with anyone, Republican or Democrat, to deliver for Ohioans.”
She emphasized Acton raised the idea of a gas tax holiday first and added, “Vivek Ramaswamy is following Dr. Acton’s bold leadership with emergency relief at the gas pump.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The legislature is embracing Ramaswamy’s plan with Ohio Senate President Rob McColley as his running mate. Amid the rising cost of gas and diesel fuel, polls show frustration with Republican leadership ahead of the midterm election.
What’s the plan for the gas tax?
Gas taxes fund work on roads and bridges around Ohio. Drivers pay 38.5 cents per gallon on gas and 47 cents per gallon for diesel. In the past several years, gas taxes have generated about $2.6 billion annually.
The Ohio Contractors Association, which represents the highway and utility construction industry was quick to warn against lost tax revenue.
“Any temporary suspension must include replacement funding that makes the state and local transportation programs whole,” Association President Chris Runyan said, “and ensures that no transportation project is delayed, deferred or canceled as a result.”
Runyan said Ohio’s transportation investments are “vital to our economy.”
“Relief for Ohio families and businesses and continued investment in the transportation system they rely on can — and should — go hand in hand.”
Ramaswamy’s plan would replace three months of lost revenue with cash from state transportation balances, then the general revenue fund, and potentially even the rainy-day fund. But McColley expressed confidence that “due to good fiscal stewardship,” the state could absorb the tax break without dipping into its reserves.
After the event, Ohio’s Office of Management and Budget clarified that the Ohio Department of Transportation has no cash balance left in its current budget.
The Highway Operating Fund has a cash balance “just under $1.6 billion and the balance fluctuates daily,” OBM Spokesman Pete LuPiba explained. “It supports $5 billion open purchase orders for operations, maintenance, and capital improvements. There is no money in the account that is not planned for future projects.”
Ohio House Speaker Matt Huffman said the total cost would likely land somewhere between $640 and $700 million.
“This is eminently achievable. It’s fiscally achievable,” Ramaswamy said. “Ohio, under Republican leadership, has thankfully been on a good fiscal trajectory that we can do this, and if we can do it, that, in this moment, means that we should.”
Huffman and Senate President McColley committed to calling their members back to the Statehouse to vote on legislation. They’re planning to have both chambers in session next Wednesday, Sept. 30.
Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine shuts down proposal to suspend state gas tax

Even if their legislation passes, lawmakers could have trouble getting Gov. Mike DeWine on board. Back in 2019, he negotiated a gas tax increase, and earlier this year he shot down a proposed gas tax holiday.
McColley said he’s had conversations with DeWine and believes the governor remains open minded about their plan.
The Ohio Capital Journal reached out to the governor’s office for comment. A spokesman said “we have not yet issued any statements on these proposals.”
Why now?
Ramaswamy, Huffman, and McColley all dismissed suggestions that their proposal is yet another bid to juice turnout for Republicans in an unfavorable political environment.
Ohio’s Republican supermajority has already advanced an amendment writing existing photo voter ID laws into the state constitution. Earlier this month President Donald Trump promised voters $5,000 checks if the GOP holds the U.S. House and Senate.
Huffman repeatedly said “this is not a radical proposal” and pointed back to the Republican gas tax holiday measure DeWine dismissed earlier this year.
“We’ve been talking about this for months,” he said. “It’s not like, hey, there’s an election coming up here. Why don’t we do something?”
The legislation Huffman referenced, however, hasn’t gotten a single hearing.
Senate President and Republican candidate for lieutenant governor Rob McColley discussing a gas tax holiday alongside Republican candidate for governor Vivek Ramaswamy (left) and House Speaker Matt Huffman. (Photo by Nick Evans, Ohio Capital Journal.)
“Frankly,” McColley said, “for us to sit by idly during a time of fiscal emergency for our families, for Ohioans, simply because there’s an election coming up, that would be an abdication of our duties.”
All three men stressed that a sharp uptick in fuel costs, particularly diesel, pushed them to act. The primary drivers of that increase are ongoing wars in Ukraine and Iran.
The former, President Donald Trump promised to end “even before becoming president,” and the latter, Trump promised would conclude “very shortly” almost six months ago.
Ramaswamy referenced “Russian refinery issues” but not the war in Iran. Pressed on whether President Trump, whose endorsement helped him clear the Republican field, needs to end the war, Ramaswamy said foreign policy is out of his hands.
“Would (I) rather not have that war? Absolutely,” Ramaswamy said. “I certainly — we’re all in that camp, right? Every American is probably in that camp.”
Democratic buy in?
Huffman promised a vote and an emergency clause to ensure the tax cut takes effect immediately. To clear that bar, however, Huffman acknowledged Republicans will need buy-in from Democrats.
“I think Democrats who vote against this are doing it at their peril,” he said. “This is a very easily understood issue: should you not have to pay gas tax for the next 90 days without interruption in roads (funding)?”
Can they do that? Ohio Senators propose novel, if questionable, Browns stadium funding plan

With Acton’s campaign claiming credit for putting the conversation front and center, some Democrats might support the idea, but some had critiques.
In a press release, Ohio House Minority Leader Dani Isaacsohn agreed that Ohioans “desperately need relief from the costs of the failed war in the Middle East,” but he said Ramaswamy’s “knee-jerk response to Dr. Acton’s plan has demonstrated no understanding of how the state government works, how the budget is structured, or how taxpayer dollars should be spent.”
Isaacsohn noted the Ohio Department of Transportation doesn’t have surplus funding and Ramaswamy’s reliance on it as a source for the tax break demonstrates “confusion” or “recklessness.”
But there’s plenty of money readily available, Isaacsohn said.
“We can enact Dr. Acton’s Gas Tax Holiday, but it has to be paid for in a way that makes sense for Ohioans,” Isaacsohn said. “A gas tax holiday could be paid for with the $600 million the Republican legislature has tried to allocate to billionaire Jimmy Haslam for his NFL team.”
Asked if he had a comment about Isaacsohn’s suggestion, Huffman laughed and said no.

title: Helene survivor: It’s time to move beyond market-based approaches to climate change
description: If you’re a millennial like me, climate anxiety is practically in your DNA. I’ve lived through my fair share of climate change-induced disasters, and 2024’s Hurricane Helene was just the latest and gravest — though most certainly not the last or worst I’ll ever experience in my lifetime. And I consider myself lucky: many people […]
text:
Flood debris piles left in the aftermath of Hurricane Helene in Bat Cave, North Carolina. (Photo by Sean Rayford/Getty Images)If you’re a millennial like me, climate anxiety is practically in your DNA. I’ve lived through my fair share of climate change-induced disasters, and 2024’s Hurricane Helene was just the latest and gravest — though most certainly not the last or worst I’ll ever experience in my lifetime. And I consider myself lucky: many people in the global south have been affected by climate change impacts for decades, yet have contributed the least to carbon emissions.
Still, I fight for a livable future for all. That livable future depends on moving away from failed market-based “solutions” and toward intentional, coordinated policies that effective address the root causes of climate change and deliver benefits to all people.
As we approach the two-year anniversary of Hurricane Helene, the question remains: How many more global disasters will it take for climate change to be seen as the emergency it is? And when will we pivot from ineffective market-based solutions to deep decarbonization in the public interest?
With the latest UN report highlighting that the world will surpass the 1.5 Celsius warming mark set by the Paris Agreement in the next few years even under the best-case scenario climate scenarios, we must limit, adapt to, and return from higher temperatures if we want to avoid even more extreme heat, flooding, and irreversible climate tipping points. The report highlights some scenarios at 2 degrees warming, leading to even graver risks like destabilization of major ice sheets, permanent degradation of the Amazon carbon sink, and irreversible disruption of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation, currents that play a significant role in regulating the climate.
As frustrating as it is, the lack of meaningful, systemic government action up to this point makes sense. As it currently operates, our economic system depends on unfettered growth and high consumption that creates externalities like pollution, public health catastrophes, and otherwise preventable accidents. While some governments have attempted to regulate them, they have been prevented from doing so fully or effectively because of corporate capture of regulatory bodies, information asymmetry, and the interrelated webs of wealth, power, and influence.
Now, if the U.S. power sector (the largest emitter of greenhouse gas emissions) embraced 80% renewable generation by 2030 while also electrifying other sectors, we could start making real progress because it could realistically reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 50% below 2005 levels. But as market-based and largely voluntary approaches currently operate, no industry incentives are sufficient to meaningfully halt the role of accumulation and consumption that have driven climate change and the extreme exploitation of the planet and its people.
Of course, a truly “free-market” approach to the climate crisis would follow the declining costs of renewable energy and lead to the uptake at scale. However, that has not happened. In 2025, over 90% of new renewable energy projects were lower cost than even the lowest-cost fossil fuel alternatives (like coal and methane gas), with gas-fired generation cost even increasing over time due to fuel price volatility. But that’s not the current state of the dominant economic system, which leans on protectionism, legal monopolization, sky-high market entry barriers, and lack of true competition to maintain oligarchy-like control of wealth, power, and giant corporations. All of this stifles innovation, progress, and the benefits to all from deep decarbonization.
A better way to decarbonize with urgency is by planning for and then building an economy that runs on 100% renewable energy. We and the rest of the world have to get serious about planning for and taking coordinated, collective governmental action to decarbonize our economy while advancing climate and energy justice for all.
From one climate disaster survivor in western North Carolina to my neighbors around the world: Our current approaches to climate change aren’t working. They’re too limited, too fragmented, and too decentralized to prevent the worst impacts and prepare for the ones that are already here or on the way soon. We need to build something new, a system that prioritizes strong, effective protections, justice, and benefits for all while allowing businesses, individuals, and communities to thrive.
Real climate solutions already exist, including coordinated planning for a 100% renewable energy sector. The matter is too urgent to continue engaging with false and failing climate “solutions.” After all, no community deserves to suffer its own Helene.
Sophie Loeb has worked in climate policy and advocacy for over 4 years. She lives in Asheville, N.C.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Legislator proposes Dolly Parton license plate in Louisiana to support literacy
description: State Rep. Mike Bayham, R-Chalmette, is proposing a special Dolly Parton license plate in Louisiana that would help fund a state literacy program for children started by the country music icon.
text:
State Rep. Mike Bayham plans to introduce legislation in 2027 to set up a Dolly Parton license plate in Louisiana. (Photo by Jason Kempin/Getty Images)State Rep. Mike Bayham, R-Chalmette, is proposing a special Dolly Parton license plate in Louisiana that would help fund a state literacy program for children started by the country music icon. 
Every Parton license plate would come with a $25 fee that would support the Imagination Library in Louisiana, Bayham said in a news release Thursday. The program mails one book a month to every child that joins the library. Children up to age 5 can sign up free of charge. 
“Dolly Parton used her extraordinary success to make a difference in the lives of children. This plate gives Louisianans an opportunity to celebrate her legacy while making a meaningful investment in our next generation,” Bayham said. 
The plates likely won’t be available until next year at the earliest. Bayham plans to introduce a bill to set them up in the next legislative session, which begins in April. 
Parton said she started Imagination Library  in 1995 to honor her father, Lee, a sharecropper and construction worker who never learned to read.  It initially only covered children in Sevier County, Tennessee, where Parton grew up, but has since expanded to many other states and countries. 

Former Gov. John Bel Edwards expanded Imagination Library to include all young children in Louisiana in 2023. 

“We won’t be done until we’re reaching every ZIP code in every parish,” said Molly Marker, state director of Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library in Louisiana in Bayham’s press release. “A specialty plate gives people anywhere in the state a way to be part of that, and it puts it on the road: on the highway, in the school pickup line, at stop signs all over.”

Bayham is kicking off his campaign for the license plate at a news conference Friday at the Audubon Aquarium and Insectarium in New Orleans. Members of the Krewe of Dolly, a Mardi Gras marching group that also works with the Imagination Library, will be in attendance.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas ramps up outreach about new Medicaid work requirements
description: Arkansas launched a new series of flyers, posters, text messages and videos Thursday about new work requirements taking effect next year for some Medicaid participants. The Department of Human Services announced a new “outreach toolkit” about the requirements that take effect for those on the Medicaid expansion program in January under the federal One Big […[...]
text:
The Arkansas Department of Human Services building on Main Street in downtown Little Rock. (Photo by John Sykes/Arkansas Advocate)Arkansas launched a new series of flyers, posters, text messages and videos Thursday about new work requirements taking effect next year for some Medicaid participants.
The Department of Human Services announced a new “outreach toolkit” about the requirements that take effect for those on the Medicaid expansion program in January under the federal One Big Beautiful Bill Act that President Donald Trump signed last year.
The requirements mandate that recipients of the federal insurance program must complete 80 hours of work, community service, higher education, work programming or a combination of the four each month, unless they meet certain exemption criteria. 
“DHS is committed to helping Arkansans prepare for changes that may affect their health care,” Department of Human Services Secretary Janet Mann said in a news release. “This toolkit provides ready-to-use educational resources for organizations and community members to spread the word about the new requirements and what they need to do to maintain their coverage.”
The toolkit includes templates of emails, text messages and blog posts that providers, nonprofit groups, insurers and others can use to share information about the new requirements. It also offers graphics in English, Spanish and Marshallese.
The department also unveiled videos that will run on digital bulletin boards in each of its county offices, and encouraged organizations to sign up for free customized promotional videos. 
Arkansas began a “soft launch” of the new requirements earlier this year, checking whether beneficiaries comply but not dropping them if they don’t.
The toolkit was produced in house using existing resources, department spokesperson Gavin Lesnick said.
Arkansas is preparing to launch the requirements as the state’s hybrid expansion faces an uncertain future. The state has asked for a temporary two-year extension of the program, which uses federal funds to purchase private insurance for low-income Arkansans, after the Trump administration rejected its renewal.
Lesnick said the federal government has not made a decision on that request yet. 
The last time Arkansas implemented work requirements for Medicaid, more than 18,000 people lost coverage before a federal judge blocked the restriction.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Gov. DeSantis-appointed trial judge faces public reprimand for shooting comment
description: A Second Judicial Circuit judge who made “intemperate and caustic comments” and lamented that he’d like to tell his deputy “to pull his gun and shoot” a trio of attorneys is being ordered to appear before the Florida Supreme Court for a public reprimand. Released Thursday, the Supreme Court disciplinary ruling tracks the Judicial Qualifying Commission’s […]
text:
Florida's Supreme Court. Sept. 8, 2023. (Photo by Florida Phoenix)A Second Judicial Circuit judge who made “intemperate and caustic comments” and lamented that he’d like to tell his deputy “to pull his gun and shoot” a trio of attorneys is being ordered to appear before the Florida Supreme Court for a public reprimand.
Released Thursday, the Supreme Court disciplinary ruling tracks the Judicial Qualifying Commission’s recommended punishment  for Judge J. Layne Smith, appointed to the bench by Gov. Ron DeSantis in June 2020. The circuit consists of six north Florida counties: Franklin, Gadsden, Jefferson, Leon, Liberty, and Wakulla.
Judge J. Layne Smith (Photo via Second Judicial Circuit)
“Although we accept the Commission’s recommendation, we emphasize that Judge Smith’s conduct fell far below the standard of professionalism that Florida judges owe to those who appear before them,” the opinion reads. 
The ruling didn’t set a specific date for Smith to appear before the court  and instead deferred the planning to the clerk of the court.
Court documents show that Smith made most of the comments on Sept. 23, 2025, during a hearing on an order to show cause on a motion to compel discovery in a Wakulla County lawsuit.
The record shows, “Smith became frustrated with the parties’ attorneys after learning they could not confirm that a party had been properly served.
“At one point, Judge Smith told the parties: ‘I would like to tell the deputy to pull his gun and shoot all three of you as far as my level of frustration right now. I really don’t want him to do that.’” Judge Smith also belittled the attorneys, referring to them as the “Keystone Cops” and the “Apple Dumpling Gang,” the record shows.
Smith recused himself from the case about one week later and on Oct. 21, 2025, self-reported his behavior, issued a public apology, and recused himself from any remaining cases involving the parties to that case.

title: Nor’easter headlines are everywhere. What will Delaware actually see?
description: The storm’s effects will vary across the state, with the greatest threat coming from tidal flooding and dangerous surf DOVER, Del. — A nor’easter drawing attention from Philadelphia and national news outlets can sound like a single storm with a single forecast. For Delaware residents, the more useful question is where they live — and how close they are to ..[...]
text:
Delaware LIVE is introducing a French Bread Total to help readers decide whether a storm calls for a run on bread, milk, eggs and the other essentials for surviving a weekend indoors. On our seven-point French Toast Scale, this storm earns a 1 out of 7 for most Delaware households.
The storm’s effects will vary across the state, with the greatest threat coming from tidal flooding and dangerous surf
DOVER, Del. — A nor’easter drawing attention from Philadelphia and national news outlets can sound like a single storm with a single forecast. For Delaware residents, the more useful question is where they live — and how close they are to tidal water.
The National Weather Service expects the greatest impacts along Delaware’s ocean beaches, bays and tidal waterways. Coastal flooding is already a concern Thursday, Sept. 24, and could recur with successive high tides. Stronger winds are possible at the beaches Friday night into Saturday. Farther inland, residents are more likely to encounter gusty winds than flooding.
Editor’s note: Delaware LIVE is introducing a French Bread Total to help readers decide whether a storm calls for a run on bread, milk, eggs and the other essentials for surviving a weekend indoors. On our seven-point French Toast Scale, this storm earns a 1 out of 7 for most Delaware households. The rating does not discount the serious flooding risk for people in low-lying coastal and tidal communities.
What is a nor’easter?
A nor’easter is an East Coast storm named for the northeast winds it typically brings to coastal areas. It can occur at any time of year and does not have to bring snow.
This storm is developing offshore. Its persistent winds are pushing water into Delaware’s bays and tidal waterways, where elevated water levels can cause flooding at more than one high tide. The storm’s exact track remains uncertain, particularly for how strong coastal winds become Friday night and Saturday.
What should Delaware expect?
Sussex County: The beaches and Inland Bays face the greatest combination of hazards. A coastal flood warning covers the Delaware beaches and inland Sussex until 2 a.m. Saturday. Forecasters expect 1 to 2 feet of water above ground level in low-lying areas near shorelines and tidal waterways. Some roads in coastal and bayside communities could become impassable. The Weather Service says more serious flooding remains possible around Rehoboth Bay and Indian River, depending on the storm’s track.
At the ocean beaches, breaking waves could reach 12 feet in the surf zone. Dangerous rip currents, beach erosion and possible dune breaches are also concerns. A high surf advisory and high rip current risk continue through Saturday evening.
Kent County: A coastal flood warning also remains in effect until 2 a.m. Saturday. Low-lying roads and communities near Delaware Bay and tidal waterways face the greatest risk. The warning does not mean all of Dover or Milford will flood.
New Castle County: A coastal flood advisory covers vulnerable areas along tidal shorelines and waterways until 1 a.m. Saturday. Away from the water, the main effect is expected to be gusty weather. The Weather Service says excessive rainfall and freshwater flooding appear unlikely at this time.
When will it end?
The current coastal flood warnings expire early Saturday, but that is not necessarily the end of the effects. Dangerous surf continues through Saturday evening, and the Weather Service says tidal flooding could persist into the weekend. Winds and conditions on the water are expected to improve Sunday. Residents near the coast should check updated alerts as the storm’s path becomes clearer.
To Go Box | Delaware’s nor’easter

When: Coastal impacts are underway Thursday. Stronger beach winds are possible Friday night into Saturday.
Where: The greatest risk is along the beaches, bays and low-lying tidal waterways of Sussex and Kent counties.
What: Repeated high-tide flooding, possible road closures, dangerous surf and beach erosion. Inland areas can expect gusty winds.
French Toast Scale: 1 out of 7 for most households. Coastal residents should take local flood warnings seriously.
What to do: Check alerts before traveling near tidal roads, never drive through floodwater and stay out of the surf while the high rip current risk is in effect.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: UK violated open records law three times in recent cases, AG finds
description: Attorney General Russell Coleman found the University of Kentucky to be in violation of Kentucky’s open records law in three different cases since August, showing the school’s continuing pattern of problems with the state law aimed at government transparency. The Lexington Herald-Leader found that in 2025, 18 of 24 appeals to records denied by public […]
text:
A statue of the University of Kentucky's mascot, a wildcat named "Bowman," sits on the campus in Lexington. (Kentucky Lantern photo by McKenna Horsley)Attorney General Russell Coleman found the University of Kentucky to be in violation of Kentucky’s open records law in three different cases since August, showing the school’s continuing pattern of problems with the state law aimed at government transparency.
The Lexington Herald-Leader found that in 2025, 18 of 24 appeals to records denied by public universities in Kentucky involved UK. 
The AG’s office published its most recent slate of open records appeals on Wednesday. In two appeals, UK was found to have not violated the law. In addition, the AG’s office found that Kentucky State University had partially violated the law.
In the first case, Professor Reuben Adotorwovor challenged UK over its denial of his request for a tenure and review committee report on him. Although the law permits people to request all documents pertaining to them, the university redacted parts of the report without providing an explanation for doing so. Coleman’s office said UK also violated the Act by failing to respond within five business days of receiving the request.
“When a public agency denies a request for public records, it must also “include a statement of the specific exception authorizing the withholding of the record and a brief explanation of how the exception applies to the record withheld,’” the AG letter said. 
UK officials did not identify what material it redacted or explain the redaction in detail, as required by state law.
The second case involved a request by a person named Samantha Jones, who asked for body camera footage related to the arrest of a student by UK police in 2022.
UK denied the request under the federal Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act, which is aimed at protecting student privacy. But the AG’s office said protected records under FERPA must be “education records,” and other courts have already ruled that FERPA does not protect law enforcement records. 
“Because the University has not met its burden to show that FERPA applies to the withheld video footage, the University violated the Act when it withheld the video footage on that basis,” the AG opinion said.
FERPA was involved in UK’s most notorious open records loss in 2021, when the student newspaper sued for investigatory records related to the alleged sexual misconduct case of a professor. UK cited FERPA in refusing to turn over the documents. The case, which started in 2016, went to the Kentucky Supreme Court, which ruled unanimously UK had violated the law by using FERPA overbroadly simply because a student might be involved.
“The Open Records Act encourages the ‘free and open examination of public records’ even where examination ‘may cause inconvenience or embarrassment to public officials or others …’ The University may find The Kernel’s (Open Records Act) requests burdensome and intrusive or even ill-advised but the University is not authorized to decide what public records must be disclosed and what records can lawfully be withheld,” Justice Lisabeth Hughes wrote in the opinion.
In the third case, Rabbi Shlomo Litvin was told his request for emails from two UK employees containing the word “Chabad” was too burdensome because it resulted in more than 2,000 documents.
As the courts have noted, “the obvious fact that complying with an open records request will consume both time and manpower is, standing alone, not sufficiently clear and convincing evidence of an unreasonable burden,” the AG opinion said.
UK spokesman Jay Blanton declined to comment on Thursday.
Amye Bensenhaver, a former assistant attorney general and co-founder of the Kentucky Open Government Coalition said UK’s lead counsel, William Thro, has long shown his antipathy to the state open records law.
“Why is UK asserting exemptions that don’t apply? Because they can and they do,” she said. “In his mind the burden rests with the requester – he is responsible for a great deal of harm, and he’s been called out. 
“I just think UK is a very poor student of open government, and learns nothing from its past mistakes, and continues to advance interpretations of the law that have been rejected, including the opinion on FERPA,” she said.
The Kentucky Lantern is in ongoing litigation with the University of Kentucky over another open records case related to a UK professor who protested the dissolution of the faculty senate. The professor left the school as part of a $375,000 agreement; UK refused the Lantern’s request for documents related to the agreement by saying the records were “preliminary,” therefore exempt.
The Attorney General upheld UK’s argument in the appeal; the Lantern has appealed that decision in Fayette Circuit Court.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico Election 2026: New Mexico governor
description: New Mexicans will elect a new governor on Nov. 3 for the first time in eight years. Source NM spoke with the two nominees — Democrat and former U.S. Interior Secretary Deb Haaland and Republican and former Rio Rancho Mayor Gregg Hull — about how they'd approach the job.
text:
Democrat and former U.S. Interior Secretary Deb Haaland, left, will face Republican and former Rio Rancho Mayor Gregg Hull, right, in the Nov. 3 general election contest to be New Mexico's next governor. (Photos by Danielle Prokop/Source NM)New Mexicans will elect a new governor on Nov. 3 for the first time in eight years.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham, a term-limited Democrat, has steered the state through a pandemic and overseen the growth of several lucrative state trust funds. She created a new state agency, the Early Childhood Education and Care Department; implemented the first statewide universal childcare program in the nation; and oversaw reforms to the state’s dated medical malpractice regulations.
She’s also dealt with challenges, including rulings against her gun control measures, criticism for her high levels of emergency spending and a troubled child welfare agency.
Democrat Deb Haaland, who previously served as a member of Congress and as secretary of the U.S. Department of the Interior, will face Republican Gregg Hull, who was the longest-serving mayor in Rio Rancho history, in the Nov. 3 general election.
While the two have run mostly cordial campaigns after winning their parties’ respective June primary contests, they’ve taken differing approaches to how they would lead New Mexico through the remainder of President Donald Trump’s term, oversee the universal childcare program and regulate controversial data center developments.
Source NM spoke with both candidates about their priorities for the office, which comes with a $169,714 annual salary. Their answers have been edited for clarity and concision.
Deb Haaland
Former U.S. Secretary of the Interior Deb Haaland poses at the Roundhouse Thursday, June 5, 2025. Haaland, who is running as a Democratic candidate for governor, told attendees at a water summit ‘the future of our communities depends on us using water wisely.’ (Danielle Prokop / Source NM)
Deb Haaland earned a decisive victory over her primary election opponent, Bernalillo County District Attorney Sam Bregman, in June with a 44% lead. That evening, as election results came in, she addressed a crowd of supporters gathered in Albuquerque’s Old Town Plaza and promised to deliver a “better New Mexico.”
In the months since then, Haaland, a Laguna Pueblo member, has often invoked her lived experience as an Indigenous New Mexican and as the head of a federal agency. She knows what it’s like to rely on SNAP and Medicaid, she’s often said, and she also knows how to lead an organization with a multibillion-dollar budget and thousands of employees.
Over the summer, she’s campaigned on a platform of affordability and has pledged to work toward creating a public option for healthcare in the state. She recently promised to enact a data center moratorium immediately upon taking office while the Legislature works in the upcoming 60-day lawmaking session to create guardrails around the industry.
Haaland has also campaigned on increasing tax credits for working families and families with children and recently pledged to support a proposed bill that would ban landlords from using artificial intelligence to “price fix.”
“I really want to put more money in people’s pockets,” she told Source NM. “We need more of a focus on New Mexicans being treated fairly.”
What is the biggest issue facing New Mexico?
I believe I answered this in the primary as affordability, and it’s worse now because gas is more expensive and people are putting gas on their credit cards. People are going into debt just to get to work.
It’s directly related to the things that Donald Trump is doing. I’m going to blame this squarely on the president.
What makes you the better choice for voters?
I am the candidate with the experience to be the next governor. I managed one of the largest departments in the federal government; 70,000 employees and an $18 billion annual budget. I did that for four consecutive years. I represented District 1 in Congress where I got five bills signed and passed into law.
I know how the federal government works. The federal government has obligations to our state, so I would be the best-suited to hold the federal government accountable.
How would you approach overseeing the state’s universal childcare program in your first term?
I would make sure that it continues. When I think about what that program would have done for me when I was raising my kid as a single mom, it would have really changed my life in a good way.
We need to boost capacity, we need to bring more professionals in, open more programs in various parts of the state and even our largest cities.
Do you see a need for reform in the Children, Youth and Families Department, and what changes would you implement?
Hiring a qualified and experienced secretary will be the first order of business. I’ll also work to build morale in the department and to fill those positions where there’s a shortage, whether it’s social workers, case workers and so forth. 
I am ready to overhaul CYFD and then implement a commission to set policies.
What issues do you want to see the state Legislature take up in the coming 60-day session?
There’s a lot of things that we need to get across the finish line.
The medical professional compacts, there are still some of those that weren’t passed.
Aside from the child tax credits and working-class families tax credits that I’ve spoken a lot about, some of my education plans are priorities. Reading coaches in schools, my Every Child Outdoor Initiative, I’d love to get started on that.
Of course I want to address healthcare, making a public option available for New Mexicans so nobody is without health insurance.
If elected, what is your first order of business after being sworn in?
I know you see governors and presidents with a big stack of executive orders to sign on day one. I don’t expect to have a great big stack of executive orders. If I win the election on Nov. 3, we’re going to immediately work on our budget.
Gov. Lujan Grisham appointed her fifth education secretary earlier this year during her tenure and the state continues to rank at or near the bottom in education. What do you think the problem is and how would you solve it?
I’m grateful for the early literacy program that we’ve been moving toward. I really feel that reading should be a top priority for our students overall. My pledge to put more reading coaches in classrooms; I really feel that this is a human-to-human endeavor that we need.
I know this because I’m a mom and I helped my child to read at an early age. If kids can read, they have the confidence to move through their entire educational journey.
What do you think Gov. Lujan Grisham has done the best in her tenure and what are you most critical of?
The things I really appreciate the most are the early childhood initiatives and the universal childcare. I could see how those can change people’s lives and help our kids, so I’m really grateful for that. I’ve been around for a while and I know that we tried to get early childhood education across the finish line for a long time, and she was able to do it.
Obviously I’m critical of Donald Trump, but I’m otherwise not one to be super critical of leaders here in our state. Gov. Lujan Grisham, some of the issues she faced were so massive. COVID, the worst fires in the history of our state. Those were things that were really urgent.
As secretary of the Interior you oversaw billions of dollars in infrastructure, conservation and clean energy projects. How would you support those projects on a statewide level?
I really am very committed to addressing our legacy pollution issue. I think everyone deserves to breathe clean air and have land they can live on and farm or what have you.
You’ve been critical of the Trump administration’s effects on New Mexico, particularly as it pertains to budget cuts on services like Medicaid and food assistance. How would you approach governing during the remainder of his second term?
The Legislature and the governor have worked hard to address the issue so that New Mexico can fill in the gaps. I want us to have navigators in the state government.
What the Trump administration will really work to do is kick people off because they aren’t recertified in the right manner. They’re going to put all these hoops in front of everyone to jump through and they want people to throw up their hands. I want to make sure that we are helping anyone and everyone we can to recertify for the programs.
Gregg Hull
Former Rio Rancho Mayor and Republican gubernatorial nominee Gregg Hull. (Danielle Prokop/Source NM)
Gregg Hull first won election as Rio Rancho’s mayor in 2014. Twelve years later, he decided not to pursue the office again as he spent this summer in a three-way contest for the Republican gubernatorial nomination.
He defeated public relations professional Doug Turner and former New Mexico cabinet secretary and current cannabis CEO Duke Rodriguez with 47% of the vote.
While campaigning for governor, he’s often touted Rio Rancho’s accomplishments in the dozen years he oversaw the state’s third-largest city. Its population grew from about 93,000 to nearly 113,000 and the city won numerous Government Finance Officers Association budget awards under his leadership.
But as a Republican who, if elected, would oversee a Democrat-controlled Legislature, he’s equally quick to tout his experience as a nonpartisan politician.
While he disagrees with Haaland and Democratic state lawmakers on certain policy proposals, such as a proposed data center moratorium, he believes he can effectively work with elected officials in both parties — like he did during his eight years as chair of the New Mexico Mayors Caucus — to steer the state through the next four years.
“Governors get in there and, this is not a criticism, they’ve never had any type of municipal-level experience,” he told Source NM. “They haven’t been down in the communities to actually figure out what it takes to get the trash picked up and potholes filled and what it takes to make sure that the stop lights are timed properly and the police force is adequately equipped.”
What is the biggest issue facing New Mexico?
Our declining population. Having a lack of economic opportunity in our state, a lack of healthcare and poorly ranked education is driving people out of our state.
You fix that by working on making sure that when people are here, they know their kids can get quality education and when they get that education, there are actual opportunities for them to work and live here.
What makes you the better choice for voters?
The experience that I’ve had working within the state of New Mexico on so many different levels. Yes, I was mayor of Rio Rancho for 12 years, but I was not a mayor in a bubble. For eight years, I was the chair of the New Mexico Mayors Caucus, where I worked with every mayor across the state. I think that’s reflective of why (former Las Cruces) Mayor Ken Miyagishima came out and endorsed me after he discontinued his gubernatorial campaign.
We haven’t had somebody with my experience actually go to the Roundhouse, I believe, since Clyde Tingley, who was president of the Council of Albuquerque at the time.
How would you approach overseeing the state’s universal childcare program in your first term?
The first thing we need to look at is making sure that the most needy of individuals get those services. I have been opposed to the fact that this childcare program is not just for the most needy in our communities, but it’s also going to the wealthiest in our state.
I think there needs to be some balance there. We need to look at those higher-income echelons and look at the originally proposed co-pay systems, because I think you could divert those co-pays into helping daycares meet the criteria to become qualified and then more of our lower-income individuals would actually benefit from the program.
Do you see a need for reform in the Children, Youth and Families Department, and what changes would you implement?
We absolutely do need to see reform in CYFD. We need a director in there that is a qualified individual who knows how to deal with child psychology and child well-being and is certified in these things. We need to help CYFD employees gain certifications and trainings that they need.
What issues do you want to see the state Legislature take up in the coming 60-day session?
The Legislature outlined some ideas that they wanted to take up with CYFD. I actually agreed with most of them. 
The only thing I want to make sure we tap the brakes on is reunification. You’ve got to make sure the child’s safety comes before reunification.
We also need to look at robust infrastructure packages that will help communities upgrade their water systems up and down the state.
If elected, what is your first order of business after being sworn in?
CYFD and the Public Education Department. I’ll work with our superintendents and our local school districts to make sure we have consistent goals of what we want to see to help improve the education scores of children in New Mexico.
Making sure that we are enabling our children to read by the third grade is critical. I’ll also work with PED to talk about how we invest more money into career and technical education.
Gov. Lujan Grisham appointed her fifth education secretary earlier this year during her tenure and the state continues to rank at or near the bottom in education. What do you think the problem is and how would you solve it?
Once you hire a PED secretary, you need the most qualified individual you can hire. As a leader, when that qualified individual tells you, ‘This is the way things should be done’ and they give you advice and bring their experience to the table, that needs to be listened to. That experience needs to be put to work.
I would propose additional deputy cabinet secretaries. We have one right now that deals with special education, but I’d like to see a deputy cabinet secretary for rural northern New Mexico, rural southern New Mexico, the metro areas and then one that’s a direct liaison with our pueblos so that we’re dealing with our Indigenous people to make sure that their cultures are being respected and that their languages are actually part of the curriculum.
What do you think Gov. Lujan Grisham has done the best in her tenure and what are you most critical of?
I’m always cautious about criticizing current elected officials. It’s easy to second guess and be a backseat driver.
I think that she’s worked very hard. She worked very hard to try to get some things done in education, she worked very hard to get some things done in public safety.
If elected, you’ll be a Republican overseeing a Democrat-controlled Legislature. How would you work across the aisle in the upcoming legislative session?
I think I’ve proven that I can work across the aisle. I have worked across the aisle because mayor is a nonpartisan position.
I’m very good at building relations by sitting down, finding common ground and working together.
You’ve said that a blanket moratorium for data centers would send the message that New Mexico is closed for business, but you’ve also said that the state needs guardrails regarding such developments. How can you accomplish that without putting a pause on development while the Legislature drafts those protections?
Here’s the thing: The ability to raise guardrails already exists. This has become a political talking point that distracts us from the real issues facing New Mexico, like healthcare, education and public safety.
Data centers or any other industry coming into New Mexico have to work through the Economic Development Department and if they’re going to qualify for any kind of state incentives, you put the guardrails into the deal. Project Jupiter had guardrails built into it. Now, did they follow through on those? From what I’m hearing, no. So then you put clawbacks in the deal. If you don’t perform the way you promised, then we pull all your incentives and we stop your project.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Republicans fighting over who should hold Oklahoma’s U.S. Senate seat after election
description: Oklahoma’s recently appointed U.S. Senator and a potential successor have been quietly clashing over who gets to serve out the rest of former Sen. Markwayne Mullin’s term after November’s election. The brewing tension revolves around a central question: Who gets to be Oklahoma’s senator for the two months after the November general election results are […]
text:
Oklahoma Gov. Kevin Stitt and Alan Armstrong pose for a photo after the governor held a press conference announcing Armstrong as his appointment to the U.S. Senate on March 24, 2026 at the state Capitol. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)Oklahoma’s recently appointed U.S. Senator and a potential successor have been quietly clashing over who gets to serve out the rest of former Sen. Markwayne Mullin’s term after November’s election.


The brewing tension revolves around a central question: Who gets to be Oklahoma’s senator for the two months after the November general election results are certified?
Is it Gov. Kevin Stitt’s appointee, Sen. Alan Armstrong? Or his elected replacement, who is likely to be current Rep. Kevin Hern?
As The Washington Sun first reported, both men want the spot.
Hern has already hired Oklahoma attorney Glenn Coffee to help make his case, just in case a legal battle ensues. Armstrong is banking on Stitt’s support to carry him.
Armstrong wants to stay through January so he can work on his goal of permitting reform; Hern wants to be sworn in — assuming he wins, which is likely but not guaranteed — in November and continue his work in Congress.
Oklahoma law, which governs how the transition is supposed to go down, is unclear about the specifics of the process.
One relevant section of Oklahoma statute (Title 51, Section 15) reads: “Every appointed officer shall hold his office until the end of the term for which the officer whom he succeeds was elected or appointed, and until his successor is elected and qualified.”
Another section (Title 26, Section 12-101 (C)(3)) says: “The candidate elected to the office at the regularly scheduled election shall be deemed to also have been elected to fill the vacancy and shall be eligible to assume the office upon the official certification of the election by the State Election Board.”
Oklahoma State Senate Pro Temp Lonnie Paxton, who authored the language in the Title 51 section, is asking for a formal opinion on the matter from Oklahoma Attorney General Gentner Drummond.
Paxton asked Drummond in a Tuesday letter if the cut-off for the appointed Senator’s term is when the state certifies election results, or when other elected office transitions usually happen in January.
He’s also asking what power, if any, the governor has to decline or delay the State Election Board’s certification of the election, once the results are determined to be true. Usually, the board certifies results within seven days of an election.
The attorney general hasn’t issued an opinion, but Paxton has made an urgent case for a response, as the general election is fast approaching.
Meanwhile, former Oklahoma House speaker and current Republican candidate for Lt. Governor T. W. Shannon has weighed in on the social media platform X.
“This should not be a tough call,” Shannon wrote. “We need to get Kevin Hern sworn in the moment his election is certified. Even a few months of additional seniority is incredibly valuable for Oklahoma.”

name: National
title: Doctors and hospitals to see lower Medicaid payments in three dozen states
description: New federal rules likely will force three dozen states to reduce their annual Medicaid payments to doctors and hospitals by a total of more than $50 billion — potentially shrinking the number of providers willing to see Medicaid patients, according to a new analysis. The analysis in the peer-reviewed Health Affairs estimates that the 17 […]
text:
New federal rules likely will force three dozen states to reduce their annual Medicaid payments to healthcare providers by a total of more than $50 billion. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo / New Jersey Monitor)New federal rules likely will force three dozen states to reduce their annual Medicaid payments to doctors and hospitals by a total of more than $50 billion — potentially shrinking the number of providers willing to see Medicaid patients, according to a new analysis.
The analysis in the peer-reviewed Health Affairs estimates that the 17 states with the highest provider reimbursement rates will have to cut their spending by between 10% and 25% of their overall Medicaid budgets. Medicaid is the joint state-federal health insurance program for people with low incomes.
“It means that more of these hospitals, (and) a few nursing homes that are wrapped up in our academic medical centers, are going to start limiting the numbers of Medicaid patients that they see,” said Debra Lipson, the independent health policy researcher who authored the report. “It’s going to make it more difficult for people who are on Medicaid to get essential care.”
Medicaid generally pays doctors and hospitals  less money than private insurers and Medicare do for the same services. As a result, many providers refuse to care for Medicaid patients.
To address this problem, the federal government in 2016 began allowing the 40 states that contract with Medicaid managed care organizations to require those organizations to pay doctors and hospitals more for certain types of care.
But in the years since, federal and state spending on these so-called state-directed payments has exploded, growing from about $27 billion in 2020 (4% of total Medicaid spending) to an estimated $97.8 billion in 2024 (12% of total spending). The federal Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services estimates that 2025 spending topped $143 billion (14% of total Medicaid spending).
The broad tax and spending measure that President Donald Trump signed in July 2025 places new limits on state-directed payments. Beginning in 2028, the law requires state Medicaid programs to reduce reimbursement rates by 10 percentage points each year until they reach either 100% or 110% of what Medicare pays. States that expanded Medicaid under the Affordable Care Act would be capped at the lower rate.
Supporters of the change say state-directed payments have produced an unreasonable windfall for doctors and hospitals.
But Lipson writes that the new limits are likely to increase the gap between Medicaid payments and the cost of caring for Medicaid patients. As a result, providers are likely to limit the number of Medicaid patients they see. Another possibility, she suggests, is that providers will try to offset the losses by negotiating higher prices with commercial insurers, raising costs for non-Medicaid patients.
The 15 states that spent more than 20% of their fiscal 2024 Medicaid budgets on state-directed payments will have to make the most significant cuts, according to the Health Affairs analysis. Those states are Nebraska, Louisiana, South Carolina, Iowa, Nevada, Arizona, Kentucky, New Mexico, Illinois, Tennessee, Florida, Georgia, North Carolina, Michigan and Mississippi.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Amid disposal hazards, Michigan lawmakers consider creating battery recycling program
description: As lithium-ion batteries play an essential role in powering the devices used in the public’s everyday lives, two members of the Michigan House are looking into establishing a battery stewardship program to ensure residents dispose of their batteries safely.  During a Wednesday meeting of the House Natural Resources and Tourism Committee, Chair David Martin ([...]
text:
Photo by Jon King/Michigan AdvanceAs lithium-ion batteries play an essential role in powering the devices used in the public’s everyday lives, two members of the Michigan House are looking into establishing a battery stewardship program to ensure residents dispose of their batteries safely. 
During a Wednesday meeting of the House Natural Resources and Tourism Committee, Chair David Martin (R-Davison) welcomed input on a set of bills he’d assembled alongside Rep. Tyron Carter (D-Detroit) to create a stewardship program to manage how batteries are disposed of at the end of their life.
Under Martin and Carter’s House Bills 6159 and 6160, battery sellers and distributors will need to establish a stewardship program approved by the Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes and Energy, or work with an established stewardship organizations in order to continue to sell and distribute batteries and products that contain them.
Michigan House Natural Resources and Tourism Committee Chair David Martin (R-Davison) during a committee meeting on Sept. 23, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)
The proposed legislation would have these stewardship organizations address battery collection, ensuring batteries are collected without any cost to customers, retailers, local governments and the state. It also needs to ensure battery collection is regular, convenient, accessible and available statewide. 
Any costs for end-of-life battery management and program administration would fall on either the stewardship organization, or the business pursuing its own stewardship efforts.
While retailers that sell batteries could act as a collection site, their participation is not mandatory. 
Testifying before the committee, Katie Raverty-Evans, vice president of chapter relations for the National Waste and Recycling Association, explained that for the waste-disposal industry, battery management is a safety issue first and foremost. 
“When lithium batteries and other batteries are placed in household trash or other containers, they can be crushed, punctured, or damaged during collection and processing, creating a potential for thermal events and fires in collection vehicles, transfer stations, recycling facilities and disposal sites,” Raverty-Evans said. 
She pointed to a report that the National Waste and Recycling Association published alongside Resource Recycling Systems which found that the improper disposal of lithium batteries led to 5,000 fires annually at recycling facilities alone. In another specific example, Raverty-Evans noted that a newly-opened recycling facility in Nashville, Tenn. was forced to close for three months after a fire.
Katie Raverty-Evans, vice president of chapter relations for the National Waste and Recycling Association and Katie Gordon, legislative committee chair for the Michigan Waste & Recycling Association testify before the Michigan House Natural Resources and Tourism Committee on Sept. 23, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)
Theo Eggermont, Washtenaw County’s director of public works, said that they’ve had more than one of their trash trucks dump their contents into a parking lot due to a battery fire this year. 
“As a government official that cares about where materials go and the impacts of those materials, that’s not an acceptable way to manage this material,” Eggermont said.
Eggermont, who also chairs the Michigan Recycling Coalition’s policy committee, said the bills would expand collection infrastructure for batteries, pay for the costs to provide services, expand access, and provide education around the risks of improper disposal and the opportunities in battery recycling.
“Batteries contain critical minerals that are needed in manufacturing, and when captured, allow us to reduce the dependence on international supply chains,” Eggermont said, noting that Michigan residents throw away an estimated 11,000 tons of batteries each year, including 29 million lithium ion batteries.
Michigan Association of Fire Chiefs President Chris Stoecklein approached the issue from a fire services perspective, noting that fire departments across the state are asked to do more with less each day.
“The safest thing for a firefighter and for the public is to never have that fire in the first place,” Stoecklein told the committee. 
Michigan Association of Fire Chiefs President Chris Stoecklein discusses the fire risks posed by improper battery disposal during a meeting of the House Natural Resources and Tourism Committee on Sept. 23, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)
Mike Witkowski, director of environmental and regulatory policy for the Michigan Manufacturers Association, opposed the bills. 
While he acknowledged the safety risks that come with the disposal and transportation of lithium ion batteries, Witkowski argued the state should build a system around what it already has in place, rather than creating additional rules and financial obligations for manufacturers. 
“Under these bills, producers would be responsible for funding collection, transport, recycling, education, administration, safety requirements, and other programs,” Witkowski said. “There’s also no statutory cap on the overall cost of that obligation, so all of that would be passed on to manufacturers or producers of these batteries without sort of a stopgap in how much it costs.”
If the Legislature determines that additional collection waste management services are needed for batteries, Witkowski argued those services should be paid by the people who use those services, including manufacturers when appropriate.
The committee only took testimony on the bills at Wednesday’s hearing and did not put the legislation up for a vote.

name: Delaware
title: Campaign to Stop Human Trafficking in Delaware starts with helping the people who may never ask for help
description: An inaugural Oct. 2 Summit in Dewey Beach will bring caregivers, clinicians, advocates and other professionals together to recognize exploitation and improve support for survivors. DEWEY BEACH, Del. — A person being trafficked may still go to work, attend school or see a doctor. What those around them may not see is the person controlling their pay, housing,[...]
text:
An inaugural Oct. 2 Summit in Dewey Beach will bring caregivers, clinicians, advocates and other professionals together to recognize exploitation and improve support for survivors.

DEWEY BEACH, Del. — A person being trafficked may still go to work, attend school or see a doctor. What those around them may not see is the person controlling their pay, housing, access to drugs or ability to leave.

That is the challenge at the center of Delaware’s inaugural Human Trafficking Awareness, Prevention and Action Summit on Friday, Oct. 2, at Hyatt Place Dewey Beach. The Delaware Coalition for Human Trafficking Survivors is bringing survivors, national experts and Delaware professionals together to improve how the state recognizes exploitation and responds to people affected by it.
Two ways exploitation can stay hidden
Imagine Elena, an adult who cleans homes. She depends on the person who hired her for a place to sleep and a ride to work. Her promised pay never arrives, but she fears losing her housing if she leaves. Someone meeting Elena might see a hard-working employee, without knowing how little control she has over her work or money. Elena is fictional, but her situation illustrates a recognized pattern of forced labor.

Now imagine Jay, a 16-year-old who accepts a place to stay from someone he trusts. That person then expects commercial sex in exchange. Jay may be frightened to tell a teacher or caregiver, or may not describe what happened as trafficking. Jay is also fictional. Jennifer Cooper, a registered nurse and forensic coordinator at Nemours Children’s Health, told Delaware LIVE that young people may not recognize food, housing or other things of value as part of commercial sexual exploitation. Under federal law, a minor induced into commercial sex is a trafficking victim even without proof of force, fraud or coercion.

Victims do not fit one age, gender or background. Trafficking also does not require kidnapping or crossing a border. The common issue is exploitation: force, fraud or coercion used to compel an adult to provide labor or commercial sex, or the commercial sexual exploitation of a minor.
What Delaware’s numbers show
The National Human Trafficking Hotline identified 29 Delaware cases involving 32 victims in 2025. In 2024, it identified 32 cases involving 61 victims. The hotline cautions that reports made to it do not measure how often trafficking actually occurs; people who never contact the hotline are outside its count.
Another measure comes from Delaware’s Office of the Child Advocate. Its contribution to the Delaware Anti-Trafficking Action Council’s 2025 report says the office screened 65 juvenile trafficking referrals, including 40 classified as suspected trafficking and 25 involving young people assessed as at risk. Those are referrals, not 65 confirmed crimes, and they cannot simply be added to the hotline total.

Together, the figures show why professionals who encounter vulnerable people need to know what questions to ask, how to respond safely and where to turn for help.
Bringing the people who respond into one room
Cooper said she helped pursue a Delaware summit after traveling out of state for advanced training. The Oct. 2 program includes tracks for mental health professionals, medical providers, direct-service workers, law enforcement and survivors. Sessions are expected to address family-related trafficking, trauma, survivor care and coordinated responses.
“I want to bring together the people who are doing the work,” Cooper told Delaware LIVE. She said organizations serving vulnerable people can benefit from knowing what others nearby are doing and where services are missing.

The summit is an opportunity for psychologists and other mental health clinicians, advocates, health care workers, educators, caregivers and community leaders to learn from survivors and from one another. It is also open to residents who want a better understanding of trafficking in Delaware. A private, invitation-only executive roundtable will take place Oct. 1; the public summit follows Oct. 2.

To Go Box

What: Human Trafficking Awareness, Prevention and Action Summit
When: Friday, Oct. 2, 2026
Where: Hyatt Place Dewey Beach, 1301 Coastal Highway
Who: Professionals, advocates, caregivers, organizational leaders and interested residents
Admission: $75 regular admission, listed as available through Sept. 30
Register: Summit registration
