name: Florida Phoenix
title: Autism Speaks chair, managed care plans up on next ABA task force agenda
description: A Florida task force that could reshape how the state provides therapy to children with special needs and autism is getting together again. The state’s applied behavior analysis (ABA) task force meets Monday and will consider testimony from a managed care panel that includes representatives from Simply Healthcare, Sunshine Health, and Humana Healthy Horizons[...]
text:
Autism awareness bracelet worn by an audience member at the Aug. 31, 2026, ABA task force meeting in Tallahassee. (Photo by Christine Sexton/Florida Phoenix)A Florida task force that could reshape how the state provides therapy to children with special needs and autism is getting together again.
The state’s applied behavior analysis (ABA) task force meets Monday and will consider testimony from a managed care panel that includes representatives from Simply Healthcare, Sunshine Health, and Humana Healthy Horizons.
It also will hear from Dr. Thomas Frazier, national board chair at Autism Speaks and a research professor at SUNY-Upstate.
The 10-member task force was created to make recommendations to the next Legislature and governor on ways to improve the “care and experience and service continuity for enrollees and families receiving ABA services, while safeguarding long term program sustainability.”
In legislative parlance, that’s code for trimming costs. 
But just how big of a budget worry is the delivery of ABA services in Florida?
State Sen. Gayle Harrell, a Republican from Stuart, pressed Florida’s top economist during a recent Legislative Budget Commission meeting about ABA services and how the costs of providing the care are affecting the state budget. That’s a panel empowered to spend money outside of legislative sessions.
Amy Baker, director of the Office of Economic and Demographic Research, said the news is encouraging, at least for now.
“What we’re starting to hear this summer … is that the escalation and costs associated with kids with autism or other related issues is starting to slow down some and soften a little bit,” Baker told Harrell. “And so, we’ll have to see if that continues, but that was pretty encouraging. I think in part that had to do with some changes that had been made to how we service those children.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
One such change was requiring Medicaid-covered ABA services to be provided by managed care plans under contract with the state. Before 2025, these services were provided on a fee-for-service basis by providers outside the managed care plans’ networks.
State Sen. Gayle Harrell via Florida Senate
Harrell pressed Baker about fraud and abuse.
“I know we’ve had a major problem with ABA services and a lot of fraud that has gone into that. Are we making adjustments for that?” Harrell asked, referencing the announcement by the DeSantis administration that it was cracking down on Medicaid fraud, waste, and abuse. 
The governor announced the state’s efforts after Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Director Mehmet Oz said on social media that “Florida has been a hotspot for health care fraud for years.”
Oz sent a letter to Florida (as well as California, Maine, and New York) seeking information about the state’s Medicaid integrity and oversight efforts.
But Baker said,  “To my knowledge, we’re not. I don’t remember any discussion of that or any issues that came up in the summer conferences related to that. So, I think the best I could say, at this point, is we’re silent on that.”
Big part of state budget
Baker told the panel members that Medicaid is always one of the critical-need drivers in the state budget. Health and human services spending in Florida, mostly provided by Medicaid, ranked as the No. 6 critical need in the Long Range Financial Outlook that Baker’s office released Sept. 11
This year’s report projects that spending on health and social programs will continue to eat a large part of the state’s general revenue commitment over the next three years, both in terms of overall dollars spent and the overall percentage of state general revenue dollars being directed to those programs.
While health and human services accounts for $1.96 billion, or 37.5%, of general revenues in state fiscal year 2027-2028, the spending requirement drops the following year to $1.53 billion (25.5%) and $1.19 billion (21.6%) in state fiscal year 2029-2030.
Those Medicaid spending estimates are based on enrollment, service utilization, the federal government matching rate (officially called the Federal Medical Assistance Percentage), medical inflation, and managed care rate changes. 
Applied behavior analysis uses structured interventions to decrease maladaptive behaviors and reinforce appropriate ones. ABA is common in the treatment of children diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder and for people with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), traumatic brain injuries, and intellectual and developmental disabilities.
Why does Florida spend so much money on treatment for children with autism and special needs?

While Baker didn’t single out ABA as a worry, Shena Grantham, Florida’s deputy secretary for Medicaid policy and quality, told the task force last month that in the past two years Florida has spent more money than any other state in the nation providing ABA services to children.
About 60,000 poor and low-income children in Florida receive applied behavioral analysis at a cost of about $2.3 billion, Grantham said, although she didn’t cite the year.
She said the state spent more on ABA services for those children than it did providing pediatric hospital care for 966,900 children, doctor visits for 1.75 million children, and prescription drugs for about 1.4 million children.
Before a child can receive ABA services through Florida Medicaid, he or she must be referred by a doctor or child psychologist. The child must undergo a comprehensive evaluation to formally diagnose or rule out autism and determine medically necessary therapies.
The task force must submit its recommendations — along with the pros and cons of each proposal — to the governor and Legislature by Dec. 31.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi Book Festival has grown from its beginning as a literary lawn party
description: Crew members from Mississippi Tent and Party Rental erect tents outside the Capitol in Jackson on Monday, Sept. 21, 2026, in preparation for the Mississippi Book Festival.
text:
The state’s capital is about to be buzzing with all things bookish, as readers and writers descend on downtown Jackson on Saturday for the 11th annual Mississippi Book Festival.
Chris Kelly, who co-founded the JXN Book Club over the summer, is “beyond excited” for this weekend’s events. He and the club’s other co-founder, Kimar Cain, hosted the festival team at its first meeting in July and are eager to serve as unofficial event ambassadors.
“It’s like being Walmart greeters,” Kelly said. “We want to be a cheerful, thoughtful presence that builds excitement and keeps people engaged.” 
Christopher Kelly, left, and Kimar Cain chat about the book they and members of the book club they started are currently reading, “Parable of the Sower” by Octavia E. Butler, at Lemuria Books, Tuesday, Sept. 22, 2026, in Jackson. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
The book festival has grown from a one-day lawn party into a major economic and cultural engine for Jackson, drawing more than 8,000 book lovers and providing a counter-narrative to negative stereotypes. It has also spurred year-round educational programs to develop Mississippi’s next generation of writers.
This year’s lineup features former “Saturday Night Live” cast member Kate McKinnon, hip-hop boss Rick Ross, fiction icon George Saunders and a multitude of Mississippi’s own.
Kenzie Ragland, a Nashville transplant who founded the “JXN Book Girlies” book club in 2024, is especially eager to meet McKinnon.
She plans to attend the festival with a couple dozen other “Girlies.”
“Last year was my first year at the festival,” Ragland said, “and I was pleasantly surprised at how big it was.”
Ragland is most looking forward to returning to “Author’s Alley,” the festival’s big tent where independent authors and artists set up shop and sell their stories. “Getting to meet so many incredible lesser-known authors,” Ragland said, was a festival highlight and reason to return. 
The book club hosts an online forum for its virtual membership, broken down into nine genre-specific groups. Ragland says each group hosts over 20 readers, with more popular genres, such as fantasy, meeting more regularly. 
A culture showcase for Mississippi
With thousands of book lovers converging on the capital city, the festival is a major economic driver.
Liz Brister, president of Downtown Jackson Partners, said the festival is just what the region’s economy needs, proving that Jackson can showcase Mississippi culture for crowds from around the country and the world.
Though Mississippi is often “typecast in negative ways,” Brister said, “we should pat ourselves on the back” for what the festival says about Mississippi. “It demonstrates to visitors and residents the creative and literary spirit unique to our state.”
Crew members from Mississippi Tent and Party Rental erect tents outside the Capitol in Jackson on Monday, Sept. 21, 2026, in preparation for the Mississippi Book Festival. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Ellen Daniels, the festival’s director, noted the event’s growing diversity of authors and panels. 
Lauren Rhoades hosts an online monthly book club featuring authors connected to the South. It is on Rooted Magazine, an online platform featuring stories about what it means to call Mississippi home. Rooted runs a monthly column by Joseph Brown, a state prison inmate who has “been fighting his wrongful conviction on Parchman’s death row for more than thirty years.”
Rhoades, who came to Jackson in 2013 with AmeriCorps, now helps oversee grants for the state Arts Commission, one of the festival’s sources of funding. She is returning to the festival for the second year in a row to discuss her 2025 memoir, “Split Baby,” which chronicles the fractures of a childhood torn between two very different homes. 
While the festival understandably features many writers who draw on the South’s literary heritage, there are also events such as a panel presented by the LGBTQ Fund of Mississippi that delves into the search for belonging, friendship and self-discovery. 
Another panel called “Fathers and Sons” features award-winning journalist Tom Junod and portrait photographer Beowulf Sheehan, both of whom have recent works involving the theme of fatherhood.
Mississippi Today will also present a discussion featuring renowned analysts of the ongoing role of race in our country. The panel, called “the Soul of America,” will be aired on CSPAN.
‘A last frontier for civil discourse’
In today’s polarized political climate, “book festivals serve as a last frontier for civil discourse,” Daniels said. “There really is something for every audience.” 
The book clubs described above provide a snapshot of the kind of engaged readers the festival brings together. However, the festival’s impact is increasingly felt in many developing writers’ lives well beyond the main event.
Tonja Murphy, the festival’s community engagement director, stressed that one of the biggest changes has been in the festival’s growing devotion to the practice of writing. 
When Murphy took on her full-time role in 2022, she was tasked with developing a new initiative called “Turn the Page,” which brings authors into public schools across Mississippi. She said the program helps students find their literary voice by bringing in engaging authors who practice creative writing with them. 
“Some of our schools are hours from Jackson, so not all students can get to the festival,” Murphy said. “Turn the Page really grew out of the festival’s own kids’ programming, when we stepped back and asked, what would it look like to take this to children across the state?”
Now in its fourth year, the program has reached classrooms from kindergarten through high school. “You know you’re doing something right when the schools regularly ask you, ‘Can we get on next year’s list?’,” Murphy said.
While Turn the Page was initially funded out of the festival’s budget, it now has its own annual fundraising campaigns, Daniels said. “Turn the Page has funders who are totally dedicated to its mission.” 
Writing workshops for all ages have become central to the festival. This year’s event has four kids’ workshops, ranging from prose and creative writing to arts and crafts, in addition to a handful focusing on different genres and skillsets for youth and adults.
“Some of our country’s greatest writers are from Mississippi,” Murphy said. “Who’s to say that a child that attends one of our programs isn’t our next literary giant?”
In a state where adult literacy rates are still among the poorest in the nation, the wide reach of programs like Turn the Page is shaping Mississippi’s own storytelling future.
That such an initiative emerged from the book festival, whose programming has grown and become more diverse in recent years, signals that the book festival is nurturing new generations of readers and writers.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Morrisey declares state of emergency for Boone, Lincoln counties after flooding
description: West Virginia Gov. Patrick Morrisey has issued a state of emergency for two counties in Southern West Virginia after heavy rains this week caused flash flooding.
text:
Gov. Patrick Morrisey looks at flooding damage in Fayette County, West Virginia on Aug. 19, 2026. The state has experienced multiple major flooding events in the last few months, including one earlier this week in Boone and Lincoln counties. (Photo courtesy of the West Virginia Office of Gov. Patrick Morrisey)West Virginia Gov. Patrick Morrisey has issued a state of emergency for two counties in Southern West Virginia after heavy rains this week caused flash flooding. 
Boone and Lincoln counties are included in the state of emergency, which will be in place 30 days unless ended early by another proclamation.
“Our emergency responders are working to protect West Virginians as flooding continues to impact communities in Boone and Lincoln counties,” Morrisey said in a news release late Wednesday night. “I urge everyone in the affected areas to remain alert, avoid flooded roadways, and follow instructions from local emergency officials. We are making state resources available to support communities and first responders wherever they are needed.” 
A series of storms beginning Monday brought repeated periods of heavy rain across the state, overwhelming streams, creeks, drainage systems and low-water crossings, Morrisey’s office said in a news release. 
The state of emergency allows  the state to coordinate and deploy personnel, equipment and other resources necessary to support local emergency response and recovery operations, the news release says.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraska Senate race has seen tough talk and shifts on Immigration
description: The Nebraska Senate race between incumbent Ricketts and Osborn has seen tough talk on immigration as they both try to win a ruby red state.
text:
A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer watches a crowd of protesters at Delaney Hall, a detention center, in Newark, New Jersey, on May 25, 2026. Employing new tactics, ICE arrested more people in July than in any previous month of the Trump administration. (Photo by Ben Ackman/New Jersey Monitor)LINCOLN — The Nebraska Senate race between frontrunners Sen. Pete Ricketts and Dan Osborn has seen tough talk on immigration throughout the campaign cycle as they both try to win a ruby red state. 
Osborn, the registered nonpartisan candidate, has stated his support for stronger border security as proof of his independent chops during his campaign, but his stance has been muddied after leaked audio clips on the issue — a problem that doesn’t seem to be going away for the former labor leader. Ricketts takes a hardline conservative stance on the border and immigration as one would expect from a Republican in a red state. 
Immigration and its enforcement were big issues during the 2024 presidential election as the Biden administration saw illegal border crossings spike at the end of 2023 but start decreasing in 2024. With Trump’s return to the White House, illegal crossings on the southern border a historic low. But U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, now the nation’s highest-funded law enforcement agency because of Trump’s tax and spending bill, has faced backlash for its tactics over the past two years, sparking protests across the country, including in Nebraska. 
A Florida Republican House member recently cut a campaign ad saying Trump’s “immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far,” a sign of the midterm environment Republicans are facing. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Nebraska, an agricultural state, hasn’t seen many major ICE raids in recent years aside from a raid on Omaha’s Glenn Valley Foods in 2025, but has dealt with misinformation and fear over ICE activity. The Trump administration eased off raids in the agriculture and hospitality industries last year, addressing concerns about the rising cost of food, according to Stateline. 
Both Ricketts and Osborn have criticized the Biden administration’s border policies and praised Trump for securing the border. They both have expressed concerns over the killing of Alex Pretti and Renee Good during Minnesota’s Operation Metro Surge earlier this year and called for an investigation.
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
Osborn has tried to make the case that neither party is doing enough to accomplish comprehensive immigration reform that’s humane and can fix the problem, “because it’s an economic issue.” 
Osborn, in an interview with the Examiner last year, used the “Big Four meatpackers” as an example of an industry that benefits from having a “wide open border with no immigration policy, because they can exploit the labor, enrich themselves, and then they donate millions of dollars to candidates so they won’t do anything about it.” 
Osborn has called for mandatory E-Verify to confirm that prospective employees can work in the United States. In a press call in June 2025, Ricketts said that while E-Verify is meant to help businesses maintain a legal workforce, it isn’t perfect, according to Brownfield Ag News. 
Registered nonpartisan U.S. Senate candidate Dan Osborn speaking in Lincoln on June 11, 2026. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)
“It’s challenging sometimes if they’re relying solely on E-Verify,” Ricketts said. “That checking is just that the Social Security number is good generally, and if there’s more ways to get better information, that would be helpful in verifying people’s ability to take employment.”
Nebraska doesn’t mandate E-Verify use, but companies with state contracts must use it. State agencies and local governments must also use it. 
Ricketts has touted Republicans’ success in reducing border crossings during the second Trump administration. During Ricketts’ time as governor, he sent Nebraska State Patrol troopers to the Texas border in 2021. 
The former governor got the endorsement of a union that represents U.S. Border Patrol agents. During that press conference, Ricketts said fentanyl seizures and human trafficking cases had increased in Nebraska during the Biden administration.
Nebraska Sen. Pete Ricketts speaks at his annual steak fry in Weeping Water on Sept. 20, 2026. (Photo by Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)
“Our border is secure. Our immigration laws are being enforced. Nebraska is safer as a result,” Ricketts said in his answer to the Examiner’s voter guide. 
Ricketts also touted his vote for Trump’s Big Beautiful Bill that increased the ICE budget as an example of his work to secure the border. Osborn has called the increase in ICE funding “wasteful spending” because the agency has no real accountability. Osborn has criticized ICE for wearing masks and for memes the agency has used to rally the GOP base. 
During the State Fair debate with Ricketts, Osborn said “we should never get used to troops in our streets.” He also emphasized that he supports ICE’s mission of keeping the community safe. 
Some audio leaks of Osborn’s comments on immigration and ICE have clashed with his public statements. In one leak from a private meeting in July with Latino and Black Democrats, he said President Donald Trump’s border wall is “a symbol of racism” that “does nothing.” 
Osborn released a statement after the border wall comment “I am clear that I support strong, effective border security. When I give President Trump full credit for securing the border, some people don’t like that. But because I’m an independent, I don’t have to blindly support the purity tests of either party. I’ll fight for a border wall where it makes sense, and other strategies where it doesn’t, like in Big Bend National Park.” 
CNN reported that Osborn said he had alerted ICE to allegations of undocumented immigrants replacing Kellogg’s striking workers during his time as a labor union leader. His campaign told CNN that Osborn never personally contacted ICE or the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, but called the local sheriff’s office to ask how to report such allegations. 
In another leaked recording from a 2025 town hall, Osborn says he sees parallels between the current scapegoating of migrants and what happened to German Jews in the 1930s. Another one has him saying that he would be “f—ed” as a candidate if he said that he wanted to “abolish ICE.”  
Osborn pushed back on the leaks, saying some take conversations out of context. The Ricketts campaign and Republicans have used the recordings  as proof in their relentless quest to paint Osborn as a “secret Democrat.” 
Three other candidates are on the ballot for the Senate race: Chuck Conboy, America First Party; Robin Richards, Working People Party; and Mike Marvin, Legal Marijuana NOW, who has suspended his campaign. Their answers are in the Examiner’s voter guide. 
The general election is Nov. 3.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Reticent in primary, Lamont hits Fazio early in general-election ads
description: Gov. Ned Lamont, seldom comfortable with the grittier aspects of political combat,  is regularly hitting Republican Ryan Fazio in TV ads.
text:
Gov. Ned Lamont, seldom comfortable with the grittier aspects of political combat, is regularly hitting Republican Ryan Fazio in a television advertising campaign that displays a rhythm and focus absent in his Democratic primary against Josh Elliott. 
On the air this week are paired 30-second ads by Lamont’s campaign: A positive piece features an amiable governor high-fiving kids as he walks through a school reciting highlights of his record on education; a negative one shows worried educators fretting about votes on education by Fazio in the state Senate. 
“Ryan Fazio — where do I even begin?” says one exasperated teacher in an ad that cuts to a second educator, who replies, “He voted against so many things that helped teachers, students and parents.” A third complains, “Ryan Fazio opposed giving free breakfast to kids in need.”


The spot is titled “Report Card.” It follows two others that contrast Fazio’s positions with Lamont’s on measures the governor signed to counter President Donald Trump’s aggressive campaign to deport undocumented immigrants and the federal cutbacks that have raised the cost of healthcare coverage.
“I found out during the primary, you get attacked, you get attacked pretty hard, and at some point, you’ve got to respond and defend yourself,” Lamont said in an interview this week. He spoke after an event highlighting another contrast: Fazio’s vote against an AI regulatory bill the governor promoted and signed.
Fazio was one of only four senators to oppose the bill that passed with overwhelming bipartisan support, saying the state should defer to federal action that seems unlikely, given the opposition of the president.
During the primary against Elliott, Lamont did not heed early warnings that the liberal lawmaker from Hamden was on track to qualify for a primary and public campaign financing unless the governor pushed back. His one hard shot at Elliott didn’t come until a week before the Aug. 11 contest.
“Yeah,” Lamont said, acknowledging the campaign was slow to hit Elliott. “But we did.”
Lamont won the primary in a landslide, 67.8% to 32.2%.  
Last week, a Quinnipiac University poll found Lamont leading Fazio by 17 percentage points, one of three public polls showing the governor with a double-digit lead. A fourth by co/efficient, a marketing and survey firm with a Republican clientele, found Fazio within 7 points.
Fazio’s ads are trying to focus voters on the high cost of living in Connecticut, a concern identified in each poll, and suggest there is no reason to expect that the governor can accomplish things in a third term that he could not in the first two.


Lamont’s two-track approach — promoting his record, while undermining his challenger’s — is hardly unconventional.
Liz Kurantowicz, a former Republican campaign operative, said using the candidate’s face and voice for positive messages and third-party “validators” to deliver criticism was standard fare for the campaign of a relatively popular incumbent.
Vinnie Mauro Jr., the New Haven Democratic chair, said neither campaign is running provocative ads designed to rile their base. The governor’s ads, he said, are what should be expected from a Democratic incumbent running in a blue state with high name recognition after eight years in office.“What he’s trying to do is say, ‘Look at me. I’ve been a steady hand on the wheel. You may agree with me on some things. You may disagree with me on other things. But in terms of what Connecticut needs and wants, I am the right guy.’ That message is the right message for the state of Connecticut,” Mauro said. “Is it going to make the left part of the party excited? No, it’s not. But that’s not his intention here.”
But Fazio says the Lamont ads attacking him are evidence the governor views the race as competitive and that he has too little to say about a third-term agenda.
“The governor, even though he’s an incumbent, even though everyone knows who he is already after eight years, is not focusing primarily on his record,” Fazio said. “He’s focusing primarily on misleading voters about me, which I think shows that despite his incumbency, he’s relatively weak.”
Four years ago, when Lamont was seeking reelection to a second term in a rematch with Republican Bob Stefanowski, the governor frustrated his campaign staff by refusing to sign off on commercials attacking Stefanowski over his background as the former CEO of a payday loan company.
A payday loan ad eventually aired, but it came from a SuperPAC funded by the Democratic Governors Association, not Lamont’s campaign. Lamont dismissed Stefanowski’s private-sector record at GE, UBS and the payday lender, DFC Global, as irrelevant, at least compared to a public record.
“Last time around, I was running against somebody who had no record. He had done something at GE, not particularly relevant. Now I’m running against somebody who’s been in the state Senate for a lot of years,” Lamont said. 
Fazio, 36, was elected five years ago to the Senate from Greenwich, the governor’s hometown. The Report Card ad is based on Fazio’s vote against a budget that increased spending for education and school meals. 
Fazio said he supports higher spending for education but found other elements of the budget objectionable. He said the governor’s ad was an example of “taking big bills, complicated votes, and picking out one thing.”
Elliott had attacked Lamont, a 72-year-old former business owner, as a beneficiary of multigenerational wealth, indifferent to the economic pressures on the poor and middle class. He also darkly suggested that Lamont’s wife, a successful venture capitalist, had profited from her marriage to the governor.
While Lamont and Fazio are running attack ads, they largely have focused on policies. Fazio, who remains unknown to a significant portion of the electorate, is running several lighthearted ads with a dual purpose of raising his profile and criticizing the governor.
Fazio is cast as a superhero in one ad, strong enough to save Connecticut from expensive electricity and high taxes tolerated by Lamont. Another portrays him as wielding defibrillator paddles in a hospital room over a patient flatlining from taxes imposed by Democrats. There are 15- and 30-second versions of the spots on television and digital media.


“His are a little more cartoonish, but you know, they’re not attacking my wife or my family or my grandfather. It’s a little different tone than where I was four months ago,” Lamont said, referring to the more personal daily assaults from Elliott. “Let’s keep it to the issues. Let’s keep it to our records.”
The governor, however, has not hesitated to draw an unpopular president into the campaign. His own healthcare ad publicizes the $500 million fund Lamont has used to offset actions by Trump or Congress undermining the Affordable Care Act. Fazio was one of eight senators, all Republicans, to vote against creating the fund.


Humor is an element in most of Fazio’s ads, with at least two featuring clips of the governor. One of the spots dinging Lamont as failing to appreciably bring down electric rates featured a clip of him making a joke that did not quite land: If electric rates were so high, people would be turning out the lights.
“My ads have employed some humor, and at the same time, in doing so, have tried to make the point that we need to cut taxes and cut electric rates to make Connecticut affordable,” Fazio said. “I’m trying to be myself. I’m trying to focus on the issues that I care about and my vision for the state, but also to try to have some fun in the process. And I think it’s attracting people’s attention, and it’s giving people a little bit of an introduction into who I am as a person.”
Fazio said the tone of his ads is appropriate.
“I’m critical of the governor’s failures to make the state affordable. I’m critical of the governor’s tax increases and electric bill increases,” Fazio said. “I don’t think politics needs to be nasty and performative.”
Twice this year, Fazio has dismissed campaign strategists, most recently parting ways with a consultant known to favor more aggressive ads. Was a disagreement over ads a factor?
“There’s been no change in tone or messaging on the campaign,” Fazio said.
The question wasn’t had the tone changed. The question was whether a disagreement over tone and messaging had contributed to the departure. Pressed, Fazio declined to comment further. 
“My answer is my answer.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi Today announces John Grisham as keynote speaker for its 10th anniversary celebration
description: John Grisham will speak at Mississippi Today's 10th anniversary celebration on Oct. 7.
text:
Internationally acclaimed author John Grisham will speak at Mississippi Today’s 10th Anniversary Celebration on Oct. 7 in Jackson.
Grisham will deliver the keynote address as the nonprofit newsroom marks a decade of mission-driven reporting and focuses on new ways to provide news coverage that serves communities across the state.
The celebration is sold out. Tickets are still available for Mississippi Today’s second annual “All In on Mississippi” summit on Oct. 8 beginning at 1 p.m. at the Two Mississippi Museums.
“John Grisham has won fans worldwide with his Mississippi-centric stories that are built around universal themes of accountability and the pursuit  of justice,” said Emily Wagster Pettus, editor-in-chief of Mississippi Today. “We are grateful to him for speaking at our event as we celebrate journalism that focuses on exposing systems that work – or don’t work – for the people of this state.”
Grisham’s remarks will frame an evening examining the impact of independent journalism while looking ahead to the challenges and opportunities facing communities across Mississippi and the region.
The event will also feature a fireside chat with Laurene Powell Jobs, founder and president of Emerson Collective, and Darren Walker, president of Anonymous Content, moderated by Bill Bynum, founding CEO of HOPE and Deep South Today board member. 
About John Grisham
John Grisham is the international bestselling author of more than 50 consecutive No. 1 novels that have been translated into nearly 50 languages. His recent books include “Framed,” “Camino Ghosts” and “The Exchange: After the Firm.” Grisham has been honored with the Library of Congress Creative Achievement Award for Fiction and twice awarded the Harper Lee Prize for Legal Fiction, and his narrative voice remains one of the most recognizable in modern literature.
Grisham was raised in Southaven and was educated in Mississippi, culminating in a Juris Doctor from the University of Mississippi School of Law in 1981. He managed a private law practice in Southaven for nearly a decade and served in the Mississippi House of Representatives from 1983 to 1990. His experiences inside local courtrooms directly inspired his 1989 debut novel, “A Time to Kill.”
Grisham serves on the board of directors for both the Innocence Project and Centurion Ministries, two national nonprofit organizations dedicated to exonerating the wrongfully convicted.
Mississippi Today 10th Anniversary Celebration
Taking place at the Two Mississippi Museums on Wednesday, Oct. 7, the celebration will honor public service journalism through an evening of conversation, music, storytelling and immersive experiences that showcase the newsroom’s work.
Guests will hear accounts of the newsroom’s impact while getting a look at Mississippi Today’s vision for the future. The celebration is made possible through sponsorship from Carol and John Palmer, Collaborative Resources and Solutions LLC, The McMullan O’Connor Fund and the Mississippi Press Foundation. 
‘All In on Mississippi’ summit
On Thursday, Oct. 8, Mississippi Today will host the second annual “All In on Mississippi” summit, focused on innovative solutions, economic opportunity and community impact.
Presented with support from JPMorgan Chase, the Foundation for the Mid South, Centuri, Butler Snow, Operation Shoestring, Mississippi Center for Justice, and Brown Bottling Group, the summit will bring together leaders from business, education, workforce development, philanthropy and journalism for conversations about Mississippi’s future.
Featured sessions include:

Boots on the Ground: Mississippi Industry, AI and the Future of Work.
A New Era for Apprenticeship Programs in Mississippi.
The Literacy Launching Point and What Comes Next.
Mississippi on the National Stage.

Additional speakers and agenda details can be found at summit.mississippitoday.org. 
Tickets and sponsorships
Celebration tickets are sold out.
Tickets for the “All In on Mississippi” summit are $25.
Organizations interested in sponsorship opportunities can contact sponsorships@mississippitoday.org.
Registration, sponsorship information and the latest event updates are available at: summit.mississippitoday.org.

title: Changes to Kentucky Employees’ Health Plan raise Republican eyebrows
description: Lawmakers raised concerns this week that a new state policy could leave retirees covered by the Kentucky Employees’ Health Plan without coverage.  Gov. Andy Beshear’s office said it’s determined to keep that from happening.  During Tuesday’s meeting of the Public Pension Oversight Board, co-chair Rep.Walker Thomas, R-Hopkinsville, said that people who don’t[...]
text:
Republican lawmakers are concerned about changes to the state retirees healthcare plan. (Getty Images)Lawmakers raised concerns this week that a new state policy could leave retirees covered by the Kentucky Employees’ Health Plan without coverage. 
Gov. Andy Beshear’s office said it’s determined to keep that from happening. 
During Tuesday’s meeting of the Public Pension Oversight Board, co-chair Rep.Walker Thomas, R-Hopkinsville, said that people who don’t make a health plan selection during open enrollment will see their coverage expire. 
In the past, he said, such people would have been defaulted to a plan, often the one they had the year prior. 
Lawmakers are mostly concerned, they said, about retirees who may not get emails or other notifications about the change — and find out too late they have lost their health insurance. 
“An illness, a family emergency or an overlooked notice can cause someone to miss a deadline. Losing health coverage is a serious consequence, especially for a retiree who is not eligible for Medicare,” Sen. Jimmy Higdon, R-Lebanon, said in a Tuesday statement. Higdon co-chairs the Public Pension Oversight Board with Thomas. 
He called on Beshear and the cabinet to “reconsider this policy and delay implementation for one year. That is a reasonable alternative that will ensure our retirees will not lose their health insurance.” 
Scottie Ellis, a spokesperson for the governor’s office, said the personnel cabinet is “working to make sure Kentucky state employees and retirees are informed and prepared to select the best Kentucky Employees’ Health Plan for their personal needs during open enrollment.” 
“As healthcare costs rise nationwide, health insurance premiums, co-pays and deductibles are increasing too, including for KEHP,” Ellis said in a statement. “Because of these major changes, employees and retirees are asked to complete a short, six-step process that takes 10 minutes or less. Weekly reminders via mail, email and social media will be sent to all members, and there will be 14 Benefits Fairs across the state to assist members with plans and sign-ups. As the process continues, steps will be taken so that, again, no one involuntarily loses coverage.” 
Open enrollment starts Oct. 5.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: The next Quabbin fight is already here
description: The part of the plan that’s arguably generating the most blowback is the process the MWRA is deploying to win approval from state officials.
text:
THE TEMPERATURE is continuing to climb in the growing feud between the state’s largest drinking water provider and communities that surround its main water source. 
The Massachusetts Water Resources Authority is seeking approval from state officials for a high-stakes push to draw an additional 20 million gallons of water per day from the Quabbin Reservoir so that, the agency says, it can serve new communities in the eastern part of the state. 
It would by far be the largest such request since the MWRA was formed in 1984 — three times as much as the next-highest approved plan to pull more water out of the state’s largest drinking water source in order to serve a new community. 
The proposal is further stoking tensions that are already playing out in a separate dispute between rural, financially strapped communities that surround the Quabbin Reservoir and the agency charged with providing clean drinking water to its customers mostly in Eastern Massachusetts. The focus of that dispute is the towns’ agreement not to develop land in the Quabbin watershed in exchange for payments in lieu of taxes from the state that grossly undervalue what the land would be worth if the municipalities were able to collect property tax revenue on that land. 
For the MWRA, a quasi-public agency that serves 61 municipalities mostly in and around Greater Boston, the new water withdrawal plan, which requires the green light from the state Water Resources Commission, makes sense all around.  
As the state pursues more housing and as municipal water sources and private wells suffer from contamination and dwindling supplies due to a two-year drought that’s only now starting to subside, the MWRA believes it can be the answer, selling more high-quality water from a Quabbin Reservoir that can withstand greater withdrawals.  
Those living near the Quabbin disagree — and are mobilizing to kill the proposal. They fear the precedent such a move would set, and it feeds their sense that the agency will only continue to take the water that they protect and send it east to support growth there while their towns in Central Massachusetts face an increasingly alarming budgetary crunch. 
“We’re not giving up until there’s fairness,” state Sen. Jo Comerford, a Democrat who represents Quabbin-area towns, said in an interview. “This is not what fairness looks like. This would set a really dangerous precedent — that’s not hyperbolic — that an entity like the MWRA can get basically a lock on the water to use at its discretion without the transparent, accountable public oversight on this precious resource.” 
Part of the contention around the plan, which will face a grilling at a public hearing next week in Belchertown, is its sheer size. The MWRA has never asked the state to approve additional withdrawals from the Quabbin at anywhere close to what the agency is now seeking.  
If nothing else, Comerford said, it’s questionable optics for the MWRA to pursue a project of this size after facing scrutiny for not requiring its customers in Greater Boston to take conservation measures during the drought while residents living in localities near the Quabbin, which don’t drink water from the reservoir, implemented stricter steps to reduce water demand and protect the watershed.  
Land around the Quabbin Reservoir is off-limits to development and other activities in order to protect the drinking water source. (Jordan Wolman/CommonWealth Beacon)
But the part of the plan that’s arguably generating the most blowback is the process the MWRA is deploying to win approval from state officials. 
Water transfers like the one proposed here are governed by a 40-year-old law known as the Interbasin Transfer Act. Typically, state officials review environmental records and water demand documents from both the “donor basin” — the water resources that will be sending water somewhere else — and the “receiving basin” — the area that will be taking in more water. The goal is to ensure that there aren’t adverse impacts to the donor basin that’s losing water and that there is a legitimate demonstrated need for the transfer to occur.  
For the first time in state history, though, the MWRA is asking the Water Resources Commission to review the agency’s donor basin proposal separately and ahead of any receiving basin requests that may come in the future. Those would still need to be individually reviewed by the commission. 
The move, if approved, would essentially grant the MWRA the ability to have the donor basin approvals in hand if and when new communities are approved to receive the water and join the system.  
It could, depending on your perspective, save on long permitting processes by avoiding the agency coming in with a new analysis every time a new community wants a share of the Quabbin, giving state officials a more holistic look at the MWRA’s goals — or recklessly sever the commission’s ability to look at the tradeoffs and impacts of the donor and receiving basins together. 
The agency’s donor basin analysis, filed earlier this year, doesn’t specifically name any additional communities it plans to bring into its system. But Stephen Estes-Smargiassi, MWRA’s interim executive director, said in an interview that Weymouth and Wayland are currently going through the process to receive water and join the agency’s network, with more to come. 
“We do want to provide water to additional communities that are in need of water, either for growth to allow more new housing, or because their existing supplies have become contaminated, and they’re looking for a way to resolve that in an efficient way,” he said. “This mechanism streamlines the process for our half of the analysis.” 
But the Quabbin communities are already on edge from the MWRA’s handling of the drought and suffer from glaringly low state compensation for land they can’t develop – and can’t tax – in order to protect a water source they don’t drink from. The towns that guard Greater Boston’s water supply, and therefore hold the keys to any economic development poised to occur there, are facing dire fiscal constraints, cutting public school workers, consolidating emergency services, and dealing with local water crises of their own that render municipal buildings unusable. 
To them, the MWRA’s maneuver feels more like an ill-considered end-around than a genuine effort to reduce inefficient red tape. 
In fact, if state officials permit the MWRA’s plan, it would have the “functional effect of rewriting the law and sidestepping the fundamental purpose” of the Interbasin Transfer Act, wrote Comerford, Sen. Jake Oliveira, and Reps. Aaron Saunders and Susannah Whipps, who represent towns around the Quabbin, in a letter to the Water Resources Commission. 
“Approving the application would create exactly what the Act was designed to prevent: extraction authority untethered from proven necessity,” the lawmakers wrote.   
The debate is injecting new life into a simmering debate on Beacon Hill. 
House Speaker Ron Mariano has long sought to expand MWRA’s service territory, particularly to include municipalities along the South Shore that he represents, only to stall out in the Senate.  
Meanwhile, pending legislation would grant the Quabbin communities a permanent seat on the MWRA board and ramp up payments to those towns. 
Gov. Maura Healey sided with the Quabbin communities’ concerns this summer, urging the MWRA in a letter to meet their “pressing needs.” In response, Estes-Smargiassi said his agency began helping Belchertown explore the feasibility of new drinking water wells — discussions that the town’s water district confirmed took place but said the project is unlikely to move forward. 
Healey’s move to wade into the dispute further complicates the picture as it relates to the MWRA’s proposal, given that the agency argues the move will be necessary to meet ambitious state housing goals and new development opportunities like a former naval site in Weymouth, a top priority for the governor.  
“This is one of those classic cases where two good, valid public policies are coming up against each other,” said Martin Pillsbury, senior environmental adviser at the Metropolitan Area Planning Council, who previously served on multiple water management task forces.  
The MWRA maintains that, even with demand growth in its existing service area and the potential expansion into new communities, there is more than enough water in the Quabbin to justify the large new withdrawals.  
The current average annual demand of approximately 200 million gallons of water per day — considerably below previous levels thanks to more efficient appliances and conservation measures adopted by the MWRA — leaves plenty of room before hitting the reservoir’s cap of 300 million gallons per day, according to the agency’s donor basin analysis. 
But those numbers obscure the reality, said Lexi Dewey, the former head of the MWRA’s water supply citizens advisory committee, who argued that the MWRA is overselling how much extra water capacity it has available.   
At various points this past summer, daily withdrawals of the Quabbin hovered around and even exceeded 300 million gallons per day, according to agency records reviewed by CommonWealth Beacon.  
Asking state officials to further deplete the Quabbin by approving withdrawal of an additional 20 million gallons of water per day without identifying any specific new communities amounts to a “serious disregard” for the intent of the law, Dewey said. 
“I’m very worried that the Water Resources Commission is going to let this go by, and there is no way that should be allowed to happen,” she said. “You don’t get to come back and appeal. If they vote for this, it’s final and it’s forever.”

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: I’m a prison math teacher. Here’s how to rehabilitate, not just incarcerate
description: When people imagine a correctional facility, they often picture bars, fences and separation from society. Those things certainly exist at Stillwater Correctional Facility. Yet after spending a year teaching with the Transformation and Re-entry through Education and Community program in Minnesota’s prison education system, I’m convinced that another reality e[...]
text:
Stillwater Correctional Facility, Thursday, Nov. 20, 2025. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)When people imagine a correctional facility, they often picture bars, fences and separation from society. Those things certainly exist at Stillwater Correctional Facility. Yet after spending a year teaching with the Transformation and Re-entry through Education and Community program in Minnesota’s prison education system, I’m convinced that another reality exists inside the prison’s walls: community. 
As Minnesotans debate the future of the aging Stillwater facility, we should be discussing just that. Prison is not comfortable, and incarceration should not be romanticized. The reality of incarceration is serious and carries lasting consequences. 
But acknowledging those realities should not prevent us from recognizing something equally important: A meaningful correctional system requires opportunities for people to grow. Nearly all of them will return to society, so they need opportunities to learn, practice and strengthen the skills required to live and work alongside others. That is where I believe Minnesota’s Department of Corrections can lead. After all, it is not called the Department of Punishment.
I recently watched a documentary about Norway’s approach to corrections. What struck me was not luxury or leniency, as critics sometimes assume. Instead, it was a simple idea: If the goal is successful reentry, then correctional institutions should help people practice the skills required to achieve it. Responsibility, cooperation, conflict resolution and contribution to something larger than oneself are not simply personal virtues. They are community skills, and if we expect people to rejoin society successfully, they need opportunities to practice. Without it, we see nearly 20% of incarcerated Minnesotans returning to prison. 
Researchers who study human development and education have consistently found that people need more than basic necessities to thrive. They benefit from opportunities to solve problems, learn new skills, contribute meaningful work and develop relationships with others. In correctional settings, those opportunities often emerge in surprisingly practical ways.
At Stillwater, students write for the Prison Mirror, the longest-running, continuously published prison newspaper in the country. Some enroll in vocational programs such as carpentry, and others take my mathematics classes while pursuing college degrees. These programs provide an opportunity to contribute, collaborate and take responsibility for something larger than oneself. Increasingly, I view these programs as opportunities to practice citizenship.
One of my students has developed a hydroponic garden inside the facility. Through donations and community support, the project has expanded and now includes outdoor growing opportunities. At first glance, it’s a simple gardening project. But gardens do not thrive on good intentions alone. Plants require daily attention. Equipment must be maintained. Problems must be solved. Decisions made today may not produce visible results for weeks. The project asks participants to think beyond the moment and invest in something that will continue growing tomorrow. The same is true of college classes, vocational programs, student journalism and many other opportunities within the facility.
I entered Stillwater as a mathematics instructor in the fall of 2025 intending to create approachable lessons for students who had often been away from formal education for decades. What I encountered instead was a learning environment marked by intellectual curiosity, courage to be vulnerable, and mutual respect for classmates.
The underlying principle is not that prison should be comfortable. It is that prison should be constructive. The punishment is the loss of freedom. What happens afterward should encourage people to develop the habits necessary to live responsibly in a community. What I have observed at Stillwater is that many incarcerated people, staff members and volunteers are actively trying to build that kind of community.
Reasonable people can disagree about the future of Stillwater’s buildings. But regardless of what happens to its limestone walls and iron bars, Minnesotans should pay attention to the lessons emerging from inside them. Strong communities are built when people are given opportunities to participate, contribute and accept responsibility for one another. My students practice those skills every day inside Stillwater, and they deserve a place in the conversation about what correction should mean in Minnesota.
When a Prison Mirror journalist asked me to summarize my first year in a single sentence, I finally wrote:
“After a lifetime of teaching in challenging environments, the most rewarding has been teaching in the Stillwater community that welcomed me and treats me as a member.”

title: A focus on maintenance and administrative fixes would improve tribal water service, report says
description: The federal government’s programs for tribal water services are hampered by a lack of follow-up to support operation and maintenance, along with overly specific qualification rules and other administrative hurdles, a new federal report says. The report, issued Wednesday by the Government Accountability Office, makes a dozen recommendations for legislative an[...]
text:
A water treatment plant and washeteria in Eek is seen in 2024. Eek is a Yup'ik villlage of about 400 people located in the Yukon-Kuskokwim region. Federal agencies, led by the Indian Health Service, have invested in water and wastewater infrastructure construction. They could save money in the long run if they assist in system operations and maintenance, a report from the Governmental Accountability Office says. (Photo provided by the Alaska Division of Community and Regional Affairs)The federal government’s programs for tribal water services are hampered by a lack of follow-up to support operation and maintenance, along with overly specific qualification rules and other administrative hurdles, a new federal report says.
The report, issued Wednesday by the Government Accountability Office, makes a dozen recommendations for legislative and administrative actions that it says would improve both the water services that protect people’s health in rural Alaska communities and elsewhere, as well as the effectiveness of the money spent to provide them.
The federal government provided a little over $1 billion in 2025 to design and build water systems in tribal communities around the nation, the report said. About three quarters of the money was from the Indian Health Service, while the Environmental Protection Agency and the U.S. Department of Agriculture provided the remainder.
However, there are some inconsistencies in application requirements from the different agencies, creating both gaps in support and administrative burdens for communities needing help, according to the report.    
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE 

One of the key recommendations concerns deteriorating and failing infrastructure. Inadequate support for operations and maintenance winds up creating more costs for the federal agencies, the report said.
“Tribal water infrastructure deteriorating or prematurely failing because of insufficient O&M can increase long-term capital costs to the federal government when it has to fund extensive repairs or replacement,” it said.
To address the problem, the GAO report recommends that Congress authorize the Indian Health Service to start a pilot program to fund operations and maintenance. If that proves effective, such funding could be sustained into the future, the report said.
Currently, the Indian Health Service considers operations and maintenance funding to be outside of its jurisdiction, the report said.
The consequences of poor operations and maintenance go beyond dollars, the report noted.
“Lack of tribal capacity to fund O&M can create health risks by reducing tribal members’ access to safe drinking water,” it said.
In Alaska in particular, there are special challenges that make it difficult for communities to keep their water systems working in good order, the report said.
One is the high cost of energy in remote rural areas. Alaska Native villages rely on electricity and fuel to keep their stored water from freezing in the winter, the report noted. Doing that, which is necessary to keep water systems operating, can consume a third of communities’ total energy costs, said the report, which relied on information provided by the Alaska Native Tribal Health Consortium.
Freeze-ups in pipes and water storage systems can be extremely disruptive in rural Alaska communities. During particularly cold weather last winter, several Northwest Arctic Borough communities lost service, with wide-ranging effects like school closures. The state issued a disaster declaration in response.
One of the communities, Ambler, went without water and sewer service for months. Repairs are currently underway.
The report made several recommendations for altering qualifications and application rules. For example, the definition of qualified tribal households is too narrow and should be broadened by Congress, the report said.
Another recommendation is for the Department of Agriculture to drop some of its financial reporting requirements, which have proved difficult for many tribal governments and which the other agencies do not require.
The report is based on site visits to tribal communities in Alaska and Arizona, as well as consultation with the Alaska Native Tribal Health Consortium and other organizations.

name: Nevada Current
title: Ford and Lombardo aren’t leading Nevada’s data center debate. They’re just trying to navigate it.
description: Both Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo and the Democrat hoping to unseat him, Attorney General Aaron Ford, have been playing catch-up on data centers. Their positions have been reactive and unimaginative. It’s as if their hearts aren’t in it. Most of the Nevada press, and some national outlets as well, generously gave Lombardo ad-ready headlines last […]
text:
On data center tax breaks, as on economic policy in general, there isn't much daylight between Lombardo and Ford. (Photos: Ford's campaign; Lombardo's office)Both Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo and the Democrat hoping to unseat him, Attorney General Aaron Ford, have been playing catch-up on data centers. Their positions have been reactive and unimaginative. It’s as if their hearts aren’t in it.
Most of the Nevada press, and some national outlets as well, generously gave Lombardo ad-ready headlines last week about the governor announcing “guardrails” on data center development. 
Under an executive order accompanying Lombardo’s announcement, existing data centers would continue to get all the tax breaks they’ve always received, but new data centers would only get most of them.
Why remove just one slice of data center tax breaks. Why not toss out the whole tax break pie?
The order also creates a “community support commitment” under which new data centers wouldn’t be eligible for all those remaining tax breaks unless the facilities minimize water use and don’t stick the public with higher electricity bills.
Why tie those conditions to tax breaks? Why not just require data centers to meet those conditions or they can’t build in Nevada, period?
If we take Lombardo at his word, the answer to the aforementioned questions is in the second “WHEREAS” of his executive order:
 “…data centers are the means by which Nevada will meet an unprecedented challenge and realize an unprecedented opportunity, one of the most significant for economic growth and fiscal diversification this State has seen in a generation…”
He seems genuinely all in.
But over the summer, Lombardo also seemed genuinely all in on the proposition that Nevada already had excellent guardrails to protect the state’s resources and citizenry from any ill-effects caused by data centers.
“You’ve probably seen stories in the news about local residents in other states reporting low water pressure or huge spikes in their energy bills after a data center gets built,” Lombardo wrote in a guest column for the Reno Gazette-Journal in June. 
“But the truth is, it isn’t happening in Nevada – because we’ve made it clear that companies investing in Nevada must do so in a way that protects our resources, our communities and our quality of life,” Lombardo wrote, referencing requirements companies must meet to get tax breaks.
Two months later, in correspondence with Democratic U.S. Rep. Dina Titus over concerns about the state’s regulatory role regarding potential data centers on federal lands, Lombardo again gushed over the state’s wonderful process for permitting and awarding tax breaks to data centers.
“Abatements are an effective tool for attracting job creating projects that strengthen and diversify Nevada’s economy,” Lombardo wrote to Titus while failing to address her specific questions. “As you are aware,” Lombardo continued, “processes at the state and local levels have a high degree of transparency and offer significant opportunities for public participation and feedback.”
But Nevada must not have really “made it clear” to companies that they must do no harm. 
And Nevada regulatory processes, let alone those dealing with tax breaks, must not have had such “a high degree of transparency” after all. 
Or at least not enough to crow about while trying to neutralize a hot-button campaign issue.
Hence the governor’s executive order last week.
Ford, as you’ve no doubt heard and seen in countless attack ads by now, sponsored the original data center tax break bill enacted in 2015. (What you might not have heard, because it isn’t included in the attack ads against Ford, is that Republicans controlled both houses of the state Legislature in 2015 and the bill passed the state Senate unanimously; to reiterate, in 2015, Anthropic, OpenAI, and hyperscaling weren’t household terms.)
Ford had to be dragged kicking and screaming back to the data center issue over the summer, declining to answer a question about tax breaks in June, and saying “I will continue to look at this” in July.
But by August, scrambling just like Lombardo (and politicians coast to coast) to gain a toehold on the issue, Ford called for a pause on approving data center tax breaks until the effectiveness of the tax breaks could be reviewed. 
At the same time, Ford released a “Data Centers Accountability Plan” outlining conditions data centers would have to meet to qualify for tax breaks. It could have served as a template for Lombardo’s executive order last week, except without the Lombardo campaign’s laughably gimmicky inclusion of eliminating one portion of the tax breaks.
And so once again we find that all the rhetoric and the breathless ads notwithstanding, on data center tax breaks, as on economic policy in general, there isn’t much daylight between Lombardo and Ford. Both say they want to use tax breaks to make data centers behave.
It can’t be said that either candidate is shaping the state’s data center discussion. They’re merely navigating it
Perhaps the discussion could be opened up a bit.
For starters, let’s never forget that data centers are being built to meet the demands of a tiny band of oligarchs. The fabulousness of their wealth is exceeded only by the creepiness of their personality disorders and the arrogance of their disregard for mere mortals who work for a living.
Instead of counting on tax breaks to coax good behavior out of data center owners, operators, and the oligarchs driving the data center infestation, demand good behavior. Stop giving them tax breaks, and penalize bad behavior with heavy penalties and fines. The AI-driven data center industry can afford it.
Instead of giving data centers tax breaks, tax them more. Gaming, mining, insurance … Nevada has a long history of imposing industry-specific taxes. Create and impose one on data centers. Again, they can afford it.
And it wouldn’t be a bad idea to make data centers owners post substantial reclamation bonds up front, just in case somebody cracks the cold fusion nut or otherwise renders them obsolete.
Ford and Lombardo may feel they’ve charted courses that will safely traverse data centers as a campaign problem. Maybe they have. But neither candidate is anywhere close to adequately confronting the issue, let alone the deplorable tech lords who are recklessly inflicting it upon us.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT Sun brace for ’emotional’ farewell as the WNBA franchise plays its final game
description: The Connecticut Sun plays its final game before moving to Houston after an impressive run for first independently owned team in the league.
text:
The Connecticut WNBA franchise will play its final game in the state before it moves to Houston next year after an impressive run for the first independently owned team in the league.
Texas will be the third stop for the franchise. The team moved to Connecticut in 2003 from Orlando. The Sun made three trips to the WNBA Finals, hosted a record four All-Star Games and Connecticut was the first team to turn a profit in the league’s history. The team, which was purchased for $10 million, was sold for $300 million.
“It’s been an emotional week,” team president Jen Rizzotti told The Associated Press. “The silver lining of the chapter closing is it forces you to look at what this franchise has meant for over two decades and make sure the story is told and the legacy lasts forever.”
The franchise is moving to the home of the former Comets, who won the first four WNBA titles. Its time in Connecticut will end Thursday when the Sun face Toronto in the regular-season finale.
[RELATED: The CT Sun is leaving. The sale has raised deeper questions.]
Rizzotti will move to Houston with the team as the president of basketball operations. She said that 75-80% of the front office staff will also make the move.
“It’s exciting to celebrate the past while also being emotional that it’s ending,” she said. “Thursday is a celebration of our fans with fan appreciation night. One game isn’t enough to show the appreciation of how much they poured into the franchise for 24 years.”
Why are the Sun moving?
The WNBA seems to have outgrown the Sun with the new collective bargaining agreement demanding standard amenities for all teams that include state-of-the-art practice facilities.
The Mohegan Tribe, which owns the franchise, sold the team to Houston Rockets owner Tilman Fertitta for $300 million.
The Sun had an offer for $325 million from a group led by Celtics minority owner Steve Pagliuca that would have moved the franchise to Boston. The WNBA basically blocked that deal from happening by saying that “relocation decisions are made by the WNBA Board of Governors and not by individual teams.”
Now the franchise is becoming the first to relocate since San Antonio moved to Las Vegas in 2017.
“It’s sad,” said former Connecticut Sun CEO Mitchell Etess in a phone interview. “I put a lot into it and to see it go is sad. It did confirm that it was a good business decision to bring it there in the first place. If I was still CEO I’d recommend we sell it for that much profit.”
Being in the smallest market in the WNBA led to difficulties for the franchise to attract top free agents. Over the past two years the team has gone from being a WNBA Finals contender to rebuilding mode.
Still, despite a 10-33 record, the Sun were drawing nearly 8,700 fans a game in the 10,000-seat arena.
Sun honored their past this season
Throughout the season Connecticut honored some of the franchise’s iconic players, including Jonquel Jones, Jasmine Thomas, Alyssa Thomas, Tina Charles along with coaches Curt Miller and Mike Thibault. The group joined other Connecticut standouts — Margo Dydek, Katie Douglas, Nykesha Sales, Taj McWilliams-Franklin, Lindsay Whalen and Asjha Jones — in the rafters at the arena.
Thibault was the last of the group to be honored as Connecticut hosted the event after last Sunday’s game against Minnesota. Whalen, Charles and McWilliams-Franklin were in attendance for that contest as well as dozens of other former employees and front office staffers.
They told stories and stayed well after the game reminiscing about the franchise. Rizzotti expects a similar celebration after Thursday’s finale.
“I know we’re going really blow the game out,” she said of celebration plans. “Lot of things we’re giving away, postgame mingles and autograph opportunities. When everybody leaves we’ll just pop Champagne on the court for the last time. I’m proud of what we built.”
Connecticut was ‘icebreaker’ with gambling partnership
Etess remembers trying to sell NBA Commissioner David Stern on moving a franchise to the Mohegan Sun. The late commissioner was concerned about putting a team in a casino, but as it turns out, he was ahead of his time.
“There was a lot of excitement at the beginning, still a casino and a professional sports team being together wasn’t well received everywhere,” Etess recalled in a phone conversation. “David Stern took a lot of the hard questions when that was happening. In retrospect, it was an icebreaker for a lot of the gambling stuff that happened since. The tribe was proud of having the team as it was great to bring national attention to the state and casino.”
The Mohegan Tribe bought the team for $10 million and with the WNBA in CBA negotiations the franchise had a few months to get everything ready to start in 2003. Thibault remembers when he was hired as the coach in January, the franchise had literally nothing.
Thibault said he had to order basketballs, uniforms and even sports bras for his players. The franchise quickly turned into contenders, reaching the WNBA Finals in 2004 and 2005.
Building a faithful fan base
Thibault joked that when the team first started fans came to games to cheer on former UConn players when they came to town, but soon they became fans of the franchise.
“The first year, we didn’t have as good attendance as we had hoped, but that changed quickly,” Etess said. “We didn’t give tickets away. After the second year we were always up there in total attendance for many, many years.”
The Sun became the first team in WNBA history to make a profit when they made it happen in 2010.
“It meant a lot to us,” Etess said. “We really focused on doing everything right, trying to run the team professionally.”
Etess is sad to see the state lose its last professional team in an area that has been a women’s basketball hotbed for so long.
“It’s odd that the league didn’t want the team to stay in Connecticut,” he said. “Connecticut is such a crucial part of women’s basketball. The state that loves women’s basketball isn’t going to have a pro team, doesn’t feel right to me.”

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: The number of food recalls are down, but individual outbreaks can be severe
description: The number of food recalls reported by the federal government have decreased in recent years. Last year, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration reported 1,500 food recalls, according to federal data. That was one of the lowest totals over the past decade, and this year is on track to be even lower — through mid-September, […]
text:
Vegetables and lettuces at a grocery store in Michigan. Lettuces and salad greens were a likely source in the nationwide cyclosporiasis outbreak, which sickened thousands of people. (Photo by Jon King/Michigan Advance)The number of food recalls reported by the federal government have decreased in recent years.

Last year, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration reported 1,500 food recalls, according to federal data. That was one of the lowest totals over the past decade, and this year is on track to be even lower — through mid-September, the FDA has reported about 950 recalls.
While the figures are down, individual outbreaks can be severe, and the Trump administration’s staffing and oversight cuts may worsen the situation.



This year, thousands of people fell sick after eating lettuce tainted with cyclospora, a parasite that causes violent spasms of watery diarrhea. The lettuce came from Taylor Farms, a Mexican operation that supplies Taco Bell, Wal-Mart and Costco, among others. More than 20 states were affected, and Kroger reported that so many people avoided buying lettuce the grocery chain’s bottomline was hit.
The FDA inspects foreign sites that grow food for U.S. consumption, but it had not inspected Taylor Farms since 2019, according to the Associated Press. Since that year, the outlet reported, the overall number of foreign food site inspections has fallen by about 35%.



While the Trump administration has cut staffing levels, it has not cut food safety inspectors at the FDA. However, it did fire staffers who handled travel arrangements for inspectors, according to the AP.
Once Taylor Farms was identified as the source of the outbreak, it took four weeks to get inspectors into Mexico — “too long to get boots on the ground,” a former top food safety official at the FDA told the AP.
Last year, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — which, like the FDA, is under the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services — announced changes to how it monitors foodborne pathogens. The CDC said its early warning system named FoodNet, a collaboration with other federal agencies and states, would no longer track six pathogens, including cyclospora. The CDC has said other systems exist to perform the same function.
The federal government has struggled to contain some food outbreaks in recent years.
In 2024, Boar’s Head deli meat, a supermarket staple, was linked to a Listeria outbreak. At least 10 people died, making it the deadliest Listeria outbreak in recent memory. Prior to the outbreak, inspectors with the U.S. Department of Agriculture, which oversees the safety of meat in the U.S. food supply, documented black mold and flies at a Boar’s Head processing plant.
ProPublica revealed in 2021 an ongoing salmonella outbreak in chicken that food safety officials allowed to continue to make people sick. A few years earlier, officials detected the outbreak, which was sending people to seek medical attention. But, according to ProPublica’s reporting, officials closed the investigation into the outbreak without alerting consumers.

Our mission is to serve the public interest by exposing dangerous and costly practices of influential agricultural corporations and institutions through in-depth and data-driven investigative journalism.
