name: Mississippi Today
title: Lawyers for Mississippi say foster care system doesn’t violate US Constitution, again ask to end federal oversight
description: Mississippi Department of Child Protection Services Commissioner Andrea Sanders discusses the needs of child services with legislators during a study group on women, children and family, held at the state Capitol, Wednesday, Oct. 2, 2024, in Jackson.
text:
Mississippi’s government said health and safety problems in the foster care system are not being intentionally ignored as the state’s attorneys continue their efforts to dismiss federal oversight over its child welfare system. 
In a Tuesday court filing, lawyers from Mississippi’s Attorney General’s Office and the private law firm Baker Donelson said the issues that a court-appointed monitor identified in a recent report do not violate the U.S. Constitution. 
The monitoring is federally required by the 22-year-old Olivia Y. v. Barbour lawsuit — in which lawyers representing Mississippi foster children have repeatedly said the state’s child welfare efforts are systematically dangerous. 
In 2018, lawyers representing both the state and foster children in Mississippi agreed to an independent monitoring program that would annually examine over 100 safety measures. The agreement says the state government can dismiss the monitoring after it has met all the safety measures for at least a year. 
In the latest report, published in July, the independent monitor found the Mississippi Department of Child Protection Services had only met 22 of the applicable 107 measures, ranging from maltreatment in state care to placing children in unlicensed homes.

Mississippi’s lawyers questioned how the monitor went about creating the report in their Tuesday filing. They said Gov. Tate Reeves and department Commissioner Andrea Sanders have not deliberately caused these safety problems. 
The lawyers argue that Mississippi’s child welfare department has worked with the state Legislature to solve these problems and that should be enough to show the state is meeting its constitutional responsibility. 
“They have identified risks, marshaled resources, enacted legislation, rebuilt staffing, modernized technology, and restructured MDCPS to protect children’s personal security and reasonably safe living conditions,” the state’s attorneys wrote in their filing. 
Marcia Lowry, the lead lawyer representing Mississippi foster children, said Wednesday that the 2018 agreement was a legal contract, one that Mississippi’s government had not yet met the standards required to end. She said lawyers for the state knew they would be measured by the agreement rather than the Constitution when they signed onto it. 
“That’s how the case is supposed to end,” Lowry said. “It’s not supposed to end by the state now saying ‘We’ve done a bunch of different things, and we think that satisfies the constitutional standard.’” 
Lawyers for the department also said the required safety measures were “aspirational” metrics and they couldn’t be used to show Mississippi’s government wasn’t trying to address foster children’s safety. 
The 2018 agreement says the monitoring is intended to “maintain the child welfare infrastructure, standards, and outcomes that Defendants must meet within specified timeframes statewide.” Lowry said all the lawyers knew that these safety standards were enforceable when they signed the contract and the “aspirational” goals were not optional. 
“We entered into this because this is what we thought they could and should agree to get to, what they should get to over a period of time,” she said. “This is what the state agreed to.”
Clint Pentecost, the Baker Donelson lawyer who submitted the late Tuesday filing, did not answer a phone call or return a voicemail from Mississippi Today by publication time. MaryAsa Lee, spokesperson for Mississippi Attorney General Lynn Fitch, did not respond to an email.
Zoey Tether, a former Mississippi foster child, sits outside her home in Pontotoc, Miss., Wednesday, Sept. 23, 2026. Credit: Anna Hu / Mississippi Today
The Olivia Y. lawsuit has lingered in the legal system for decades while Mississippi children continue to enter and exit the state’s child welfare system. Zoey Tether spent some of her teenage years in Mississippi’s foster care system, cycling through at least 10 foster care placements until the state found her a permanent home. She said at one of those placements, the adults responsible for her gave her so much medication that she could barely stay awake. 
Now 21 years old and living in Pontotoc County, she’s gotten to know other Missisisppi former foster children. She said they all have plenty of stories like hers, where they feared for their well-being as the state said it would keep them safe. 
“Where are these reasonably safe places?” Tether asked when told about the state’s filing. “One out of 10 is not reasonable.”
She said whether intentional or not, the consequences of unsafe living conditions are carried by people like her — kids who often have no choice over where they end up. For a state agency charged with those responsibilities, Tether said it’s hard for her to even think about allowing any margin of error. 
“What you miss is children and their lives,” she said.
Chief U.S. District Judge Sul Ozerden will decide what happens next in the lawsuit. Lawyers for the state asked Ozerden to either end federal foster care oversight or hold a hearing for the case, one where each side could present more evidence. Lowry said she and the other lawyers would be prepared for a hearing if Ozerden opts for one. 
Anna Hu contributed reporting to this story from Pontotoc.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC governor recognized for preserving records, making them easy to access
description: COLUMBIA — During his tenure as South Carolina’s attorney general, now-Gov. Henry McMaster fought in court to retrieve a trove of Civil War gubernatorial papers taken from the government’s possession in 1865. He argued the case through U.S. Bankruptcy Court, U.S. District Court and subsequent appeals, said Eric Emerson, director of the state Department of […[...]
text:
South Carolina State Archivist Eric Emerson, right, presents Gov. Henry McMaster, left, with a national award recognizing his contributions to state records preservation Wednesday, Sept. 23, 2026, at the state Department of Archives and History. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — During his tenure as South Carolina’s attorney general, now-Gov. Henry McMaster fought in court to retrieve a trove of Civil War gubernatorial papers taken from the government’s possession in 1865.
He argued the case through U.S. Bankruptcy Court, U.S. District Court and subsequent appeals, said Eric Emerson, director of the state Department of Archives and History.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
As governor, he backed efforts to preserve the seven state constitutions adopted throughout South Carolina’s history, beginning with a temporary framework enacted in 1776 and culminating in the document ratified in 1895 that still governs the state.
And he supported state budget requests to hire more archivists and make records stored on microfilm accessible online.
It’s for this work that state archivists across the country recognized him with their association’s Advocacy for Archives Award.
McMaster became the first governor in the Council of State Archivists’ 37-year history to receive the award given to government employees and officials who spent their careers committed to archives and record keeping.
“We’ve had members of Congress and U.S. senators, but this is the first time for a governor,” said the association’s executive director Joy Banks.
To know history, someone has to record it, McMaster said in accepting the award Wednesday during the organization’s conference in Columbia.
Inside the state Department of Archives and History in Columbia as seen Wednesday, Sept. 23, 2026. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)
“Without a knowledge of history, without people preserving that history, then it’ll be lost,” he added. “And if it’s lost, then we’re all lost.”
Beyond historical documents, Emerson said the governor also has cooperated with the state’s archives agency to preserve present-day records from his own administration, as well as that of former Gov. Nikki Haley.
Over the past several months, Emerson said the governor’s office has transferred all paper records to the agency and is in the process of transferring digital records.
When Haley was appointed as President Donald Trump’s first U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, it was McMaster’s staff who transferred her gubernatorial records as McMaster transitioned in January 2017 from lieutenant governor to the Governor’s Mansion.
“He was pivotal in making sure that those records were preserved and so really set the standard,” Emerson said.
Haley, early on in her tenure, faced criticism after public records requests from media outlets revealed her office routinely deleted emails.
In response, Haley signed a new records retention policy with the state archives — the first of its kind in 40 years.
Eric Emerson is pictured Wednesday, Sept. 23, 2026, at the state Department of Archives and History. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)
Emerson called executive correspondence, whether written or digital, “vital to what state government is doing.”
“Government records are really an essential component of democracy,” Banks added. “Without the preservation, the protection, and making accessible the record to the people, then you lose that picture of who we are as a country,”
She said the national association also strives to educate the next generation on the importance of government transparency,
“These records are theirs. The government is theirs,” Banks said. “The things that are held in these archives and records management centers across the country create the receipts to let us know the work that we’ve elected public servants to do and lets us hold them accountable to things.”

title: Flock surveillance cameras raise constitutional questions, bipartisan US senators say
text: WASHINGTON — A vast and growing network of artificial intelligence-driven Flock cameras could violate constitutional privacy rights, U.S. senators on a Judiciary Committee subcommittee said during a Wednesday hearing.GOP Sen. Josh Hawley of Missouri, the chair of the Crime and Counterterrorism Subcommittee, said the point of the hearing was to find out “what is going on with the expanding surveillance network that appears to be going coast to coast in this country.”Hawley said he invited the CEO of Flock Safety to testify, but he did not appear. Senators heard from a woman wrongly arrested over a fatal car crash after a Flock camera captured a photo of her vehicle three miles from the crash site.They speculated that more people could be falsely accused based on inaccurate information gathered by the devices. They also said Fourth Amendment violations were likely because the law enforcement agencies that use the service are able to use the data to track movements without a warrant.  “If you haven’t heard of Flock, all I have to say is Flock’s probably heard of you,” Hawley said. “I’m sure we’re all in the database.”Flock did not respond to States Newsroom's request for comment. What is Flock?Flock cameras track and record every motor vehicle that comes into view, including its license plate number, make, model, bumper stickers and color. They can also capture images of people.  The information is then uploaded to a database that any law enforcement agency that contracts with the company can access without a warrant. There are more than 120,000 Flock cameras installed across the country from highways to outside grocery stores, according to the American Civil Liberties Union. The only U.S. state that does not have a Flock camera is Hawaii.Media outlets such as The Washington Post have documented abuses of the service, including law enforcement officers using the devices to stalk ex-girlfriends.U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has also tapped into Flock data through local law enforcement officials to read license plates for immigration-related searches, even though Flock denies having a contract with ICE. The backlash to the possibility of mass surveillance has been strong, with NPR reporting vandalization of Flock cameras.Arizona sheriff brushed off, he saysOne of the witnesses at Wednesday’s hearing, Ross Teeple, the sheriff of Pinal County, Arizona, said he ultimately decided to end a contract with Flock because he had raised privacy concerns the company did not adequately address. Some of his constituents said they were worried that people could be identified in images taken by Flock cameras. He said when he asked the company about how people could be clearly seen in the images, he felt the company brushed aside his concerns and told him the image resolution was not good enough to recognize a person.“I'm looking at camera pictures where I could recognize the person on the camera, but that was their claim …, and there was just too much disinformation from them and dishonesty,” he said. “I was trying to get answers from them, and they would not give me answers… and there were too many concerns. So we just decided not to continue our contract.”False accusationHawley said his main worries were personal privacy and that people have the right to be treated as innocent until proven guilty. He pointed to one of the witnesses, Lindsey Isaacs of Florida, who was wrongly accused of being involved in a car accident that killed three people because a Flock automated license plate recognition camera saw her vehicle about three miles west of the crash scene. The car involved in the crash was a Dodge Durango, the same make and model as Isaacs’. But hers was black, while the car in the crash was maroon, as described by a witness. Law enforcement still arrested her at her home. She spent three days in solitary confinement and then moved to another maximum-security unit for 10 days before she was released and state prosecutors dropped charges, she told the panel.“In my case, a Flock camera captured my vehicle a few miles from the scene of a terrible crash,” she said. “That piece of information became part of an investigation that ultimately led to my arrest on three counts of vehicular homicide and 13 days in jail for a crash I had nothing to do with.”Hawley said what he finds “so troubling" is that many drivers or people walking by are being surveilled and they’ve done nothing wrong. “It sounds as if, based on the reports we've heard, it's treating every citizen in America, I mean, by now, surely almost all of us have been scanned and logged as if we are criminals, yet without any due process, without any reasonable suspicion, without any articulable suspicion whatsoever,” he said. “This just seems very, very strange, to put it mildly, and something I think this committee really needs to hear about.”Abortion trackingNew Jersey Democratic Sen. Cory Booker asked if Flock cameras could be used to track women in states with strict abortion laws.ACLU’s Chad Marlow, senior policy counsel, said that it would be easy to track people searching for those services. Hawley agreed with Booker and also questioned how easy it would be to create a database of certain people, such as those who attend gun shows.“When you have this amount of data available, the temptations to use it are going to be absolutely incredible, if not irresistible,” he said. Marlow said the scenarios that Booker and Hawley cited are closer than they think. “If you build it, they will come,” he said. “I so much appreciate that you're bringing (up) abortion care seekers and gun owners because they are part of the same community when it comes to the threat of mass surveillance. This is something we need to be worried about because when you create the temptation, when you create the option for population control, at some point someone's going to use it.”

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont should watch for three scenarios as Trump targets the midterms
description:
Whether elections proceed fairly, get delayed or go forward despite interference, the stakes for American democracy are high this November.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont should watch for three scenarios as Trump targets the midterms.
text:
This commentary is by John Bossange, who lives in South Burlington.
Every day we read or hear about the chaos and confusion surrounding this November’s election, especially regarding the campaigns and races for national offices. Here in Vermont, our campaigns seem relatively peaceful and respectful. Our voting process for many village, town and state positions, and for our one U.S. House seat, has not been polluted by doubt and unfounded conspiracy theories alleging fraud, as has happened in other states.  
Still, Vermonters will be voting in November too, and may witness the same efforts to undermine confidence in the election results. I believe we may also see one of the three possible scenarios in states vital to the Trump administration’s attempt to maintain its control of the U.S. House and Senate.
In the first scenario, Trump and his MAGA followers will allow elections to be held because they are confident they will win key governorships, local Senate and House seats, and federal Senate and House races in enough states to remain in control of the U.S. House and Senate.  
With the court-sanctioned ability to limit polling sites and mail-in ballots, require voter IDs and post U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and other federal agents at pivotal county voting locations, combined with thousands of newly appointed election deniers as ballot-counting clerks, the MAGA faction feels reassured they’ll win the popular vote. Intimidation and confusion are key to MAGA candidate victories, and no lower court order to back off will be followed.
In the second scenario, Trump and the MAGA leadership will postpone November’s elections, claiming there is too much fraud and illegal voting potential to ensure the results honestly reflect the will of the voters in key counties and states.  
Trump and his cohort are already searching for alleged illegal voter registrations, fomenting doubt to create a false rationale for the president to order key state governors to follow his demands. States control their elections, not the federal government, and enough red-state governors will fall in line as they have during the Trump years.

READ MORE

In the final scenario, elections will proceed regardless of the Trump administration’s attempts to influence the voting process and the outcomes. Many inside the White House, the administration’s family members, loyalists in Congress and those appointed to key agencies and departments have now made their millions through real estate deals, investments in offshore accounts and alleged insider trading. It’s always been about personal enrichment and financial gain, not America, just as it was during the Gilded Age.
I remain optimistic for America because of scenario three. I am hoping for an implosion within the MAGA leadership ranks, but if that does not occur soon, then I believe that desperation and fear of convictions will unite them in panic, and they will leave our great nation in a mass exodus. I am also optimistic that the Democratic National Committee (DNC) leadership will be forced to allow a leader in the mold of Lyndon B. Johnson to restore America. The current Democratic Party multimillionaire and billionaire leaders share many of the same financial goals as their Republican and MAGA friends, and this could prevent key areas of tax and investment reforms. The DNC leadership lives in the shadow of the political tragedy it created by promoting the candidacy of former President Biden in the first half of 2024.
In this optimistic scenario, we can then get busy restoring the U.S. Constitution, freed from the voice of the MAGA leadership crowd and the DNC stranglehold on potential Democratic leaders and candidates. For starters, we’ll need to rid ourselves of the curse left behind by Citizens United, restore the 1965 Voting Rights Act and eliminate the unitary executive doctrine the Supreme Court has advanced.  
Abolishing the archaic Electoral College and challenging Christian nationalists will also be key elements in restoring and truly unifying America. Our country was founded on the Enlightenment ideas of freedom and equal opportunity, not on religion or race.
Finally, we will need to plug the holes in our U.S. Constitution that worried our founding fathers with additional amendments to prevent another Trump-like character from taking advantage of the good faith and trust any president needs to ensure that America’s bold experiment of an imperfect and forever evolving democracy continues for another 250 years.

title: Judge skeptical of White House ban of 3 news outlets but holds off on ruling for now
text: WASHINGTON — U.S. District Court Judge Timothy J. Kelly indicated during a Wednesday hearing he may order the Trump administration to reinstate White House press passes for reporters from three news organizations who had their credentials revoked this weekend. Kelly, of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, said at the beginning of a 45-minute hearing that he is largely bound by circuit court rulings that ensure journalists with White House press passes have due process rights before their access to the complex could be rescinded. “The government says those cases … were wrongly decided,” Kelly said. “Maybe they were, maybe they weren’t. But certainly as a district judge I have to apply them and I think it is fair to say that the processes that the Circuit Court laid out in those two cases … (weren’t) followed here.”Kelly said at the end of the hearing he will release his ruling as soon as he can, though he did not give any more details about how soon that might be. President Donald Trump nominated Kelly during his first term and the Senate confirmed him following a broadly bipartisan vote in September 2017. This case began Monday when CNN, MS Now and Politico sued the Trump administration for barring their reporters from entering the White House grounds. The news organizations asked the district court to grant them either a temporary restraining order or a preliminary injunction that would require the White House to return the press passes, allowing the journalists to work from the complex once again. ‘Very essence of the First Amendment’Theodore J. Boutrous, Jr., a partner at Gibson Dunn who represented the news organizations, said the president’s decision to revoke the press passes of 78 journalists represented an “unprecedented, unreasonable and severe punishment.”  “What the government is objecting to … is that very essence of the First Amendment,” he said.  Boutrous said claims from the White House the president’s decision was based on national security concerns only came after the lawsuit was filed, not when the decision was announced Friday, or over the weekend when it was implemented. Trump said Friday in response to questions from reporters in the Oval Office that his ban wasn’t in response to any specific story but “really just cumulative stories over the last two years.”“They're smart people, but they purposely write negative news. And they do that because they want to try and diminish the Republicans and a Republican administration,” he said. “And honestly, we've done a fantastic job. Look at the numbers, look at the economic numbers. We have more money coming into our country today than ever before.”Boutrous argued during the hearing that while the president holds the right to criticize reporters and news organizations as much as he wants, the administration cannot “use the power of the government to punish them for their expression.” In response to questions from the judge about whether there would ever be a circumstance where the White House could revoke a press pass, Boutrous said if someone was a spy, represented a physical threat, or a national security threat, “there would of course be authority by the White House to deal with that.”But he also referenced the Pentagon Papers, and said he didn’t believe that type of reporting on national security issues would justify revoking a reporter's White House press pass.The White House’s decision to revoke press passes for reporters from those three news organizations has led the major television networks that rotate daily coverage of the president to stop doing so. The decision has limited what videos of the president are released through that television pool system. DOJ argues access ‘a privilege, not a right’Michael Velchik, senior counsel in the civil division of the Justice Department, said the Trump administration would oppose a ruling  requiring the White House to return the press passes and allow reporters from those news organizations to resume coverage there. “Access to the White House is a privilege not a right,” he said. Velchik seemed to suggest that if the judge were to require the White House to reinstate the press passes, it shouldn’t happen during the next few days, when Chinese President Xi Jinping is scheduled to be in Washington, D.C., to meet with the president.The White House, he said, had also sent letters to CNN, MS Now and Politico on Tuesday, informing them why their press passes were revoked and giving them the chance to reply by Friday evening. Democrat sees ban as part of patternU.S. House Administration Committee ranking member Joe Morelle, D-N.Y., said during a separate virtual press briefing on Wednesday that he believes the ban of the news outlets was part of a pattern of Trump misusing government power to attack perceived opponents.“The Trump administration has flagrantly abused the immense power of the federal government against organizations and institutions whose work, whose clients or viewpoints it disagrees with,” he said. “We don't need to look any further than this outrageous attempt by the president to silence CNN, MS Now, Politico and others.”Jacob Fischler contributed to this report.

name: Source New Mexico
title: Data shows New Mexico students making gains in literacy, while math and science trail behind
description: New Mexico public school students made significant gains in reading and literacy over the last year, while math showed modest gains and science remained largely stagnant since 2022, according to recently released data presented to state lawmakers on Wednesday.
text:
New Mexico Public Education Department officials presented new assessment data to state lawmakers on Sept. 23, 2026, showing significant gains in reading and literacy over the last year, modest gains in math and stagnant results in science. Pictured above: students at Valley View Elementary School in Las Cruces. (Leah Romero for Source NM)New Mexico public school students made significant gains in reading and literacy over the last year, while math showed modest gains and science remained largely stagnant since 2022, according to recently released data presented to state lawmakers on Wednesday.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The New Mexico Public Education Department’s 2025-2026 school accreditation data  evaluates 10 elements, such as attendance, staffing, financial accountability, governance and student outcomes. Its statewide assessment results, the NM Vistas school report cards, evaluate academic achievement, student growth, attendance and graduation rates. The two accountability systems inform the PED and federal government about which schools need additional support and resources to improve student outcomes.
According to Wednesday’s presentation to the Legislative Education Study Committee by Lynn Vásquez, senior manager of assessment, research, evaluation and accountability for the PED, New Mexico students improved literacy proficiency by 10 percentage points to 44% between 2022 and 2026. Math proficiency improved only one percentage point to 26% during the same time, and science remained at 34%.
Early literacy “is where we have the greatest opportunity to change long-term trajectories for students,” Vásquez said during the meeting in Anthony. “I will also point out that the grade level that had the biggest growth was, again, kindergarten.”
Representatives Joy Garratt (D-Albuquerque) and Catherine Cullen (R-Rio Rancho) both pointed to the stagnant science scores, calling the subject “overlooked” and “underfunded,” respectively.
“Science gets overlooked because of the drive for math and language arts, reading,” Garratt said during the meeting. “We’re a state where science, emerging science, is vital, it’s exciting. You can’t do science without hands-on [experience.]”
PED Secretary Mariana Padilla added that science is one of the subject areas that can get kids excited and engaged in learning. “They tend to be hands-on. They allow you to hopefully get outside, get dirty, explore the world around you and really overlooking those content areas are really doing, I think, a disservice to our students,” she said.
The PED reported that 252 of the 830 schools in the state received approved accreditation status during the 2025-2026 pilot accreditation year, while 578 were approved with conditions. None failed to receive approval. At the same time, 17 schools improved their NM Vistas ratings and 67 were given designations requiring further support.
Vásquez’s report also noted that certain risk factors, such as economic disadvantages and chronic absenteeism, were associated with lower performance, but do not necessarily define student potential. “Risk is not destiny,” she said, and added that even high performing schools still have students that experience risk factors.
Rep. Brian Baca (R-Los Lunas) said he would like to see more emphasis on attendance interventions in earlier grades because patterns of chronic absenteeism are already established by the time students reach high school.
“We already have years of disengagement, so what I want to focus on is our elementary,” Baca said during the meeting. “I think that’s where we have an opportunity—early identification, early intervention and supports through our MLSS System (Multi-Layered System of Supports) is where we can make a lot of these changes.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Iowa Corn Growers Association asks for diesel relief as harvest kicks off
description: As Iowa farmers begin harvesting their crops, corn growers in the state are asking Iowa congressional delegates to help lower the cost of diesel fuel, which has risen sharply with trade disruptions from the war in Iran. Iowa Corn Growers Association President Steve Kuiper wrote in a letter to Iowa’s senators and four representatives that […]
text:
Iowa Corn Growers Association asked lawmakers for relief from high diesel fuel costs. Pictured is a fuel pump June 23, 2026. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital dispatch) As Iowa farmers begin harvesting their crops, corn growers in the state are asking Iowa congressional delegates to help lower the cost of diesel fuel, which has risen sharply with trade disruptions from the war in Iran.
Iowa Corn Growers Association President Steve Kuiper wrote in a letter to Iowa’s senators and four representatives that while harvest should be a “positive” time of year for farmers, “the concern of affordability looms large.” 
“This is accelerating the economic and mental stress farmers are feeling,” Kuiper said. “We are asking for your assistance in lowering the cost of a key input, diesel, that every combine, tractor and semi utilizes during the culmination of the growing season.” 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
According to AAA data for Iowa, average diesel prices in Iowa were $6.27 per gallon in Iowa – nearly twice as expensive as this time last year. 
The conflict in Iran has lead to significant trade disruptions as cargo ships struggle to pass through the Strait of Hormuz, a prominent oil, fertilizer and natural gas trade path. 
The resulting heightened fuel prices drove some Republicans, including Iowa Reps. Mariannette Miller-Meeks and Zach Nunn, to vote with Democrats in favor of requiring congressional approval if the president is to continue the war with Iran.
In the letter, corn growers asked lawmakers to push the Trump administration to “further release oil from the U.S. Strategic Oil Reserve.” 
The administration approved in March the release of 172 million barrels of oil from the reserve in response to the war in Iran. The Strategic Oil Reserve, according to the U.S. Government Accountability Office, is an emergency reserve of crude oil for the nation that has been drawn upon during crises. A GAO report in June said the reserve held less than 350 million barrels. 
Miller-Meeks said farmers and truckers need relief now, and then the nation needs to focus on increasing domestic drilling for oil, selling year-round E15 fuel and ending the “open-ended war.” 
“When a patient is hurt, you stop the bleeding first. Then you fix what caused it,” Miller-Meeks said in an emailed statement. “Iowa farmers are filling combines this week at the highest diesel price this state has ever seen, while oil companies ship record amounts of American diesel overseas. We must immediately suspend the federal and state gas tax, sell American diesel to Americans first, and get relief to the farmers and truckers who cannot wait.”
Stop diesel exports 
Sen. Chuck Grassley, of Iowa, called for an embargo on the export of U.S. diesel to provide relief for U.S. farmers. President Donald Trump said Tuesday he would support the ban, though some officials and industry professionals have argued an export ban won’t help to lower fuel prices. 
In a social media post Wednesday, Grassley said he hopes the White House doesn’t listen to “Big Oil” claims that a diesel export ban wouldn’t work. 
“Big Oil doesnt need 2 charge sky-high diesel prices 4 Iowa farmers + truckers just filling up They shld cut price 4 US diesel&get the $$ frm other countries,” Grassley wrote on X. 
Rep. Ashley Hinson, who is running for Iowa’s open Senate seat, also supported an export ban via a social media post Monday. Hinson also said the House, which has recessed until after the midterm elections, should “immediately” return to Washington D.C. to “pause diesel exports, suspend the gas tax, fully unleash E15 and biodiesel, and work on a diesel relief program for truckers and farmers.” 
“Iowans are being squeezed and shouldn’t have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran,” Hinson wrote on X. “We need to use every option at our disposal to provide some relief from high prices.” 
Hinson is running against Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek for Senate, who has called for a pause on diesel exports, gas taxes and to open gas reserves. 
The letter from Iowa Corn Growers Association also asked the Iowa delegation to “investigate legislative mechanisms” for waivers that would allow farmers to use dyed diesel fuel, intended for off-road uses, in on-road vehicles during “economic hardships.”
Off-road diesel fuel is a tax-exempt fuel that can be used for things like a combine or heavy machinery, but is illegal to use in vehicles that travel on a road.
Nunn said the U.S. has “to bring down the price of diesel.” In a social media post, Nunn suggested selling “American energy to Americans first” in addition to supporting biofuels and to holding oil companies accountable for “gouging.” 
Miller-Meeks, Nunn and Hinson are all running in midterm elections considered “toss-up” races by the Cook Political Report. 
The PAC for Iowa Corn Growers Association recently endorsed Republicans Hinson, Miller-Meeks and Nunn in their races.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Audit finds Pa. Department of Aging’s oversight of county offices lacking
description: A spokesperson for the Department of Aging questioned the timing of the report as Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro seeks reelection in November.
text:
Pennsylvania Auditor General Timothy L. DeFoor speaks during a news conference at the Pennsylvania Capitol in Harrisburg, Pa., on Wednesday, Sept. 23, 2026, announcing the findings of a performance audit of the Pennsylvania Department of Aging. The audit examined the department’s oversight of elder abuse investigations conducted by Area Agencies on Aging. (Commonwealth Media Services)A new system for evaluating the performance of county offices that investigate claims of elder abuse fails to protect the commonwealth’s senior citizens, an audit found.
It was conducted by state Auditor General Timothy DeFoor, who released the results Wednesday. 
The Pennsylvania Department of Aging, which was the subject of the audit, offered a 30-page response to the findings, saying that the auditor general’s office conducted its probe as the agency was rolling out the new system. 
As a result, the Shapiro administration said, the report doesn’t accurately reflect the department’s work, processes or legal responsibilities. The new system, called the Comprehensive Aging Performance Evaluation (CAPE) was only seven weeks old when the audit began in January 2024, the department said.
“An entire cycle of monitoring had not occurred under the new system and therefore, any audit of its effectiveness is neither complete nor accurate,” the response, included in the audit report, said.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
DeFoor, a Republican, said the Department of Aging delayed the audit for about six months during which, it was slow to make documents and employees available to auditors.  It was conducted from January 2024 to June 2025.
He added that the department rejected his office’s findings and recommendations and questioned the integrity of the auditors and whether they followed government auditing standards in their work.
“​​This is very disappointing,” DeFoor said, “Especially considering the significant scrutiny the Department of Aging has been under from whistleblowers, news media, and senior citizen advocates about the inadequacies surrounding CAPE.”
A spokesperson for the Department of Aging questioned the timing of the report as Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro seeks reelection in November. His Republican opponent is state Treasurer Stacy Garrity.
“The Auditor General has been in office for nearly six years and has only completed a handful of audits on state agencies over his term — but today, he decided to release an inaccurate, misleading report just weeks before an election,” spokesperson Karen Gray said. “In a craven and transparently political move, the Auditor General completed this report months ago but decided to release this report today in a desperate attempt to help his political allies.”
DeFoor said the department’s response to the audit continued to disappoint him. 
“I hope PDA will take a good look in the mirror and do what’s best for older Pennsylvanians,” DeFoor said in a statement. “Now isn’t the time to point fingers and make personal attacks. It is time to do what’s right and improve the system they created to oversee investigations of elder abuse.”
Department of Aging Secretary Jason Kavulich spoke about CAPE at an event in Northumberland County earlier this month. He said it replaced an ineffective legacy system that rated county Area Agencies on Aging (AAA) on a pass/fail basis and t did not provide adequate oversight. The prior system also lacked guidance for AAAs on what steps were needed to become compliant.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“CAPE not only provides those granular details to ensure a AAA is able to improve, but it also delivers historic levels of transparency and accountability of the AAA network,” the department said in a release.
The commonwealth has 52 AAAs that provide an array of services including investigating claims of neglect, physical or mental abuse, and fraud and financial abuse.
The objectives of the audit were to determine whether the Department of Aging monitored AAAs regarding investigations of elder abuse under the Older Adults Protective Services Act and whether AAA staff received the required training. 
The auditor general’s office made 10 findings and 39 recommendations for the Department of Aging and three for the General Assembly regarding changes to the program.
Among them, the office said the CAPE process doesn’t effectively assess risk of harm or mistreatment, its follow-up and record retention requirements provide limited oversight, and it needs stronger oversight of death reviews.
DeFoor also noted the Department of Aging considers its 20-day investigation window to be a goal, rather than an obligation and its lack of a timeline for financial exploitation investigations leaves seniors at risk of greater harm.
The office also said CAPE’s 18-month evaluation cycle is out of sync with the statutory requirement to evaluate AAAs annually. 
Deputy Auditor General Gordon Dillinger said Wednesday the office’s recommendations to the Department of Aging include ways to improve its monitoring, training, record retention, meet its own deadlines, improve quality assurance and increase transparency. 
The recommendations to the General Assembly focus on strengthening the Older Adults Protective Services Act, improve the review process for suspicious deaths, and create a task force to gather input from stakeholders and cooperate with the department to ensure seniors are protected from financial exploitation and abuse.

title: University of Iowa develops AI strategy with amplifying human potential in mind
description: The University of Iowa is crafting a new artificial intelligence framework in order to better understand the technology’s impacts, good and bad, and identify opportunities for innovation across all areas of campus, university leaders say. The university has launched a new website and project support program through its artificial intelligence strategy. The I[...]
text:
The University of Iowa has launched a new website and project support program through its artificial intelligence strategy. (Photo illustration by Surasak Suwanmake/Getty Images)The University of Iowa is crafting a new artificial intelligence framework in order to better understand the technology’s impacts, good and bad, and identify opportunities for innovation across all areas of campus, university leaders say.
The university has launched a new website and project support program through its artificial intelligence strategy.
The Iowa City university announced this month it is rolling out a strategy for AI exploration and use across academics, research and clinical operations, with Associate Provost for Faculty and Strategic Operations Barry Thomas saying they are focusing on amplifying the power of human beings.
Roxanna Curto, president of the UI Faculty Senate, said she’s seen AI usage become more commonplace among her colleagues in the past couple of years, and university officials involved in crafting the AI strategy should be “commended” for just how comprehensive it is.
“They’ve really taken it seriously, you know, they’ve assembled a lot of groups to explore the questions, and there’s a lot of faculty involvement,” Curto said. “It’s just sort of a number of approaches that they’re taking.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Thomas said conversations around the larger context and impact of generative AI in higher education began in late 2022 and by spring 2024, the university had formed an AI steering committee with Thomas as a co-chair.
After learning more about how AI “cross-cut the institution” in a way where it would need to be acknowledged in the university’s overall strategic plan, the university in summer 2025 created a larger strategic plan committee with stakeholders across campus and the outside community. In this time, Thomas said researchers from different academic areas had already begun using AI as a tool in their work, and continue to do so today.
“The pace of change with these technologies has been extraordinary, as has the adoption in sort of a wide range of ways, and so of course that has led to ongoing changes in the way we’ve been thinking and approaching (our strategy), and what we need to respond to,” Thomas said.
A website housing AI policies, guidance and resources for faculty, staff and students has already been launched as part of the strategic plan, Curto said, and the university announced at the start of September it is using $1 million in public-private-partnership funding over three years to enhance access to AI tools for project teams and offer training and professional development.
Events like student debates, listening sessions and an AI in teaching and learning summit will create discussions acknowledging both the pros and cons of AI, Thomas said, as there are “uncertainties” to the upsides and downsides of the technology. The university’s new certificate in artificial intelligence also welcomed its first cohort this fall.
Curto said she believes the officials working on the AI strategy are trying to figure out how to reach all faculty and students with their plan when AI usage is “so discipline dependent,” as a clinical researcher would utilize tools differently than a French literature professor like her.
Behind the work to provide resources and guidance on AI is the goal of amplifying “human potential,” Thomas said, and harnessing that potential to take advantage of new opportunities responsibly. That means supporting every discipline in instruction, research and discovery, developing AI expertise and giving students the training they need to enter a workforce that will expect them to be AI literate.
“As an institution, it’s important that we are continually monitoring and fostering that dialogue on campus, providing and enabling our faculty, staff, and students to explore these opportunities, to help lead to a deeper understanding, whether that is through our ability to harness the tools for great discovery or to study their downsides,” Thomas said. “I’m pretty excited about where this has gone because I think it really fits with the role that a university should have.”

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC service members need more affordable housing, military leaders say
description: Military leaders praised the state's education efforts while worrying about having enough housing for service members.
text:
Veterans' Affairs Secretary Todd McCaffrey, Gov. Henry McMaster and House Speaker Murrell Smith, R-Sumter, oversee a conference of South Carolina military leaders at the University of South Carolina alumni center in Columbia, S.C., on Wednesday, Sept. 23, 2026. (Photo by Skylar Laird/SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — South Carolina’s military forces are growing, but they need more places to live, military leaders told top lawmakers Wednesday.
Affordable housing, education and support for military spouses are among the biggest concerns service members face when relocating, leaders of South Carolina’s military installations said during a round-table meeting with the governor and legislators as part of an annual conference.


SC military installations
The military bases represented at Wednesday’s meeting were:

Beaufort Naval Hospital in Port Royal
Coast Guard Charleston in North Charleston
Fort Gordon in Augusta, Georgia
Fort Jackson in Columbia
Joint Base Lindsey Graham in North Charleston
Marine Corps Air Station Beaufort in Beaufort
Marine Corps Recruit Depot Parris Island in Port Royal
National Guard
Shaw Air Force Base in Sumter County

Source: Veterans’ Affairs office


The conference is meant to identify military bases’ biggest successes and challenges in South Carolina, with the goal of giving lawmakers ideas on how they can help out.
Participants come from military installations across South Carolina, as well as Fort Gordon located just across the border in Augusta, Georgia. A law passed in 2024 officially added it to South Carolina’s list of installations qualifying for state grants.
This year, most of their needs centered not around service members themselves but around their families. Making sure communities have resources for families is key for encouraging people to enlist and to work at South Carolina’s bases, leaders said.
“You recruit a service member, but you retain a family,” said retired Army Maj. Gen. Todd McCaffrey, who leads the state Department of Veterans’ Affairs.
That’s especially true as South Carolina’s population continues to boom, McCaffrey said.
The Palmetto State has seen a surge in population in recent years, with one of the highest growth rates in the country. That squeezes an already tight market, making buying a home even harder in already pricey parts of the state. Those areas include Beaufort County, which has Marine Corps Recruit Depot Parris Island and the state’s Marine Corps Air Station, and Charleston, with Joint Base Lindsey Graham, which was renamed last month to honor South Carolina’s late senator.
Along with the strains of a growing population, more service members are being assigned to South Carolina, installation leaders said.
Beaufort, especially, has seen a surge in Marines assigned to the air station there. It’s expected to grow from about 4,700 Marines to as many as 6,000 in the next four years, said Col. Trevor Feltor, the station’s commander.
Even more service members might come to South Carolina as the war in Iran continues, military leaders said.
“That causes compression, and compression could be a challenge if you don’t have the infrastructure, you don’t have the housing, the schools,” McCaffrey said. “You hear that from these military members.”
When the number of service members grows quickly, bases run out of space to house them all.
That often leaves people scrambling to find leases or mortgages they can afford nearby for themselves and their families, said House Speaker Murrell Smith, whose district includes Shaw Air Force Base.
“We’re going to have to take on the issue of how we’re going to house people in military communities, especially when we’re in a time of war and we have been transitioning on and off the bases,” the Sumter Republican said.
He floated the idea of expanding the state’s Palmetto Heroes homebuyers’ program, which helps active-duty military, teachers, nurses, law enforcement and other public sector employees buy homes.
SC approves $72M in low-interest loans to help its ‘heroes’ buy homes in the state

The program offers $10,000 in forgivable down payment loans and low, fixed-rate mortgages until funding is depleted. This year, the $74 million SC Housing had to spend ran out after less than a month, the quickest in the program’s history, according to the agency.
Smith didn’t give details on how legislators might look to expand the program to further help service members, and McCaffrey didn’t offer specific ideas. But both agreed affordable housing was a major challenge for military members.
“You’ve got to be able to take care of families, you’ve got to be able to take care of service programmers, and you’ve got to be able to generate readiness,” McCaffrey said.
Concerns about housing for service members often center around those with families, but fresh recruits often need somewhere to live, too, several base leaders said.
Many service members don’t have driver’s licenses or cars, having gone straight from high school to basic training, said Capt. Jason Anderson, deputy commander of Joint Base Lindsey Graham. If they can’t stay on the base, which sometimes happens when they run out of space, that makes it even more essential to have housing nearby, he said.
Beaufort Naval Hospital is dealing with that pressure during renovations of its onsite barracks, said Capt. Juan Rosario, the military hospital’s commander. Around 20 sailors had to move off base during the improvements, and the hospital struggled to help them find places to live that they could afford, he said.
“Parents expect me as a leader to help their children, to keep them safe, so that they can do what they were called to do, and that is to serve our nation,” Rosario said. “In order to do that, I need to find an affordable, safe house where I can put them.”
For service members with families, making sure their spouses have job opportunities and their children have access to high-quality education is essential to keeping South Carolina a military-friendly state, leaders said.
“The reality is, when these young people decide to join the military and have families, they have an expectation — and, frankly, they’re right, I think — to have the kind of housing, the schools and the job opportunities that all Americans want to have,” McCaffrey said. “South Carolina’s working really hard to provide that.”
In July, the federal government relaunched the SpouseWorks program to help spouses of active-duty military members get jobs when they relocate. The program offers career coaches, job boards and scholarships for career-advancing degrees.
Statewide, K-12 public schools that go above and beyond to help military families can receive a Purple Star designation. Criteria for becoming a Purple Star school include designating a liaison to help with military-specific challenges, providing extra training for school staff and making sure policies are in place that allow transfer students to join sports and clubs throughout the year.
A state law passed last year also gives children from military families enrollment preference in charter schools that use a lottery system.
Programs like those “give Marines a valuable peace of mind,” said Col. Clark Mitchell, of Parris Island. “It allows them to focus on the mission, knowing their family is supported by a grateful community.”

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: MAP: Arkansas’ most populous county passes data center regulations
description: Pulaski County’s top elected official has seven days to decide whether to veto new regulations on data centers approved by the county’s quorum court. The majority-Democrat panel in Arkansas’ most populous county voted 11-4 Tuesday night in favor of the new rules. County Judge Barry Hyde, a Democrat, has seven days to veto it. The […]
text:
An audience member attending a Pulaski County Quorum Court agenda-setting meeting holds a sign opposing data centers on June 9, 2026. (Photo by Ainsley Platt/Arkansas Advocate)Pulaski County’s top elected official has seven days to decide whether to veto new regulations on data centers approved by the county’s quorum court.
The majority-Democrat panel in Arkansas’ most populous county voted 11-4 Tuesday night in favor of the new rules. County Judge Barry Hyde, a Democrat, has seven days to veto it. The measure was written by Wendell Griffen, a former circuit and appeals court judge and current Democratic nominee for county judge, and sponsored by Justice of the Peace Julie Blackwood, a Democrat. 
According to the Arkansas Democrat-Gazette, Hyde did not say whether he planned to sign the measure and appeared skeptical of it during Tuesday’s meeting. The regulations can also become law without Hyde’s signature if he does not sign or veto them after seven days. 
The regulations touch on noise, and water and power use, requiring prospective data center projects to submit to the county electrical load analyses, water and wastewater plans, land-use suitability studies and a decommissioning plan, among other requirements. Prospective data center projects are required to demonstrate that the development won’t “materially impair” utilities and other public infrastructure that serve surrounding properties under the new regulations, but do not limit the amount of water or power a project can use.
Since the quorum court first considered data center regulations for Arkansas’ most populous county in May, the opposition to the power-hungry computing hubs has grown, with polling showing increasingly broad unpopularity among Americans. 
That unpopularity has pit pro-data center interests such as the Little Rock Regional Chamber of Commerce against Pulaski County residents opposed to the AVAIO data center project in the unincorporated part of the county. 
AVAIO is one of six planned data center projects in the state. Two of those projects, in West Memphis and Clarksville, are already under construction.
The effort to regulate data centers in Pulaski County has seen fits and starts, even as Little Rock passed its own requirements over the summer. Data center opponents rejoiced in June after a temporary moratorium appeared to pass, only for the county clerk to announce days later that there had been a vote miscount. 
Debate has also raged over whether to exempt the AVAIO project from the regulations. Blackwood told the Arkansas Times that AVAIO would be required to comply with the new regulations.
The fight over data centers has cut across party lines, with elected officials in other states losing their seats amid the backlash.
The push to build more and more data centers comes as internet giants like Google, Open AI and Meta seek to capitalize on the rapid growth of artificial intelligence models. While data centers have existed for decades, powering everything from email to social media, the AI models created by tech companies require massive amounts of computing power.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Van Buren County deputy accused of excessive force
description: An Iowa man is suing the Van Buren County Sheriff’s Office, alleging excessive force was used against him by one of its officers. John Michael Orndoff, 25, of Milton, is suing Van Buren County and Deputy Adam McIntyre, who has been employed by the county since 2018. According to the lawsuit, McIntyre was working on […]
text:
(Photo by David Talukdar/Getty Images)An Iowa man is suing the Van Buren County Sheriff’s Office, alleging excessive force was used against him by one of its officers.
John Michael Orndoff, 25, of Milton, is suing Van Buren County and Deputy Adam McIntyre, who has been employed by the county since 2018.
According to the lawsuit, McIntyre was working on Oct. 15, 2024, when he observed Orndoff driving a vehicle without license plates. Before McIntyre could initiate a traffic stop, Orndoff parked the car and began walking away. After speaking to the county dispatch staff, McIntyre learned that Orndoff’s driving privileges had been revoked, and informed Orndoff that he was being cited for driving with a revoked license.
Orndoff objected and asked to speak to the county’s chief deputy, according to the lawsuit. McIntyre denied the request, then took hold of one of Orndoff’s arms and directed him to place his hands behind his back. “Orndoff did not immediately comply, but did not strike, threaten or in any way assault McIntyre, and did not attempt to flee,” the lawsuit asserts. “Within seconds of first taking hold of Orndoff, and after a single warning, McIntyre threw Orndoff head-first to the ground …  Because McIntyre was controlling Orndoff’s arms, Orndoff was unable to break his fall or to protect his head as he was driven to the ground.”
According to the lawsuit, Orndoff’s head struck the concrete and he was immediately rendered unconscious before convulsing.
“Orndoff sustained a severe head injury, including a skull fracture and brain bleed, as a result of the takedown,” the lawsuit asserts. “Orndoff posed no immediate threat to McIntyre or to anyone else; Orndoff was unarmed, and Orndoff was not actively resisting arrest or attempting to flee but was, at most, passively resisting.”
Orndoff was taken to Van Buren County Hospital and then transferred by air to the University of Iowa Hospitals and Clinics in Iowa City, according to the lawsuit.
Court records show Orndoff was later charged with, and convicted of, driving with a revoked license and interference with official acts.
The lawsuit seeks unspecified damages for alleged violation of Orndoff’s constitutional rights and for alleged assault and battery. The county has yet to respond to the lawsuit, and Van Buren County Attorney H. Craig Miller declined to comment on the allegations.
Court records indicate that in July, Orndoff was charged with livestock neglect. Police alleged that along with a veterinarian, they investigated several complaints of animal neglect on Orndoff’s property and found a young cow in an emaciated condition that was suffering from a lack of feed and potable water. The veterinarian noted the cow’s visible spine, ribs, and pelvic bones, as well as signs of muscle wasting. “This animal is in need of immediate sustenance and veterinary care,” Dr. Emma Fryauf Fallis wrote in her report on the cow’s condition.
Four weeks after the charge of livestock neglect was imposed, it was dismissed by the court at the request of county prosecutors, although Miller said he could not comment on the reasons for the request.
Orndoff is currently facing a charge of failure to properly dispose of dead animals. A county deputy alleges a dead pig was found in a feed bag on Orndoff’s property and a “skinned animal” of some kind was found hanging from a tree in his yard. According to the deputy, Orndoff said he was using the dead animals to feed to his dogs.
Orndoff has pleaded not guilty to the charge. A trial date has yet to be scheduled.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Demuth-affiliated political action committee receives $10 million infusion
description: A super PAC backing Republican House Speaker Lisa Demuth’s campaign for Minnesota governor received a $10 million cash infusion in recent weeks, cutting into Sen. Amy Klobuchar’s longtime financial advantage in the race. Restore Sanity — a political action committee that has provided the most significant outside money in support of a statewide Republican can[...]
text:
House Speaker Lisa Demuth, R-Cold Spring, announced she is running in the August GOP primary election during a press conference in front of the Minnesota Capitol. (Photo by Michelle Griffith/Minnesota Reformer)A super PAC backing Republican House Speaker Lisa Demuth’s campaign for Minnesota governor received a $10 million cash infusion in recent weeks, cutting into Sen. Amy Klobuchar’s longtime financial advantage in the race.
Restore Sanity — a political action committee that has provided the most significant outside money in support of a statewide Republican candidate in years — received $10 million in the past four weeks from the Restoration of America PAC, which is primarily funded by Wisconsin billionaire duo Richard and Elizabeth Uihlein. The Uihleins own one of North America’s largest distributors of shipping and packaging supplies.
The Uihleins have donated $70 million this election cycle in favor of GOP candidates and causes, making them the fifth-largest donors in the midterm election so far, according to the Washington Post.
The Restore Sanity PAC has spent nearly $4.4 million on digital and TV ads in support of Demuth’s campaign for governor and nearly $1.8 million on ads against Klobuchar’s campaign, according to campaign finance reports released Wednesday that detail spending and fundraising up to Sept. 15. The independent expenditure committee has raised $14.1 million, of which over $13 million came from the Uihlein-funded PAC. Restore Sanity has nearly $7 million in cash in the final weeks leading up to the Nov. 3 election.
The cash infusion suggests at least some big-money Republicans see glimmers of hope here in Minnesota, where Democrats haven’t lost a statewide race since 2006 but have been weighed down since by embarrassing stories about the looting of the state’s safety net by fraudsters.
Klobuchar, who is ending a 20-year Senate career to run for governor, has raised over $12.5 million since launching her campaign at the end of January and has spent $9 million, mostly on consulting and ads. Her campaign has over $3.5 million in cash.
Demuth’s gubernatorial campaign has raised nearly $2.6 million this year, half of which came from a $1.3 million public subsidy payment last month. The state provides the subsidy to candidates who agree to spending and fundraising limits. Klobuchar opted out of the subsidy, which allowed Demuth to receive a larger payment. Klobuchar didn’t participate in the subsidy because she would have had to cap her fundraising.
Klobuchar’s cash advantage will likely be compounded by Democratic-Farmer-Labor-aligned allies like the Alliance for a Better Minnesota, which has historically been backed by wealthy benefactors like Rockefeller heiress Alida Messinger and public-sector unions.
The Alliance for a Better Minnesota PAC has raised $3.55 million this year and has spent over $1.3 million on digital ads against Demuth.
In addition to the governor’s race, all 201 seats in the Minnesota Legislature will be on the ballot in November, so the rival legislative caucuses and political parties are fundraising and will spend big to gain control of state government.
House Democrats have raised $5.6 million this year and have $3.2 million in cash in the final weeks before the midterms. House Republicans have raised over $2 million this year and have about $2 million in cash.
Senate Democrats have raised $5.7 million and have nearly $5.2 million in cash. Senate Republicans have raised nearly $3 million this year and have $3.8 million in cash.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Louisiana community colleges face faculty poaching from new industry
description: Major companies investing in Louisiana are looking to the state’s community and technical colleges to supply their workforce, and they are also poaching the instructors who teach there, the school system’s leader said this week.  A series of major industrial projects are coming to Louisiana, touting numerous high-paying jobs that require specialized training[...]
text:
Louisiana Community and Technical College System President Richard Nelson. (Greg LaRose | Louisiana Illuminator)Major companies investing in Louisiana are looking to the state’s community and technical colleges to supply their workforce, and they are also poaching the instructors who teach there, the school system’s leader said this week. 
A series of major industrial projects are coming to Louisiana, touting numerous high-paying jobs that require specialized training, most notably the Hyundai steel plant in Ascension Parish, the Meta Hyperion data center in Richland Parish and a Space X launch facility in Vermilion Parish. 
Their staffing demands are straining the state’s ability to train enough students to ensure the new jobs go to Louisianians, Louisiana Community and Technical College System President Richard Nelson told the Board of Regents at its monthly meeting Tuesday. 
Another challenge for the system as it tries to fill those jobs is the companies hiring highly-skilled tradespeople from community colleges who are training the next generation of workers, higher education leaders said at a budget hearing Tuesday. 
“We can’t produce 10 times, 100 times more welders or plumbers if everyone is poaching all of our faculty,” Commissioner of Higher Education Kim Hunter Reed said. “So that issue has to be resolved, and companies need to stand in partnership with us as we try to do this work.” 
In addition to luring away faculty, Nelson said some companies are hiring students before they complete their training to meet their need for workers with even basic technical skills. 
Entry-level positions at the Meta data center start at $44,200 a year, according to figures from Louisiana Economic Development. The annual pay for lowest-paid workers at the SpaceX facility will be $78,000, while Hyundai has not made entry-level compensation for its steel mill jobs public.
Nelson said the demand for workers is so high that the system would have to double its enrollment for Louisiana residents to fill the available jobs. The system enrolls more than 100,000 students annually and awards credentials and degrees to over 30,000 students a year. 
To meet the workforce demand, Nelson said the LCTCS budget would have to increase more than $100 million annually. Its budget for the current academic year is $340 million. 
“What (we) really have to do is build that infrastructure to provide a much greater level of workforce than what we’ve been used to,” Nelson said. 
Nelson said the additional money could be used to pay skilled faculty enough to remain in their jobs, to build new training facilities and provide students with wraparound services, such as childcare and transportation.  
Starting up new programs to meet the needs of the companies currently hiring is more expensive than maintaining existing programs, according to Nelson. The cost primarily falls on the state rather than on the businesses, he said. 
Providing the funding needed to train their workers should be part of the conversation when big employers are looking to come to Louisiana, Nelson added.
“Once they sign the paperwork, well, now you have to actually provide the people, and it’s going to be over a period of years after that,” he said. “If there’s no funding to do that, what position are we in?”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Federal judge tosses Nessel suit accusing fossil fuel industry of anti-trust violations
description: Earlier this year, Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel joined a number of states across the country in taking legal action against the fossil fuel industry when she filed a suit against four of the world’s energy companies and a major oil lobbying group accusing them of violating state and federal anti-trust laws to discourage competition […]
text:
Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel speaks at a press conference on her lawsuit, alongside 25 other state attorneys general and governors, for a restraining order on the pause for SNAP benefits on Nov. 1. Oct. 29. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance. Earlier this year, Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel joined a number of states across the country in taking legal action against the fossil fuel industry when she filed a suit against four of the world’s energy companies and a major oil lobbying group accusing them of violating state and federal anti-trust laws to discourage competition from renewable energy. 
However, a U.S. District Court judge on Tuesday determined Nessel lacks the standing to pursue federal anti-trust claims, granting in-part a motion to dismiss the case.
In the suit filed on behalf of the state of Michigan, attorneys for the state alleged that BP, Chevron, Exxon Mobil, Shell and the American Petroleum Institute had violated the Sherman Antitrust Act, the Clayton Antitrust Act and the Michigan Antitrust Reform Act. 
The suit argues the defendants had conspired with each other for decades to preemptively limit competition from renewable energy in order to maintain dominance over the energy market, resulting in harm to Michigan residents through overpriced energy, a lack of energy options on the market and increased costs to implement measures to counter the negative effects of fossil fuel use.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In her order, Judge Jane M. Beckering of the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Michigan determined that even if Michigan had adequately pleaded a conspiracy, “the antitrust laws protect against none of the injuries for which Michigan seeks a remedy, except for overcharges for energy.”
Beckering wrote that the state had plausibly alleged that the fossil fuel companies stifled innovation in and adoption of renewable energies, but ultimately determined that the state failed to show proximate cause proving that this conspiracy led to higher costs for Michigan residents.
“This decision adds to the growing list of federal and state courts that have dismissed climate lawsuits,” Chevron’s attorney, Theodore J. Boutrous Jr., said in a statement. “These climate suits are baseless no matter plaintiffs’ attempts to concoct new litigation theories, like these meritless antitrust claims.”
In a statement to Michigan Advance, Nessel Press Secretary Danny Wimmer noted the attorney general’s disagreement with the decision.
“Our office is reviewing the opinion in full and considering our options.” Wimmer said.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: GOP general treasurer candidate pledges greater scrutiny of RI pension system
description: In politics, having connections can sometimes be the easiest way to get something done. But the Republican nominee for general treasurer, Micholas Credle, says you shouldn’t have to “know a guy” to get answers about how Rhode Island manages its money. Credle, who ran unopposed in the GOP primary, stood in the State House rotunda […]
text:
Micholas Credle, the Republican nominee for Rhode Island general treasurer, speaks at a State House press conference attended by other GOP candidates and retirees on Sept. 23, 2026. At far left is Rhode Island GOP Chairman Allyn Meyers. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)In politics, having connections can sometimes be the easiest way to get something done. But the Republican nominee for general treasurer, Micholas Credle, says you shouldn’t have to “know a guy” to get answers about how Rhode Island manages its money.
Credle, who ran unopposed in the GOP primary, stood in the State House rotunda Wednesday, alongside other Republican candidates and a handful of retirees, and pledged to bring greater transparency to how the state oversees its pension investments and other financial initiatives.
“Answers should not depend on connections,” Credle said during a press conference that drew only two reporters. “Rhode Islanders should not have to guess what happened to their money, they shouldn’t have to chase documents or know somebody to know something.”
A retired U.S. Army officer who was born in North Carolina, Credle grew up in Illinois and Indiana, and moved to Rhode Island in 2019. But he said Wednesday that he considers himself a Rhode Islander nonetheless.
“I live here, I pay taxes, I serve here,” said Credle, who resides in Providence.
The first-time office-seeker then offered his own example of a “guy” whose record, he said, should prompt Rhode Islanders to ask questions.
“I know a guy who holds public office and has been entrusted with responsibility,” Credle said. “I know a guy whose public record has generated questions about transparency and the stewardship of public resources.”
When announcing his bid for a second term earlier in April, General Treasurer James Diossa said he had worked to “protect the financial future of all Rhode Islanders,” highlighting the growth of the state’s pension fund and other efforts to manage the state’s money. 
But Credle said Rhode Islanders deserve more than assurances about how their money is being managed.
“Open the books,” he demanded. “Release every record.”
Credle also challenged Diossa to debate him, saying the sitting office holder has declined to acknowledge his candidacy or answer his questions.
Diossa was seen outside the State House about 10 minutes after Credle left the building. Asked by Rhode Island Current whether he would debate his Republican opponent, Diossa replied only that his campaign strategy is “traveling the state interacting with the voters.” He declined to comment on Credle’s press conference.
Credle said greater scrutiny of the state’s pension system is needed because many retirees remain frustrated with the state overhaul more than a decade ago championed by then-General Treasurer Gina Raimondo and enacted by the General Assembly. The changes suspended the 3% annual cost-of-living increases retirees had received before 2011 and instead tied increases to the pension’s funding level, investment returns and inflation.
“This is a miscarriage of justice,” Sandra Marzilli Paquette, a retired special educator who helped found the Advocates for COLA Restoration and Pension Reform group, said in an interview after the press conference. “People cannot afford medications. People cannot afford heat. They cannot afford to fuel their cars.”
Pensioners received a one-time 2% COLA adjustment after a 2015 settlement. Subsequent changes to the COLA structure came in 2023 and 2024, with the latter providing a fully calculated annual COLA to retirees who retired on or before June 30, 2012.
Paquette said she and other members of her group are supporting Credle because she believes retirees need someone in the Treasurer’s Office who will listen to their concerns and examine the pension system’s finances.
“He is acknowledging the fact that what occurred in 2011 should not have occurred, and he is acknowledging the fact that when he is [in office], he is going to look into this,” Paquette said of Credle. “He is going to see what went wrong, what our assets are.”
Credle  has worked in executive compensation and described himself Wednesday as an educator and “financial student.” He has also served as chairman of the Ward 12 Republican City Committee in Providence.
Early voting begins Oct. 14 ahead of the Nov. 3 general election.
