name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Critics say NC’s property tax amendment could do more harm than good
description: There will be much at stake in November when North Carolinians go to the polls. The state has one of the nation’s most closely-watched U.S. Senate races. A win by former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper — a Democrat matched against Michael Whatley, former chairman of the Republican National Committee — could help change the […]
text:
(Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)There will be much at stake in November when North Carolinians go to the polls.
The state has one of the nation’s most closely-watched U.S. Senate races. A win by former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper — a Democrat matched against Michael Whatley, former chairman of the Republican National Committee — could help change the balance of power in the Senate.
But for some homeowners, particularly those living on fixed incomes, rising property taxes will also be top of mind on Election Day. That’s when voters will be asked to consider a Republican-backed constitutional amendment requiring state lawmakers to pass laws limiting the maximum amount that local leaders can increase property taxes. 
The amendment, Republican leaders said, grew out of homeowners’ growing discontent about high property taxes. Seniors in particular are having a tough time aging in place because high property taxes are forcing them out of homes, they said.
Rep. Erin Paré (Photo: NCGA)
“It was because of the outpouring of concern over years … from constituents, mostly seniors, but pretty much everybody,” State Rep. Erin Paré (R-Wake) told NC Newsline. “I think even my friends from the other side of the aisle can attest to that, that they [constituents] just were seeing their property tax bills go up, and it was kind of unpredictable.” 
As NC Newsline previously reported, the House Select Committee on Property Tax Reduction and Reform recommended adding the constitutional amendment to the ballot. House Speaker Destin Hall (R-Caldwell) created the committee to examine tax reform as a result of constituent complaints.
Hall and other Republican leaders blame local governments for excessive increases.
“Families are getting ripped off as some, but by no means all, local governments rake in billions more than inflation and population growth warrant,” Hall said in the spring.
Local government officials, progressive advocacy groups and Democratic lawmakers who oppose the measure say that limiting the amount of tax revenue local governments can collect could have dire consequences for local governments, which could be forced to cut services. 
Local property taxes help pay for vital needs like public safety, education, and public health.
Alexandra Sirota (Photo: NC Budget & Tax Center)
“It would undermine local decision-making about how communities fund schools, emergency services, libraries, and more, even as communities are trying to respond to rising costs.” Alexandra Sirota, executive director of the NC Budget and Tax Center, said in a statement. 
Sirota added that the property tax amendment “wouldn’t provide meaningful relief to homeowners” but would “give outsized breaks to corporate property owners and high-value properties.”  
The League of Women Voters NC also weighed in against the property tax amendment, expressing concern that “restricting local property-tax revenue could affect funding for public education, elections and other local services and/or increase reliance on fees.” 
“LWVNC opposes the property-tax levy amendment because it would shift greater authority over local funding decisions to the state while leaving the actual limits, formulas and possible exceptions to future legislation,” the organization said in a statement.
A recent report by the NC Housing Coalition, a nonprofit housing advocacy group, estimates that counties and municipalities would have lost nearly $1 billion for essential services if a 2% levy limit had been in place during the most recent revaluation cycle. 
Meanwhile, the average homeowner would have only saved $7 a month or $84 a year. But Duke Energy would have saved $10 million, and several data centers more than $1 million each, according to the coalition’s analysis. 
Samuel Gunter (Photo: NC Housing Coalition)
“Supporters of this bill are arguing that this is going to substantially relieve the property tax burden, especially on vulnerable homeowners,” said Samuel Gunter, executive director of the housing coalition. “We wanted to investigate that claim.”
The housing coalition also found that 73 of North Carolina’s 100 counties would have lost property tax revenue under a 2% levy and that 24 counties would have seen tax revenues fall by 10% or more. 
The coalition used a 2% levy limit to make its case because the Tax Foundation, a conservative-leaning tax policy nonprofit, used that number when it pitched the idea of a levy limit to the House committee looking into property tax reform.
“We’re not saying that this would be the exact impact on a county or on a city of a future levy limit, but instead trying to help us see what it would have really looked like, and what its impact would have been, and what could that tell us about this proposed amendment,” said Hudson Vaughan, the primary author of the coalition’s analysis.
Paré said it’s important to remember that the amendment only gives lawmakers the authority to set a levy limit. The General Assembly will work out the details if voters approve the amendment, she said.
“That could be a wide variety of things going into some type of formula that gives us whatever levy limit we believe makes sense,” Paré said. “That could be well beyond 2%, that could be some sort of population growth, plus inflation, plus something else formula. It’s just very, very early to say what that could look like.”
NC groups launch campaign to defeat two tax amendments on November ballot

Despite that uncertainty, and even though the housing coalition’s analysis shows individual homeowners aren’t likely to save much and could lose critical services, the amendment looks likely to win approval. 
A recent Elon University poll found that 72% of likely voters favor the amendment limiting property tax increases, while 14% oppose it. Another 14% were unsure. 
Two other amendments — one requiring photo IDs for all forms of voting and another lowering the cap on the state’s personal income tax rate from 7% to 3.5% — are also likely to be approved.
“All the amendments on the ballot, we’re finding have much stronger for than against,” Jason Husser, director of the Elon University Poll, told NC Newsline.
Vaughan acknowledged that it will be difficult to defeat the amendments.
Hudson Vaughan shares property tax updates with Orange County residents. (Photo: Greg Childress/NC Newsline)
“I think it will be an uphill battle to defeat them because of how misleading they are, and how challenging it is to reach the general public about the complexities of what these really are and what they mean,” Vaughan said. “There’s a lot of folks who are understandably struggling right now, and so anything that seems like it will cut the amount that they have to pay for something is going to be appealing.”
A more immediate remedy for the property tax dilemma is to improve and expand  existing programs that give tax breaks to seniors and disabled taxpayers, Vaughan said.
“Fixing those programs would go a long way towards really helping the folks who need it most, and keeping folks who are on fixed income and who are struggling to stay in their homes in their homes and in their communities that have greatly benefited from their presence for a long time,” Vaughan said.
Paré has also championed legislation to  improve programs that provide tax breaks for seniors and disabled citizens. She said more flexibility is needed in the state’s homestead exemptions programs because current exemptions are inadequate for urban areas where properties often carry higher values.
“I think the biggest pressure is coming from seniors who have been living in their homes for 50 years, and especially in Wake County,” Paré said. “You’re in your 80s and you paid off your house decades ago and you have to pay for property taxes that you can’t afford now because your tiny house in downtown Raleigh is worth all this money.”

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Republicans sue again to demand records in NJ noncitizen voting blunder
description: The Republican National Committee sued New Jersey election officials in a bid to compel them to produce voter records.
text:
The Republican National Committee sued New Jersey election officials in a bid to compel them to produce voter records. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)The Republican National Committee has sued New Jersey’s top election official and five county election supervisors for withholding voter records it says are public under federal law.
The committee on Tuesday accused Lt. Gov. Dale Caldwell, who oversees elections as secretary of state, and election administrators in Bergen, Hudson, Middlesex, Somerset, and Union counties of violating the National Voter Registration Act of 1993.
The committee filed requests for 13 categories of voter records on July 31, 10 days after Gov. Mikie Sherrill (D) revealed the state registered thousands of noncitizens to vote and that about 300 of them cast ballots. Sherrill has blamed a software error at the Motor Vehicle Commission, where customers can be automatically registered to vote.
But Caldwell’s office didn’t respond for six weeks, and then largely denied the requests, the lawsuit charges. The county election officials also failed to provide most of the records sought, it says.
Under the National Voter Registration Act, records relating to the “implementation of programs and activities conducted for the purpose of ensuring the accuracy and currency of official lists of eligible voters” are considered public records that must be disclosed upon request, the lawsuit says.
Joe Gruters, the committee’s chairman, noted that Sherrill admitted the state goofed in registering noncitizens.
“Now, election officials are hiding the records that would tell voters how it happened,” Gruters said in a statement. “The RNC won’t stand for it. Garden State voters deserve the truth, and we’re taking these left-wing officials to court to demand answers.”
The committee wants a federal judge to declare New Jersey election officials in violation of the National Voter Registration Act and compel them to produce the records sought. Tuesday’s lawsuit is the second the committee has filed seeking answers about the goof. They also sued in state court in early July before Sherrill went public with it; that case remains pending.
A spokesperson for Caldwell did not return a request for comment.
Steve Sigmund, a Sherrill spokesman, blasted the latest lawsuit.
“While Gov. Sherrill is working to clean up the voter rolls and protect our elections, Republicans are still following the same Trump MAGA playbook,” Sigmund said. “Gov. Sherrill has made clear that the Trump Administration should not have access to the personal identifiable information of millions of New Jersey voters, and the courts have agreed.”
The Trump administration sued Caldwell earlier this year seeking unredacted voter records under the National Voter Registration Act, but a federal judge dismissed the case in July, saying federal law that mandates election officials turn over some types of records to the federal Election Assistance Commission upon request does not extend to New Jersey’s digital voter registration system.
Michael Symons, spokesman for the Attorney General’s Office, said the office is “committed to ensuring that our elections are free, fair, and secure.”
“Our election officials undertake extensive efforts to maintain voter rolls and ensure all eligible voters, and only eligible voters, can vote. We look forward to defending our elections against this partisan lawsuit, which is a fishing expedition for the personal information of New Jersey voters,” Symons said.
The records Republicans sought include policies and procedures governing New Jersey’s maintenance of voter rolls; lists of voters removed and why; and communications between state agencies identifying registered voters discovered to be deceased, relocated, and not citizens.
Besides the committee, the lawsuit’s plaintiffs include Sen. Anthony Bucco, the state Senate’s GOP leader, and Rep. Thomas Kean, a Republican now in a tight race to retain his congressional seat in the 7th District.
They’re represented by two lawyers from a Virginia-based firm founded by Harmeet Dhillon, who President Donald Trump appointed to head the Department of Justice’s civil rights division. Dhillon, who’s also a former Republican National Committeewoman, has claimed noncitizens’ votes “cancel out” Americans’ votes and vowed to prosecute anyone involved.
Claims of widespread noncitizen voting have been repeatedly debunked — a Republican former elections official from Arizona testified to a House subcommittee hearing last week that such claims are exaggerated — but recent polling suggests the allegations are working to erode public confidence in the electoral system.
Besides Caldwell, the county election officials named as defendants are Debra M. Francica, elections superintendent in Bergen County; Maryanne Kelleher, elections superintendent in Hudson County; Scott Snyder, commissioner of registration in Middlesex County; Anthony J. DeCicco, commissioner of registration in Somerset County; and James Foerst, commissioner of registration in Union County.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Whitmer directs MSP to investigate fatal crash following ICE pursuit in Grand Rapids
description: Gov. Gretchen Whitmer has directed the Michigan State Police to investigate the circumstances surrounding a car crash in Grand Rapids that killed a man. The Grand Rapids Police Department and local activists both say the crash occurred while the driver was fleeing a traffic stop involving U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents. The victim was […]
text:
Michigan State Police logo | Photo by Jon King/Michigan AdvanceGov. Gretchen Whitmer has directed the Michigan State Police to investigate the circumstances surrounding a car crash in Grand Rapids that killed a man. The Grand Rapids Police Department and local activists both say the crash occurred while the driver was fleeing a traffic stop involving U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents.
The victim was Mario David Coronado Juárez, according to U.S. Rep. Hillary Scholten (D-Grand Rapids) and local activists with Movimiento Cosecha GR. At a press conference on Tuesday evening, Gema Lowe, an activist with Movimiento Cosecha, said that Coronado Juárez was a father of three children and in his mid-30s.
ICE’s role in the crash led Grand Rapids Police Chief Joe Trigg to request that state police assist with the investigation, because local police are more limited in their ability to obtain information from federal agents.
“Given the circumstances of this incident, the Governor has directed the Michigan State Police to conduct an independent review of the law enforcement actions surrounding this situation in coordination with the Grand Rapids Police Department’s investigation,” the governor’s chief communications officer Kaylie Hanson said in a statement. 
A spokesperson for the governor did not answer specific questions regarding the abilities of state police to investigate the actions of federal agents in ways that local police cannot and about the powers of state police to hold federal agents accountable, depending on the outcome of the investigation.



Quotation







It needs to stop. How many more are going to die? How many more do we have to send home? This needs to stop. We are asking for justice today.


– Karla Barbari, a member of the Guatemalan community in Grand Rapids


The crash occurred around 7:10 a.m. Sunday near Century Avenue SW and McKendrick Street, which police say turned fatal when Coronado Juárez, the driver of the car, hit a tree as he was fleeing ICE agents and his car caught fire.
Activists at the press conference called his death part of “a massive, ongoing escalation in ICE violence across Grand Rapids, the region, and the country,” and blamed the immigration agents’ actions for the car crash that killed Coronado Juárez.
“ICE agents, Immigrations and Customs Enforcement agents, were chasing him and he was terrified,” Lauren Coman, a local organizer with GR Rapid Response to ICE and No Detention Centers in Michigan, said. “It was evident from the moment the footage was shown that the same vehicles we at GR Rapid Response to ICE see kidnapping our neighbors all over Grand Rapids and parking at 517 Ottawa were at the scene: a white Dodge Durango, a charcoal Dodge Durango, and a compact sedan. ICE was in fact called in this accident, and the reason that Mario is no longer with us.”
Lauren Coman, an organizer with No Detention Centers Michigan, demanded sanctuary city policies in Grand Rapids and an end to Grand Rapids Police Department officers working alongside ICE agents. Aug. 11, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.
Local organizers and members of the Guatemalan community at the press conference emphasized the tragedy of Coronado Juárez’s death.
“He was focused on working, providing for his family, and saving enough money to begin building a home for them in Guatemala,” Lowe said of Coronado Juárez. “Mario was a devoted family member who dreamed of creating a better future for his children, just like anyone, just like us and any of you. He was described for those who knew him as humble, hardworking, and deeply committed to his family.”

Lowe added that Coronado Juárez’s family wants his remains to be sent home to Guatemala. The group is hosting a vigil on Thursday evening with his family members to demand justice for his death and to help reunite his remains with his family.
Activists allege Grand Rapids police are working with ICE despite city policy 

“His family is asking for justice. They want his remains and they want justice,” Karla Barbari, a member of the Guatemalan community in Grand Rapids, said tearfully. “It needs to stop. How many more are going to die? How many more do we have to send home? This needs to stop. We are asking for justice today.” 
Scholten, whose district includes Grand Rapids, sent a letter on Tuesday to David Venturella, the acting director of ICE, asking for further information on the circumstances surrounding the crash, including the stated reason for the pursuit and whether there was a preexisting warrant, order of removal or ongoing investigation into the subject of the vehicle chase. 
She also asked for details on whether or not the pursuit was classified as high-risk, an ICE practice that has drawn criticism from elected officials around the state for endangering both those involved and the surrounding community. 
Scholten further requested that ICE “make relevant footage and records available to this office, local law enforcement, and the family of the deceased,” and asked the agency to confirm that all body-worn camera footage, dashcam footage and incident reports are retained. 
U.S. Rep. Hillary Scholten (D-Grand Rapids) speaks to reporters after visiting the North Lake Processing Center in Baldwin, Mich. Feb. 17, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.
“No traffic stop should end with a fatality. Something went wrong, and we need to know what and how. I have sent a letter to Immigration and Customs Enforcement demanding immediate answers about what happened and a transparent investigation into facts we don’t yet know, so that we can prevent something like this from ever happening again,” Scholten said in a press release. “The purpose of federal law enforcement is to make our communities safer. We must make sure that is happening. I will continue to monitor this situation closely and remain in close contact with federal and local law enforcement until our community gets the answers we deserve.”
Scholten faced criticism in recent months from some local elected officials and community leaders, who published a statement in mid-August saying that Scholten’s stance in opposition to the abolition of ICE was harmful to the West Michigan community. 
“Coalitions of immigrants, their families, friends and the networks they are embedded in throughout the community are antagonized by the continued propping up of ICE,” the statement read. “We hope this is an opportunity for the Congresswoman to be a unifier and firmly reject the notion that ICE has made our communities safer in any capacity, or that it was ever meant to be.”
Scholten responded with a statement of her own, saying that she understands the concerns of constituents about “increasingly aggressive” immigration enforcement and the need for accountability, but that she continues to believe that abolishing ICE as an agency is not the answer to those concerns.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Could Mississippi State and Ole Miss repeat the glory of the 2014 football season?
description: Mississippi State quarterback Kamario Taylor (1) rolls out to pass during an NCAA college football game against South Carolina Saturday, Sept. 19, 2026, in Columbia, S.C. Mississippi State won 41-34.
text:
So, here we are, three weeks into the college football season, and some Mississippi football fans are asking themselves: Could we be looking at another 2014 season?
Rick Cleveland
Remember? For nearly two months, Mississippi was the talk of college football. Ole Miss began the season ranked 18th and rose to as high as No. 3. Mississippi State began the season unranked and rose to No. 1. No. 1! The Bulldogs stayed there for five weeks. Five weeks! For two weeks in October, State was ranked No. 1 and Ole Miss No. 3. Poor ol’ Mississippi was the toast of college football. We were living a dream.
If you remember that, you remember this: And then we woke up. LSU burst the Rebels’ bubble, beating Ole Miss 10-7 at Baton Rouge on Oct. 25, after the Rebs led into the fourth quarter. Alabama – isn’t it always Alabama? – knocked off the previously 9-0 Bulldogs 25-20 on Nov. 15. It wasn’t that close.
Those 2014 Bulldogs, led by St. Dak Prescott, would wind up ranked No. 11 in January with a 10-3 record. Those Rebels, after losing to TCU 42-3 in the Peach Bowl, would wind up 9-4 and dropped all the way to 17th in the final Associated Press poll.
Flash forward to today. Ole Miss, 3-0, has risen to No. 4 after vanquishing LSU 32-24 last Saturday night in Oxford. You could make the case the Rebels should be higher. Who else in the country has already defeated two nationally ranked teams? Nobody, that’s who. State, 3-0, has broken into the AP poll at No. 24 after back-to-back road victories over Minnesota and South Carolina.
Who knows how either will finish? Both face so many football landmines, beginning with this Saturday when Ole Miss goes to No. 21 Florida and State hosts No. 19 Missouri. Later, Ole Miss still must play five more ranked teams, including State. After Missouri, State still faces Alabama (currently No. 8), LSU (currently No. 10), somehow unranked Oklahoma, and No. 1 Texas, all in the month of October. It doesn’t seem fair.
So, in answer to the question asked in the first paragraph of this column: No, I don’t believe we are looking at another 2014 season. The schedules are too brutal, too early. I don’t think we’ll see the two Mississippi teams both ranked among the top teams in college football. I don’t think Ole Miss or State will rise to No. 1 –  and certainly not for a five-week run.
But the possibility is there. These are two really good college football teams, with the most important ingredient a team needs to make a championship run. That is, each has a quarterback who can step up when it matters most and win games.
Mississippi quarterback Trinidad Chambliss (6) passes against LSU during the second half of an NCAA college football game in Oxford, Miss., Saturday, Sept. 19, 2026.  Credit: AP Photo/Rogelio V. Solis
Last Saturday began with Ole Miss coach Pete Golding speaking the truth on ESPN “College Gameday.” Said Golding, “If you ain’t got a quarterback, you’re screwed. I don’t care what level it is.” 
Both State and Ole Miss are far from screwed. Trinidad Chambliss and Kamario Taylor are remarkably talented; both seemed to have that “it” factor all great quarterbacks have.
Quick aside: When I was packing up my backpack in the Vaught-Hemingway press box in the wee hours of Sunday morning, one of the dozen or so national writers covering the game stopped and told me, “You need to book your tickets to New York for the second weekend in December.” 
I asked why, and he said, “You are probably going to have two finalists for the Heisman: Trinidad and Kamario.”
That is a possibility if both can remain healthy through the SEC football’s version of the Bataan Death March. Both showed why on Saturday.
Taylor, just a sophomore, went first: Down 16-0 before nearly 80,000 howling fans, he threw for four touchdowns to rally State to a 41-34 road victory over South Carolina. Then came Chambliss: After LSU rallied from a 24-7 halftime deficit to tie the score, Chambliss drove the Rebels 75 yards for the winning touchdown and scored it himself on a 14-yard scamper. 
Both will need similar performances to win this Saturday. At the Swamp in Gainesville, Ole Miss faces a highly talented, 3-0 Florida team that is a three-point favorite to beat the Rebels. State plays host to a Missouri team that demolished visiting State 49-27 last year. State is a 5.5-point favorite over a Missouri team that is still missing tailback Ahmad Hardy, the Mississippian who ran around, through and over the Bulldogs for 300 yards last season.
For Ole Miss and State to do a 2014 do-over, both would have to win tough games Saturday. And then, it will  only get harder.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Georgia should build on housing progress by centering families
description: Every day at United Way, we meet families who are doing everything right. They’re working, raising children, contributing to their communities and still struggling to find housing they can afford. For many, the challenge isn’t simply buying a home. It’s finding a safe, stable place to live that fits their budget and allows them to […]
text:
As state lawmakers prepare for next year's legislative session, our guest commentary author writes that there is an opportunity to focus on the policies that can make the greatest difference for working families. Photo by Grace Cary/Getty ImagesEvery day at United Way, we meet families who are doing everything right. They’re working, raising children, contributing to their communities and still struggling to find housing they can afford. For many, the challenge isn’t simply buying a home. It’s finding a safe, stable place to live that fits their budget and allows them to build toward the future.
That’s why housing policy matters so much. It touches nearly every aspect of a family’s well-being, from financial stability and educational outcomes to health and workforce participation.
Recently, Congress took an important step by passing the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, the first significant federal housing legislation in more than three decades. While no single law will solve Georgia’s housing challenges overnight, it represents meaningful progress and creates an opportunity for states to build on that momentum.
Georgia continues to experience strong population growth, and our housing supply has struggled to keep pace. That imbalance affects families across the income spectrum, particularly those who are already making difficult choices between housing, childcare, transportation and healthcare.
As lawmakers prepare for next year’s legislative session, there’s an opportunity to focus on the policies that can make the greatest difference for working families. That means supporting housing production, streamlining permitting where appropriate, addressing infrastructure needs and reducing unnecessary barriers that make it more difficult or more expensive to build homes.
The recent federal legislation also established new guardrails for institutional investment in the single-family housing market, responding to concerns that have been raised in communities across the country. With that framework now in place, Georgia has an opportunity to evaluate how those changes work in practice while keeping its attention on the broader challenge that continues to affect families every day: there simply are not enough homes to meet demand.
Communities need a variety of housing options. Some families are ready to purchase a home. Others need the flexibility of renting while they save, relocate for work, recover from financial hardship or care for loved ones. A healthy housing market includes opportunities across that spectrum, ensuring people can find housing that meets their needs at different stages of life.
For organizations like United Way, the goal has never been to champion one particular housing model or another. Our focus is on outcomes. We want families to have stable housing, children to grow up in safe neighborhoods, employers to attract workers and communities to remain places where people of all income levels can live and thrive.
That is why collaboration matters. Housing affordability is too important to become an endless cycle of revisiting yesterday’s debates. Families are looking for practical solutions that increase supply, improve affordability and expand opportunity.
Georgia has an opportunity to build on the progress already made. By keeping the focus on increasing housing availability, reducing unnecessary obstacles to development, and ensuring communities have the resources they need to grow responsibly, lawmakers can help more families find stable footing.
When more Georgians have access to housing they can afford, the benefits extend far beyond the front door. Stronger families create stronger neighborhoods, stronger employers, and stronger communities. That is a goal everyone can support.

Round one brackets for 2026 contest featuring top manufacturing products made in Nebraska. (Courtesy of Nebraska Chamber of Commerce and Industry)LINCOLN  — The top 16 products have been revealed for the 2026 “Coolest Thing Made in Nebraska” competition — ranging from license plates to popcorn and what is billed as the world’s first miniaturized robotic-assisted surgery system.
“Nebraska makes some incredible products and the people who make them deserve to be celebrated,” said Joseph Young, president and CEO of the Nebraska Chamber of Commerce and Industry, an organizer of the contest.
License plates manufactured in Lincoln by Cornhusker State Industries, a program of the Nebraska Department of Correctional Services, are among the top 16 finalists competing for the 2026 title of ‘coolest thing’ made in Nebraska. (Courtesy of Nebraska Chamber of Commerce and Industry)
Voting continues through Oct. 4 for the first round of the bracket-style competition that features the top 16. Advanced rounds will follow, with the winner to be announced Oct. 29 at the chamber’s Manufacturing Summit in La Vista.
The multi-phase competition, now in its fifth year, is designed to shine light on the manufacturing industry, which Young calls a major economic engine for the state that supports more than 100,000 jobs and communities statewide.
He said the contest “lets us have some fun while telling a much bigger story: Nebraska manufacturers are innovative, competitive and making products that have an impact far beyond our state.”
All finalists will be invited to display products at the summit. Registration is open to the public.
Narrowed from a statewide pool by a judging panel of business and nonprofit leaders, this year’s top 16, and where they’re made: 

 FiberCut – Bish Enterprises, Giltner
 Avail Tow Bar – Blue Ox, Pender
 Hi Rail Excavator and Snowblower – Ceres Group, Omaha
 Ram Air Turbine Hub – Collins Aerospace, York
 Nebraska License Plates – Cornhusker State Industries, Lincoln
 Modular Housing – Family Built Homes, Gering
 Fresh, Stone Milled Flour – Grand Republic Milling Company, Gering
 Excedrin – Haleon, Lincoln
 Precision Hunter Ammunition– Hornady Manufacturing, Grand Island
 TAU-XR – Lindsay Corporation, Lindsay
 Marble Pack-Off – Marble Technologies, Lincoln
 Nirbuilt Airboats – Nirbuilt Airboats, Ashland
 Animal Health IV Fluids – Nova-Tech, Inc., Grand Island
 Popcorn – Popcorn County, USA, North Loup
 PyraMAX Transmission Structures – Valmont Industries, Columbus
 MIRA- miniRAS – Virtual Incision, Lincoln

The winner will join the ranks of other “coolest” Nebraska-made products: a Grand Island-produced combine series by Case IH (2025), Valley Irrigation’s center pivot irrigation machine (2024), Rocket Mobility’s all-terrain tracked wheelchair made in Columbus (2023) and Kawasaki’s subway car built in Lincoln to run on the rail tracks of New York City (2022).

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Nonprofit launches Eastern Kentucky birding ‘hotspots’ to encourage bird documentation
description: A land conservation nonprofit in Kentucky is using grant funding to add signs near birding “hotspots” in Eastern Kentucky that people can use to document birds through an app supported by an ornithology lab at Cornell University.  The Kentucky Natural Lands Trust is using part of a $10,000 grant from the Cornell Lab of Ornithonology […]
text:
Cardinals were recognized as the state bird of Kentucky in 1926. (Getty Images)A land conservation nonprofit in Kentucky is using grant funding to add signs near birding “hotspots” in Eastern Kentucky that people can use to document birds through an app supported by an ornithology lab at Cornell University. 
The Kentucky Natural Lands Trust is using part of a $10,000 grant from the Cornell Lab of Ornithonology to place six signs at various Eastern Kentucky trailheads and spots as a part of the “Pine Mountain Birding Trail” along the Pine Mountain mountain ridge that stretches about 125 miles from Tennessee through Kentucky. 
One of the signs placed along the Pine Mountain Birding Trail in Eastern Kentucky. (Courtesy Joe Manning, Kentucky Natural Lands Trust)
Visitors can use QR codes on the signs that direct people to the Cornell lab’s eBird app where users can document birds they see, create birding checklists and share the data as a part of a crowd-sourced effort.
The nonprofit describes the region as “one of the most biodiverse temperate regions” in the world and a “key link in an intercontinental migration route” for hundreds of millions of birds every year, according to a Tuesday press release.
In a provided statement, Sara Barker, the Land Trust Bird Conservation Initiative Program Leader at the Cornell lab, said the lab wanted to work with an organization like the Kentucky Natural Lands Trust that is “rooted in the land, trusted by local communities, and equipped to work across property lines to safeguard and elevate awareness of this region’s extraordinary biodiversity.” 
“Central Appalachia’s forested ridges are among the most critical — yet often overlooked — corridors for birds in the Mississippi Flyway,” Barker said. “The partnership between the Kentucky Natural Lands Trust and Cornell Lab is turning Pine Mountain into meaningful data for hemispheric bird conservation.”
The sign locations are at the Chained Rock trailhead in Bell County; the Blanton Forest State Nature Preserve in Harlan County; the Pine Mountain Settlement School in Harlan County; Kingdom Come State Park in Harlan County; Little Shepherd Trail in Letcher County; and the Bad Branch State Nature Preserve in Letcher County. 
The grant funding has also been used to offer guided birding hikes, free public workshops and other programming and research, according to a release from the Kentucky Natural Lands Trust. The nonprofit lists the Kentucky Energy and Environment Cabinet, Kentucky State Parks and the Pine Mountain Settlement School as partners involved in the birding trail.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: “Go and Do Likewise:” Beshear’s book touts Christian values (except when it comes to Bevin)
description: If there are one or two of you out there who still have doubts that Gov. Andy Beshear will run for president in 2028, doubt no more. This week, he officially released “Go and Do Likewise: How We Heal a Broken County,” joining the Presidential Hopeful section of your local bookstore already stocked with choices […]
text:
Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear, flanked by Lt. Gov. Jacqueline Coleman and his family, takes in the celebration at his reelection party on Nov. 7, 2023, in Louisville. (Austin Anthony/Kentucky Lantern)If there are one or two of you out there who still have doubts that Gov. Andy Beshear will run for president in 2028, doubt no more. This week, he officially released “Go and Do Likewise: How We Heal a Broken County,” joining the Presidential Hopeful section of your local bookstore already stocked with choices such as “Young Man in a Hurry: A Journey of Discovery” by Gavin Newsom, “Where We Keep the Light: Stories From a Life of Service” by Josh Shapiro, “Crisis of the Common Good: The Fight for Meaning and Connection in a Broken America,” by Chris Murphy. You get the idea – first you set up a PAC, then write a book with a colon in the title and you’re halfway to New Hampshire.
“Go and Do Likewise: How We Heal a Broken Country,” was released this week by Gov. Andy Beshear. (Photo courtesy St. Martin’s Press)
Luckily for these busy men, 1) Donald Trump has provided an excellent opening to talk about such hopeful, healing topics, and 2) there are many talented ghost writers out there. Mark Tabb, who is thanked by Beshear in the acknowledgements, keeps a light touch and a fast pace with the greatest hits of the Kentucky governor. 
Luckily for Tabb, Beshear has a truly unusual number of high-drama moments from his years in office, which also provide him with excellent examples of his Biblical themes, the good Samaritan etc. From COVID to the West Kentucky tornadoes to the Eastern Kentucky floods, Kentuckians shine in crises – neighbors helping neighbors – in all the ways that are antithetical to the Trumpist individualism that has poisoned our public discourse.
Trump will not be on the ballot in 2028 (we hope) so it’s interesting the book is so focused on him, but it’s clear that Trumpism is what Democrats will have to continue to run against, and thus is how Beshear has structured the book. (He may not have imagined Trump’s polls being this low as he and Tabb wrote it.)
Luckily for us readers, Beshear is not so filled with the Holy Spirit that he leaves out any thoughts of payback. Kentucky’s favorite bad guy, former Gov. Matt Bevin, is referred to throughout as Trump Lite, and their political tussles are highlighted with more candor than previously encountered.
There is, for example, the time then-Attorney General Beshear was crossing the Capitol parking lot when he ran into then-Gov. Bevin, and chastised him for not doing his job after a Louisville child was hit by a stray bullet.

“Eyes wide, Bevin leaned toward me and snarled, ‘Spare me your talking points. If you want to get political, I’ll knock your f—— head off!’ 
I stared directly into his bugged-out eyes. ‘Are you threatening me, Governor?’ I said as calmly as I could but, raising my voice, added, ‘Cause I don’t take kindly to being threatened.’ 
He shot back, ‘I didn’t threaten you.’ 
‘You just said you’d knock my head off,’ I replied. I could see in his face Bevin knew he’d made a mistake, not that he’d admit it. Ever. Instead, he shook his head and scoffed, ‘Is this how you people act?’”
 


	It turns out “you people” are Democrats, and Beshear uses the moment to further explore the ongoing political divide expertly manipulated by Trump and the ever charming Trump Lite.
But Bevin is not the only politician who doesn’t like to admit he made a mistake. In the book, Beshear mentions only a few of his own, such as Tupac Shakur’s unemployment application during COVID. He does not write about the entire debacle over unemployment benefits, or the many problems in his Department of Juvenile Justice so aptly documented by the Lexington Herald-Leader, or the various travesties around the Kentucky Wired program.
But generally speaking, people writing books before they run for president aren’t going to explore those themes.
The most affecting chapters are about abortion rights advocate Hadley Duvall, who almost certainly made the difference in his second gubernatorial election, the mass shooting at Louisville’s Old National Bank that killed one of his closest friends, and America’s civil rights history, and the removal of the Jefferson Davis statue from the Capitol. 
I think it’s smart of Beshear to talk about his faith because so many people perceive the Democratic Party as one full of atheists; his willingness to talk about God is part of what has created a genuine rapport with Kentuckians. One of Beshear’s greatest strengths is his ability to do the right thing while seeing clearly how to reap political rewards from it. For example, his daily COVID briefings brought real comfort to thousands of people, and beamed his awkward dad jokes and Mr. Rogers persona into an indelible image that clearly helped him win a second term in a deep red state.
What’s still unclear is whether Beshear, despite the sharp political instincts and prodigious fundraising, has the charisma to appeal to people outside Kentucky, and whether this book will help him do so. He’ll sell plenty of copies; on Wednesday, Tom Loftus reported that in addition to the Kentucky Democratic Party spending $10,000 to buy books, Beshear’s PAC, In This Together, bought $9,000 worth of them. Will your average voter in Iowa or South Carolina join this group? In the runup to a presidential campaign, does it even matter?

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Gov. Landry’s order waives some limits on off-road diesel use to lower fuel costs
description: Farmers and timber harvesters can use off-road diesel fuel for all purposes for the next 30 days under an executive order Gov. Jeff Landry issued Wednesday.
text:
A farmer harvests corn beside Iowa Highway 163. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Farmers and timber harvesters can use off-road diesel fuel for all purposes for the next 30 days under an executive order Gov. Jeff Landry issued Wednesday. 
The governor cited soaring prices for diesel fuel as the reason behind his action. He’s also called on the Trump administration and Congress to halt all diesel exports for 90 days to address the high costs.  
“We’re not going to sit on the sidelines while Louisiana farmers are paying record prices to harvest the crops that feed our families and support our economy. We have an opportunity to provide immediate relief, and that’s exactly what we’re doing,” Landry said in a statement from his office.
The executive order applies to what’s known as dyed diesel, which is intended for off-road uses such as tractors, heavy equipment and irrigation systems. Louisiana does not apply its 20-cent-per-gallon motor fuel tax to off-road diesel, which is tinted red to distinguish it from regular diesel fuel
Landry’s executive order is in effect through Oct. 22 and applies to vehicles registered as Class 2 (forest products) and Class 5 (farm use). The governor has also directed the state revenue department to ask the Internal Revenue Service for relief from any penalties that might result from the state suspending its off-road diesel use limitations. The federal government tax on diesel is 24.4 cents per gallon, though it is not assessed on off-road fuel.
The average price per gallon for diesel fuel in the U.S. has exceeded $6 for the past two weeks, setting a new record. According to the governor’s office, this level is 112% higher than LSU AgCenter forecasters projected when they calculated their forecast for farmers’ crop budgets in 2026.
Higher demand for diesel in European markets is behind the higher prices, according to market analysts. The global supply has been disrupted by Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine as well as the ripple effects of the conflict between the U.S. and Iran.   
President Donald Trump said Tuesday his administration would make a decision soon about whether to embargo U.S. fuel exports in response to high prices. The refining industry has said it would most likely curb production of diesel if foreign shipments are stopped, which analysts say would not create the desired cost relief.

name: Delaware
title: Delaware wins SNAP deadline case while facing high payment error rate
description: Judge rejects USDA’s timetable and clarifies immigrant eligibility, but federal rules aimed at improving state payment accuracy remain in place DOVER, Del. — Delaware has won a court ruling that prevents the Trump administration from counting certain food assistance errors against states under a deadline a federal judge found unlawful. The victory protects t[...]
text:
Judge rejects USDA’s timetable and clarifies immigrant eligibility, but federal rules aimed at improving state payment accuracy remain in place
DOVER, Del. — Delaware has won a court ruling that prevents the Trump administration from counting certain food assistance errors against states under a deadline a federal judge found unlawful. The victory protects the state from potential future costs tied to that deadline, but it does not resolve a separate problem: Delaware’s SNAP payment error rate was 16% in fiscal 2025, well above the national average.
The Sept. 17 ruling also confirmed that certain lawful permanent residents, including people who were previously refugees or granted asylum, remain eligible for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program without waiting five years. It did not overturn the 2025 federal law requiring states with high payment error rates to pay a share of SNAP benefit costs.
The case for state accountability
Congress changed SNAP last year to give states a stronger financial reason to determine eligibility and benefit amounts accurately. Under the law, states with error rates of at least 6% can be required to cover 5%, 10% or 15% of benefit costs, depending on their rate. The requirement generally begins Oct. 1, 2027.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture reported a national payment error rate of 10.62% for fiscal 2025, representing $10.1 billion in improper payments. The measure includes benefits paid above and below the correct amount. It is not a fraud rate.
“These payment error rates are further proof that state accountability is severely lacking in SNAP,” Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins said when USDA released the figures. She said the department wanted states to curb waste while serving needy families and protecting taxpayers.
Delaware’s error rate
Delaware’s fiscal 2025 rate was 16%, compared with the 10.62% national rate and the law’s 6% cost-sharing threshold. That makes payment accuracy a substantial issue for the state, independent of its dispute with USDA over the new law’s implementation. The figure does not mean 16% of Delaware recipients committed fraud; it includes overpayments and underpayments.
Delaware’s rate is high enough to qualify it for a delay in the new benefit cost-sharing requirement. That gives the state more time to improve accuracy before it must begin paying a share of benefits under that provision. The delay comes from the law itself, separate from the court ruling.
Why the judge rejected USDA’s deadline
The lawsuit focused on how USDA put the 2025 law into effect. SNAP rules provide a 120-day adjustment period during which certain errors arising from a policy change are excluded from a state’s payment error rate. USDA said the period began July 4, 2025, when the law was enacted, and ended Nov. 1.
But USDA did not issue its guidance on noncitizen eligibility until Oct. 31, leaving states one day under that timetable. Other instructions arrived weeks or months after USDA said the clock had started. U.S. District Judge Mustafa Kasubhai ruled that the department had not given states adequate notice. He set aside its deadline and required a full adjustment period following proper implementation instructions.
The judge also found that USDA’s October guidance wrongly indicated that some lawful permanent residents were ineligible for SNAP or subject to a five-year waiting period. USDA issued a clarification in December. The ruling confirms that lawful permanent residents who were previously in specified humanitarian categories retain their exemption from the waiting period, provided they meet other SNAP requirements.
What Jennings’ criticism means
“This entire ordeal was a blatant attempt by the Trump Administration to take food away from families in need, to destroy a plank of the social safety net, and to degrade our state’s financial standing,” Attorney General Kathy Jennings said in announcing the decision.
Jennings’ accusation goes beyond what the judge decided about the administration’s intent. USDA says it is seeking to reduce improper payments, save federal money and hold states accountable for administering SNAP accurately. The court nevertheless found that USDA’s initial guidance misstated eligibility for some lawful permanent residents and that its deadline unfairly exposed states to future costs.
The distinction does not erase the effects of the broader 2025 law. The Congressional Budget Office expects its tighter eligibility and work rules to reduce the number of people receiving SNAP. Its projected $187 billion in federal savings over 10 years includes those changes; it is not an estimate of fraud eliminated. The court ruling establishes that USDA went beyond a lawful implementation of the changes at issue, but it does not establish that denying food to needy families was the administration’s purpose.
For Delaware, the ruling means USDA cannot use the deadline the judge rejected to count implementation errors against the state. Delaware must still follow the new law and address its high payment error rate. Both facts matter to understanding what the state won — and the work that remains.
TO GO BOX | The SNAP ruling

Who: Delaware Attorney General Kathy Jennings joined other states in suing the Trump administration over USDA’s SNAP guidance and deadline.
What: A federal judge set aside USDA’s deadline for counting certain implementation errors and clarified eligibility for some lawful permanent residents.
When: The ruling was issued Sept. 17, 2026.
Where: The decision came from the U.S. District Court for the District of Oregon and addresses USDA guidance to states.
Why it matters: Delaware avoids errors being counted under the rejected deadline, but its 16% fiscal 2025 payment error rate remains high. The federal law requiring states with high error rates to share SNAP benefit costs remains in effect.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Mixed signals for housing costs in Alaska
description: Apartment rents in Alaska rose 2.1% over the past year, the most modest increase in five years, according to analysis by the state Department of Labor and Workforce Development. The statistics on rental costs are part of a package of articles about housing costs published in the September issue of Alaska Economic Trends, the monthly […]
text:
A sign seen on April 9, 2025, advertises rental availability at an apartment building in Anchorage's Turnagain neighborhood. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)Apartment rents in Alaska rose 2.1% over the past year, the most modest increase in five years, according to analysis by the state Department of Labor and Workforce Development.
The statistics on rental costs are part of a package of articles about housing costs published in the September issue of Alaska Economic Trends, the monthly magazine of the department’s research section.
Rental statistics, based on prices recorded in March of this year, show some striking geographic differences.
The Wrangell-Petersburg area in Southeast Alaska had the cheapest rent of the 11 cities and areas analyzed, with a median monthly rate of $1,288 for a two-bedroom apartment. Bethel, a rural hub in Western Alaska, had the highest rents, with a median of $2,030 a month for a two-bedroom apartment.
Kodiak, Anchorage, the Fairbanks North Star Borough and Juneau were behind Bethel with monthly median rentals above $1,700.The Matanuska-Susitna Borough, just north of Anchorage, was on the low side for median rents, at $1,567 a month, but it had the biggest yearly increase, measured at 12.8%.
That reflects demographic characteristics in the bustling borough, where many residents are commuters who work in Anchorage, said Gunnar Schultz, a state labor economist and one of the authors of the housing-cost stories.
“Mat-Su obviously has been growing in contrast to most of the rest of the state,” he said. “So I think that that obviously puts upward pressure on price.” Proximity to Anchorage is another contributor because it means money is coming into the borough from the state’s largest city, he said.
The analysis is part of the department’s regular monitoring of housing costs. The rental comparisons covered much but not all of the state; the North Slope Borough and Bering Strait region, for example, were not included.
For homebuyers in Alaska, there are some economic headwinds, according to the economists’ analysis. Mortgage costs are much higher than they used to be, they said.
For a 30-year fixed rate mortgage on a $415,000 Alaska home — the median value — the monthly payment in 2025 was about $2,050. That is 84% higher than the estimated median monthly mortgage payment in 2019, the analysis said.
A big driver is the rise in home values, from an average of about $300,000 in 2019 to an average of $415,000 just six years later. Another factor is the increase in interest rates, from a median under 3% in 2020 to 6.5%in 2023, the analysis said.
But while home values and thus monthly mortgage costs increased, so did wages in Alaska.
The result of all those combined changes was that purchasing a home became marginally more affordable in 2025 than in the two years prior, according to the analysis.
Alaska’s Housing Affordability Index,  the number that represents how many people earning the average monthly are needed to make mortgage payments, dropped a bit in 2025 to 1.37. That is down from last year’s index of 1.39 and from the 2024 index of 1.4, which was the highest in recent years. But it is above the indexes measured in previous years; from 2019 to 2021, the index was below 1, indicating that a single person earning average Alaska wages had enough money to afford monthly mortgage payments.
Despite the slight improvement in the affordability index, buying a house remains a hefty burden in Alaska, Schultz said. “It’s still so much higher than it was during COVID and before,” he said.
A slight decline in interest rates last year was a contributing factor to the small improvement in housing affordability. However, interest rates are now heading up, the analysis pointed out.
Also affecting housing affordability is the availability of homes, and on that subject, there is positive news for would-be buyers, according to the economists’ analysis.
Housing construction in 2025 hit a 10-year high after years of increases that followed the big drop during the COVID-19 pandemic. A total of 2,261 single-family and multifamily housing units were built last year, the analysis said. That compares to 1,747 in 2020 and 1,726 in 2021. Home construction has been steadily rising since those years, according to the data.
The Alaska Economic Trends articles did not compare housing costs in the state to those nationwide, but the U.S. Census Bureau has some U.S. statistics that provide some contest.
Nationally, home ownership costs remained flat from 2020 to 2024, while rents increased by $100 more a month to a median $1,413 during the period, according to the Census Bureau. The analysis considers areas around the nation with populations over 5,000, so most of Alaska’s rural communities are not included.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico behavioral health committee closes in on goal of approving 13 regional health plans
description: The committee tasked with rebuilding New Mexico’s behavioral healthcare infrastructure has approved 11 of 13 regional plans, the committee chair told lawmakers on the interim Legislative Finance Committee during their Tuesday meeting.
text:
The Behavioral Health Reform and Investment Act’s executive committee, pictured on Aug. 5, 2025, has approved 11 of the 13 regional plans to rebuild behavioral health infrastructure, committee Chair Nick Boukas told state lawmakers on Sept. 22, 2026. (Source NM file photo)The committee tasked with rebuilding New Mexico’s behavioral healthcare infrastructure has approved all but two regional plans, the committee chair told a panel of state lawmakers Tuesday.
Nick Boukas, the committee chair and director of the state Health Care Authority’s Behavioral Health Services Division, told lawmakers on the interim Legislative Finance Committee that he and his colleagues have signed off on 11 of the state’s proposed 13 regional behavioral healthcare plans.
Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham signed Senate Bill 3, known as the Behavioral Health Reform and Investment Act, into law in 2025. It created 13 behavioral health regions mirrored after the state’s 13 judicial districts. Local officials with counties, tribes and cities within each region have crafted unique plans to identify their communities’ biggest gaps in behavioral healthcare and to set goals for addressing them.
The law is aimed at bringing providers back to New Mexico, particularly rural areas, after former Republican Gov. Susana Martinez accused several providers of fraud, which led to a mass departure.
While needs vary from region to region, Boukas said that they have largely held four priorities in common: expanding access to behavioral health treatment and recovery services; strengthening youth, family, school and caregiver support; addressing housing and transportation; and building and retaining a behavioral health workforce.
New Mexico lawmakers express frustration with long process to rebuild behavioral health system

A Tuesday LFC brief says the state invested $565 million for behavioral health services in 2025, yet has “little data” to indicate whether outcomes are improving or whether “access is better today than it was when the state began making these investments.” So far, the 13 plans carry a price tag of $110 million, according to the brief.
Some lawmakers in attendance expressed frustration over the slowgoing process, which has become a common theme in this summer’s legislative hearings on the matter.
“We’ve spent a whole lot of money with zero results yet,” Rep. Mark Duncan (R-Kirtland) told Boukas.
Boukas told lawmakers that the seemingly slow nature of SB3’s implementation is to be expected.
“When I say that this is working, it’s that we’re getting folks to start talking to each other. None of the programs have rolled out yet to where we can start collecting data,” he said.
The Behavioral Health Reform and Investment Act Executive Committee is scheduled to meet in Santa Fe on Oct. 6. Boukas previously told Source NM he hopes to have all 13 regional plans approved by the end of the year.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraska can cut property taxes. It can’t eliminate the bill.
description: Affordability is on nearly everyone’s mind. With homeowners and prospective homeowners looking for every way they can to save on the necessities of life, it is only natural to consider that expense that is itself a perennial topic in Nebraska: how to reduce the property tax burden. But lowering property taxes is not easy, and […]
text:
A tax statement with 'special messages' box regarding past due taxes. (Courtesy of Lancaster County Treasurer)Affordability is on nearly everyone’s mind. With homeowners and prospective homeowners looking for every way they can to save on the necessities of life, it is only natural to consider that expense that is itself a perennial topic in Nebraska: how to reduce the property tax burden. But lowering property taxes is not easy, and the simplest-sounding solutions come with hard compromises for our communities. When property tax revenue declines, so does the funding available for the local services and investments that shape our daily lives.
In Nebraska last year, $5.6 billion of property taxes was levied in Nebraska:

$3.3 billion was levied in support of local school districts, including bonded indebtedness. 
$975 million was levied for counties.
$653 million was levied for cities. 
The remainder was levied by townships, fire districts, natural resource districts, educational service units, community colleges and miscellaneous districts like libraries and ag societies. 

While the state of Nebraska partially offset those levies with over $1 billion of relief (through mechanisms like the property tax credits and the homestead exemption), that is still a lot of money for a state of just over 2 million people. Nearly every dollar raised through property taxes, however, stays in the local economy, funding the local workforce and purchasing local goods and services.
Strong schools. Safer neighborhoods. Reliable roads. Modern libraries. Parks and recreation. Emergency services. These are not abstract benefits. They are the foundations of thriving communities, and property taxes pay for them.
In Nebraska, the property tax debate affects more than homeowners. Farmers, ranchers and rural communities also feel the pressure of property taxes. Local property tax revenue helps support the critical infrastructure urban and rural Nebraska communities depend on. For homeowners, property taxes assess an illiquid household asset; for farmers and ranchers, they tax the productive land required to make a living. As Nebraskans consider additional property tax relief, the challenge is not simply how to lower the tax bill, but also how to ensure our communities can continue funding the services and infrastructure Nebraskans demand.
Eliminating or significantly reducing property taxes does not eliminate the cost of providing public services. It simply shifts that cost somewhere else and through a different revenue source. A common refrain is that local governments need to “tighten their belts,” as if local governments can simply disregard duties and services mandated by the state. Further, if things that impact our quality of life are reduced or eliminated in the name of property tax relief, we have seen those communities less and less likely to retain the next generation of citizens and property owners.
Alternatively, shifting funding to sales or income taxes introduces severe budget volatility, as these revenues generally fluctuate more with economic conditions, making long-term budgeting more difficult.
Property taxes offer something especially valuable: stable, locally controlled and locally invested funding. Residents elect the officials who set budgets and tax rates, giving taxpayers a far more direct role in how their community’s money is raised and spent, as opposed to asking the state legislature for money to fix a bridge or to hire a special education teacher. Locally elected officials want lower property taxes, too. They live in the communities they serve, own property and pay the exact same taxes they levy.
That local connection matters. It allows communities to set priorities based on their own needs rather than relying more heavily on decisions made at the state level. Replacing local tax authority with state funding or other revenue sources inevitably shifts decision-making to the state Capitol. As the old saying goes, “Whoever has the gold makes the rules.” 
Property taxes are more than a line on a tax bill. They are one of the primary tools communities use to invest in the places people call home. As we consider property tax reform for Nebraska, the most important question is not “How much should we cut?” but more accurately, “What do we need to pay for, and who should pay for it?”
A sustainable path forward requires two things:

Broadening our economic base: Growing local business, housing and agricultural development allows the cost of essential services to be shared across more people and more property, lowering the individual burden naturally.
Aligning state and local responsibilities: If the state asks local property owners to carry duties that are statewide in scope, the state should assume and fund them. Conversely, if certain local programs are deemed too expensive for local taxpayers to sustain, communities should have the choice to scale them back locally.

At the end of the day, basic infrastructure and public safety are expensive needs. Meaningful property tax relief begins with growing our communities and conducting an honest assessment of local government’s responsibilities – not an uncalculated shift of the bill.
