name: Missouri Independent
title: The Muehlebach in Kansas City keeps coming back for taxpayer subsidies
description: Kansas City’s Muehlebach Hotel hosted every president from Theodore Roosevelt to Ronald Reagan. Harry Truman ran much of his political operation from the penthouse suite. It’s where he signed the Truman Doctrine in 1947 and awaited election results in 1948. Once referred to as White House West, it’s one of Missouri’s most storied buildings. The […]
text:
The historic 12-story Hotel Muehlebach building in Kansas City (photo by Patrick Tuohey).
Kansas City’s Muehlebach Hotel hosted every president from Theodore Roosevelt to Ronald Reagan. Harry Truman ran much of his political operation from the penthouse suite. It’s where he signed the Truman Doctrine in 1947 and awaited election results in 1948. Once referred to as White House West, it’s one of Missouri’s most storied buildings.
The building has also been bailed out by taxpayers at least three times in 34 years.
It’s 2026, and it’s time once again to subsidize the Muehlebach Hotel!
This time, the Kansas City Business Journal reports that Flint Development secured a 25-year property tax abatement to turn several floors of the Muehlebach Hotel into apartments. The project also received a sale-leaseback bond structure in which the Land Clearance for Redevelopment Authority issues up to $51.5 million in taxable industrial revenue bonds, paid back by the developer.
LCRA holds title to the property for the lease term — construction plus 25 years — which provides the property tax exemption. At the end of the lease, the title reverts to the developer. The project also includes a sales tax exemption on construction materials, an additional subsidy on top of the abatement.
And the result, of course, is going to be great! Hunter Harris, a partner with Flint, said in a statement, “The Muehlebach project will not only provide essential housing for local residents, but will also act as a primary driver for community vitality in the area. We are committed to delivering a community that meets the rigorous demands of today’s residents while contributing to the overall economic health of Kansas City.”
In 1992, Kansas City used tax increment financing to tear down Muehlebach Towers and renovate the hotel. A 1996 Business Journal piece about several subsidized projects downtown, including the Muehlebach, quoted UMB President Alexander Kemper as saying, “I think there’s a lot of great dynamic growth going in downtown Kansas City, and it’s about time.” The story also quoted Sean O’Byrne, then a broker for one of the properties to receive TIF, saying, “Grand Boulevard could become that in more than just name.”
Alas, the hotel opened in 1998 and struggled. David Martin at The Pitch wrote: A 1995 bond issue paid for renovations to the Marriott and a new Muehlebach Tower. Taxes generated by the hotels were supposed to retire the debt. Inadequate demand for rooms, however, has forced the city to find an additional $5 million to satisfy creditors.
Years later, in 2018, Platform Ventures proposed a $114 million plan to redevelop the whole block. It would turn the neighboring Kansas City Club building into a hotel, turn the Muehlebach into 117 apartments and build a new parking garage and office building. The city authorized a tax abatement: 75% off for 10 years, then 37.5% for 15 more, plus $12.6 million in historic tax credits.
It was going to be magnificent! The same effusive Sean O’Byrne, now vice president of business development for the Downtown Council of Kansas City, told the Star, “This is hitting on every cylinder that we want as far as downtown revitalization.” He gushed, “It’s also bringing back a wonderful landmark in the Muehlebach tower, something that’s been vacant for more than 25 years.” He’s as ebullient as he was 22 years earlier.
The Star also quoted Greg Flisram, executive director of LCRA at the time, as saying the project “would bring ‘new life’ to that part of downtown and especially the Muehlebach building.”
The Kansas City Club portion did get built, opening in 2020 as Hotel Kansas City. The Muehlebach didn’t.
In a recent Star piece, City Council member Kevin O’Neill defended ongoing public costs for the Power & Light District, saying, “we have one hell of a downtown because of the investment made.” If that’s true, why are we still subsidizing these projects?
I wish the new developers of the Muehlebach all the luck in the world. But history teaches us to be skeptical of taxpayer subsidies promising transformational success. A better way: Let developers do their best, with their own money, to meet the needs of the market. And if the market is telling us something is a bad investment for private investors, it’s a bad investment for public dollars, too.
With apologies to Truman, these bucks need to stop.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Carbon capture proposals draw mixed responses from environmental groups in Michigan House committee
description: As Michigan continues to examine its options for meeting its 100% clean energy goal, members of the state House gathered to consider a slate of bills to give the state authority over efforts to capture and store carbon emissions. The House Energy Committee heard testimony from Reps. Parker Fairbairn (R-Harbor Springs) and Cam Cavitt (R-Cheboygan) […]
text:
State Rep. Parker Fairbairn (R-Harbor Springs), Utility Workers Union of America Renewable Energies Director James Harrison, and state Rep. Cam Cavitt (R-Chebyogan) sit before the House Energy Committee on Sept. 22, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)As Michigan continues to examine its options for meeting its 100% clean energy goal, members of the state House gathered to consider a slate of bills to give the state authority over efforts to capture and store carbon emissions.
The House Energy Committee heard testimony from Reps. Parker Fairbairn (R-Harbor Springs) and Cam Cavitt (R-Cheboygan) on House Bills 6247–6249, which aim to establish a state-based framework for carbon capture, utilization and sequestration efforts. 
These projects capture carbon dioxide from sources such as power plants and industrial facilities. The emissions are either reused or injected into geological formations including depleted oil reservoirs or saline aquifers.
Fairbairn told committee members that the state is uniquely suited for carbon capture, utilization and storage, noting that Michigan has access to geological formations including deep saline reservoirs, porous basalts and depleted oil fields, which can be used to store liquid carbon dioxide. 
Michigan is also an energy and manufacturing hub, Fairbairn said, noting that this technology provides a pathway for these facilities to reduce their carbon emissions.
He also pointed to the state’s clean energy law that requires electrical providers to meet a 100% clean energy standard by 2040. The law includes nuclear energy and natural gas plants using 90% effective carbon capture technology in its definition of clean energy resources.
While the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency oversees permitting for injection wells like those used in carbon sequestration, shifting that oversight to the Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes and Energy would allow the state to process those permits more quickly, Fairbairn said. 
Fairbairn also noted that DTE Energy and Consumers Energy, two of the state’s largest energy utilities, support the proposals because they would provide the state with the regulatory framework needed to ensure their natural gas plants comply with Michigan’s clean energy law.
James Harrison, the renewable energies director for the Utility Workers Union of America, said the technology can help preserve jobs in industries that are difficult to fully transition to electricity, such as manufacturing, cement, steel, refining and chemicals.
However, the policies drew a mixed response from environmental groups.
James Harrison, director of renewable energies for the Utility Workers Union of America, testifies in favor of legislation to give the Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes and Energy authority over carbon capture and sequestration efforts during a meeting of the House Energy Committee on Sept. 22, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)
Wibke Heymach, senior midwest regional policy manager for Clean Air Task Force, offered support for the bills, noting that carbon capture technology represents one commercially available option for industries that would otherwise continue producing emissions.
“Michigan is home to several industrial facilities that emit harmful air pollutants, including particulate matter, sulfur oxides, and nitrogen oxides. CCS retrofit projects on industrial facilities can improve local air quality by reducing these emissions while capturing CO2,” Heymach said.
Ben Poulson, the state government affairs director for the Michigan League of Conservation Voters, stood in opposition to the proposals, questioning whether they created the proper framework for the growing carbon capture industry.
“The United States is existing in a period of electricity demand growth, largely driven by data centers, and if those are powered by carbon-producing technologies, it means further sources of carbon pollution,” Poulson said. “It’s smart that we are thinking about how to reduce carbon pollution, and as both these demand technologies and storage technologies scale, we’re going to see more facilities, more wells, more pipelines, more transportation of compressed carbon dioxide and more private investment from people looking to place carbon pollution.”
Whenever the state moves from regulating an emerging technology into a commercial industry, it’s important to make sure the state’s system of regulations is designed around the risk and incentives that come with that expansion, Poulson said.
Ben Poulson, state government affairs director for the Michigan League of Conservation Voters, raises concerns on a slate of bills to give the state regulatory authority over carbon capture and sequestration efforts before the House Energy Committee on Sept. 22, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)
Echoing concerns from the Clean Air Task Force, Poulson argued the 20-cent fee per ton of carbon injected for storage was too low, drawing parallels with the state’s low waste tipping fee, which has resulted in a significant amount of waste from other states and Canada ending up in Michigan landfills.
The bills also do not address the source of the carbon that would be sequestered, Poulson said. 
“If we are to store carbon here in Michigan, Michiganders deserve to know that the storage process is actually reducing the amount of atmospheric carbon, and that the process of capturing and storing is not creating more carbon than it stores,” he said. “And they also deserve to know that we are prioritizing pollution that could not easily be reduced otherwise.”
In a statement to Michigan Advance, EGLE Director of Communications Dale George noted that while they did not take a position or submit testimony on House Bills 6247–6249 during Tuesday’s hearing, the agency has consistently supported legislation to enable carbon capture, utilization and storage permitting at the state level, and would continue to work with lawmakers toward that end.

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming courts investigate extent of personal data exposed in cybersecurity breach
description:
While the breach of third-party software did not impact the judicial branch’s current internal system, data from certain cases between 2015 and 2025 may have been exposed. 
The post Wyoming courts investigate extent of personal data exposed in cybersecurity breach appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
The Wyoming Judicial Branch says it’s awaiting more details regarding the scope of a cybersecurity breach of a third-party software company that may have included a decade’s worth of data from the state’s court system. 
West Publishing Corporation, which the Wyoming Supreme Court and Wyoming district courts previously used for case management, was recently hacked, exposing court records from several states, including Wyoming. 
“Our internal team completed a preliminary review of the data shortly after we received notification of the incident involving West Publishing to gauge what we could, including a high-level view of what information and time frame were exposed,” Jacob Just, communications director for the Wyoming Judicial Branch, told WyoFile in an email. “That gave us a general sense that data was exposed for cases between 2015 and 2025, and exposed [personally identifiable information] was likely limited to names, dates of birth, and addresses.” 
However, Just said, the judicial branch is awaiting the full analysis to confirm that information. How long that may take is unknown, he said, but at that point, the judicial branch “will work with West Publishing on any potential direct notifications that need to be made.”
Just also reiterated that the breach did not impact the judicial branch’s networks or systems currently in use by the courts. 
For the most part, the Wyoming Supreme Court is responsible for reviewing appeals from district court decisions in civil and criminal cases. The high court also hears petitions for extraordinary relief from lower court decisions, and it occasionally answers questions certified to it from federal courts. 
Meanwhile, Wyoming state district courts are the trial courts of general jurisdiction in the state with the exception of small claims cases, misdemeanors and civil cases under $50,000. That means district courts deal with the most serious and controversial cases in the state. 
While the judicial branch awaits the analysis, West Publishing is providing 12 months of free credit monitoring and identity theft protection services to those potentially affected by the breach. Those services can be arranged at CTrackNotification.com.
The post Wyoming courts investigate extent of personal data exposed in cybersecurity breach appeared first on WyoFile .

name: Daily Montanan
title: Why roadless areas matter for wilderness preservation
description: We should all be deeply concerned about the most recent challenge to the integrity of America’s national forests—the proposed repeal of the 2001 U.S. Forest Service Roadless Area Conservation Rule. This could open up nearly 45 million acres of our public lands to road-building, logging, mining and development. Roadless wildlands protected under this rule pro[...]
text:
A view of the Ten Lakes Wilderness Study Area in northwest Montana. (Micah Drew/ Daily Montanan)We should all be deeply concerned about the most recent challenge to the integrity of America’s national forests—the proposed repeal of the 2001 U.S. Forest Service Roadless Area Conservation Rule. This could open up nearly 45 million acres of our public lands to road-building, logging, mining and development.
Roadless wildlands protected under this rule provide abundant benefits to nature and to people. In their current status, roadless areas provide critical wildlife habitat, mature contiguous forests, magnificent scenic vistas, clean water, carbon storage, and recreation opportunities. However, one often overlooked and very important benefit is that roadless areas are critical to the preservation of wilderness character, including the “qualities” and “values” in wilderness.
On Aug. 18, 2026, U.S. Department of Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins announced the Trump administration’s proposed rule that would completely repeal the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule. Inventoried Roadless Areas are wild areas within national forests where new road building, reconstruction and logging are generally prohibited, with some notable exceptions. The general prohibition on roadbuilding allows these places to remain in a mostly natural condition with limited development and infrastructure. These roadless areas are not currently designated wilderness but are often located adjacent to wilderness areas. Tens of millions of acres of these roadless areas are also currently recommended as wilderness in the Forest Service’s own forest plans or proposed for wilderness designation via legislation currently pending in Congress, such as the Northern Rockies Ecosystem Protection Act.
Roadless areas provide a de facto buffer to protect wilderness from the impacts of industrial forest management and other resource extraction occurring on nearby National Forest System lands. The Wilderness Act is silent on the issue of buffer zones around designated wilderness where activities detrimental to the preservation of wilderness character could be limited. However, many subsequent wilderness laws have specifically prohibited the establishment of protective buffer zones. While not perfect, and with notable loopholes, Inventoried Roadless Areas provide an elegant solution to the issue of buffers that meet this need for protection from impacts occurring outside the wilderness boundary to preservation of wilderness character inside, “as an area where the earth and its community of life are untrammeled” by humans.
Critical to this reasoning is that wilderness character inside designated wilderness can be, and often is, impacted by activities that occur outside wilderness. Those impacts are many. For example, they include impacts to solitude from the sights and sounds of development and activities occurring outside the wilderness boundary—from things such as logging, mining, road construction, gravel pits, shooting ranges, motorized recreation, and highly developed trailheads for recreational access.
Additionally, natural conditions and wildness inside the wilderness boundary line can be damaged or enhanced by the presence or absence of suitable wildlife habitat in adjacent areas. Animals and plants located inside wilderness need habitat beyond the administrative boundary of wilderness to move within their home range or for adaptation to climate change. Roadless areas provide these natural conditions and offer the benefit of an expansion of their available habitat.
Inventoried Roadless Areas have been serving as buffers that often prevent the most egregious, as well as many lesser, insults to wilderness character. The absence of Inventoried Roadless Areas adjacent to wilderness would make it much more likely that industrial forest management would take place right up to the wilderness boundary. In wilderness areas that do not have this buffer, industrial forest management already does often occur right up to the line.
To dig in deeper and think about how repeal of the Roadless Area Conservation Rule might impact a wilderness near you, check out this map showing the location of Inventoried Roadless Areas across national forests. Click on the layer list to add “Forest Service Wilderness areas.” Think about what these areas mean to you in their current, roadless condition and then imagine how they and adjacent wilderness areas would change if roads and related development were allowed. It’s shocking to see how much of America’s remaining wildlands on national forests would be threatened by industrial development if the Roadless Area Conservation Rule is repealed.
The public comment period for this proposal is open until Oct. 6. Click here for talking points and to submit your own public comments.
We must keep these places roadless—for their own sake and for their contribution to the preservation of wilderness.
Suzanne Cable is a Wilderness Watch board member. She retired in January 2024 after a 30-year career with the United States Forest Service, finishing her career as the forest-wide program manager for Recreation, Trails, and Wilderness on the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest.

name: WyoFile
title: The home place
description:
Humans yearn for a place that has meaning, that connects us to the earth and to our people, writes columnist Walt Gasson.
The post The home place appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Opinion

I had a conversation recently with a friend. Somewhere in the palaver, I used a phrase that I thought everyone knew. Turns out they don’t — or at least, he didn’t. This happens to me every so often. Terms like “bull hauler” or “blue roan” or “shotgun chaps” are well-known in the Wyoming lexicon, but maybe not so much outside our beloved rectangle. In this case, the term was “the home place.” It was just an honest misunderstanding, but it started me thinking. Perhaps I should explain.
It seems to me that one of the most defining characteristics of human beings is a sense of place. We long to belong somewhere. Some people are born there and never leave. Some spend their whole lives in search of it. But in all cases we humans yearn for someplace that has meaning, that connects us to the earth and to our people. In the absence of this connection, we feel adrift. We need a home place.
For my family and me, that’s in southwestern Wyoming. One particular spot in that great wide open has particular significance for us. It has been our retreat for five generations. It has provided not only a sense of place, but a place of sense — somewhere we could stop for a day or a weekend or a week to look at ourselves as individuals and as a family. It has offered us peace and quiet and some distance from our neighbors. But more important, it has offered us both the freedom of the wilderness and the comforting blanket of family traditions. It has been the site of a few honeymoons, the best birthday parties, a lot of back-breaking labor, countless fishing trips and elk hunts, and some of the most memorable moments of our lives. It’s our home place.
The fireplace at the Gasson family cabin, built from South Pass rose quartz and Big Sandy Creek river rock. (Kim Gasson)
And we built it, or at least we helped. The technical knowledge came from those artists in logs, the Williams brothers. They ran the last of the little scab sawmills in our end of the country, located a ridge or two over from us, and they cut the logs for the cabin there. They milled them and cut them onsite, turning lodgepole pine into a cabin in one summer. With rose quartz from South Pass for the fireplace and granite river rock from Big Sandy Creek for the chimney, we had a small cabin built from the land on which it stood. And so it stands today, in large part unchanged. Between that first year and now have come the memories, volumes of memories. 
Many of my own home place memories are somehow tied to wildlife, the products of a lifetime of fascination with wild critters and the places they live. I remember the way my dad looked when he fished, standing on one of the granite boulders that rimmed Big Sandy Lake. He wore a light wool plaid shirt against the morning cool and his old, battered felt hat. He seldom spoke when he was fishing, and the only sounds I recall were the whisper of the wind and the light “plop” of a Colorado spinner hitting the surface of the water. We fished a lot in our 12 years together. I suppose that we were like fishermen everywhere — sometimes we caught a lot and sometimes we got skunked. I cannot remember how many fish we caught on any given day, but I remember how it felt to be fishing with my dad, and I would give a great deal to be able to do that just one more time. 
After his death, my mom and I continued to go to the home place. My mom was always a part of it. Even in her 80s, she returned every summer to renew her relationship with it. She told me once that it was hard to be there for a while after Gus died. It is a tribute to the strength of my mother that her love for it endured. But it is no great surprise. If you look through the accumulated memories of this family and its special spot, you will see that my mother is a part of many of them. She was there, hauling rock for the fireplace. She was there, fishing with my dad. And she was there to be a single parent to an angry young man who would rather go hunting and fishing than go to school.
The home place remained in the background as I met Kim, went to college, and left our hometown for Laramie, Pavillion, Gillette, Cheyenne and finally Laramie. But we have always come back. Indeed, it became the scene of some of the best parts of our life together. We spent the first night of our honeymoon, out of gas in a borrowed Bronco watching the moon rise and set over the high desert on the way to the cabin. We would spend a week there together every September, hunting antelope and sage grouse on frosty mornings when the aspens were kissed with gold. After 53 years of marriage, we still spend the best part of September at the home place.

The Gassons’ fifth-generation log cabin, built with lodgepole pine milled near the site using butt-and-pass corners. (Kim Gasson)

Kim’s touch there has always been unmistakable. From the defensible space that took us two decades to complete that now protects us from the inevitable wildfire to the second hardwood floor, the rustic decks both front and back, and the handmade quilts and curtains, she has shaped the home place into a warm and welcoming haven that reflects who we are and where we are. She has sculpted it, not so much in her own image but in the image of our family and our connection to the land.
It was only natural that our children should be a part of the home place, and that it should be a part of them as well. First Jenny, followed by Beth and then Sarah. These girls were rocked to sleep in the big chair by the window. Each bathed in the waters of South Temple Creek and slept under the stars as the coyotes yipped in the midsummer night. They caught their first fish there, and we recorded each one in photographs. Each of the girls shows a bit of who they are in these pictures. Jenny is quiet and holds a small brook trout delicately with a shy smile. Beth at the same age has a similar small trout, but she has a grin from ear to ear and a death grip on her fish. Sarah is 8, covered in fish blood and slime, wrestling a whopper of a cutthroat.
Our son Clark represents a special case. Born to two high schoolers in the early 1970s, he was adopted shortly after his entry into this world. It was a closed adoption, long on secrecy and judgment but short on compassion. It was also the hardest and most painful decision of our lives. We never saw him, never held him, never even knew what happened to him. He was simply gone, and the pain of losing him was indescribable. But through a series of events that can only be described as miraculous, he came back to us at age 46. And he came with his family to the home place.
With us and with their own families, they all return. Like fish returning upstream to their home waters, they return to the home place. And they bring with them a love for the land and an ethic for the use of that land. They grew up knowing the value of a sense of place and valuing a place that makes some sense. Like the old axe that’s been in the family for 50 years — only replaced the handle three times and the head twice — the home place remains a priceless part of our lives. Each generation has used it, maintaining some things, adding or subtracting others to meet their needs. But the love of the family and the love of the land have remained constant. We seem to have passed that constant on to our own children, and they have in turn passed it onto their children. It may be the most precious gift we can give them — a legacy of love.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: As health insurance costs soar, some Idaho healthcare workers pay for medical care out of pocket
description: This story was first published by KFF Health News on Sept. 22, 2026. Joshua and Ashley Durham run a family medicine practice, and for the first time in their lives, they have no health insurance. When the Durhams began their practice at the end of 2023 — he as a primary care physician and she […]
text:
Ashley and Joshua Durham used the Affordable Care Act marketplace for their health insurance after they began their family medicine practice in Boise, Idaho, in late 2023. But the couple say they opted out of health insurance for their family of four this year after they saw their ACA premium payments jump to nearly $1,600 a month. (Photo by Hayat Norimine/KFF Health News)This story was first published by KFF Health News on Sept. 22, 2026.
Joshua and Ashley Durham run a family medicine practice, and for the first time in their lives, they have no health insurance.
When the Durhams began their practice at the end of 2023 — he as a primary care physician and she as a pharmacist who handles the billing — the couple bought coverage for themselves and their two kids on the Affordable Care Act marketplace. But they said their monthly premiums for a similar health plan for this year rose several hundred dollars to nearly $1,600.
Top insurance official recommends task force for studying Idaho’s most critical healthcare issues

They decided to pay out-of-pocket for their medical expenses instead, leaning on $50,000 they had set aside in a health savings account over several years.
“It’s nerve-racking,” said Joshua Durham, 47. “It just takes, you know, one little accident, and then you got a big fat bill.”
The healthcare industry traditionally has more of its workforce on medical insurance than many other fields. Nationwide, 7% of all healthcare workers were uninsured in 2024, compared with 11% of all adults under 65, according to a KFF analysis of the most recent American Community Survey data. And doctors were especially unlikely to forgo health insurance, with just 2% uninsured.
But even healthcare workers are feeling the pinch as health insurance costs rise each year, with employers expecting that costs will jump an additional 8.2% for 2027.
The Republican-led Congress also opted last year not to renew Affordable Care Act marketplace credits enacted during the covid pandemic. While subsidies remain in place for people with low incomes, the pandemic-era credits helped reduce many consumers’ premium payments, especially those working in small businesses such as independent medical practices. Nearly half of marketplace enrollees worked for small businesses or were self-employed in 2024; some of the most common occupations included chiropractic care and dentistry.
Jack Dillon, executive director of the Association for Independent Medicine, which represents 4,000 physician-led practices, said premium increases have become untenable for small businesses, whether employers seek coverage through the marketplace or directly from insurers.
“The cost has become so astronomical,” Dillon said. “You’re looking at it and saying, ‘What’s the value?’”
As health insurance continues to become less affordable, Dillon said, more healthcare employers may seek alternatives to their standard coverage, such as providing higher hourly wages or providing only minimal plans.
The number of people without insurance in the U.S. is expected to increase by roughly 15 million over 10 years because of the expiration of the expanded ACA subsidies and $1.1 trillion in estimated cuts resulting from President Donald Trump’s signature One Big Beautiful Bill Act, according to the Congressional Budget Office.
Healthier people are the most likely to opt out of insurance. That leaves insurance covering a smaller pool of people who tend to be sicker and need more expensive care. So insurers raise prices to cover the remaining enrollees, which fuels even higher premium costs.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
 ‘Healthcare Is a Business’

Samantha LeGault, a nurse practitioner at a health clinic in Boise, said her employer-offered plan’s premium payment rose from $700 to $1,500 a month this year to insure herself, her husband, and four of their kids. LeGault has Crohn’s disease and two of their daughters also have medical conditions, so she said her family has no choice but to continue to pay for that health coverage.
But she decided to skip dental insurance to save money, and she prioritizes dental visits for her children over herself.
She had already struggled to set aside retirement savings and had switched her children from a private school they liked to public school to cut down on costs. Then the new health insurance costs tightened her budget even more. She estimated that about one-fifth of her income now goes toward her monthly premium payments.
“I know how the clinics work, that I am an expensive patient,” LeGault said. “At the end of the day, healthcare is a business in the United States.”
Samantha LeGault, a nurse practitioner for a health clinic in Boise, says her medical insurance premium costs rose from $700 to $1,500 a month this year to cover her, her husband, and four of their kids. She has Crohn’s disease, and two of her daughters also have medical conditions. She continues to pay for health coverage but opted to skip dental insurance to reduce their monthly expenses. (Photo by Hayat Norimine/KFF Health News)
The Durhams have three other employees in their practice. Two of them receive health insurance through their spouses, Ashley Durham said. The Durhams said they pay $420 monthly toward their physician assistant’s premiums.
As a primary care physician, Joshua Durham said he doesn’t need regular doctor visits, because he can diagnose and treat himself — and, if needed, the rest of his family, though he acknowledged that’s frowned upon. The American Medical Association’s code of ethics generally discourages doctors from treating themselves or relatives but makes exceptions for emergency situations or short-term, minor problems. Ashley Durham said she’s filled prescriptions for her family.
Arthur Caplan, a bioethicist and professor emeritus at New York University’s Grossman School of Medicine, said that as more people are “turning toward relatives because they can’t access or easily see a regular doctor,” it may make sense to revisit that aspect of the code of ethics.
 Out-of-Pocket Expenses

Healthcare workers with less advanced medical certifications than the Durhams often don’t have the option of treating themselves or family members — or don’t have savings to fall back on for healthcare expenses. And many healthcare professionals, such as Jill Kordick, a 64-year-old retired healthcare executive in Norwalk, Iowa, aren’t willing to go without the safety net of insurance.
In her work, Kordick saw hospitalizations become financially devastating for patients, so she said she would never opt out of health insurance — even for just the 16 months before she’d become eligible for Medicare at age 65.
Last year, she qualified for the enhanced Affordable Care Act tax credits, allowing her to pay $75 a month for health coverage. Her premiums rose to $800 a month this year when those subsidies expired.
Because she has a $10,000 deductible, she put off going to the doctor for weeks when she had a sinus infection this year, until it ultimately evolved into an ear infection. She said she regularly rethinks, and sometimes returns, nonessential groceries in her shopping cart. And she keeps her house’s thermostat at 80 degrees in the summer to cut down on air conditioning costs.
Kordick said healthcare is a universal struggle in this country, regardless of how familiar patients are with the industry. “It’s disheartening that it’s as broken and fragmented as it is,” she said.
The Durhams have seen the impact of unaffordable healthcare on their patients. They said they try to lend some leeway to patients when they can — a luxury they have, operating their own practice. In one case, Ashley Durham said, she wrote off $1,160 in bills for a single father whose son didn’t have health insurance rather than send their bills to a collection agency.
“It’s hard, because as a human I want to help them out,” she said. “At the same time, we need revenue for our office.”
Joshua Durham is more nervous about going uninsured than his wife. As a child, he witnessed his parents struggling to pay medical bills for their family of nine in south-central Idaho. Durham recalled that his dad, who was a carpenter, helped build a surgeon’s house to pay for an operation.
Today, Durham also sometimes exchanges work for care. He said he gets free eye exams from an uninsured optometrist and offers him free primary care.
He worries about a worst-case scenario: a car crash, a sports injury, a serious diagnosis.
“Do I have pancreatic cancer today?” Durham said wryly.
So far, the couple has paid around $9,000 total for expenses out of their health savings account this year, including physical therapy to help with the thoracic outlet syndrome that affects Durham’s neck and shoulder, mental health appointments, and contact lenses. The expenses were higher than the Durhams anticipated. But it was still less than what their monthly premiums would have cost them.
Their decision has paid off, Joshua Durham said. At least for now.
The Durhams used the Affordable Care Act marketplace for health insurance for their family of four last year. This year, they chose to pay out-of-pocket for care instead when the cost of their premium payments jumped. (Photo by Hayat Norimine/KFF Health News)
Are you struggling to afford your health insurance? Have you decided to forgo coverage? Click here to contact KFF Health News and share your story.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Blackburn campaign drops legal threat of Registry over reappointments
description: Days after threatening to take Tennessee’s Registry of Election Finance to court over a public records request, gubernatorial candidate U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn dropped the demand for communications dealing with board reappointments. An initial request for records filed by Blackburn attorney Brandon Smith turned up nothing substantive between Registry boar[...]
text:
An attorney for Republican gubernatorial candidate U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, pictured here at a Memphis event with President Donald Trump,  threatened to sue the Tennessee Board of Campaign Finance over a public records request but dropped the demand one day later. (Photo: John Partipilo)Days after threatening to take Tennessee’s Registry of Election Finance to court over a public records request, gubernatorial candidate U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn dropped the demand for communications dealing with board reappointments.
An initial request for records filed by Blackburn attorney Brandon Smith turned up nothing substantive between Registry board member Tom Lawless, who died suddenly during a weekend trip to New York City, and Executive Director Bill Young regarding gubernatorial appointments of Democratic board member Paige Burcham Dennis and Republican David Golden. The Registry sent no responses to an expansive request by Smith, telling him it had none to provide, mainly because appointments are handled by word of mouth.
Young said Tuesday that Assistant Director Lance Frizzell handles details dealing with appointments but acknowledged that he spoke about the matter with Lawless, who said he would call the governor’s office about appointments, before his untimely death.
The terms of Golden and Burcham Dennis run out at the end of the year, and their reappointments would be made Jan. 1, 2027, unless new gubernatorial appointments are made based on nominations by the state’s Republican and Democratic parties.
A spokesperson for the Blackburn campaign did not respond to questions by the Lookout Tuesday asking whether she was trying to circumvent the governor’s reappointments and make her own.
Blackburn’s campaign hasn’t had a good relationship with the Registry in the last week, blasting the board for forwarding a sworn complaint to the Attorney General’s Officer for an investigation into dark-money spending that targeted her during the Republican primary. A Blackburn spokesperson said the Registry shirked its responsibility by declining to mete out punishment.
Comparably, Blackburn caused a stir in August when she said she would appoint her replacement to the U.S. Senate, if she wins the gubernatorial race. If she resigns from the federal seat before an inauguration, Gov. Lee could make the Senate appointment, creating potential for conflict between the two.
Young said Tuesday he didn’t know exactly why the Blackburn campaign was seeking records but noted the Registry provided a response. 
After receiving no records from the Registry, Smith sent an email letter Sept. 15 to the agency saying, “The notion that not a single communication exists across all nine categories strains credulity.” He further wrote that, “Should the Bureau fail to provide an adequate response, we will not hesitate to pursue all available remedies” under state law, which involves seeking a court order for public records. He gave a Sept. 29 deadline.
The initial request dealt with records of communications between Young, the Bureau of Ethics and Campaign Finance Director, Lawless, whose death creates a vacuum on the board, Gov. Bill Lee’s office, other Registry board members, state lawmakers and others relating to the reappointment of Burcham Dennis and Golden.
The letter asks Registry staff to go through a wide-ranging search of records on personal devices, email accounts and personal messaging applications used for public business and specifies Young’s and Lawless’s cell phones and email accounts.
But early Tuesday morning, Smith sent a follow-up email to the Registry’s legal counsel canceling the public records request.
The Registry’s attorney, Seth May, sent Smith a letter Monday saying the Registry doesn’t appoint members and that appointments “generate almost no paperwork.” He added that “almost all relevant” communications are done in person or over the phone.
Young also sent a letter to the chairs of the Tennessee Democratic and Republican parties Monday notifying them of the expiring terms of Burcham Dennis and Golden. The Republican and Democratic party executive committees can provide the governor three nominees each to fill the posts, and he requested that each group give the governor enough time to fill the posts before the terms expire.
The governor can request a second list of nominees, Young’s letter says. Young added that he and Assistant Director Lance Frizzell recommend reappointing Golden and Burcham Dennis because of their “exemplary and diligent service.”

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Immigrant advocates seek immediate halt to THP traffic stops conducted in tandem with ICE
description: Immigrant advocates went to federal court Tuesday seeking an immediate order blocking the Tennessee Highway Patrol from conducting traffic stops in tandem with federal immigration agents. In its federal lawsuit, the Tennessee Immigrant & Refugee Rights Coalition and seven Tennessee taxpayers alleged the THP is violating state law and the U.S. Constitution by[...]
text:
Speaker Maria Oceja founder of Vecindarios 901, a Memphis-based grassroots organization, speaks at a press conference held by the Tennessee Immigrant and Refugee Rights Coalition Tuesday before a hearing in federal court over the organization's lawsuit seeking to stop the Tennessee Highway Patrol from conducting joint traffic stops with Immigration and Customs Enforcement. From left, 
Alejandra Hodge TIRRC Board Member, Viridiana Marin, Bill Friskics-Warren of Music City Migra Watch, Rev. Travis Meier and immigration advocate Ashley Warbington. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Immigrant advocates went to federal court Tuesday seeking an immediate order blocking the Tennessee Highway Patrol from conducting traffic stops in tandem with federal immigration agents.
In its federal lawsuit, the Tennessee Immigrant & Refugee Rights Coalition and seven Tennessee taxpayers alleged the THP is violating state law and the U.S. Constitution by making traffic stops of motorists suspected of being noncitizens solely based on their ethnic or racial appearance and then allowing Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents — riding along or stationed nearby — to demand immigration papers and detain drivers.
“The THP is using its traffic stop powers to help ICE do something that the Supreme Court has forbidden: to conduct ‘roving patrol[s]’ in which officers stop motorists on roads in the interior of the United States to check immigration status absent any substantial reason to think they lack status,” read their motion for a preliminary injunction blocking the joint traffic stops.
State attorneys defending the Tennessee Highway Patrol and the Tennessee Department of Homeland Security argued in court filings that state troopers have only engaged in legal traffic stops, based on probable cause of a traffic or criminal violation, and defended the cooperative effort between state troopers and ICE agents.
“Interagency law enforcement collaboration is not taboo,” they wrote in legal filings. State attorneys urged the court to reject the “extraordinary demand” that THP cease cooperative efforts with ICE . “THP’s collaboration with federal counterparts makes Tennessee safer,” they wrote.
Immigrant rights group sues Tennessee Highway Patrol over motorist stops

The state attorneys also raised procedural objections, arguing the plaintiffs lack legal standing to file the lawsuit, the federal court lacks jurisdiction to hear the lawsuit and the state has sovereign immunity against the legal claims.
In court on Tuesday, Assistant Attorney General Samantha Morris argued that ICE agents riding along with state troopers was not a constitutional violation, noting that interagency collaborations are common. Morris compared the practice to bringing drug-sniffing K-9 dogs on patrol to deploy when troopers conducting stops then have reasonable suspicion of potential drug violations.
Michael Holly, who represents the plaintiffs, said the comparison was apt “in a way.” Except, he said, a “drug dog doesn’t have a salary or an agenda.”
U.S. District Judge Aleta Trauger told attorneys Tuesday she hoped to “issue a fairly quick decision.”
The lawsuit was filed May 18, about a year after the THP and ICE conducted a week-long operation they dubbed “Operation Flood the Zone” focused on one Nashville neighborhood with a large immigrant population.
Dashcam and bodyworn camera videos obtained by a consortium of investigative news outlets later revealed troopers made pejorative remarks about their targets, described the Nashville operation as “hunting’ time,” competed among designated teams of ICE officers and troopers to make the most arrests and marked detainees’ arms with sharpies to indicate which team could take credit for the arrests.  
Questioned months later by state lawmakers about alleged misconduct during the operation, THP Colonel Matt Perry said the agency has since rejected overtures from ICE to conduct future joint operations. 
The Tennessee Highway Patrol, however, continues to work in tandem with ICE and other federal agencies as part of the Memphis Safe Task Force, convened last September via an executive order from President Donald Trump. In that role, the THP has conducted tens of thousands of traffic stops in Memphis. Neither the task force nor the THP has released data on how many of those traffic stops led to immigration arrests.
The injunction sought by the immigrant advocates and taxpayers, if granted, would prevent the THP from conducting traffic stops in tandem with ICE in its role as a member of the Memphis Safe Task Force.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Alabama task force finalizes recidivism definition for future vote
description: A group seeking a formal definition for recidivism told the Alabama’s Joint Re-Entry Task Force Tuesday that they would stick with the same recommendation they made to the task force in June. That defines recidivism as returning to the custody of the Alabama Department of Corrections “for commission of a new crime” within three years […]
text:
Alabama Bureau of Pardons and Paroles Director Cam Ward speaks during Reentry 2030 event at the Perry County Correctional Facility in Uniontown, Ala., on Friday, Oct. 6, 2023. Alabama’s Joint Re-Entry Task Force plans to formally adopt a definition for recidivism that other agencies have already adopted. (Will McLelland for Alabama Reflector)A group seeking a formal definition for recidivism told the Alabama’s Joint Re-Entry Task Force Tuesday that they would stick with the same recommendation they made to the task force in June.
That defines recidivism as returning to the custody of the Alabama Department of Corrections “for commission of a new crime” within three years of being released for an earlier conviction.
“Every state uses that same definition,” said Cam Ward, director of the Alabama Bureau of Pardons and Paroles and chair of the Reentry Task Force, in an interview following the meeting. “The Bureau of Justice, which is a branch of the Department of Justice, has always used that definition. If we were to go out and use a separate definition altogether, you could not compare us to other states. It would be apples and oranges.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Ward and others want to adopt a formal definition for recidivism to gauge the success of intervention programs that Alabama has applied. Ward said Alabama has a recidivism rate of 27%. That would place it 15th in the nation for that metric, which improved from 34% in recent years, according to The Council of State Governments Justice Center.
“I think the investment in more resources on job training, mental health and substance abuse, that is what is moving the needle,” Ward said.
Adopting that definition also allows state officials to compare its metric against other states and learn about their re-entry programs that Alabama can then adopt.
“There is nothing wrong with copying best practices from other states,” Ward said.
Members of the subcommittee seeking to define the word received feedback from several committee members.
Some had concerns about how to define “a new crime” within the context of the definition. Ward suggested at the meeting in June that a Class A misdemeanor be the threshold for committing a new crime. Others, like Bennet Wright, executive director of the Alabama Sentencing Commission, said it would be hard to even determine whether a person had committed a new misdemeanor because of gaps in the existing system that tracks offenses in the state.
“You have different data structures that you may or may not have access to,” Wright said in an interview following the meeting. “There is no statewide repository of municipal data information.”
Despite that, Wright said the subcommittee recommended the same definition of recidivism because it is the same one that the ADOC uses.
Ward made cutting Alabama’s recidivism rate in half one of the central goals for ABPP. The board has partnered with the Council of State Governments Justice Center on an initiative called Reentry 2030 to improve outcomes for people who were released from ADOC custody.
The task force will vote on the new language at the next quarterly meeting, although the date has not been announced.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: ​ID number would have to appear on Colorado mail ballots if amendment passes
description: Coloradans who vote with a mail ballot must sign the ballot envelope. If voters approve a proposed constitutional amendment in November, they would also need to include an ID number on the envelope.  Amendment 84 would require voters to write the last four digits of their Social Security number, their Colorado driver’s license number or […]
text:
Volunteers at the Denver Clerk and Recorder's office remove ballots from a ballot box container during the Colorado primary election on June 30, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Fraieli/Colorado Newsline)Coloradans who vote with a mail ballot must sign the ballot envelope. If voters approve a proposed constitutional amendment in November, they would also need to include an ID number on the envelope. 
Amendment 84 would require voters to write the last four digits of their Social Security number, their Colorado driver’s license number or their REAL ID number on their mail ballot envelope to ensure it is counted.
Suzanne Taheri, a conservative attorney and former deputy secretary of state, is backing the initiative alongside Chuck Broerman, a conservative former El Paso County clerk, through the Colorado Voter Trust Initiative. The initiative is funded by the Coalition for American Prosperity and Growth, a “dark money” group. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The amendment would affect only mail ballots, which are automatically mailed to every registered Colorado voter. The vast majority of Coloradans do not vote in person. Those who do already need to present a valid ID at the polls. As a constitutional amendment, the measure would need 55% of the vote to pass. 
Supporters of the measure say it creates a secondary verification method to confirm a ballot belongs to the right voter, reinforcing confidence in elections. Taheri did not respond prior to publication to Newsline’s questions about the goals, logistics and costs of the measure.
Opponents say the proposal adds privacy concerns for voters without further securing Colorado’s election process. The measure will lead to disenfranchisement, because more ballots could end up rejected and not counted over discrepancies in what voters put on their ballot envelope, they say. 



Quotation







Having these extra administrative barriers, strict new ID mandates or additional verification hurdles will only make it harder for eligible Latinos and other citizens to participate.


– Christo Luna, director in Colorado of Mi Familia Vota


Two issue committees formally filed with the Colorado secretary of state’s office to oppose the measure, and voter advocacy organizations have also voiced their opposition, including the League of Women Voters of Colorado, Mi Familia Vota and Common Cause Colorado. The Colorado Democratic Party also opposes it. 
Secretary of State Jena Griswold’s office said it does not comment on ballot measures since it runs and certifies elections in the state, even measures like Amendment 84 that would affect her office. 
Nonpartisan legislative staff’s analysis of the measure estimated it would increase spending for county clerks by $2.5 million in the first year and up to $1.2 million in future years. The costs include additional work hours for election judges to verify ID numbers, a curing process for voters to fix discrepancies, and a redesign of ballot materials and envelopes. The secretary of state’s office would also see increased costs if the amendment passes. 
Matt Crane, executive director of the Colorado County Clerks Association, said the organization is still working to understand the logistical and fiscal impact Amendment 84 would have on county clerks, he said.
County clerks would need to redesign their mail ballot envelopes, and it’s unclear what that would cost, Crane said. They’re also working to determine how the amendment would affect different communities, like college students who might not have a Colorado license or know their Social Security number. 
The association tries to avoid taking positions on ballot measures since it’s the “independent referee for elections,” Crane said, but occasionally it will. Some clerks have voiced support for the measure, while others are against it. 
‘Solution in search of a problem’
Colorado’s existing signature verification process for mail ballots is already secure and recognized as “a gold standard,” Christo Luna, director in Colorado of Mi Familia Vota said. 
“Having these extra administrative barriers, strict new ID mandates or additional verification hurdles will only make it harder for eligible Latinos and other citizens to participate, increasing the risk that legitimate ballots are rejected unnecessarily,” Luna said. “We do feel that if this passes, it’s definitely going to be a big problem here in Colorado.”
The new requirement would discourage people from voting, given concerns about their sensitive identification information, Luna said. He said it would also diminish community and government trust.



Quotation







Amendment 84 is a politically motivated attempt to make it harder for people to vote and will result in eligible Colorado voters having their ballots rejected and votes not counted.


– Aly Belknap, executive director of Common Cause Colorado


Aly Belknap, executive director of Colorado Common Cause, said a requirement to place personally identifiable information on a ballot can put Colorado voters at risk of having their identities stolen or compromised. Voters already provide an ID number when they register to vote, she said. 
“Amendment 84 is a politically motivated attempt to make it harder for people to vote and will result in eligible Colorado voters having their ballots rejected and votes not counted,” Belknap said in a statement. 
It would draw out the time it takes election officials to process and count votes, Belknap said, delaying official election results. 
The League of Women Voters of Colorado opposes Amendment 84, because Colorado already has a secure and reliable system to verify mail ballots, Beth Hendrix, executive director of the League, said. All it will do is lead to the rejection of more ballots from eligible voters.
“This measure, it won’t make our elections safer,” Hendrix said. “It just makes them harder to navigate, and it puts eligible Coloradans’ votes at risk over simple clerical errors.”
Hendrix expects the measure would result in a substantial work load increase for election workers, too.
Handwriting varies from person to person, Hendrix said, and the necessity for elections staff to verify ID numbers creates more opportunities for a ballot to be rejected. Colorado has a system in place for voters to “cure” their ballots if a signature is rejected, and a similar system would be needed to cure ID numbers election officials cannot read or match to an eligible voter.  
“The whole point seems to be to keep noncitizens from voting,” Hendrix said. “ And noncitizens do not vote. It is illegal for them to do that, and the proven cases where it has happened, I mean, the numbers are so minuscule that they would not threaten any election. So this is a solution in search of a problem.”
Thousands of Coloradans need to cure their ballots through the signature verification process each election, and that number can increase if election officials need to verify another item like an ID number. 
The Bell Policy Center, a liberal nonprofit advocacy organization, said in its explanation of the measure that while ID numbers offer a “more objective form of voter verification” than signatures, the requirements “do nothing to improve election security given the lack of evidence of mail voter fraud.”
“However, they do create new barriers to voting for eligible voters who may not have certain forms of ID, including people who are older, low-income, live in rural areas, disabled, and are from communities of color,” the Center’s explainer says.

title: Growth in ‘early-career’ residents is quicker in Tennessee counties bordering big cities
description: Counties near Tennessee’s biggest cities saw the fastest growth rates for “early-career” adults ages 25 to 44 since 2020, according to a report released by the Tennessee State Data Center Monday. The center, part of the University of Tennessee’s Boyd Center for Business and Economic Research, analyzed population estimates from the U.S. Census Bureau from […]
text:
Wilson County saw the fastest growth of "early-career" residents out of any Tennessee county from 2020 through 2025, according to a report released by the Tennessee State Data Center on Sept. 21, 2026. (Photo: Wilson County Facebook)Counties near Tennessee’s biggest cities saw the fastest growth rates for “early-career” adults ages 25 to 44 since 2020, according to a report released by the Tennessee State Data Center Monday.
The center, part of the University of Tennessee’s Boyd Center for Business and Economic Research, analyzed population estimates from the U.S. Census Bureau from 2020 to 2025.
Overall, the state saw an 8.9% change in the 25-44 age group between those years, compared to just 1.2% growth for the same age bracket between 2010 and 2015.
Tennessee’s Department of Economic and Community Development defines a county as “rural” if it has less than 50 percent of its population living in a 2020 Census Urbanized Area of more than 50,000 people. The center’s analysis found that Tennessee’s 78 rural counties showed an increase of 65,812 people — 11.3% — in the 25-44 age group over the 5-year period. The state’s 17 urban counties saw the age group grow by 92,957 people, a 7.7% increase.
Tennessee State Data Center Director Timothy Kuhn said the report purposefully does not address potential reasons for population increases or decreases.
“Population estimates themselves don’t really answer the question as to why someone might choose to relocate to any particular area,” Kuhn said. “The answers to that question tend to be more qualitative.”
Wilson County, which abuts Davidson County’s eastern edge, saw a 27.67% jump in early-career adults — the largest of any county. Maury County, located south of Williamson County, followed with a 23.94% increase. Counties near Knoxville and Chattanooga also saw boosts in this age bracket.
“This is an age group where people are really engaged with the labor force,” Kuhn said. “They’re completing their education and they’re forming households and forming families and taking lots of important life steps. So when you see this population group going up, that’s an important indicator for a community.”
Gains in the 25-44 age group were much smaller in West Tennessee, and some rural counties in the grand division saw dips in the early-career population.
In Lake County, the group’s population dropped 15.25% from 2020 to 2025. Haywood County saw a 7.39% decrease, and Weakley and Hardeman counties decreased a fraction of a percent. Shelby County had a 1.77% loss.
Fayette County recorded the largest gain west of the Tennessee River with 12.26%.
The data indicates that the majority of increases in the 25-44 age group are due to in-migration, or people moving in from other areas, Kuhn said.
The fastest-growing age group in the state is still retirees — aged 65 and older — which increased by 14.7% since 2020.
“A much larger component of that is due to a larger cohort of people aging into the 65-plus group,” Kuhn noted. “It’s really the front end of the baby boom — people that were born in 1946. Every year they’re replacing a smaller cohort ahead of them, and there’s larger cohorts coming in, so it makes the population grow faster.”
All counties saw positive growth in population aged 65 and older between 2020 and 2025. Williamson County recorded the largest percent growth in that population segment at 30.5%, followed by Montgomery County with 29.3% and Maury County with 28.9%.

text:
The Ohio burgee. (Getty images file photo.)Every morning in the Ohio Capital Journal’s free newsletter, The Eye-Opener, we round up the news and commentary from across Ohio and around the country and world that is catching our attention. We call this feature Catching Our Eye, republished here.
Please subscribe to our free daily newsletter to get all the Ohio news you need to know right to your inbox every weekday morning.
If you already subscribe, please share with your family and friends so they know about the Ohio Capital Journal too: https://ohiocapitaljournal.com/subscribe/
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 Catching Our Eye

• Public corruption running rampant. ProPublica reports, “The FBI Anti-Corruption Squad Was Circling Susan Collins — Until Trump Got in the Way.”
Probe: In 2024, the FBI sought to launch a sweeping pay-to-play investigation examining interactions between Sen. Susan Collins and a top donor, records and emails show.
Confession: The donor, an ex-defense contractor, told agents his company won millions in federal contracts by bankrolling campaigns of powerful politicians.
Shutdown: After Donald Trump returned to office, the investigation died, a casualty of his purge of the FBI. Its closure shut a potential window into how Washington works.
• Gas tax holiday? The Statehouse News Bureau’s Jo Ingles and Karen Kasler report, “Lawmakers could suspend Ohio’s gas tax soon, in plan announced by GOP candidate for governor.”
State lawmakers are apparently planning to interrupt their election-season recess to come back to Columbus and pass a bill to suspend Ohio’s gas tax. The announcement came from Republican candidate for governor Vivek Ramaswamy, whose running mate is the president of the Ohio Senate.
News of this plan came a few hours after Democratic candidate Amy Acton issued a call for a gas tax holiday on social media. The state’s current tax is 38.5 cents on gas and 47 cents on diesel. AAA reports the average price in Ohio is $4.49 for a gallon of regular gasoline and $6.82 for a gallon of diesel.
• JD Vance kicks 750,000 people off their health insurance. The New York Times reports, “Trump Officials Eject 750,000 From Obamacare Markets, Claiming Fraud.”
The Trump administration has ejected more than 750,000 enrollees from the Affordable Care Act insurance marketplaces, Vice President JD Vance announced on Tuesday, claiming that many were receiving premium subsidies they did not qualify for and that some were not even real people.
• Failing to understand Ohio education policy. In a Columbus Dispatch opinion column, Mike Curtin writes, “Vivek Ramaswamy gets no more than an ‘F’ when it comes to education. Here’s why.”
Any candidate who proclaims “a world-class education is your birthright as an Ohioan” is mouthing worthless platitudes absent a promise and a plan for fully funding high-quality, universal pre-K.
• The Paper. The Ohio Newsroom’s Erin Gottsacker reports, “In a landscape of local news loss, the Toledo Blade is looking for a buyer.”
If the Toledo Blade isn’t sold by the end of this year, the 190-year-old newspaper will stop publishing.
Block Communications, the paper’s owner, announced the decision to staff in an email earlier this month, according to the newspaper.
“Unfortunately, an extremely difficult decision has been made,” wrote Block Communications’ president and chief operating officer Jodi Miehls. “The Block Family’s continued investment to keep the Blade open is no longer an option. The financial losses the Blade has endured for years are simply not sustainable.”
• HIV decriminalization. The Buckeye Flame’s Ken Schneck reports, “HIV decriminalization supporters to hold first-ever Advocacy Day at Ohio Statehouse.”
Ohio still has six laws on the books that criminalize living with HIV. And the laws are actively enforced.
