Read the story on VTDigger here:  A celebration of “maple-fired” punk highlights challenging times for Vermont’s live music.
text:
Dead Street Dreamers performing at The Underground, courtesy of The Underground
For Dan O’Day, “there’s no better feeling” than performing live music for a crowd and feeling the energy go out and come back to you. 
“I think about these moments of just having people sing along to your songs, know your music, cheering you on,” he said. “I think I took a lot of it for granted — that stuff that normal people don’t get to ever experience is that feeling of that pure love of performing and getting that reaction from it.” 
O’Day is the lead songwriter for Steppin’ Razor Blades, a two-tone ska band formed of musicians from all over New England. Steppin’ Razor Blades is one of nine local punk and ska (an upbeat form of punk and reggae) bands slated to perform at “Skunkfest,” a brand-new festival that plans to celebrate both the music and the “do-it-yourself” ethos of punk. 
Skunkfest — a portmanteau of ska, punk and festival — is slated to take place Sept. 26 in Randolph, outside of The Underground, a local music venue, thanks to the combined efforts of The Underground and tattoo parlor Black Meadow Gallery and Tattoo. 
To the festival’s organizers and performers, the festival demonstrates the thriving punk ecosystem and deep connection between punk and Vermont culture. One band, Vallory Falls, proudly describes itself as “maple-fired punk rock.” 
But the festival also comes at a time of uncertainty for the future of punk in particular and live music in general. Venues across the state have been struggling, and The Underground is a part of that trend. In fact, owner Vincent Freeman said the club’s regular live shows will be going on an indefinite hiatus by the end of the year. 
The Underground began as a recording studio 15 years ago, offering a recording space and audio engineering to local musicians, Freeman said. But during the pandemic, he began hosting weekly livestreamed concerts in the basement. 
Freeman and Kate Branstetter, co-owner of Black Meadow, have been talking about organizing a festival for years, inspired in part by local punk flea markets and smaller concerts. 
Alongside the music, Branstetter has put together a punk-themed craft and makers’ market. “We’re looking at a flea market of band memorabilia, and homemade DIY crafts, and paintings that are asking intense questions, and graffiti art,” she said. 
The festival will also have a “fixer tent,” where visitors can see live demos of how to repair their own items. To Branstetter, that do-it-yourself attitude is one way that punk intersects with Vermont culture. 

McAsh performing at The Underground, courtesy of The Underground

“Vermont is a place for the nostalgia of the original punk and ska scene, because we’re just a little bit more removed from a lot of stuff, (so) we’re used to being DIY and crafty and scrappy,” she said. 
Vermont also influences the music of some of the bands coming to Skunkfest. Riley Rae Burridge, manager and drummer of Vallory Falls, said that the band’s latest EP, “Porchlights and Field Lights,” has songs like “Citronella” with lyrics that are partly based around life in Vermont: “At the base of this green ridge, Citronella candlelight / As the flames die down, I’ll hold you close.” 
But as passionate as she is about Vermont, Burridge is worried about some signs of a decline in the punk scene here, especially when it comes to places to see and hear bands. Radio Bean in Burlington closed earlier this year. Jim’s Basement and 242 Main, other popular Burlington punk venues, have both closed in the past 10 years. 
“A lot of folks tell me that Burlington used to be like the main scene for punk bands,” she said. “And right now, we’re kind of in a place where we’re trying to figure out what to do and what to go on with.”
Freeman said he’s been struggling with both his insurance costs and the cost of music licensing for song covers. With those expenses and others, he’s been barely breaking even on weekly shows.
“We were a (bring-your-own-booze) venue, and then yeah, my insurance company just dropped me overnight and said, ‘Hey, we’re not going to cover you anymore,’” he said. 
He’s also the father of a 14-month-old child and feels like he doesn’t have the capacity anymore to run a part-time venue.
“The other end of this DIY culture is … there aren’t these large organizations that are financially backed doing this; it’s all our musical creative community,” he said. “We have an idea and we want to roll with it and are super passionate about it, but eventually we burn out because we don’t see enough support.” 
These issues are part of national-level changes in the music industry, such as the increased concentration of venues into the hands of large corporations, and Freeman doesn’t know how Vermont will move forward with them. But he’s proud to support local businesses where he can, such as by using Seven Days’ ticketing platform rather than Ticketmaster. 
And he still believes that live music is “crucial” to human connection. 
“As an avid concert goer, it’s such a cathartic exercise physically and mentally to attend a concert,” he said. “You can just let out everything that’s weighing on you, any negative energy, and also celebrate the positive energy.”
Burridge said despite punk’s loud and prickly reputation, she’s found punk shows to be incredibly safe, and she’s felt very accepted as a trans person in the community. 
“A lot of people think punk and think like, ‘Oh, it’s scary. Oh, there’s a lot of folks that just look mean, look like they’re gonna hurt me.’ It is not like that. It is one of the most caring communities in the entire state,” she said.

title: Dorothy (Dot) Naylor
description:
She was a lifelong learner, an innovator before innovation was cool, and generally a feisty woman who regarded obstacles as challenges to be overcome her whole life.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Dorothy (Dot) Naylor.
text:
Born: 01/24/1939
Newport, Rhode Island
Died: 09/07/2026
Berlin, Vermont
Details of service:
There will be a Celebration of Life on June 5, 2027 at Memorial Hall on Mirror Lake in Calais.
In lieu of flowers the family is asking you consider a donation to one of the following organizations:
Rural School Community Alliance or
North Calais Memorial Hall Association 207 G.A.R. Road, Calais Vermont

Dorothy (Openshaw) Naylor of Berlin, previously of Calais, passed away peacefully at Woodridge Nursing and Rehabilitation on September 7, 2026 after a long and well-lived life. 
Dorothy was born at Newport Hospital in Newport, Rhode Island on January 24, 1939, to James A. and Dorothy (Harvest) Openshaw. She moved with her family to Southampton, Massachusetts in 1941 where she attended the local elementary school and graduated from Northampton School for Girls in 1957.
Dorothy attended several universities including Cornell and New Mexico before landing at University of Massachusetts (Amherst) from which she graduated in 1961.  While at UMass she met and married her lifelong partner and love, Ben Naylor.  Together with their infant daughter (Sonja) they moved to Manhattan, Kansas in the summer of 1961. While there, Ben continued his studies and their family grew to include three sons. In 1967 Ben had completed his studies and they’d had enough of flat, featureless, windy land, so they moved the family back east and settled at Kents Corner in Calais before moving to Collar Hill in 1972 where they resided for over 50 years. 
Dorothy went by different names. Her father nicknamed her Lass when she was born because, as he said, “She was slow as molasses in January,” in a riff on her birthday and her tardy entrance to the world. Despite the nickname, she could never be considered sluggish, stagnant, or unproductive. For most of her adult life she was known as Dot (or Aunt Speck by some cheeky nieces and nephews). In her later years she was known as Dorothy at her request.
In addition to her several names, Dorothy wore many hats throughout her long and active life. She taught 5th & 6th grades at East Montpelier Elementary School for 20+ years, she served on multiple boards and committees, she partnered with Ben in homesteading their land and developing a thriving small business. She was a lifelong learner, an innovator before innovation was cool, and generally a feisty woman who regarded obstacles as challenges to be overcome her whole life.
Dorothy began her teaching career in the Four Corners (one room) School House. At the time it was an overflow building for the modern elementary school. She walked her students two-tenths of a mile to and from the main building several days a week for specialty classes such as PE, art, and the like. After a couple years overlooking the field across the road she envisioned a Nordic skiing program that would simultaneously teach winter survival skills, so she applied for a grant, bought cross-country ski sets and taught many generations of students how to ski and enjoy the winter.
Throughout her life Dorothy embraced serendipity. One day in 1976 she bought too many peaches from the co-op and turned them into a thriving boutique jam business now owned by son Kelt and his wife Kristina. In the beginning Dorothy hand wrote all the labels. Those labels are now digitally printed using her handwriting for the font. As the business grew, she delivered and managed, while Ben handled production and product development. Now this jam, and many other specialty food products, can be found on store shelves throughout New England.
Dorothy had a healthy respect for civic engagement and town service – she served on many boards – most related to education.  She and Ben were involved in the citizen committees that created the modern Calais Elementary School and U32; both built in the early 1970s.  She later served on the Calais School board during the contentious merger required by Act 46. She continued engaging in the fight to maintain local schools right up to the very end, attending school board meetings virtually from her nursing home.
Maybe it was immersion in a place where tourism is an economic staple, maybe it was just her personality; in any case Dorothy actively avoided crowds, mainstream tourism, and other “touristy” events. She and Ben took three very memorable vacations in their life. The first and most momentous in 1994 when they toured Antarctica on a retired Russian research vessel. They were caught up in international intrigue when the ship was impounded in the Falkland/Maldive Islands and Argentina refused to allow passage through their airspace to Tierra del Fuego in Chile!
Though she was always active, she was never too busy to wander their property in Calais or sit on the porch of their cottage on Lake Champlain with a gin & tonic.
Dorothy is survived by her three children: daughter, Sonja N. Andrews, (Ross), Calais, VT; son, Kelt M. Naylor, (Kristina), Dummerston, VT; son, Benjamin E. Naylor, (Jennifer), Petersburg, NY as well as 7 grandchildren: Lillian and John (Rebecca) Andrews, Caroline and Max Naylor, Aleana, Sophia (Lucas), and Eli Naylor, and one great grandson, Harvest Andrews. Dorothy was predeceased by her beloved husband, Ben Naylor, her infant son Kurt W. Naylor, her parents and siblings, Judy (Openshaw) Findeisen and James A. Openshaw, Jr.

title: Michigan Smart Trade Alliance tracker shows over $26 billion in tariff-driven costs paid statewide
description: The Michigan Smart Trade Alliance has launched a tracker estimating that Michigan households have incurred more than $26 billion in tariff-related costs since January 2025, or about $6,419 per household.  That number is based on the National Taxpayers Union Foundation’s state tariffs tracker, which uses import and duty data from Trade Partnership Worldwide a[...]
text:
U.S. Customs station at the Blue Water Bridge in Port Huron, Michigan. (Photo by Jon King/Michigan Advance)The Michigan Smart Trade Alliance has launched a tracker estimating that Michigan households have incurred more than $26 billion in tariff-related costs since January 2025, or about $6,419 per household. 
That number is based on the National Taxpayers Union Foundation’s state tariffs tracker, which uses import and duty data from Trade Partnership Worldwide and U.S. Census Bureau household counts. According to the alliance’s website, the tracker “reflects only the highest of several published, credible estimates of tariff costs to Michigan households.” The website also notes that other analysts and the White House put the number lower, while some dispute that tariffs impose any net cost after accounting for other economic effects. 
“The costs on Michigan families is taking a toll in the form of higher costs and frustration with trade policies and tariffs that are holding our economy back,” said Michigan Smart Trade Alliance spokesperson John Sellek in a press release. “It’s time to end the trade war with Canada, get both sides to the negotiation table, and find a solution that will end this affordability crisis in Michigan.”
Michigan Smart Trade Alliance tracker estimating Michigan household costs incurred by tariffs. (Screenshot)
The tracker projects an average increase of $488.4 per second across Michigan in statewide tariff costs. That number is a calculation, not a demonstration of constantly updating data — it divides the last confirmed total from the National Taxpayers Union Foundation, $23 billion, by the 545 days in that data period, to find the average per-second cost, and projects that amount forward.
The website also notes that the tracker was created using artificial intelligence.
The group also released the results of an early July Ipsos poll of 559 likely voters, which showed that, across party lines, voters were in strong support of statements that they would be more likely to support a candidate who says, “I support smart trade that protects Michigan jobs” and support congressional action to increase trade with trusted allies such as Canada and Mexico when it protects jobs and lowers costs.
“Anyone who is running for office right now should consider themselves on notice: Voters in Michigan across the political spectrum want smart trade and an end to erratic trade policies that raise prices and make it difficult or impossible for businesses to plan for the future,” Mark Fisk, another spokesperson for the Michigan Smart Trade Alliance, said. 
Another poll commissioned by the organization and conducted by EPIC-MRA in June showed similar pushback on tariffs, with a 70% to 20% margin saying that “state and federal lawmakers should pursue a different trade policy that reduces tariffs and lowers costs for consumers.” 
However, opinions in that earlier poll varied along party lines — “A 79% to 12% majority of Democrats, 58% to 31% of Independent voters oppose tariffs, while an 81% to 13% majority of Republicans said they support tariffs,” according to the alliance’s website.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Mass. unemployment agency ‘mismanaged’ call center performance, ‘failed’ to quickly pay claimants, auditor concludes
description: The auditor’s report unveils how even before the agency was thrust into turmoil with record-breaking poor performance during a time of a relatively stable job market, out-of-work Massachusetts residents weren’t receiving the help they needed in a timely fashion.
text:
IN THE MONTHS AFTER Massachusetts adopted a new platform meant to improve the unemployment assistance system for both jobless Bay Staters and state workers managing claims, disbursement of those benefits trickled to a nation-leading low. 
The issues, as it turned out, had been festering in the years before that 2025 system update, a new report from Auditor Diana DiZoglio reveals. 
Those snags ranged from claimants stuck on hold for over an hour to poor access to in-person assistance in communities around the state to long lags in the issuance of payments for qualified residents staring down unemployment. 
As a result, the report concludes, Massachusetts risks losing federal funding as well as saddling vulnerable claimants with delayed access and lost trust. 
DiZoglio’s review of the Department of Unemployment Assistance was mainly limited to two years between 2022 and 2024. That’s before the agency implemented a new benefits system which, as chronicled by CommonWealth Beacon this year, led to the slowest rate of payments in the country. 
Lengthy delays at DUA have reverberated around Beacon Hill, where lawmakers report being inundated with complaints from constituents about the agency’s lack of responsiveness.  
However, legislative leaders have done little to tackle the problem. A pair of first-term lawmakers have been pushing for months to convene a special commission that would examine the issues, but it now appears even that modest proposal is dead until the start of the new term in 2027 at the earliest. 
Yet the auditor’s report unveils how, even before the agency was thrust into more recent turmoil with record-breaking poor performance during a time of a relatively stable job market, out-of-work Massachusetts residents for years weren’t receiving the help they needed in a timely fashion. 
“When hardworking people lose their jobs, unemployment insurance becomes a lifeline that allows them to continue to pay bills while they search for a new job,” DiZoglio said in a statement. “When those benefit payments are delayed, job search resources are unavailable, and complaints are not tracked and prioritized appropriately, the system fails job seekers and taxpayers alike.” 
Matthew Kitsos, a DUA spokesperson, said the agency is “committed to improving customer experiences and ensuring eligible claimants receive benefits in a timely fashion.” He added in a statement that DUA has “taken significant steps to address challenges head-on,” including launching a pilot program to process claims more efficiently and hiring more adjudicators and seasonal staff. 
For the vast majority of claims, DUA did not meet the federal performance standard that calls for issuing 93 percent of benefits within 35 days of a claim in any of the 24 months that DiZoglio reviewed. In April 2024, that number dropped below 70 percent, the lowest month included in the audit. 
The agency implemented a new system in May 2025 that Gov. Maura Healey vowed would catapult the state into “national leadership” for the delivery of benefits. But the percentage of payments issued to claimants within 35 days only plunged deeper to 42.5 percent last September, an all-time state low. The data has since improved over time, with 83 percent of benefits now paid within 35 days as of July, the most recent month with data available.  
Unemployment benefits themselves are paid through a tax on Massachusetts employers, while the federal government funds the administration of that assistance across the states. 
On call wait times, DiZoglio’s report criticized DUA for a failure to demonstrate that “call log data was being monitored at all” to evaluate performance.  
Out of more than 700,000 calls over a one-year period, the report found that it took 30 minutes to respond to about half of all inbound calls either from a call center agent or an automated voice prompt. Wait times exceeded an hour for about a quarter of the calls. 
Claimants hung up on DUA call centers around 30 percent of the time during some months in 2024 — six times as much as the 5 percent standard, “indicating challenges in managing call volume and access to service,” the report notes. 
Kitsos said that call wait times are now down from an average of two hours to between four and 11 minutes. 
DUA, citing budget and staff constraints, also failed to offer in-person assistance at three regional offices in Brockton, Springfield, and Lawrence, which were used for appeal hearings, during the audit period. 
That meant claimants had to travel in some cases 200 miles roundtrip to Boston, further increasing wait times and delaying access to benefits, DiZoglio noted.  
Rep. Joshua Tarsky, a first-term Democrat who co-sponsored the legislation to establish a special commission on unemployment insurance, said in an interview that the auditor’s report further validates the push to scrutinize the system – even though his bill likely won’t advance this year, he conceded. 
“These unemployment benefits aren’t abstract,” said Tarsky, who plans to re-file the bill alongside Rep. Hadley Luddy next session. “They are monies for people who are wanting to buy food, diapers, pay for their heat. It’s something that you can’t just, if it’s working inefficiently, let it go. We need to actually fix this so that our constituents can get the money they need and get the benefits that they’re entitled to.” 
The auditor also alleged that DUA violated state public records law by only retaining call log data for 13 months instead of three years, limiting the agency’s ability to “review and evaluate its call-handling performance.” Kitsos said that DUA disagrees with the auditor’s interpretation of records retention requirements and maintained that the agency is in compliance with the law. 
Nor did DUA take necessary steps to guard against fraud, which has become more prevalent since the 2020 pandemic. The agency didn’t complete the required number of claim reviews in fiscal years 2023 and 2024 — DUA cited a reassignment of six staff investigators to support the launch of the new system as the reason — which “could increase the risk of DUA not identifying improper payments.” 
And DiZoglio zoomed farther out, reaching back to a major Gov. Charlie Baker-era mishap in which the prior Republican administration erroneously spent more than $2 billion in federal Covid funds for unemployment benefits.  
Despite an agreement between Gov. Maura Healey and the feds to pay much of that money back over 10 years, DUA has not sufficiently kept the US Labor Department updated after the new platform launched — a problem “given the exorbitant amount of taxpayer dollars involved,” the report finds. 
To course correct on the issues that DiZoglio identified, the report recommends that DUA should routinely review call log data, implement system alerts for missing information from claimants, offer in-person assistance at regional offices, identify the underlying issues driving delays in benefit payments, and consider hiring additional staff members.
